Machine learning applied to the optimization of biomass char-based 
supercapacitors: Effect of experimental parameters on 
supercapacitor performance
Jing Chen
a , b

Experimental conditions

Biomass char
ABSTRACT
To address the optimization issue of experimental parameters during the experimental preparation of biomass 
char supercapacitors, this study applied six different regression models (four machine learning models and two 
deep learning models) to predict the specific capacitance of biomass char supercapacitors. The results indicate 
that the Transformer model performs best in terms of prediction accuracy, with an R
2 
(coefficient of determi -
nation) of 0.9609, an MAE (mean absolute error) of 16.8599, and an RMSE (root mean square error) of 19.4569. 
Furthermore, analysis indicates that among the experimental parameters, the activation temperature exerts the 
most significant influence on the specific capacitance. The carbonization temperature and carbonization time 
exhibit a strong coupled relationship with the specific capacitance: at low carbonization temperatures, 
carbonization time shows a positive correlation with specific capacitance, whereas at high carbonization tem -
peratures, carbonization time correlates negatively with specific capacitance. A high heating rate demonstrates a 
strong negative correlation with specific capacitance. This study employs regression models to analyze experi -
mental parameter data, thereby providing novel approaches for optimizing experiments aimed at designing 
superior supercapacitors.
1. Introduction
As developed and developing nations progressively implement their 
strategic objectives of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality, countries 
are gradually reducing their reliance on fossil fuel energy sources, 
decreasing the share of thermal power capacity, and pursuing greener, 
lower-carbon methods of electricity generation [ 1 ], which has fostered 
the continuous advancement of renewable energy, with particular 
emphasis on enhancing the utilization of wind and solar power [ 2 ]. 
However, unlike thermal and nuclear power these renewable energy 
sources lack the stable power output and easy-to-implement power 
regulation capabilities of generation methods. Their electricity output is 
thus subject to fluctuations due to temporal and spatial factors [ 3 ]. 
Consequently, the integration of green yet intermittent power genera -
tion methods such as wind and solar energy into the grid gives rise to a 
series of new grid challenges, including voltage fluctuations, frequency 
instability, and diminished grid frequency regulation and peak load 
management capabilities [ 4 ]. The construction of energy storage power 
plants (such as supercapacitor energy storage, electrochemical energy 
storage, pumped hydro storage, thermal energy storage, and.) is one of 
the most effective methods for addressing these issues [ 5 ].Among these, 
supercapacitor energy storage stands out as the most promising and 
sought-after energy storage device for grid frequency regulation due to 
its high power density, rapid charge-discharge capabilities, and 
extended cycle life [ 6 ]. The preparation of supercapacitors typically 
employs char-based materials. Biomass char, as a low-carbon-footprint, 
environmentally friendly, and cost-effective carbon-rich material, ex -
hibits favorable capacitive physicochemical properties, together with 
the potential of abundant functional groups, and a tunable pore struc -
ture. Consequently, it has been extensively explored for the fabrication 
of high performance supercapacitors [ 7 ].
However, biomass char derived from simple carbonization processes 
often suffers from underdeveloped pore structures, limited functional 
groups, and suboptimal surface morphologies. As a result, super -
capacitors fabricated using such char materials show suboptimal energy 
storage performance, which hinders their practical application in grid

frequency regulation [ 8 ]. Over the past decade, scientists have 
employed a wide array of methods to prepare porous char materials with 
enhanced performance characteristics. These approaches encompass 
adjustments to carbonization temperature, time, and heating rates 
during biomass carbonization; modifications to activation temperature, 
time, heating rates, and activator ratios during the activation process; as 
well as optimization of activators, heteroatoms doping, and metallic 
elements modification [ 9 – 13 ], all these strategies are designed to 
enhance the physicochemical properties of biomass char, thereby 
fabricating high-performance supercapacitors. Xiaodi Han et al. utilized 
chestnut shells as raw material to investigate the effect of varying acti -
vator ratios on supercapacitor performance. Porous char produced with 
an activator ratio of 4 exhibited a specific capacitance as high as 448 F/g 
under test conditions of 0.5 A/g [ 14 ]; Sabin Aryal et al., investigated the 
effect of different carbonization temperatures on the specific capaci -
tance of supercapacitors using Prunus persica (peach) seed stones as raw 
material. At a carbonization temperature of 800 
◦
C, they produced 
activated porous char with the highest specific surface area (788.01 
m
2
/g) and measured a specific capacitance of 299.2 F/g under test 
conditions of 1 A/g [ 15 ]. T. Rajesh Kumar et al., conducted 26 sets of 
experiments using waste American poplar fruit as feedstock to deter -
mine optimal parameter combinations. They investigated the influence 
of five experimental parameters — carbonization temperature, activation 
temperature, activation time, carbonization time, and activator ratio -
— on supercapacitor performance. The resulting biomass char based 
supercapacitors exhibited an extraordinarily high specific capacitance of 
423 F/g at 1 A/g [ 16 ]. Owing to the large number of variable experi -
mental parameters, the substantial workload involved, and the coupled 
effects between these parameters, it is challenging to investigate their 
interrelationships through individual experiments alone. Consequently, 
researchers have begun employing alternative methodologies to opti -
mise the production process of biomass char based supercapacitors. 
Machine learning regression algorithms represent one of the most 
widely adopted approaches [ 17 ]. These algorithms can process large 
volumes of complex data, analyse non-linear relationships between data 
points, and generate models that reflect the intricate relationships be -
tween input and output data. This enables us to analyse the coupled 
relationships between factors influencing supercapacitor performance 
through these models, thereby establishing more optimal experimental 
methods for fabricating higher-performance supercapacitors. Ahmed 
Emad-Eldeen et al. utilized a biomass char based supercapacitor dataset 
comprising 130 samples (encompassing material physicochemical 
properties and test conditions) to compare the training efficacy of seven 
machine learning algorithms and eight deep learning algorithms on a 
test set. The results indicated that machine learning algorithms are more 
effective in the field of supercapacitor performance prediction [ 18 ]. 
Peng Liu et al. compiled experimental data from 669 biomass char based 
EDLCs published between 2017 and 2023, encompassing 14 input fea -
tures including experimental parameters, pore structure, chemical 
composition, and measurement conditions. They employed eight ma -
chine learning models, including CatBoost, to predict specific capaci -
tance, with a particular focus on exploring the influence of biomass 
porous char microstructure on specific capacitance [ 19 ]. Yuxuan Sun 
et al. collected data on 157 biomass porous char samples prepared using 
potassium salt activators and nitrogen doping (including experimental 
conditions, physicochemical properties, and testing conditions). 
Employing three machine learning models for training, they revealed 
that heating rate is the most critical factor influencing the specific 
capacitance of biomass char, optimized the preparation process for 
biomass porous char and designed experiments to experimentally vali -
date the models [ 20 ]. Although these studies employing machine 
learning regression algorithms to optimize supercapacitor performance 
have achieved some progress, the input features in these studies include 
both experimental variables and pore structure parameters. These two 
features are not mutually independent(the experimental variables can 
affect the pore structure); the coupling effects among parameters 
inevitably influence the final model prediction outcomes, making it 
challenging to independently reflect the impact of individual experi -
mental parameters on supercapacitor performance [ 21 ].
Therefore, in order to independently explore the influence of 
experimental parameters on the performance of biomass char based 
supercapacitors, this study selected only seven experimental parameters 
derived from the carbonization and activation processes as input vari -
ables. This limited set of input variables poses a significant challenge for 
training a high-performance regression prediction model [ 19 ]. Never -
theless, the specific capacitance prediction model trained on such a 
dataset — with high feature independence — can more accurately reflect 
the influence of each experimental parameter on supercapacitor per -
formance. This facilitates analysis of the coupling relationships among 
parameters and identification of optimal parameter. Finally, experi -
ments were designed based on the optimized experimental parameters 
obtained from the model to validate the model ’ s outputs and the con -
clusions of the model analysis. Collectively, this work holds a great 
significance for the fabrication of high-performance biomass char based 
supercapacitors.
2. Materials and methods
The research content of this paper encompasses data collection, 
database establishment, model selection, as well as model training, 
analysis, and interpretation. This study selected six machine learning 
regression models, covering two major technical directions: deep 
learning and ensemble learning. Among them, deep learning models 
included two neural network architectures: Transformer and Gate 
Recurrent Unit (GRU). Ensemble learning-based models comprised four 
regression models: XGBoost, Random Forest (RF), CatBoost, and 
LightGBM. Three evaluation metrics were employed to assess the pre -
dictive efficacy of these models for the specific capacitance of biomass 
char based supercapacitors. The predictive performance of the six 
models was compared to identify the optimal model. Finally, the optimal 
model was analyzed via three model interpretability methods, exploring 
the key factors influencing the specific capacitance of biomass char 
based supercapacitors and their trends of influence. This provides 
theoretical guidance for the experimental parameter optimisation of 
higher-performance biomass char based supercapacitors.
2.1. Data collection and processing
Machine learning regression tasks require a dataset with sufficient 
sample size and high-quality samples. A sufficiently reliable dataset can 
significantly enhance the predictive performance and reliability of the 
model [ 22 ]. In this study, all data were collected from relevant literature 
on biomass char based supercapacitors published between 2021 and 
2025, Keywords such as ‘pre-carbonization ’ , ‘KOH activation ’ , ‘super -
capacitor ’ , and ‘porous char ’ were used to search relevant papers in 
various literature search engines(e.g., Web of Science, X-MOL, ELSEV -
IER). The specific capacitance of biomass char based supercapacitors is 
influenced not only by the experimental preparation process but also by 
factors such as the type of activator employed during activation and the 
testing conditions applied during testing. Therefore, to ensure consis -
tency and eliminate confounding variables, all selected samples were 
porous char materials prepared using KOH activation. Testing was 
conducted under a three-electrode configuration with 6 M KOH solution 
as the test electrolyte. The selected data points were all specific capac -
itances measured at a current density of 1 A/g. As most data related to 
supercapacitor specific capacitance in the literature were presented as 
images, the data were digitized and extracted using GetData Graph 
Digitizer 2.22 software and the impact of Graphic digitization noise was 
analyzed in S1. A total of 144 sample data points were collected from 36 
papers concerning biomass char based supercapacitors(Table.S7).

Oil palm leaf-derived hierarchical porous carbon
for “water-in-salt” based supercapacitors: the
eﬀect of anions (Cl − and TFSI −)i n
superconcentrated conditions †
Arisa Phukhrongthung,a Pawin Iamprasertkun, b Aritsa Bunpheng,b Thanit Saisopa,c
Chakkrit Umpuch, d Channarong Puchongkawarin, d Montree Sawangphruk e
and Santamon Luanwuthi *a
This study investigates the use of a hierarchical porous carbon electrode derived from oil palm leaves in
a “water-in-salt” supercapacitor. The impact of anion identity on the electrical performance of the
carbon electrode was also explored. The results show that the prepared carbon had a hierarchical
porous structure with a high surface area of up to 1840 m
2 g−1. When a 20 m LiTFSI electrolyte was
used, the carbon electrode had a speci ﬁc capacitance of 176 F g −1 with a wider potential window of
about 2.6 V, whereas the use of a cheaper 20 m LiCl electrolyte showed a higher speci ﬁc capacitance of
331 F g −1 due to the smaller size of the Cl − anion, which enabled inner capacitance. Therefore, the anion
identity has an e ﬀect on the electrochemical performance of porous carbon, and this research
contributes to the understanding of using “water-in-salt” electrolytes in carbon-based supercapacitors.
The study's ﬁndings provide insights into developing low-cost, high-performance supercapacitors that
can operate in a wider voltage range.
1. Introduction
Supercapacitors, a class of electrochemical energy storage
devices, have attracted tremendous interest due to their high-
power density (4000 –10 000 W kg
−1), excellent cycle stability
(50 000–100 000 cycles), good reversibility and low
maintenance.1–4 They have great potential for use in a wide
range of applications such as electric vehicles, portable elec-
tronics and high-power tools. 2,5,6 However, the poor energy
density (1 –10 W h kg −1) of supercapacitors hinders their prac-
tical applications.3,4,7 Therefore, increasing the energy density of
supercapacitors is a key challenge. Principally, the super-
capacitor is categorised into double-layer capacitors (EDLCs)
and pseudocapacitors. EDLC materials generally store energy
electrostatically by the adsorption of the ions at the electrode/
electrolyte interface, while electrical energy is stored in pseu-
docapacitor materials through a faradaic reaction at the surface
(also refer to the ions intercalation
8). Although the EDLC
possess a low energy density compared to the pseudocapacitor,
it exhibits superior rate capability and cycling stability.
7,9,10 Still,
the performance of the supercapacitor in both categories
mainly depends on electrode materials and the type of
electrolytes.
7,11
Carbon-based materials have been promising materials for
EDLC owing to their large surface area (1000 –3500 m 2 g−1),4,12
good electrical conductivity (up to 10 6 Sm −1 depending on the
carbon structures), 12–14 and excellent chemical stability. 10,15
Various carbonaceous materials such as carbon nanotubes, 16–18
porous carbon, 19,20 and graphene 21,22 have been intensively
developed in the past few years. Among these, porous carbon
shows exceptional characteristics such as high accessible
surface area and short di ﬀusion pathways, which could be
advantageous for improving the capacitance and rate capability
of supercapacitors.
20,23 In general, hierarchical porous carbon
usually contains at least two kinds of pores; that is mostly
micropores (<2 nm) and mesopores (2 –50 nm).
23 Micropores
provide the interface for charge accumulation, while mesopores
facilitate ion and electrolyte di ﬀusion.
23,24 Additionally, the
porous carbon can be prepared from biomass materials which
are renewable and low-cost. Numerous types of biomass such as

peanut bran, 25 corncob,26 lotus seedpods, 27 pea skin, 28 Hout-
tuynia,29 bamboo,30 water hyacinth leaves, 20 walnut shell, 31
orange peels,32 etc. are used as carbon precursors for producing
porous carbon. The speci c area of the carbon prepared from
these biomass materials is ca. 700–1650 m2 g−1.20,25–32 However,
these biomass materials are not vastly available in Southeast
Asia and do not potentially create an economic valorisation.
Also, the carbon synthesis is performed at high temperatures
(700–1000 °C). Thus, searching for feasible biomass which is
cheap, easily accessible and obtained from economic plants is
necessary.
Oil palm is one of the economic plants in Southeast Asia. The
oil palm plantation generates great quantities of waste, espe-
cially oil palm leaves; they are discarded on the land and
sometimes burned in the agricultural area. In Thailand, more
than 10 million tons of oil palm leaves per year have not been
utilised.
33 The oil palm leaves are rich in lignocellulose and can
be used as a carbon source for the synthesis of porous
carbons.34 Hence, it has a great potential to increase the value of
the oil palm leaves by using them as carbon precursors in this
work. Also, in previous studies, the carbon materials were
mostly prepared via a step of high-temperature carbonisation
(1000–1400 °C). This method is a high energy-consuming and
cost-ineﬀective. An alternative approach such as hydrothermal
carbonisation (HTC) has been employed in this work to syn-
thesise the carbon since HTC is facile and has low energy
consumption; it operates at medium temperature (160 –250 °C)
and uses water as a reaction medium.
35,36
Yet, another simple approach to improving the energy
density of supercapacitors is the use of appropriate electrolytes.
High-voltage organic electrolytes are widely used for increasing
energy density.
37–39 However, they are toxic, highly ammable
and volatile. 7 These problems can be addressed by employing
an aqueous electrolyte. Although aqueous electrolyte is non-
ammable and environmentally feasible, 40 the working
voltage is limited by the water splitting reaction at around
1.23 V.
41 The trendy superconcentrated electrolytes, so-called
“water-in-salt” (WIS) electrolytes, have been studied to tackle
the limited voltage of aqueous electrolytes. The WIS electrolyte
was rst introduced by Suo et al.
42 Superconcentrated lithium
bis(triuoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI) was used as an
electrolyte for lithium-ion batteries, thereby the stability voltage
window can be expanded to 3.0 V. In such a high concentration
condition, the hydrogen and oxygen evolution reactions are
suppressed due to small numbers of free water molecules.
42,43
Moreover, the reduction of the H 2O/Li+ molar ratio strongly
aﬀects the solvation structure of the electrolyte.44 The concept of
the WIS electrolyte was also applied to supercapacitors by
B´elanger's and many research groups to enhance energy
density.
45–48 For instance, Hasegawa et al. prepared carbon
monolith-based supercapacitors with 5 M LiTFSI. The
symmetric supercapacitor can operate at 2.4 V and deliver an
energy density of 24 W h kg
−1.47 Other high solubility salts such
as sodium perchlorate (NaClO 4),49 potassium uoride (KF), 50
sodium nitrate (NaNO 3)51 and lithium chloride (LiCl) 52 could
also act as WIS electrolytes. The use of superconcentrated
NaClO
4 in supercapacitors, for example, could expand the
voltage window up to 2.30 V. 49 Therefore, WIS electrolytes have
been an interesting electrolyte choice for employing in porous
carbon-based aqueous supercapacitors. To our best knowledge,
hierarchical porous carbon prepared from oil palm leaves and
applied as an electrode in WIS based supercapacitor have not
been reported before. The e ﬀect of porous carbon properties
and the types of salt on the performance of the aqueous
supercapacitors is rarely discussed.
In this work, oil palm leaf-derived hierarchical porous
carbon was prepared using hydrothermal carbonisation
coupled with KOH activation (Fig. 1). The weight ratio of KOH/
carbon was varied in order to modify the porosity of the
carbons. The obtained carbon successfully possessed a devel-
oped structure with ultrahigh porosity containing numerous
micropores and mesopores. The oil palm leaf-derived hierar-
chical porous carbon demonstrated an extremely high speci c
surface area of up to 1928.85 m
2 g−1. The electrochemical
performance of the porous carbon-based supercapacitors was
studied in two di ﬀerent types (anions) of water-in-salt electro-
lytes (LiTFSI and LiCl). With the use of the appropriated WIS
electrolyte, the potential window of the supercapacitors was
expanded to 2.6 V (20 m LiTFSI). However, the oil palm leaf-
derived hierarchical porous carbon showed the highest
specic capacitance of 331.40 F g
−1 with the window voltage of
1.9 V when using 20 m LiCl as the electrolyte. These results
demonstrated the in uence of the concentrated anions on the
electrochemical performance of the porous carbon electrode.
Hence, such excellent capacitive performance con rms the
potential to use oil palm-derived porous carbon as an e ﬀective
electrode in high-voltage aqueous supercapacitors.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials and chemicals
Oil palm leaves (containing 7% of ashes which are 5.91% of Si,
0.45% of Ca, and 0.36% of Mg, Fig. S1 †) were collected from
a local plantation in Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand. All the
chemicals were analytical grade and used without further
purication. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 85%) was purchased
from LobaChemie. Nitric acid (HNO
3, 69.0%), ethyl alcohol
(C2H5OH, 99.9%) and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 37%) were
purchased from J.T.Baker, Reagents Duksan and Merck,
respectively. Carbon black Super P (99.9%), polyvinylidene
uoride (PVDF) and 1-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (C
5H9NO or NMP,
99.5%) applied for electrode preparation were purchased from
Alfar Aesar, Sigma Aldrich and QReC, respectively. Lithium
triuoromethanesulfonyl (LiTFSI, $99.0%) and lithium chlo-
ride (LiCl, 99.99%) from KEMAUS were used as electrolytes for
the electrochemical supercapacitor study.
2.2. Synthesis of carbon materials
2.2.1. Pre-treatment of oil palm leaves. In order to remove
unwanted impurities, oil palm leaves were soaked in 1 M HNO
3
for 1 h before being washed with deionized (DI) water until its
pH stables at around 7. The clean oil palm leaves were then
dried in an oven (Memmert, Germany, UN30) at 105 °C for 4 h.

storage, biomass-derived porous carbons have emerged as eco-
friendly alternatives to conventional electrode materials. This study
shows that activated carbon prepared by one-step activation
exhibits an enhanced specific surface area and pore volume. The
optimum parameter for ameliorating the structural and electro-
chemical properties is 60 min of microwave heating. The specific
surface area, pore volume, and mesopore volume of the resulting
activated carbon (EUAC1−60) achieve 1589.0 m

validates its exceptional stability with capacitance retention of 89.90% and Coulombic efficiency of 117.21% after 10,000 cycles. The
zinc ion hybrid supercapacitor with the EUAC1−60 cathode and Zn foil anode displayed an excellent energy density performance of

1. INTRODUCTION
Given the pressing global need for energy, dwindling fossil fuel
reserves, and deteriorating environmental conditions, consid-
erable attention should be given to enhancing the efficiency of
energy storage and conversion apparatus.
1
Among the various
energy storage devices available, rechargeable batteries (e.g.,
nickel metal hydride batteries and lithium ion batteries),
conventional capacitors, and supercapacitors comprise the
three primary categories. While rechargeable batteries
commonly exhibit high energy density, their inferior power
density and limited life prevent them from meeting the
requirements for high power output and fast charging/
discharging scenarios. Conventional capacitors, by contrast,
were unable to satisfy the practical requirements due to their
significantly low energy density.
2
Supercapacitors, in contrast,
are swiftly evolving into potential energy storage technologies
and are attracting considerable interest. These devices exhibit
rapid charge−discharge velocity, exceptional circulation
stability, and the ability to bridge the gap
3
between high-
energy density cells
4
and traditional power density capacitors,
5
rendering them applicable in a broad array of sectors,
encompassing telecommunications gear, hybrid vehicles,
6
smart grids, high-speed rail,
7
and spacecraft.
8
As a fundamental
element of supercapacitors, electrode materials play a pivotal
role and directly influence the electrochemical behavior of
supercapacitors. Nevertheless, the exploration of novel
electrode materials exhibiting superior performance, eco-
friendly attributes, and low cost is an imperative issue to be
addressed, which has considerably impeded the industrial
development of supercapacitor devices.
9
In the context of supercapacitor applications, an optimal
electrode material is required to possess an appreciable specific
surface area to absorb more electrolyte ions and augment its
electrochemical functionality. Furthermore, the electrode
material must also exhibit superior conductivity and rapid
charge−discharge efficiency within a short duration. In light of
these prerequisites, porous carbon, due to its adjustable
morphology and superior conductivity, is deemed a promising
supercapacitor electrode material.

strategically guided by its multifaceted advantages in
sustainability, pore structure engineering, and electrochemical
functionality. Unlike conventional alkaline activators (e.g.,
KOH) or metal salts (e.g., ZnCl
2
), H
3
PO
4
provides an
environmentally benign activation pathway with minimal
generation of corrosive byproducts, aligning with green
chemistry principles while reducing postprocessing haz-
ards.
24,25
Its unique activation mechanism, involving dehy-
dration and cross-linking reactions at moderate temperatures
(≤500 °C), enables the simultaneous development of a
hierarchical pore architecture: microporous domains to
maximize charge storage capacity and mesoporous channels
to facilitate rapid ion diffusion, thereby synergistically
enhancing both specific capacitance and rate perform-
ance.
26−28
Furthermore, the phosphorus-containing functional
groups (e.g., C−O−PO
3
) introduced during H
3
PO
4
activation
not only improve interfacial wettability for efficient electrolyte
penetration but also contribute to pseudocapacitance through
reversible redox reactions.
29
The activating process is divided
into one-step and two-step activation.
30
During one-step
activation, biomass is impregnated with the activator prior to
the carbonization process. The activator interacts directly with
biomass by cleaving the aryl ether bonds. Concurrently, gas
release is accelerated by dehydration and condensation
mechanisms associated with hydrolyzed glycosidic bonds
present in hemicellulose and cellulose.
31
In addition,
phosphate and polyphosphate moieties are formed by H
3
PO
4
conjugation with organic components within the biomass
source, which subsequently facilitates the expansion of the
precursor into the porous structure.
32
Alternatively, a two-step
activation procedure involves carbonization and subsequent
impregnation in the activator, followed by activation at an
elevated temperature to produce activated carbon. Throughout
the two-step activation protocol, pyrolysis results in the release
of volatile components and facilitates the production of pores
within activated carbon. However, certain tar constituents
partially block the developed pores. The physicochemical
characteristics of activated carbon generated by one-step versus
two-step activation may show considerable differences,
potentially affecting supercapacitors’ performance. However,
systematic investigations of the effects of these two methods on
the physical and chemical properties of activated carbon are
rarely conducted.
Eucommia Ulmoides Oliver (EUO) stands as a significant
economic tree species exclusively found in China. The
cultivated area of this species covers over 95% of the
worldwide EUO resources, yielding substantial annual biomass
assets.
33
However, improper use of these biomass resources
can lead to serious resource wastage and environmental
contamination dilemmas. Hence, there is a growing need to
convert EUO wood into value-added products. Research
efforts have been devoted to harnessing EUO wood as a
sustainable precursor for high-performance supercapacitor
electrodes, with a particular focus on structural and process
optimization strategies. These endeavors encompass systematic
investigations into pore structure engineering of biomass-
derived activated carbons,
34
comparative analyses of thermal
activation methodologies,
35,36
and mechanistic studies of
H
3
PO
4
-mediated activation protocols.
37
However, critical
knowledge gaps persist regarding the fundamental differences
between one- and two-step activation approaches in governing
the hierarchical porosity and charge storage behavior of EUO
wood-derived carbons. A systematic understanding remains
essential for rational design of biomass-based electrodes with
tailored energy-power characteristics.
In this study, we have developed a method using both one-
and two-step activation procedures with H
3
PO
4
as a chemical
activator to manufacture EUO activated carbon. The optimal
activation technique (one-step or two-step activation) is
selected based on the distinct pore structure of the activated
carbon, and microwave heating technology is used to
investigate the effects of heating time on the pore architecture
characteristics of the activated carbon. By contrasting the
structural differences between activated carbon and biochar,
the intrinsic correlations between the structural properties of
activated carbon and its electrochemical performance are
unveiled. In a three-electrode system, the electrochemical
performance of EUO activated carbon is evaluated using cyclic
voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge−discharge [galvano-
static charge/discharge (GCD)], and electrochemical impe-
dance spectroscopy (EIS), and key metrics such as specific
capacitance, capacitance retention, Coulombic efficiency, and
energy density of the activated carbon electrode material are
obtained. This work initiates a sustainable strategy to
transform underutilized EUO wood biomass into hierarchically
porous carbons through H
3
PO
4
-microwave synergy, offering a
dual advantage of coefficient fabrication and remarkable energy
storage performance. Our findings not only advance the
rational design of biomass-derived supercapacitor electrodes
but also establish a model for converting agricultural forestry
residues into high-value carbon materials for next-generation
energy devices.

bark and foliage are carefully removed and subjected to a
drying procedure at 105 °C for 24 h. The dried wood is then
processed into a wood meal (40−60 mesh sizes). H

of
analytical purity (99.90%) was purchased from Energy Co.,
Ltd. (Shanghai, China).

Biomass‑derived nanostructured carbon materials 
for high‑performance supercapacitor electrodes
Mehrnaz Ebrahimi1 · Hassan Hosseini‑Monfared1  · Mehran Javanbakht1 · Fatemeh Mahdi1
Received: 12 November 2022 / Revised: 24 December 2022 / Accepted: 28 December 2022 / Published online: 10 January 2023

Abstract
To achieve a higher energy density for the supercapacitor without degrading cycle stability, functionalization of biomass 
based-AC with oxygen-containing groups was applied. Nanostructured carbon materials were produced from barley straw 
biomass waste using the activation-functionalization by  FeCl3 and urea via the pyrolysis method in a tubular reactor at 
900 °C. The electrode made up of carbon BCF-U in the three-electrode cell in aqueous KOH electrolyte showed high-
specific capacitance of 515 F  g–1 at current density of 2 A  g−1  and in aqueous  Na2SO4 electrolyte the capacitance of 379 F 
 g−1  at 3 A  g−1 . The BCF-U electrode showed cycling stability, retaining more than 99% capacitance after 5000 cycles in 1 M 
 Na2SO4 electrolyte. The fabricated symmetric supercapacitor device with carbon BCF-U showed a high-energy density of 
10.7 Wh  kg–1 and a power density of 720 W   kg−1  in aqueous 6 M KOH. Different characterizations were carried out to show 
that the functional group and morphological features of the activated carbon were closely related to the superior capacitive 
performance by enhancing diffusion of electrolyte ions. The analysis proved the formation of graphitic nature with mixed 
micro- and mesoporous textures in addition to carbon nanotube, carbon nano rod, and graphene. These unique features make 
synthetic activated and functionalized samples possess good adsorption capacity for electrical double layer capacitors. The 
results demonstrate that nanostructured carbon materials derived from a low-cost biomass waste can serve as an economical 
carbon feedstock for production of high-performance electrode material for supercapacitors.
Keywords Supercapacitor · Barley straw-derived carbon · Carbon nanostructures · Functionalization
1 Introduction
Lignocellulosic biomass is readily available, low cost, and 
bio-renewable with great potential for the preparation of 
carbon materials, biofuels, and biochemicals [1 ]. Mega 
gram amounts of lignocellulosic biomass residue are gener-
ated through forestry and agricultural activities annually in 
world [2]. Converting lignocellulosic biomass into added-
value products such as biochar provides less dependency 
on petrochemical resources while providing a sustainable 
waste management alternative. Application of biochar to soil 
can improve organic matter in soil [3 , 4]. Biochar presents 
other important features such as low cost, high surface area, 
porosity, high electrical conductivity, and high chemical 
stability [5], which have stimulated tremendous interest in 
preparation of the valuable activated carbon-based electrode 
materials for supercapacitors [6].
Replacing fossil fuels with renewable and sustainable 
resources is an urgent strategy for society to retard the global 
warming rate. Moreover, this changing strategy responds the 
ever-increasing global energy crises which are rising due 
to economic and population growth. It is critical to expand 
the production of sustainable and renewable clean energy 
technologies. The main renewable energy sources, includ-
ing wind, solar, and hydropower are fluctuating because of 
weather conditions. Therefore, there are unique challenges 
to store and supply renewable energy on a stable way. Elec-
trochemical supercapacitors (ES) are efficient energy storage 
systems for many applications due to their superior power 
density, stability, cycle lives, and fast charging/discharging 
ability without any risk of explosion [7, 8]. Supercapacitors 
are employed in various fields, such as transport systems, 
military devices, computers, and medical and industrial 
instruments [9 ]. By their charge storage process, all the 
 * Hassan Hosseini-Monfared 
 hahomonfared@gmail.com
1 Department of Chemistry, Amirkabir University 
of Technology (Tehran Polytechnic), Tehran 15875-4413, 
Iran
17364 Biomass Conversion and Biorefinery (2024) 14:17363–17380
1 3
carbonaceous materials exhibit electrochemical double-layer 
capacitor (EDLCs) type behavior based on the adsorption of 
ions at the electrode interface [10, 11].
To reuse waste biomass in energy storage equipment, 
Cheng et al. prepared a series of porous carbons (CSCs) 
with high surface area (1754 to 1987  m2  g−1 ) by the car -
bonization of  ZnCl2-pretreated chestnut shells and evalu-
ated their electrochemical performances [12]. Among all 
the CSC-based supercapacitors, the sample CSC-7 exhib-
ited the best electrochemical performance with the spe-
cific capacitances of 105.4 F  g−1  at 0.1 A  g−1  and 92.0 
F  g−1  at 10 A  g−1 . Obtaining the capacitance as large as 
92.0 F  g−1  at high-current density is good, but the capaci-
tance improvements just by increasing the surface area 
were not remarkable. In another study, Cao et al. prepared 
porous activated carbon (AC) from corn stalk pith with the 
high-specific surface area (2495  m2  g−1 ) using potassium 
hydroxide [13]. The electrode made by this sample showed 
low inner resistance of 1.0 V and the specific capacitance 
of 323 F  g−1  in 6 mol  L−1  KOH electrolyte at a current 
density of 0.1 A  g−1 . The surface area enlargement resulted 
to high-specific capacitance. In 2019, a tubular porous car -
bon was prepared by Chen without any doping from straw 
cellulose waste with NaOH activation [14]. The prepared 
carbon had a high-specific surface area and displayed 
specific capacitance of 313 F  g−1  in 6 M KOH at 0.5 A 
 g−1  for supercapacitors. The tubular porous carbon-based 
supercapacitor device provided a high-energy density of 
8.67 Wh  kg−1  at a power density of 3.50 kW   kg−1  in 6 M 
KOH. Furthermore, Yakaboylu et al. prepared porous acti-
vated carbons from hybrid willow and miscanthus grass 
by pyrolysis, oxidative torrefaction, and KOH chemical 
activation [15]. Analyses of the prepared carbon revealed 
the presence of oxygen (about 11 to 19%), various sized 
porosity, and high surface area of 3265  m2/g. The prepared 
two-electrode symmetrical supercapacitors were stable 
in a 6 M KOH aqueous electrolyte for 1000 cycles and 
showed specific capacitance up to 162 F/g at 100 mA/g. 
In another study, Lin et al. prepared phosphorus-doped 
porous carbon from biomass sawdust [16]. The P-doped 
carbon material exhibited fine specific capacitances of 
292 F  g−1  at low current density 0.1 A  g−1  and the high-
energy density of 10.6 W h   kg−1 . Furthermore, Li et al. 
noticed the importance of templating agent and prepared 
porous carbons from sodium alginate and calcium algi-
nate to study the effect of different regulation component 
(sodium/calcium) on the electrochemical properties of the 
obtained charcoals as EDLC [17]. The higher capacitance 
of about 313 F  g−1  was obtained with sodium alginate-
derived porous carbon when the KOH/C ratios were 2 and 
4. The surface area of the prepared electrode material was 
very high with respect to the previously reported stud-
ies and the observed capacitance and power density were 
comparable; at low current density range (50 − 250 mA/g), 
the energy density, and power density were 17.5 W·h/kg 
and 209 W/kg, respectively. An alternative strategy that 
has been used to enhance the capacitive feature of AC is 
the functionalization. Bandosz et al. used melamine and 
urea to study the combined effect of N- and O-enriched 
AC of coconut shell on electrochemical performance of 
supercapacitors [18]. They found that EDLC behavior is 
mainly achieved with the O- and N-containing functional 
groups located in pores between 5 Å and 6 Å. Functional 
groups pyrrolic-N, pyridinic-N, and quinone-O showed the 
most enhancing effects on capacitance. Furthermore, Xing 
et al. have already reported the preparation of nanoporous 
carbons (the surface area 600–2600  m2  g−1  and pore-struc-
ture ~ 2.1 nm) from sunflower seed shell by impregnation-
activation/carbonization-activation processes and used 
as electrode material for EDLC in 30% KOH [19]. The 
carbons made by impregnation-activation process showed 
better capacitive behavior at high current density (244 F 
 g−1  at 0.25  Ag−1  and 171  Fg−1  at 10 A  g−1 ) which was 
ascribed to the abundant macroscopic pores and less inte-
rior micropore surface. The capacitive performances of 
these carbons are better than ordered mesoporous carbons.
In comparison to rechargeable batteries and fuel cells, 
the commercially available supercapacitors suffer from the 
low energy density (~ 10 Wh  kg−1 ) [20]. Therefore, there are 
plenty of research to improve the energy density of super -
capacitors [21]. In this study, to achieve a higher energy 
density for the supercapacitor without degrading cycle sta-
bility, functionalization of biomass based-AC with oxygen-
containing groups was applied. Carbon surface functional 
groups may contribute to the enhanced capacitance [22]. 
This research not only offers a method for the conversion of 
biomass waste into added-value products such as graphene 
and CNT, but also provides a highly efficient method for the 
functionalization of the carbonized biomass for enhanced 
electrochemical energy storage devices.
2  Experimental section
2.1  Material characterization
Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra were taken using a 
544 Rayleigh WQF-520 Spectrometer. Raman spectra were 
collected using a Teksan TakRam N1-532 Raman spectrom-
eter with excitation wavelength 532 nm from a laser beam. 
X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of powders were recorded 
on a Philips PW-1730 using a Cu Kα source (λ = 0.1542 nm) 
at a scanning speed of 10°  min−1  over a 2θ range of 10 − 80°. 
The interlayer spacing  (d002) was determined using the 
Bragg’s Eq. (1) [23].

Biomass‑derived carbon electrodes from sugarcane bagasse 
for supercapacitor applications
Kajal Gautam1 · Mohit Bhatt2 · Akarsh Verma3  · Anil Kumar Sinha2
Received: 21 January 2025 / Revised: 8 March 2025 / Accepted: 19 March 2025 / Published online: 26 March 2025

Abstract
This research investigates the application of carbon materials derived from sugarcane bagasse, a form of biomass, for the 
advancement of supercapacitor electrodes. Carbon electrodes were synthesized by carbonizing biomass waste at 500 °C with 
varying durations (3, 4, 5, and 10 h) and pre-treatment using glacial acetic acid, HCl, and NaOH. The resulting materials were 
designated as C-1, C-2, C-3, and C-4 respectively. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was employed to analyze the structural properties 
of the materials, while Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy were used 
to evaluate their optical characteristics. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed to examine the morphology and 
structural characteristics of all samples. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was conducted to surface chemistry, and 
elemental composition of materials. Electrochemical performance was assessed using cyclic voltammetry (CV), charging 
discharge, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Sample C-4, synthesized at 500 °C for 10 h, exhibited the 
best electrochemical performance, with high specific capacitances of 226.7 F/g at 1 mV/s, excellent rate capability with 65% 
capacitance retention at 100 mV/s, and excellent cyclic stability and coulombic efficiency of 100% over 5000 cycles. These 
findings underscore the effectiveness of biomass-derived carbon electrode for high performance supercapacitor applications.
Keywords Biomass-derived carbon · Sugarcane bagasse · Supercapacitors · Electrochemical performance
1 Introduction
Supercapacitors, also known as electrochemical capacitors, 
have gained substantial recognition for their exceptional 
power density, rapid charge–discharge capabilities, and 
impressive cycle life, positioning them as critical compo-
nents in energy storage technologies [1 ]. Unlike conven-
tional batteries, supercapacitors excel in applications that 
demand swift energy delivery and high-power output, such 
as regenerative braking systems in electric vehicles, grid 
energy storage, and various consumer electronics [2 , 3]. 
Supercapacitors, unlike the conventional capacitors, deliver 
significantly more energy density because of adsorption of 
charges during charging cycle. This is unlike the storage 
mechanism in conventional capacitors, which store energy 
only by the electrical polarization of dielectric [4]. Carbon-
based materials are extensively employed as electrodes in 
supercapacitors due to their high electrical conductivity, 
large surface area, and excellent electrochemical stability 
[5–7]. These properties are crucial for achieving high capac-
itance and efficient charge storage. Various forms of carbon, 
like activated carbons [8], carbon nanotubes (CNT) [9], gra-
phene [10], reduced graphene oxide [11], and carbon-based 
composites [5 ], have been used as electrodes for superca-
pacitors, each offering unique advantages and limitations [5, 
12]. Activated carbons, derived from various sources includ-
ing biomass, are the most common electrode materials for 
supercapacitors. Activated carbon, also known as activated 
charcoal or activated coal, is highly porous form of carbon 
with high surface area exceeding 2000  m2/g [13], tuneable 
pore morphology, and amenable for surfaces functionalized,

which enables substantial charge storage through electro-
static interactions and double-layer capacitance [14– 16]. 
Additionally, these materials find applications in water/air 
purification [17, 18], odor remover [19], and as catalyst [20]. 
Carbon nanotubes and graphene offer superior electrical 
conductivity and mechanical strength, making them suit -
able for high-performance supercapacitors [5 , 21, 22]. The 
sustainability of energy storage materials is an increasing 
concern, and biomass-derived carbon materials are emerging 
as an eco-friendly alternative [15, 23]. Sugarcane bagasse, a 
by-product of sugar industries, is an abundant and low-cost 
biomass source that can be converted into carbon materials 
through carbonization. This process not only recycles agri-
cultural waste but also reduces the environmental impact 
associated with conventional carbon production methods 
[24, 25]. Biomass-derived carbon materials offer several 
advantages over traditional carbon sources. First, they are 
derived from bio-waste, which contributes to sustainability 
and reduces material cost [26]. Second, the synthesis process 
allows morphology engineering like pore size and surface 
functionalisation to maximize device charge storage capac-
ity. Finally, the use of biomass reduces environmental impact 
by lowering carbon footprints and mitigating greenhouse 
gas emissions associated with traditional carbon production 
[24, 27].
Biomass-derived carbon materials, such as those 
obtained from sugarcane bagasse, grass, wood, and other 
plant-based sources, have emerged as promising electrode 
materials for supercapacitors due to their high surface area, 
abundant functional groups, and sustainable nature [ 23, 28, 
29]. These biomass-derived carbons often possess a hierar -
chical porous structure, which enhances ion diffusion and 
electrolyte accessibility, leading to superior electrochemi-
cal performance [30]. Additionally, the intrinsic heteroatom 
doping (e.g., oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur) in these materials 
improves charge storage capacity by introducing pseudo-
capacitive behavior and increasing electrical conductivity 
[31]. Studies have demonstrated that sugarcane bagasse-
derived activated carbon exhibits a high specific capaci-
tance and excellent cyclic stability, making it a competitive 
alternative to conventional carbon-based electrodes [13, 
15]. Furthermore, grass-derived biochar has been shown to 
deliver outstanding electrochemical performance due to its 
high graphitic content and tunable porosity [32]. The renew-
able and cost-effective nature of biomass-derived carbons 
makes them highly attractive for sustainable energy stor -
age applications in supercapacitors [ 28, 32]. In this quest, 
Anand et al. [33] synthesized heteroatom-doped activated 
carbon from walnut shells, achieving a high specific sur -
face area and a hierarchical pore structure that enhanced 
ion transport and electrochemical performance. Their mate-
rial exhibited a gravimetric capacitance of 271.4 F/g at 0.5 
A/g. In another work, Alwi et al. [34] investigated waste 
sugarcane bagasse (WSB) as a cost-effective and sustain-
able precursor for porous carbon in supercapacitors. To 
enhance its electrochemical performance, they hybridized 
WSB-derived carbon with silicon dioxide (SiO₂), a low-cost 
pseudocapacitive material. The optimized nanocomposite 
electrode demonstrated a high specific capacitance of 362.3 
F g⁻ 1 at 0.25 A/g, demonstrating the potential of WSB-
derived composites for high-performance energy storage 
applications. Singh et al. [35] developed a series of highly 
porous sulfur-doped activated carbon (WSC/S) derived 
from sugarcane bagasse. The WSC/S exhibited a large 
specific surface area with high mesoporosity, enhanced 
wettability, and abundant redox-active sites, which con-
tributed to superior supercapacitor performance. The high 
mesopore content facilitated efficient ion transport, ena -
bling the WSC/S electrode to achieve a remarkable spe-
cific capacitance of 282.25 F g⁻ 1 at 0.1 A g⁻ 1 with excel-
lent cycling stability, retaining over 96% capacitance after 
10,000 cycles. These materials demonstrate the potential of 
biomass-derived materials as efficient energy storage solu-
tions for energy storage applications. In this study, activated 
(AC) carbon electrodes were synthesized from sugarcane 
bagasse by treatment with glacial acetic acid, hydrochloric 
acid, and sodium hydroxide to remove impurities from the 
raw material and then carbonizing the biomass at 500 °C 
for different time durations 3, 4, 5, and 10 h. The resulting 
electrode materials were designated as C-1 (500 °C, 3 h), 
C-2 (500 °C, 4 h), C-3 (500 °C, 5 h), and C-4 (500 °C, 
10 h). The structural properties of the carbon materials 
were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), revealing a 
graphitic structure of material. Fourier-transform infrared 
(FTIR) provided insights into the functional groups and 
photoluminescence (PL) provides optical characteristics of 
the materials. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) con-
firmed that sample C-4, synthesized at 500 °C for 10 h, 
exhibits a crossed sheet-like morphology. This morphol-
ogy is consistent with the characteristics of hard carbon, 
which is beneficial for enhancing ion transport and elec-
trochemical performance in energy storage devices such 
as batteries or supercapacitors. Hard carbon typically has 
a disordered structure with micro- and mesopores, facili-
tating the insertion and extraction of ions during charge 
and discharge cycles. The crossed sheet-like morphology 
provides a large surface area, improving electrolyte access 
and reducing the diffusion path for ions, thereby enhancing 
electrochemical performance. Electrochemical tests dem-
onstrated that sample C-4 achieved specific capacitances 
of 226.71 F/g at 1 mV/s and 147.80 F/g at 10 A/g, surpass-
ing the performance of several other biomass-derived car -
bon materials reported in the literature (shown in Table  1). 
Carbon electrodes derived from agricultural residues gen-
erally exhibit lower capacitance compared to the perfor -
mance of our materials [36]. Additionally, carbon materials

ABSTRACT
By offering a green and sustainable option to reusing biomass, the creation of energy harvesting/storage sys-
tems from biomass/waste materials has signi ﬁcant scienti ﬁc and technological implications. To achieve the
required applications in the ﬁelds of supercapacitor and conversion, microstructure management is crucial
for carbon-based materials. Here, a facile production of heteroatom-doped porous carbon (HAPC) from
Enhydra ﬂuctuant leaves as electrode material for supercapacitor is demonstrated. Large speci ﬁc-surface area
and good pore-size distribution were achieved. An exceptional speci ﬁc-capacitance ( C
sp) 428 F/g at 1 A/g in
an acidic electrolyte was achieved. The solid-state symmetric-supercapacitor device (SSSD) produces the high-
est C
sp of 113 F/g and 73.88 Wh/kg energy –density at 1 A/g, whereas 5.11 kW/kg power-density was achieved
at 10 A/g. The SSSD exhibits outstanding durability, where it holds 94% of its Csp after 10,000 charge/dis-
charge series.
1. Introduction
A global goal is now to produce and store energy ef ﬁciently, eco-
friendly, and sustainably. Numerous rechargeable devices have been
created, and electrochemical-related technology has garnered a lot of
attention as an ef ﬁcient method for electrical energy storage. Because
of their large power capacity, outstanding coulombic reversibility
(98% or more), exceptional cyclability, and environmentally benign
characteristics, supercapacitors play a signi ﬁcant role in energy har-
vesting/storage. The pseudocapacitors and double-layer capacitors
are the two primary groups of supercapacitors based on the charge-
storage mechanism [1–4]. So, in the recent decade, the main chal-
lenges are to explore biocompatible sources which are renewable,
eco-friendly, cost-effective, and high-adsorption electrode materials,
having fast ion and/or electrode transport, and also ﬁlled with tunable
microstructure/surface chemistry [5]. Biomass is a renewable, crucial
precursor to produce carbonaceous materials for energy harvesting/
storage device applications. Therefore, nowadays researchers put more
attention into processing biomass-derived materials for their attract-
able storage properties including their extensive accessibility, being
renewable, and also cost-effective starting ingredients. As a result, var-
ious types of applications are exploited for these kinds of properties
including carbon-dioxide capture [6], hydrogen storage [7], dye-sensi-
tized solar cells [8], water treatment [9], and most importantly energy
storage [10,11]. More importantly, these are useful for their attract-
able integral homogeneous, also speci ﬁc biological properties that
are applied as patterns for constructing active electrode materials con-
necting well-deﬁned geometries. Besides this, products containing car-
bon precursor as a major quantity and also the well-balanced networks
are signi ﬁcant for the metabolic process of making biowaste-based
electrode materials. Because of this, they are appropriate for applica-
tions involving electrochemical charge/discharge that require rapid
ion movement. Recently, diverse types of biomass or biowaste-derived
carbon materials are indispensable in the fabrication of self-doped
hierarchical porous carbon-based electrodes and this gets increasing
interest as a warming theme for energy harvesting/storage and conver-
sion-related ﬁelds [12].
Biomass-derived porous graphite carbon materials (BPGCs) are
renowned as new justi ﬁable carbon materials for their well-develop-
ment of porous structure, interesting graphitic structure, doping with

different heteroatoms, etc. [13]. Considering electrochemical energy
storage and conversion, there are three different systems that have
been classi ﬁed and investigated to utilize the BPGCs including fuel
cells, lithium-ion batteries, and supercapacitors. Although, after
detailed study, the porous carbon materials have some limitations like
(i) a low degree of graphitization with a poor graphitic structure,
resulting a less conducting and transmission of ions and electrons,
(ii) low speci ﬁc-surface areas, (iii) lack of heteroatoms for doping,
etc. The above-mentioned limitations have imperfect the proper
“green” applications in energy harvesting/storage and conversion as
well as environmental pollution protection [14].
BPGCs materials contain a broad range of “green” applications
owing to their outstanding electrical conductivity, upgraded crys-
talline orientation, and also exceptional physicochemical possessions
which could facilitate ion diffusion [15]. However, graphitic carbon
materials have some dif ﬁculties including their costly nature and poor
porous structure. To be stunned by these applications, excellent porous
graphitic structures of carbon materials with appropriate heteroatoms
doping are developed. Therefore, heteroatoms-self-doped porous bio-
mass carbon materials have been fabricated as ef ﬁcient electrodes
for symmetric electrochemical supercapacitors as they feature extre-
mely large energy –density in both aqueous and organic-based elec-
trolytes. As a result, they exhibit signi ﬁcant potential for energy
harvesting/storage and conversion-related applications [16,17].
Supercapacitors (SCs) are the most proper devices as they have
energy storage as they have large power-density and excellent cyclic
electrochemical stability [18]. Although in the past decades, activated
carbon materials have been utilized as electrode materials in superca-
pacitor applications but in recent decades biomass-derived activated
carbons (ACs) attract much more attention. When heteroatoms like
B, S, O, N, and P are introduced into the carbon skeleton for construct-
ing the porous structure of carbon elements, the electrochemical per-
formance of SCs increased. Doping with N and O in the
supercapacitors results in a better comprehensive activity instead of
using other heteroatoms like B or S [16,19]. For synthesizing ACs,
the most used methods are chemical, physical, or chemical-physical
activations [20]. These ACs have some useful properties such as a high
surface area with larger pore volume and unique electrochemical
behavior for choosing as supercapacitors. However, these have some
disadvantages e.g., a large number of chemical reagents are needed
in the chemical activation path. In these reactions, the using excess
candidates are not recycled easily and cause environmental pollution.
Sometimes, the dead and fallen leaves were successfully used for pro-
cessing the ACs by the same method of activation using abundant alka-
lis or acids but these are so common [21]. To resolve the above
problems, unique nano-structures of biomass-based materials are cho-
sen for the ACs production only through facile one-step carbonization
in the absence of any other agents. Nowadays, to construct functional
carbon materials, molecular modi ﬁcation-based gel precursors are the
most favorable preparation method. And for this, various types of gels
are used.
In this study, we applied a straightforward production of HAPC
skeleton from leaves of Enhydra ﬂuctuant, and the produced active car-
bon matrics were utilized as active materials for energy harvesting/
storage purposes. The synthesized carbon materials had a good pore
size and distribution with a large speci ﬁc-surface area. Synthetic por-
ous carbon has exceptional speci ﬁc-capacitance ( C
sp), measuring
428 F/g at a current density of 1 A/g under H 2SO4 electrolyte. This
is owing to the porous carbon's high active surface and pore volume.
Active electrode materials' electrokinetic research reveals the largest
capacitive input to total charge storage. Produced HAPC matrices uti-
lized in the construction of the solid-state symmetric-supercapacitor
device (SSSD) exhibit the highest Csp of 113 F/g at 1 A/g with a wide
voltage frame of 2 V. The as-fabricated SSSD exhibits maximum 73.88
Wh/kg energy –density at 1 A/g current density and 5.11 kW/kg
power-density at 10 A/g current density. Even in an acidic electrolyte,
the manufactured SSSD exhibits outstanding rate capability and dura-
bility. Subsequently 10,000 nonstop charge/discharge cycles, the gad-
get still retains 94% of its Csp. The synthesized HAPC skeletons have a
substantial possibility to bridge the electrochemical performance gap
between conventional electrolytes because of their extremely interest-
ing electrochemical performance than formerly described carbona-
ceous electrodes using a simple carbonization process.
2. Experimental
2.1. Chemicals
All chemicals are of the AR grades and were all used without fur-
ther puri ﬁcation. Ammonium chloride (NH 4Cl, 99.9%), concentrated
hydrochloric acid (HCl, 99.9%), and potassium hydroxide (KOH,
99.9%) were all furnished by Sigma Aldrich. De-ionized water was uti-
lized to prepare the aqueous solutions.
2.2. Synthesis of heteroatom-doped porous carbon (HAPC) skeleton
The raw green leaves of Enhydra ﬂuctuant were collected, and the
extra impurities, that were adhered to the composed leaves, were
removed by washing them in double distilled water. After that, the
leaves were chopped into little slices and dried in the sun for a week.
The dried raw green leaves were crushed in a high-speed mixing-grin-
der to produce dust from the leaves. Before the materials were car-
bonized in the subsequent procedures, the as-produced dust was
activated by NH 4Cl and KOH. NH 4Cl and green leaves powder were
combined. First, a 1:1 stoichiometric mass ratio of ammonium chloride
and dust of green and raw leaves were mixed together in a mortar. The
mixture was then maintained in a drying oven under vacuum and pure
Argon (Ar) atmosphere at ∼80 °C for 24 h. Later, KOH was added to
the mixture in the stoichiometric mass ratio of 1:1 and thoroughly
mixed to create a homogenous mixture. The mixture was then main-
tained in the vacuum oven under the same conditions. The pre-acti-
vated leaves were carbonized at various temperatures; 800, 900, and
1000 °C in a continuous Ar gas ﬂow applying a constant heating tem-
perature rate of 5 °C/min; they were then held at the annealing tem-
perature for two hours. Later, under a continuous Ar gas ﬂow, the
product was left cooling naturally to reach room-temperature. To get
rid of any unreacted components, the resulting ingredients were
washed for numerous periods applying 10% HCl and distilled water.
After that, distilled water was used to wash away the black substance
in order to neutralize it. The produced sample was ultimately desic-
cated in a desiccator. Also known as H-PC EF-800, EF-900, and EF-
1000, these synthetic HAPC materials are carbonized at 800, 900,
and 1000 °C, respectively. Supplementary Materials contain the mate-
rial characterization and other electrochemical measurements.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Formation of HAPC materials from Enhydra ﬂuctuant leaves
Different chemical components can be found in the raw, green
leaves of E. Fluctuant . It has various medicinal properties. It is a plant
with great therapeutic potential and numerous positive properties,
including anticancer, antioxidant, and antidiabetic, antibacterial,
anti-diarrheal. The existence of phytochemicals such as ﬂavonoids,
alkaloids, phenol, tannins, saponins, and carbohydrates can be cred-
ited to these activities [29,30]. Raw green leaves include a variety of
nutrients, including pectin, crude ﬁber, carotenoids, moisture, fat,
and polyphenols [29,30]. In the synthesis, carbohydrates are the main
source of carbon precursors.

Biomass-derived activated carbon from Cyperus pangorei for high-performance 
supercapacitor electrodes  
N. Maheswari1* & S. Nandhini2 
1Shree Ramchandra College of Engineering, Lonikand, Pune-412216, Maharashtra, India 
2Department of Physics, M. V. Muthiah Government Arts College for Women, Dindigul-624001, Tamil Nadu, India 
*E-mail: nmahi.phys@gmail.com 
Received 30 June 2026; accepted 15 July 2026 
Activated carbon was successfully prepared from Cyperus pangorei  through a simple and cost-effective thermal 
decomposition method using ghee as a ca rbonization aid. The obtained carbon was annealed at 500 °C for 3 h and 
characterized by scanning electron microscopy  and Fourier transform infrared spec troscopy (FTIR). SEM analysis revealed 
aggregated carbon particles, while FTIR confirmed the pr esence of oxygen-containing surface functional groups. The 
electrochemical performance of the prep ared carbon electrode was evaluated usi ng cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic 
charge-discharge, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and cycling stability studies using PVA / Na 2SO4 gel electrolyte 
within a potential window of 0–1.5 V. The electrode  exhibited a maximum specific capacitance of 476 F g -1 and maintained 
excellent capacitive behaviour even at a high current density of 25 A g -1. The enhanced electrochemical performance is 
attributed to the combined contribution of electric double- layer capacitance and surface redox activity associated with 
oxygen-containing functional groups. The results demonstrate that Cyperus pangorei-derived carbon is a promising low-cost 
and sustainable electrode material for supercapacitor applications. 
Keywords: Activated carbon, Biomass carbon, Cyperus pangorei, Energy storage, Electrochemical performance, Supercapacitor  
Introduction 
The growing demand for sustainable energy storage 
systems has stimulated extensive research on advanced 
electrochemical energy storage devices. Supercapacitors, 
batteries, and conventional capacitors are widely used in 
energy storage technologies based on electrochemical 
energy conversion processes 1-3. Among them, 
supercapacitors have attracted significant attention 
owing to their high power density, rapid charge-
discharge capability, long cycle life, operational safety, 
and environmental friendliness 4. These characteristics 
make them suitable for applications in consumer 
electronics, backup power systems, electric vehicles and 
renewable energy storage. 
The performance of supercapacitors is strongly 
influenced by the nature of  the electrode material. 
Various electrode materials, including activated 
carbons, carbon aerogels, carbon nanotubes, graphene-
based materials, conducti ng polymers and transition 
metal oxides, have been investigated for supercapacitor 
applications. Recently, bi omass-derived activated 
carbons have attracted c onsiderable attention as 
sustainable electrode materials for high-performance 
supercapacitors owing to their low cost, renewability, 
tunable pore structure and e nvironmental friendliness. 
Recent reviews have highlighted the significant 
progress achieved in the synthesis, activation strategies, 
and electrochemical performance of biomass-derived 
carbon materials for energy storage applications
5-6.. 
Activated carbons are among the most widely used 
electrode materials because of their high specific 
surface area, excellent electrical conductivity, chemical 
stability and low cost
7. Activated carbons can be 
produced from a variety of carbon-rich precursors, 
particularly biomass wastes, which offer the advantages 
of abundance, renewability, and environmental 
sustainability
8. Numerous biomass sources such as 
palm-tree cobs, plum kernels, cassava peel, sugarcane 
bagasse, rice husks, olive stones, date pits, fruit stones 
and nutshells have been successfully utilized for the 
preparation of activated carbons
9. 
Cyperus pangorei commonly known as korai grass, 
is an abundant lignocellulosic biomass containing 
holocellulose, cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, waxes, 
and moisture
10. Owing to its high carbon content and 
widespread availability, it represents a promising 
precursor for the preparati on of activated carbon. It 
contains cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, which are 
known to produce a high carbon yield upon thermal 
decomposition. In addition, the fibrous structure of 
INDIAN J CHEM TECHNOL, JULY 2026 
 
 
516
Cyperus pangorei facilitates the formation of porous 
carbon during carbonization, providing a large number 
of electroactive sites for electrolyte-ion adsorption. The 
utilization of this agricultural biomass not only reduces 
waste disposal problems but also offers a sustainable 
and environmentally friendly route for the production 
of low-cost carbon electrode materials for supercapacitor 
applications. The development of porosity in activated 
carbons can be achieved through physical activation 
using oxidizing gases such as steam or carbon dioxide or 
through chemical activation employing activating agents 
such as phosphoric acid and zinc chloride
11. 
In the present work, biomass derived carbon was 
prepared from Cyperus pangorei  through a simple 
thermal decomposition process using ghee as a 
carbonization aid. To the b est of our knowledge, the 
electrochemical performance of carbon derived from 
Cyperus pangorei using a simple thermal decomposition 
route with ghee-assisted car bonization has not been 
systematically investig ated for supercapacitor 
applications. Various biomass precursors, including 
agricultural wastes, lignocellulosic materials and plant-
derived residues have been explored to prepare porous 
carbons with high surface area and abundant functional 
groups, which enhance electrolyte ion accessibility and 
charge storage capability. However, challenges such as 
controlling pore structure, improving electrical 
conductivity and developing simple eco-friendly 
synthesis strategies still limit their practical applications. 
Therefore the exploration of novel biomass resources 
and sustainable processing routes remains essential for 
designing high-performance carbon electrodes. 
The present work demonstrates an inexpensive and 
sustainable approach for converting an abundantly 
available natural biomass into a high-performance 
carbon electrode material. The structural and 
morphological characteristics of the prepared carbon 
were investigated using Fourier transform infrared 
spectroscopy (FTIR) and scanning electron microscopy 
(SEM). The electrochemical performance was evaluated 
using cyclic voltammetry, galvanostatic charge-
discharge, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and 
cycling stability measurements in PVA / Na
2SO4 semi-
gel polymer electrolyte. This study highlights the 
potential of an unexplored biomass precursor for 
developing cost-effective and environmentally friendly 
supercapacitor electrodes. 
 
Experimental Section 
Biomass derived carbon was prepared from Cyperus 
pangorei through a thermal decomposition method. 
Fresh Cyperus pangorei  was collected from nearby 
agricultural fields and dried using a solar dryer to 
remove moisture. The dried biomass was 
subsequently carbonized in a quartz crucible under 
atmospheric conditions. During the carbonization 
process, a small quantity of ghee was added as a 
carbonization aid to facilitate uniform combustion and 
enhance the carbon yield. The resulting carbonaceous 
material was collected and annealed at 500 ºC for 3 h. 
The annealing treatment promoted the development 
of porosity through the selective removal of volatile 
and reactive carbonaceous species, leading to the 
formation of carbon with an enhanced porous 
structure. The obtained carbon powder was then 
ground thoroughly and used for structural, 
morphological and electrochemical characterization. 
FTIR spectra of the prepared carbon were recorded 
using a PerkinElmer Spectrum BX II spectrometer in 
the wave number range of 400–4000 cm ⁻¹ to identify 
the surface functional groups present in the material. 
The surface morphology of the carbon was examined 
using a TESCAN VEGA-3 LMU scanning electron 
microscope. 
Electrochemical measurements were carried out 
using a conventional three-electrode system (Fig. S1). 
The working electrode was prepared by mixing the 
carbon material, carbon black and polytetra-
fluoroethylene (PTFE) binder in a weight ratio of 
80:15:5. Ethanol was added to obtain homogeneous 
slurry, which was uniformly coated onto a graphite 
sheet (1 cm × 1 cm) and dr ied at 70 °C for 12 h. The 
mass loading of the active material was approximately 
1 mg. 
The prepared electrode served as the working 
electrode, while a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) and 
a platinum wire were used as the reference and counter 
electrodes respectively. Po ly vinyl alcohol (PVA) 
containing 1 g Na
2SO4 was employed as the gel 
electrolyte. Electrochemical performance was evaluated 
using a CHI660D electrochemical workstation. A PVA / 
Na2SO4 gel electrolyte was employed to provide ionic 
conduction between the working, reference and counter 
electrodes. Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic 
charge-discharge (GCD), electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy (EIS) and cycling stability measurements 
were performed to investigate the capacitive behaviour 
of the prepared carbon elec trode. The el ectrochemical 
measurements were carried out in the potential range of 
0–1.5 V. This potential window was selected based on 
preliminary experiments, which showed stable

Supercapacitors with super high power density, speedy charge-

Biomass Porous Carbon Derived from Celery Leaves with
High Capacitance for Supercapacitor
Jiaqi Wu, Zihan Ma, Guangning Wang,* and Tingting Chen*
[a]
To develop environmentally friendly and high-performance
supercapacitors, the low-cost, high-capacitance renewable
electrode material is at present viewed as one of the most
challenging tasks for obtaining the next-generation of energy
storage devices. Therefore, in this study, Celery leaves, a
common biomass vegetable, are used to prepare activated
carbon for high voltage and high-capacity supercapacitors
through a simple method. Due to their high surface area and
abundant nitrogen and sulfur heteroatoms, hierarchically
porous carbon materials can simultaneously realize high
capacity and long-cycling durability. The specific capacitance
has been recorded to be up to 753.0 F g
� 1
at 0.5 A g
� 1
with
capacity retention as high as 96.7 % even after 5,000 cycles.
Also, the assembled symmetric cell provided a high energy
density of 17.36 Wh kg
� 1
at 250 W kg
� 1
. The effects of yellow
and green colors and different activation temperatures on the
properties of electrode materials were systematically studied.
The results showed an excellent electrochemical performance
in biomass carbon electrode materials, which would facilitate
the development of a high-quality energy system and a green
supercapacitor.
Introduction
With the worsening of the environment and depletion of
resources, the human society is in crisis. Therefore, there is a
critical need to develop high energy conversion efficiency
storage devices. Supercapacitors (SCs) have attracted attention
because of the merits of large power density, good cycling
stability, fast charging, and discharging.
[1]
Thus, the super-
capacitor is being used in various ways for electronics as well
as electric vehicles with hybrid drive and pulse technology.
[2]
However, the SCs have low energy density, which limits the
range of the original application. Generally, it is proportional to
the supercapacitor’s energy density with capacitance and
voltage window.
[3]
The potential window can be increased by
assembling an asymmetric supercapacitor. Although high
capacitance electrode materials have been widely used in the
positive electrode of the asymmetric supercapacitor, it is
difficult to obtain negative electrodes that have high capaci-
tance. Generally, carbon materials with large negative potential
windows are used as negative electrode.
[4]
Carbon materials,
such as, graphene, carbon nanotubes, porous carbon, etc. are
versatile. They are not only non-toxic, chemically stable, and
readily conduct electricity, but also have peculiar properties
can accelerate electrolyte ions diffusion.
[5]
However, the low
capacitance of traditional carbon materials reduces the energy
density of SCs. Finding a negative electrode with high
capacitance remains a challenge, which limits the development
of SCs. Specifically, increasing the specific surface areas (SSA)
can improve the capacitance and rate performance by adjust-
ing the pore distribution of carbon.
[6]
The wettability can be
increased by doping heteroatoms on the carbon surface, and
the electrolyte-accessible areas can be enlarged.
[7]
However,
these electrode materials are usually prepared using expensive
and unsustainable raw materials.
[8]
Given all these require-
ments, biomass is seen as a high-efficiency carbon precursor
because of its economical and continuable potential. Using
special processes, well-distributed pore size and physicochem-
ical stability were exhibited in some biomass-derived carbons.
[9]
They have the advantages of large potential windows, stable
physicochemical properties, easy synthesis, and are often used
as a positive pole in asymmetric SCs.
[10]
Additionally, biochar
raw materials tend to contain a mass of oxygen-containing
functional groups, such as C � O, C = O, and carboxyl groups,
improving their performance over traditional carbon
materials.
[11]
For example, Wu et al. used albizia flowers to
prepare hierarchical porous carbon microrods for SCs. The
specific capacitance (Cs) reached 406 F g
� 1
at a current density
of 0.5 A g
� 1
in a 6 M KOH electrolyte.
[12]
It could improve
capacitance performance and energy storage in SCs by
selecting suitable biomass precursors and catalysts. Regarding
SCs, biomass is a promising electrode material. However, there
are still many factors preventing its further use: finiteness of
geographical distribution, production, and transportation.
[13]
Celery, which is widely planted in China, naturally has several
elements that can be doped, and people always eat celery
stalks but discard celery leaves as garbage. Celery stem had
been used to prepare porous carbon in supercapacitors with
good charge storage capacity, but unfortunately it was
prepared by expensive freeze-drying and the SSA was only
507.73 m

.
[14]
Celery stem is usually eaten and celery leaves
are wasted, and celery leaves and celery stems have different

Therefore, a quick absent template method was developed
to efficiently synthesize porous carbon by carbonizing celery

the effects of activator and carbonization temperature on the
formation of biomass carbon pores were investigated. Also, the
impact of yellow leaves and green leaves on the electro-
chemical performance of SCs was investigated in detail.

Materials characterization. Scanning electron microscopy
(SEM) was used to study the morphology of celery-derived

[15]
Therefore, suitable temperature and activator
