Potassium gluconate‑assisted synthesis of biomass derived porous 
carbon for high‑performance supercapacitor
Yu Feng1 · Ge Li1 · Xiaoliang Wu1 
Published online: 20 June 2023 
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2023
Abstract
Porous carbon has attracted enormous attentions as electrode materials for supercapacitor due to its sufficient porosity and 
large specific surface area. In this paper, we reported a convenient approach for the preparation of activated porous carbon 
(APC) by one-step activation method using bacterial cellulose as carbon source and potassium gluconate as activator. The 
obtained porous carbon possesses a unique porous framework with suitable specific surface area and rich oxygen content. 
Benefiting from the unique structure, the obtained electrode shows a high specific capacitance of 437 F  g−1  at 0.5 A  g−1  
and excellent electrochemical stability. More interestingly, the constructed APC-700//APC-700 symmetrical supercapacitor 
exhibits a high energy density of 23.5 Wh  kg−1  and good cycling stability in 1 M  Na2SO4 aqueous electrolyte. Therefore, the 
work provides a new and facile method to prepare porous carbon-based electrode materials from biomass for supercapacitor.
Keywords Bacteria cellulose · Potassium gluconate · Hierarchical porous carbon · Supercapacitor
1 Introduction
Along with the fast increasing of portable electronic devices 
and new energy vehicles, high-efficiency energy storage 
devices have become a promising choice. Among current 
energy storage equipment, supercapacitors have gained 
extensive research as a result of their high power density, 
fast charging and discharging rate and good electrochemical 
stability [1 –5]. Porous carbon with excellent conductivity 
and high specific surface area are often the first choice for 
commercialized electrode materials [6 –9]. But traditional 
porous carbon materials are often derived from non-renew-
able fossil energy. In recent years, for the sustainable devel-
opment, biomass porous carbon materials, which have the 
advantages of wide source, green and low cost as a suitable 
alternative material are widely used in electrode materials, 
such as eggshell [10], plant straw [11], poplar catkins [12] 
and various pollens [13].
Bacterial celluloses (BCs), a porous network nanoscale 
biopolymer synthesized by microbial fermentation, can be 
efficiently produced by metabolism of acetic acid bacteria 
[14]. In addition, bacterial cellulose has a natural porous net-
work nanostructure. This network porous structure ensures 
high specific surface area and low electron transport resist-
ance of carbon electrode materials [15–18]. Recently, bacte-
rial cellulose-derived electrode materials have been studied 
by researchers. Such as, Wang et al. prepared a new type of 
flexible electrode by using bacterial cellulose as a biologi-
cal template with KOH as activator. The prepared electrode 
exhibits a specific capacitance of 241.8 F  g−1  [19]. Pei et al. 
synthesized nanobelt-carbonized bacterial cellulose nano-
composite by activating bacterial cellulose with  V2O5. The 
prepared electrodes display a specific capacitance of 281 
F  g−1  at 0.25 A  g−1  [20]. However, the traditional way to 
activate bacterial cellulose is mainly through alkaline acti-
vators. This method is mainly activated by external etching 
under high temperature conditions. Therefore, the obtained 
carbon materials often have uneven pore distribution in the 
microstructure and poor connectivity between pores, further 
restricting the electrochemical property of the materials. The 
obtained electrode has a specific capacitance usually low 
300 F  g−1 , which is far from meeting the needs of practi-
cal applications. Accordingly, it is worth looking forward 
to exploring an efficient, convenient and economical way 
to prepare high performance bacterial cellulose electrode 
materials.

 wuxiaoliang90@163.com
1 College of Chemistry, Chemical Engineering and Resource 
Utilization, Northeast Forestry University, 26 Hexing Road, 
Harbin 150040, People’s Republic of China
2114 Journal of Porous Materials (2023) 30:2113–2120
1 3
Herein, we  developed a convenient method for the 
preparation of porous carbon by one-step activation method 
using bacterial cellulose as carbon source and potassium 
gluconate as activator. The optimized electrode possesses 
a distinct hierarchical porous structure with suitable spe -
cific surface area and rich oxygen content. Benefiting from 
the unique structure, the obtained electrode exhibits high 
specific capacitance and excellent electrochemical stabil-
ity. More interestingly, the constructed APC-700//APC-700 
symmetrical supercapacitor exhibits high energy density and 
good cycling stability.
2  Experimental sections
2.1  Synthesis of the porous carbon
The bacterial cellulose was added into distilled water and 
stirred for 24 h, followed by freezing and evacuating in the 
vacuum freeze dryer. After drying, 1 g bacterial cellulose 
were added into 0.5 mol  L−1  potassium gluconate solution 
and stirred magnetically for 12 h. The obtained product was 
filtered and freeze-dried. The dried product was pyrolyzed 
at 600 °C, 700 °C and 800 °C for 2 h with a heating rate 
of 5 °C   min−1  in  N2 atmosphere, respectively. Then, the 
obtained product was dried after washed with 2 M HCl for 
12 h and deionized water. Then, the samples were named 
as APC-x (which x represents the activation temperature). 
For comparison, the bacterial cellulose was directly carbon-
ized at 700 °C in  N2 for 2 h, and the obtained sample was 
recorded as PC.
Characterization ways and electrochemical characteriza-
tion were recorded in supporting information.
3  Results and discussions
Scheme  1 illustrates the synthetic route of APC-x. The dried 
BC was soaked in 0.5 mol  L−1  potassium gluconate solu-
tion, and activated at high temperature after freeze drying. 
After removing impurities with dilute HCl, the hierarchical 
porous framework was formed. The microstructures of the 
obtained materials were explored by scanning/transmission 
electron microscopy (SEM/TEM). As seen in Fig. S1a, the 
materials from the direct carbonization of bacterial cel -
lulose (PC-700) shows a big block-like structure without 
obvious pore structure. After introducing potassium gluco-
nate as activator, the SEM images of the APC-700 materi-
als (Fig.  1a, b) reveal a three-dimensional interconnected 
hierarchical porous structure compose of rich micrometer 
sized macropores between carbon skeleton, which can as 
ion-buffering regions to shorten the diffusion distance of 
ions. As reported in the literature [21], potassium gluconate 
is used as an activator, when the temperature is below 500, 
it is mainly the decomposition of organic matter. when the 
temperature is above 600, the generated potassium carbon-
ate will enhance its activation ability with the increase of 
temperature, further generating potassium oxide and carbon 
dioxide, further enlarging the pore structure. In addition, as 
shown in Fig.  1c, d, TEM further confirms that the APC-
700 samples possess the three-dimensional interconnected 
porous structure with massive macropores. The APC-600 
(Fig. S1b) and APC-800 samples (Fig. S1c) possess the 
similar three-dimensional interconnected porous structure 
with APC-700. Furthermore, as shown in Fig. S2b, c, the 
corresponding elements mapping images regarding SEM 
show that the samples are composed of C and O elements.
The crystal structure of the obtained carbon materials 
was explored through X-ray diffraction (XRD). As seen 
in Fig.  2a, all materials have a weak peak at 43.5° and a 
broad peak at 23.6°, representing the 002 and 101 crystal 
planes of carbon, respectively [22, 23]. As the temperature 
increases, the (002) crystal plane reflection intensity of the 
samples gradually decreases, indicating that the degree of 
graphitization reduces gradually and the increase of tem-
perature causes more amorphous and disordered structures 
in the carbon samples [ 24]. The element compositions of 
the obtained samples were tested by X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy (XPS). As shown in Fig.  2b, it is obviously 
evident that all the APC samples are composed of C and O 
elements. As the temperature increases, the oxygen content 
decreases from 13.84 at% (APC-600) to 11.24 at% (APC-
700) and finally to 8.86% (APC-800). The C 1 s spectra of 
APC-700 (Fig.  2c) consists of four different peaks centering

Abstract
Background: Porous carbon electrode (PCE) is identi ﬁed as a highly suitable electrode material for commercial application due
to its production process, which is characterized by simplicity, cost-effectiveness and environmental friendliness. PCE was syn-
thesized using torch ginger (Etlingera elatior (Jack) R.M. Smith) leaves as the base material. The leaves were treated with differ-
ent concentrations of ZnCl
2, resulting in a supercapacitor cell electrode with unique honeycomb-like three-dimensional
(3D) morphological pore structure. This PCE comprises nano ﬁbers from lignin content and volatile compounds from aromatic
biomass waste.
Results: From the characterization of physical properties, PCE-0.3 had an impressive amorphous porosity, wettability and 3D
honeycomb-like structural morphology with a pore framework consisting of micropores and mesopores. According to the struc-
tural advantages of 3D hierarchical pores such as interconnected honeycombs, PCE-0.3 as supercapacitor electrode had a high
speciﬁc capacitance of up to 285.89 F g −1 at 1 A. Furthermore, the supercapacitor exhibited high energy and power density of
21.54 Wh kg −1 and 161.13 W kg −1, respectively, with a low internal resistance of 0.059 Ω.
Conclusion: The results indicated that 3D porous carbon materials such as interconnected honeycombs derived from the aro-
matic biomass of torch ginger leaves have signi ﬁcant potential for the development of sustainable energy storage devices.

INTRODUCTION
The recent attention paid to the continuous improvement of
supercapacitors as electrical energy storage devices, in terms
of electrodes and electrolytes, is because of their advanced perfor-
mance with superior energy and power capacities compared to con-
ventional capacitors and batteries.
1 Some of these innovations
include graphene, 2 graphene oxide, 3 activated carbon/porous
carbon,3 carbon aerogel,4 conductive polymer5 and metal oxide.6
Activated carbon materials with unique geometries such as
nanoﬁbers,
7 nanotubes,8 nanoballs,9 nanosheets10 and nano-3D11
have become of interest due to their thermal stability and electro-
chemical conductivity.12,13 Three-dimensional (3D) activated carbon
materials with connected hierarchical pores have shown great
potential because of their superior microstructure with adjustable
porosity and excellent electrochemical performance.12,14 The pro-
duction of activated carbon with a 3D pore structure has been car-
ried out through simple, uncomp licated and time-consuming
approaches, including carbonization, chemical activation and phys-
ical activation.
15
Previous studies have demonstrated that 3D hierarchically inter-
connected porous activated carbon rich in micropores can be pro-
duced from biomass waste materials using simple methods,
leading to improved electrochemical performance.
16,17 The
selection of biomass as the base material for supercapacitor elec-
trodes is driven by global concerns about creating sustainable
technologies.
18 This is due to its abundant presence, natural
microporous structure and environmental friendliness as an elec-
trical energy storage device.
19 Aromatic biomass with a distinctive
odor, resulting from its lignin content and volatile compounds,
composed of abundant aromatic structures has become the focus
of attention in this ﬁeld.20 For example, Cao et al.21 used a popular

7411

sawdust waste with abundant aromatic structures to produce a
3D carbon skeleton with improved porosity and speci ﬁc capaci-
tance. Taer et al .22 also considered using citronella leaves as an
aromatic biomass-based carbon precursor to produce a 3D inter-
connected porous carbon with high electrochemical performance
through a one-step integrated pyrolysis process (physical
carbonization–activation) with ZnCl
2 impregnation.
The study reported here focused on using aromatic biomass
waste, obtained from agricultural residues rich in lignin, cellulose,
hemicellulose and volatile elements, as the base material for pro-
ducing porous carbon for supercapacitor electrodes. Torch ginger
leaves were selected as an example of potential agricultural waste
for this purpose. In a previous report, torch ginger plant parts,
namely ﬂowers, rhizomes, leaves, bark, stems and roots, were
optimized as natural antioxidants and antibacterial agents.
23-26
However, the use of torch ginger leaf wastes as a material for mak-
ing porous carbon, especially for electrodes in supercapacitor cell
components, is still in its early stages. 27,28 Torch leaves have a
characteristic dark-green color and are 80 cm × 18 cm. They are
a good source of carbon-producing nanocellulose 29 and the con-
version into 3D porous activated carbon is simple and uncompli-
cated. The process involves continuous carbonization and
physical activation to produce activated carbon with a
honeycomb-like hierarchical pore structure rich in interconnected
micropores.
The activated carbon was produced from aromatic biomass
waste from renewable torch ginger leaves, using a simple and
harmless one-stage integrated pyrolysis process (carbonization –
physical activation). The 3D porous honeycomb structure was
obtained based on different activator concentrations. Chemical
activation was done using ZnCl
2 with low concentrations (0.1,
0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 mol L −1) mixed with torch ginger leaf carbon
through a chemical activation process, which contributed to con-
trolling the formation of pore structures. In this process, no com-
plicated and very tedious template methods were required to
produce interconnected pore microstructures. The increase in
speciﬁc capacitance and energy and power densities of the
obtained porous carbon electrode (PCE) was also supported by
the attractive features of the hierarchical pore system. This
included good amorphous properties, high wettability and provi-
sion of active sites between the electrode and suitable electrolyte
during the electrochemical process. The selection of the precursor
of the aromatic biomass of torch ginger leaves as a material for
making carbon electrodes was a very suitable and promising
strategy for sustainable, renewable, environmentally friendly
and cost-effective energy storage devices.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Basic materials
An amount of 5 kg of torch ginger harvest waste in the form of old
leaves was collected from community plantations in Pekanbaru,
Riau. The green-brown leaves with a distinctive aroma were cut
to <5 cm to make processing easier. Subsequently, the samples
were dried in the sun and an oven for 5 days to dehydrate them.
Additional materials
The torch ginger leaf waste was treated to create a porous carbon
base material for supercapacitor electrodes using ZnCl
2 impreg-
nation at different concentrations of 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 mol L−1M
as an activating agent. A total of 1 mol L −1 H2SO4 was used as a
source of electrically charged ions to ﬁll the carbon pores. The
acidity level of the samples was measured using pH indicator
strips. These three materials were purchased from Merck KgaA,
Germany. Chemical activation and sample neutralization were
carried out by adding distilled water as an activator solvent and
sample puriﬁcation.
Electrode manufacturing
The dried torch ginger leaves were pre-carbonized by heating at a
temperature of 250 °C for 2.5 h to brittleness and producing char-
coal. Subsequently, the carbon was ground to a particle size of
<60 μm using mortar and ball milling. The samples were chemi-
cally activated with ZnCl
2 at concentrations of 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 and
0.7 mol L −1 using a Thermo Scienti ﬁc hot plate stirrer at 80 °C
and 300 rpm rotation. This process was begun by dissolving the
ZnCl
2 activator with distilled water for 1 h, followed by mixing
30 g of carbon and stirring for 2 h. The carbon of activated torch
ginger leaves was heated in an oven for 2 days to rehydrate the
remaining water content during chemical activation. The samples
were printed into coins with a solid texture and not brittle using a
hydraulic press at a pressure of eight tons with a holding time of
2 min. A unique honeycomb-like 3D hierarchical pore structure
rich in interconnected micropores was generated through one-
stage integrated pyrolysis, namely carbonization and physical
activation using a Payuntech furnace. Carbonization was carried
out from room temperature to 600 °C under the in ﬂuence of
nitrogen gas to vaporize elements other than carbon in the sam-
ple. This was followed by physical activation up to a temperature
of 850 °C under the in ﬂuence of carbon dioxide gas to open the
pore structure of the carbon. Finally, each sample was neutralized
(pH = 7) using distilled water with a scale-washing technique to
characterize its physical and chemical properties. Figure
1 shows
a schematic of the preparation of supercapacitor PCEs based on
torch ginger leaf aromatic biomass with high potential for further
development.
Physical characterization
The basic physical properties of PCEs based on torch ginger leaves

. The study aimed to assess the potential of these biochar-based

1. Introduction 
Energy consumption worldwide has been steadily increasing, with 
levels reaching 575 quadrillion (BTU) in 2015 and projected to reach 
736 quadrillion BTU by 2040. But unfortunately, current energy re -
sources are insufficient to meet this demand and may result in signifi -
cant energy crises due to issues such as non-renewable nature of natural 
resources, environmental effects, and higher energy requirements [1,2] . 
It is imperative and pressing to prioritize the development of energy 
solutions that are efficient, inexpensive, simple to produce, and eco- 
friendly, including energy storage devices such as fuel cells, batteries, 
capacitors, and supercapacitors [3 – 6] . 
Amongst the energy storage devices, supercapacitors have several 
exceptional characteristics. These are fast charging and discharging, 
long and stable cycles, superior power and energy density that distin -
guish them from others. Due to these features, supercapacitors are seen 
as a complementary storage device to capacitors, fuel cells, and con -
ventional rechargeable batteries. The excellent performance of 
supercapacitors makes them useful in many applications, such as 
portable and consumer electronics, transportation, aerospace, and sen -
sors [7 – 9] . 
Based on energy storage mechanism, supercapacitors are categorized 
into two types which are electrical double layer capacitors (EDLCs) and 
pseudo-capacitors [10] . The performance of supercapacitors is highly 
influenced by the properties of the active electrode materials [11] . 
Carbon-nanotubes (CNTs), carbon-nanofibers (CNFs) and biomass 
derived graphene like carbon are some promising active materials for 
electrode that can be employed for electrical double layer capacitors 
(EDLCs). In contrast, pseudo-capacitive behavior mainly relies on 
carbon-based materials like metal oxides, metal hydroxides and con -
ducting polymers. Due to these material redox reactions occur during 
the charging and discharging processes [12 – 17] . 
Various carbon enriched materials are being used for energy storage 
in supercapacitor applications. Conventionally biomass derived gra -
phene like materials owe the characteristics like high conductive nature, 
high surface area and mechanical flexibility [18,19] . However, the

Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) are known for their structural flexi -

However, when LDHs aggregate, it can result in reduced energy density 
and diminished cycle stability. 
Amongst the carbon-based materials ACs are the most widely used 
materials for energy storage in supercapacitor applications for a long 
time. Owing to the characteristics like abundant availability, renew -
ability, large specific surface area, stable electrochemical performance, 
eco-friendliness ACs are in high demand due to their ability to provide 
outstanding electrochemical efficiency [23,24] . Utilizing the natural 
structure of biomass, which offers a continuous, interconnected, and 
hierarchical arrangement, has become increasingly popular in recent 
years. Previously mollusk shell was used to produce microporous carbon 
having honeycomb like structure through a cheap and environment 
friendly process. Inherited and interconnected hexagonal channels of 
these shells provide a promising electric conductivity to enhance elec -
tron diffusion and efficient electrolyte penetration. Owing to these 
properties it has a significant potential for improving capacitive per -
formance [25] . Due renewable nature of biomass, it can be converted 
into many useful products like bio oil, gases and biochar via different 
thermochemical conversion techniques like torrefaction [26] , pyrolysis, 
gasification and hydrothermal conversion [27] . When produced under 
controlled and optimal conditions, biochar generated via pyrolysis can 
result in high-quality material in different fields. According to studies to 
produce biochar some methods are used, the torrefaction process yields 
the highest percentage of biochar, exceeding 35%, pyrolysis up to 34% 
and gasification with approximate percentage of 10%, respectively [28] . 
This bio-char based material produced via pyrolysis can be modified by 
various surface modification techniques which are discussed in detail in 
[29] . These surface modified biochar based materials produced from 
biomass feedstocks can be utilized in variety of ways for potential 
application [30,31] . 
.Researchers are trying to produce activated carbon (AC) from 
different lignocellulosic biomasses including sugarcane bagasse, rice 
husk, bamboo, walnut shell, coconut shell, empty banana fruit bunch 
[32] . Potential of biomass for bioenergy prospective has been elaborated 
in a previous study which provides a comprehensive knowledge of 
biomass utilization for value added products [33] . 
The production of activated carbon involves using different carbon- 
rich sources as precursors, including but not limited to woody and 
nonwoody, coal, and petroleum pitch [34] . ACs can be produced by a 
two-stage process. Formerly, the carbon-rich material undergoes low- 
temperature carbonization, and in the second stage, it undergoes acti -
vation at a higher temperature. Activated carbon can be created using 
physical or chemical activation methods. Surface modification by a 
physical activation method uses steam, air, or oxygen at high tempera -
tures to activate biochar. In contrast, a surface modification via chemical 
activation technique involves the treatment of the biomass precursor 
feedstocks with an activating agent such as an acid, a base, or a salt in an 
inert atmosphere [35] . Various biomass waste materials, including 
fruits, husks, shells, vegetable waste, animal waste, and microorgan -
isms, have been utilized to produce activated carbon. These materials 
have been used in various applications related to energy and the envi -
ronment [36,37] . 
Many biomass feedstocks including shells, stalks, have been used to 
make ACs. The produced ACs have shown potential as electrode mate -

In Pakistan, after citrus and mango, Date Palm is third most impor -

mt/year. Pakistan is the seventh highest producer and exporter of dates 
in the world [44] . Waste being generated from date agro industry and 
date processing industry include immature date fruit fell from tree, (DS), 
spoiled dates, lost dates and date press cake [45] . This waste can cause a 
serious environmental burden as well as the loss of raw materials. DS is a 
rich source of carbon and also containing cellulose and lignin content

ash content DS were selected as a precursor for biochar (BC) production. 
The novelty of this research lies in the production of activated carbon

ABSTRACT  
Porous carbons possess considerable appeal and are in high demand as materials that can be produced from 
biomass waste. This study presents the transformation of Tectona grandis (Teak) sawdust into porous carbon 
materials, referred to as Tectona grandis sawdust-derived porous carbon (TPC), through a cost-effective FeCl
3
- 
assisted carbonization process, followed by a KOH activation. TPC samples were synthesized by carbonization at 
different temperatures (650 – 850 
◦
C) and characterized comprehensively. Structural analysis via X-Ray diffrac -
tion (XRD), Raman, and Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) revealed a progressive enhancement in 
graphitic structure and reduction of functional groups with increasing activation temperature. Field emission 
scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) displayed the development of intricate hollow tube-like porous networks 
in TPC-850, with the highest specific surface area (1767.66 m
2
/g) and pore volume (1.43 cm
3
/g). Electro -
chemical investigations showcased the superior performance of TPC-850 as a supercapacitor electrode due to its 
high graphitic nature, large surface area, and well-structured porosity. The galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD) 
measurements exhibited a high specific capacitance of 572 F/g at 0.5 A/g in a 6 M KOH electrolyte. The high- 
frequency semicircle and low-frequency steeper region in electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) further 
indicated reduced resistance and enhanced ion diffusion in TPC-850. Significantly, TPC-850 demonstrated 
remarkable electrochemical cyclic stability, retaining 95.83 % of its initial capacity even after undergoing 4500 
cycles at a scan rate of 500 mV/s. The findings underscore the viability of TPC-850 as a high-performance 
supercapacitor electrode material, providing insights into harnessing renewable resources for advanced energy 
solutions. This work highlights the potential of utilizing waste biomass for energy storage applications and 
demonstrates the feasibility of converting it into efficient porous carbon materials with substantial graphitization 
and porosity.   
1. Introduction 
Over the last few decades, the depletion of fossil fuels, environmental 
contamination, and the release of greenhouse gases has led to significant 
health risks and disruptions in ecosystems. As a response, researchers 
are increasingly investigating environmentally friendly and sustainable 
systems for energy storage and conversion [ 1 – 4 ]. Renewable energy 
sources are being integrated into the energy sector, aiming to mitigate 
environmental pollution by reducing reliance on traditional, fossil fuel- 
based power methods [ 5 – 7 ]. Hence, there has been a growing fascina -
tion with nanomaterials due to their electrochemical characteristics, 
cost-effectiveness, simplicity in production, extensive surface area, and 
improved electrical as well as magnetic behaviour [ 8 , 9 ]. In particular, 
porous activated carbons derived from organic waste have emerged as a 
significant and innovative concept. This is primarily attributed to their 
widespread applications in eco-friendly electrochemical sensors, fuel 
cells, solar cells, catalysis, and energy storage devices such as batteries 
and supercapacitors [ 10 – 13 ]. Furthermore, these carbon materials are 
cost-effective, environmentally friendly, easily accessible, possess high 
carbon content, exhibit excellent electrical conductivity, and showcase 
remarkable physicochemical properties [ 4 ]. Specifically, the distinctive 
crystal structure found in carbon materials derived from biomass plays a 
crucial role in facilitating the swift movement of electrolyte ions within 
electrodes. This characteristic renders them highly promising materials 
for use as electrodes in supercapacitors [ 14 ]. 
Numerous comprehensive studies ( Table 2 ) have showcased the 
viability of carbonaceous materials derived from biomass as a compet -
itive and advantageous resource for applications in supercapacitor

[ 15 ]. This interest arises from its remarkable attributes, such as high 
power density, enhanced operational safety, and extended cycle life -
span, which have led to extensive research and exploration in this area 
[ 16 ]. Out of all the carbonaceous materials derived from biowaste, 
activated carbon produced from a lignocellulosic source stands out as 
the preferred choice. This is due to its expansive specific surface area, 
adjustable pore structure, notable chemical stability, and favourable 
electrical conductivity [ 17 , 18 ]. However, there is a need to further 
investigate readily available biomass sources, and there is still signifi -
cant potential for enhancing the preparation strategies. Simultaneously, 
a comprehensive understanding of the origins and mechanisms under -
lying this activity remains to be seen. Therefore, further efforts are 
required to develop straightforward techniques that utilize cost-effective 
biomass precursors. This will result in the creation of durable electrode 
materials suitable for energy-related applications [ 19 ]. 
The production of biomass-derived carbon through the conventional 
method of direct pyrolysis involves three main stages. Initially, at tem -
peratures below 100 
◦
C, rapid weight reduction occurs, which can be 
attributed to water evaporation. Subsequently, within the temperature 
range of 315 
◦
C to 400 
◦
C, a significant amount of gases is generated, 
concurrent with the development of the fundamental carbon frame -
work. As the temperature continues to rise, the organic components 
within biomass cells undergo transformation, leading to the creation of 
conjugated carbon atoms and forming a char structure [ 19 , 20 ]. 
Furthermore, the creation of carbon with sp
2 
hybridization and the 
generation of gases during this process can contribute to enhancing 
conductivity and the development of a porous framework [ 21 ]. These 
effects can be advantageous for utilizing these materials in electro -
chemical applications. Nevertheless, the direct carbonization/pyrolysis 
approach faces challenges in producing carbon materials with inherent 
porosity and a substantial surface area. Typically, activation processes 
are necessary for the products to acquire these desired characteristics 
[ 22 ]. In the process of preparing activated carbon, commonly employed 
activating agents include steam, CO
2
, ZnCl
2
, H
3
PO
4
, K
2
CO
3
, and KOH 
[ 23 , 24 ]. Among these options, KOH holds a distinct advantage. This is 
because its utilization induces more localized reactions with the pre -
cursor material, resulting in the creation of higher porosity in the 
resulting activated carbon [ 25 , 26 ]. 
In this report, we present a straightforward, inexpensive, and un -
complicated approach to creating porous carbon, referred to as TPC, 
using Teak sawdust as the starting biomass. This process involves 
treating the biomass with FeCl
3 
for carbonization, followed by KOH 
activation at varying temperatures. This treatment results in the for -
mation of high surface area porous carbons. Our study demonstrates that 
the TPC-850 variant displays remarkable porous and surface properties, 
high specific capacitance, excellent cyclic stability, and impressive 
performance when used in a 6.0 M KOH system. As a result, this un -
complicated technique holds significant promise for transforming 
organic waste into porous, graphitic carbon materials, with substantial 
potential for applications in sustainable and renewable energy 
technologies. 
2. Experimental methods 
2.1. Materials 
Potassium hydroxide pellets, ferric chloride, and hydrochloric acid 
were obtained from Loba Chemie. Absolute ethanol was sourced from 
Changshu Hongsheng Fine Chemicals. N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP) 
and poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) were acquired from Sigma- 
Aldrich, and TIMCAL C-NERGY SUPER C65 was purchased; all chem -

used throughout the experiments to prepare all the solutions. Tectona 
grandis (Teak) sawdust was collected from Beerangod, Honnavara,

producing Tectona grandis sawdust-derived porous carbon (TPC). 
2.2. Synthesis of TPC 
Tectona grandis sawdust was sun-dried for a week and ground into a 
powder. It was then thoroughly washed multiple times with ultrapure 
water, followed by ethanol, and subsequently dried in an oven before 
being pulverized. The carbonization of pulverized sawdust was done in 
the first step, followed by chemical activation in the second step. In the 
first step, pulverized sawdust was mixed in a 1:1 ratio with FeCl
3

C for about 24 – 48 h. Then it was carbonized in an argon gas

◦

◦

Abstract: The present work reports the synthesis of biomass derived activated carbon and its elec-
trochemical behaviour in different electrolytes. Ricinus communis shell (RCS) was used as a raw
material in this study for the synthesis of activated carbon (AC) following a high-temperature acti-
vation procedure using potassium hydroxide as the activating agent. The physical and structural
characterization of the prepared Ricinus communis shell-derived activated carbon (RCS-AC) was
carried by Brunauer-Emmett-Teller analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, Fourier Transform Infrared
Spectroscopy, Raman Spectroscopy and Scanning Electron Microscopy. The synthesized AC was elec-
trochemically characterized using various techniques such as Cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic
charge–discharge (GCD) tests, and Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements in
different aqueous electrolytes (KOH, H2SO4, and Na2SO4). The results show that the double layer
properties of the RCS-AC material in different electrolytes are distinct. In speciﬁc, the working elec-
trode tested in 3 M KOH showed excellent electrochemical performance. It demonstrated a speciﬁc
capacitance of 137 F g−1 (at 1 A g−1 in 3 M KOH) and exhibited high energy and power densities of
18.2 W hkg−1 and 663.4 W kg−1, respectively. The observed capacitance in 3 M KOH remains stable
with 97.2% even after 5000 continuous charge and discharge cycles, indicating long-term stability.
The study conﬁrmed that the synthesized RCS-derived activated carbon (RCS-AC) exhibits good
stability and physicochemical characteristics, making them commercially promising and appropriate
for energy storage applications.

1. Introduction
A huge amount of effort has been made in the recent years to develop renewable,
environmentally sustainable, affordable, and dependable energy systems. The gradual
deterioration of the atmosphere and the depletion of fossil resources have drawn the
attention of researchers and scientists towards the exploration of renewable energy [1–5].
There are two kinds of electrochemical devices: batteries and capacitors, both of which are
promising energy storage systems. Depending on the charge management mechanisms
used, all energy storage technologies have certain advantages and disadvantages. Batteries
have a low power density but a high energy density, whereas traditional capacitors have a
high-power density but a low energy density [6–8]. A supercapacitor (SC), also known as
an electrochemical capacitor, is an intermediary between the battery and the traditional
capacitor that provides signiﬁcant advantages such as enhanced strength and energy ﬂow,
high reliability, ﬂexible operating temperature, and environmental friendliness [9,10]. The
energy storage process in EDLCs depends on the efﬁcient electrostatic accumulation of
charges at the electrode-electrolyte interface and during this charge-storage procedure, there
Catalysts 2023, 13, 286. https://doi.org/10.3390/catal13020286 https://www.mdpi.com/journal/catalysts
Catalysts 2023, 13, 286 2 of 13
is no charge transfer. Fast redox processes involving charge transfer at the electrode and
electrolyte interfaces controls the amount of energy is stored in pseudocapacitors [11,12].
The development of numerous electrode materials for supercapacitors have been reported
in the literature which can be categorised as composite materials [13–17], carbon materials
derived from biomass [ 18], conductive polymers [ 19], and transition metal oxide [ 20].
Carbon materials from biomass are frequently used in these electrode materials because of
their low cost, nontoxicity, abundance of source, and long cycle life. The most frequently
reported electrode material is activated carbon derived from biomass [21,22], which has
been used in industrial capacitors.
Due to the wide range of electrochemical and physicochemical properties obtained
depending on the precursor and activation method used, activated carbon-based materials
are frequently used as electrodes [23]. Activated carbon prepared from various biomass
such as human hair [24], bean dregs [25], dead neem leaves [26], tobacco rods [27], corn-
stalk core [28], cassava peel [29], fungi [30], pine cone petal [31], silk [32], rice husk [33],
microalgae [34], sugar cane bagasse [35], eggshell [36] etc. has been previously reported
in literature. The high packing density, high surface area, higher porosity, and high
chemical and physical stability of these activated carbons are some of their common char-
acteristics [37]. The porous nature of AC materials is considered to be advantageous for
supercapcitor applications, with microporous materials having a greater impact on charge
transfer processes. The material’s surface area and the electrolyte’s stability are the main
factors responsible for the high capacitance values. Electrolyte is found to be one of the
most effective elements in supercapacitor performance. There are three categories of aque-
ous electrolytes commonly used: base, acidic, and neutral liquids. Aqueous electrolytes
outperform organic-based and ionic liquid electrolytes in terms of power density while
limiting energy density [38]. Electrochemical capacitors tested with aqueous electrolytes
provide additional advantages over other electrolyte systems, such as low cost, high-ionic
conductivity, safety, and environmental friendliness.
In neutral electrolytes, the working potential window extends above 1.2 V to 2.2 V
while it is restricted to 1.2 V in acidic and basic electrolytes [ 39]. The protonation or
deprotonation of the functional groups is what gives carbonaceous materials derived
from biomass their altered surface properties in aqueous electrolytes. Despite signiﬁcant
advancements, some obstacles still exist, including a low energy density and a small
potential window for aqueous based electrolytes.
The current work is focussed on the investigation of the effect of aqueous-based
electrolytes on the capacitance performance of carbonaceous material derived from biomass.
The capacitance of the material is inﬂuenced by the relationship between the average pore
size of the material and the effective size of the electrolyte ion. Ricinus communis shell
is used as a precursor to prepare the highly porous carbon by pre-carbonation followed
by KOH activation. The prepared carbon material has a better ionic conductivity and
a good speciﬁc surface area as the electrode material. It demonstrated good capacitive
performance when used as supercapacitor electrode materials in aqueous electrolytes,
such as 3 M KOH, 1 M H 2SO4, and 1 M Na 2SO4. The established relationship between
carbon electrode structures and electrolyte composition will help in understanding the
impact of carbonaceous electrodes derived from biomass on the storage properties of
symmetric supercapacitors.
2. Results and Discussion
The structural and phase of the prepared activated carbon was investigated by XRD
analysis (Figure 1a) and as observed from the ﬁgure, RCS-derived activated carbon (RCS-
AC) displays diffraction intensities, indicating the predominance of amorphous structures.
It is clear that there are sharp shifts of (002) peaks at around 23 ◦ and 43◦ corresponding
to various N and O heteroatom contents. The (002) peak represents graphitic stacking
originating from randomly oriented aromatic carbon. This might be due to the high
temperature activation process.

1. Introduction 
Non-renewable resources and energy sources such as oil and coal are 
becoming increasingly depleted because of the rapid development of the 
social economy. At the same time, environmental issues such as various 
exhaust gases and the greenhouse effect caused by these energy sources 
have become a global source of concern and an increasingly serious 
social issue. In the last decade, the energy crisis and environmental 
protection issues have intensified, and the demand for new energy 
sources and feasible environmental protection measures has grown. To 
meet the ever-increasing demand for efficient energy storage and envi -
ronmental pressures, it is urgent to seek sustainable clean energy 
generated from renewable resources [ 1 – 6 ]. Among various energy 
transformation and storage devices, supercapacitors (SCs), also known 
as ultracapacitors, have attracted great attention due to their higher 
power delivery ( > 10 kW kg
� 1
) and longer cycling life ( > 100,000 cycles) 
compared to batteries, simple principle, and safe operation [ 1 ]. There -
fore, SCs have been widely studied and developed in many fields in 
recent years, such as uninterruptible power supplies, portable consumer 
electronic devices, electric vehicles, industrial power and energy man -
agement, and load-levelling [ 4 , 7 , 8 ]. 
Generally, electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) and pseudo -
capacitors are categorized as supercapacitors based on their charge- 
storage mechanisms. Energy is stored in EDLCs through the reversible 
adsorption of electrolyte ions on an active material; therefore, the 
capacitance of an EDLC relies heavily on the surface area of the electrode 
material and pore framework (porosity and size distribution), which 
needs to facilitate the access of electrolyte ions [ 9 ]. Unlike EDLCs, 
pseudocapacitors achieve energy storage through fast and reversible 
faradaic redox reactions, which take place at or near the electrode sur -
face. To meet the needs of high-energy supercapacitors, the choice of 
pseudocapacitive material with electro-active species is crucial to

It is widely acknowledged that the electrode material is one of the 
most important factors influencing supercapacitor performance. A large 
number of carbon-based electrode materials, such as AC [ 10 – 12 ], mes -

ABSTRACT
Biomass-derived carbon aerogels have attracted considerable attention for applications in CO
2 
capture and 
supercapacitors (SCs). However, these carbon aerogel materials often suffer from an insufficient number of active 
sites. In this study, a novel N, P co-doped porous carbon aerogel with a hierarchical structure was synthesized 
using cellulose biomass as the raw material, a NaOH/urea system as the solvent and activator, and urea and urea 
phosphate as heteroatom dopants. Owing to the synergistic effects of heteroatom co-doping and the hierarchical 
pore structure, the optimal sample, NPCA-600 – 0.5, exhibited a large specific surface area of 582.9 m
2
/g and a 
high pore volume of 0.187 cm
3
/g. It demonstrated a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 2.89 mmol/g (25 
◦
C, 1 bar), 
along with high CO
2
/N
2 
selectivity and excellent recyclability, retaining 91 % efficiency after 10 cycles. As a SC 
electrode, NPCA-600 – 0.5 achieved a high specific capacitance of 238 F/g at 1 A/g, maintaining 80 % of its initial 
capacitance after 5000 cycles at 10 A/g. This work not only provides a promising adsorbent and electrode 
material for CO
2 
capture and supercapacitors, but also offers valuable insights for the design of advanced carbon- 
based materials.
1. Introduction
As the global population grows and industrialization expands, the 
demand for energy has led to the consumption of vast amounts of fossil 
fuels, resulting in significant greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions [1,2] . 
This situation has triggered a severe energy crisis and exacerbated the 
greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide, in particular, stands out as the pri -
mary GHG (75 % of total GHG emissions) responsible for climate change 
and accelerated global warming [3,4] . In view of the above problems, 
the development of efficient CO
2 
capture technologies and energy 
storage devices emerges as a potent approach to alleviate the energy 
crisis and mitigate climate change [5,6] .
Based on the capture process principles, several CO
2 
capture 
methods, including chemical absorption [7] , membrane separation [8] , 
and gas – solid adsorption [9] , have undergone extensive research and 
application. Of these, gas – solid adsorption technology has emerged as a 
compelling option, thanks to its high absorption rate, convenient 
regeneration system, energy efficiency, and environmental friendliness 
[10] . Porous carbons are highly regarded as promising CO
2 
gas – solid 
adsorption materials. Their high chemical and thermal stability, exten -
sive specific surface area, adjustable pore structure make them a top 
choice [11] . Furthermore, carbon materials usually possess a layered 
porous structure alongside a substantial specific surface area. Micro -
pores and small mesopores can enhance the storage of charge ions. 
While meso-macro pores provide mass transfer channels to facilitate the 
transport of charge ions in solution [12,13] . This configuration facili -
tates the efficient transfer of ions and electrons, as well as the accu -
mulation of charge, thereby rendering them an excellent candidate for 
energy storage materials [14 – 16] .
In recent years, carbon aerogel-type porous carbon, with its three- 
dimensional structure, high surface area, high electrical conductivity 
and stable physicochemical properties, has been identified as an 
emerging class of functional materials for CO
2 
capture and super -
capacitors [17 – 19] . Zhai et al. [20] prepared the starch-based carbon 
aerogel. When used as an electrode material for supercapacitors, it 
showed excellent electrochemical properties, reaching a specific 
capacitance of 211.5 F/g at 0.5 A/g. Ji et al. [21] prepared a biochar- 
silicon hybrid aerogel using carbon nanotubes and silicon as raw ma -
terials. The hybrid aerogel exhibited good CO
2 
adsorption performance, 
with a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 2.74 mmol/g at 25 
◦
C and 1 bar. 
Moreover, carbon aerogel-type adsorbents and electrode materials 
derived from renewable biomass sources like cellulose [22] , chitosan

[23] , lignin [12] , and starch [20] have gained increasing attention. 
Cellulose is a macromolecular polysaccharide consisting of glucose 
molecules, and it is widely present in the cell walls of green plants and 
algae [24,25] . As a highly favored renewable biomass material, cellulose 
boasts remarkable attributes such as biodegradability, non-toxicity, 
lightness, and ease of chemical modification [4] . These properties 
collectively render cellulose an appealing feedstock for the production 
of biomass-derived carbon aerogel materials.
However, carbon aerogels ’ limited surface active sites result in low 
CO
2 
absorption capacity or low specific capacitance when used as ad -
sorbents or electrodes [26,27] . Previous research has indeed demon -
strated that doping carbon surfaces with heteroatoms significantly 
boosts CO
2 
capture and electrochemical performance [5,6,14] . N doping 
is the most commonly employed method to improve CO
2 
adsorption and 
discharge capacity by enhancing surface alkalinity and forming pseudo- 
capacitance [13,28] . N doping mainly occurs in the carbon skeleton in 
the form of pyridine-N (N-6), pyrrole-N (N-5), oxide-N (N-X) and gra -
phene (N-Q) [29] . Unlike N atoms, P atoms have a larger radius than 
carbon atoms, which enables them to create vacancy defects and alter 
the electronic structure within the carbon framework. This modification 
enhances the interaction between the adsorbent and CO
2 
molecules and 
provides additional pseudocapacitance [30,31] . Different from single- 
atom doped, co-doped multiple heteroatoms may amplify charge 
transport through the synergistic action of multiple impurity atoms and 
produce more efficient reaction sites [10,32] . Hence, the modification of 
carbon aerogel materials by utilizing the synergistic effect of co-doped 
heteroatoms is an effective approach.
Accordingly, the objective of this study is to develop a novel N, P co- 
doped cellulose-based carbon aerogels for CO
2 
capture and super -
capacitors. Cellulose was selected as the biomass precursor, and the 
NaOH/urea system was used as the pore-forming agent and cellulose 
solvent with urea as the nitrogen source and urea phosphate as the 
phosphorus and nitrogen source. The effects of carbonation temperature 
and heteroatom doping on CO
2 
adsorption and supercapacitor perfor -
mance were systematically determined by adjusting the mass ratios of 
urea phosphate to cellulose and the activation temperature. In addition, 
CO
2 
adsorption thermodynamics and kinetics, as well as CO
2 
cyclic 
adsorption properties and selectivity were systematically evaluated. 
Results indicate that the prepared N, P co-doped porous carbon aerogel 
(NPCA) exhibits a hierarchical porous structure, abundant surface- 
active sites, a good CO
2 
adsorption ability, high selectivity, good 
regeneration, and good capacitance performance.
2. Experimental Section
2.1. Materials
Cellulose (average particle size of 50 μ m) was purchased from 
Aladdin Industrial Co. (Shanghai, China). NaOH, urea, hydrochloric acid 
(HCl), N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), 
and acetylene black were obtained from Kelong Chem. Co. (Chengdu, 
China). Urea phosphate was bought from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical 
Co. (Shanghai, China). KOH was purchased from Changliao Chem. Co. 
(Chengdu, China). All reagents were utilized in their original state 
without any further purification.
2.2. Preparation of N, P co-doped carbon aerogels from cellulose
A solution of NaOH (2.50 g), urea (3.83 g) and water (27.0 g) were 
precooled and then cellulose powder (3.83 g) was added. The solution 
was stirred magnetically for 1 h until cellulose was completely dissolved. 
Subsequently, a urea phosphate aqueous solution (10 mL, 0.025 � 0.1 g/ 
mL) was added dropwise and stirred for another 1 h. The gel was then 
frozen at � 25 
◦
C for one day and dried in a freeze-dryer for 2 days to 
obtain a cellulose aerogel precursor.
In order to prepare NPCA, the aforementioned precursor was then 
transferred to a tube furnace and heated under N
2 
protection for 2 h at 
600 
◦
C with a ramp rate of 5 
◦
C/min. Subsequently, the materials were 
washed thoroughly with 1 M HCl and a large volume of DI water until 
the pH of the filtrate became neutral. Finally, the cellulose-derived 
carbon aerogels were dried overnight at 80 
◦
C. The final carbon aero -
gels were labeled as NPCA-T-n, where T represents the activation tem -
perature ( = 500, 550, 600, 650, and 700 
◦
C), and n represents the urea 
phosphate/cellulose mass ratio ( = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1). For comparison, a 
control carbon aerogel, designated as NPCA-600 – 0 (urea phosphate =
0), was also prepared at 600 
◦
C using a similar synthetic procedure. 
Fig. 1 presents a schematic representation of the synthesis of carbon 
aerogel.
2.3. Characterization
The crystalline structure of the materials was analyzed using X-ray 
diffraction spectroscopy on a DX-2007 X (Haoyuan Instruments Co., 
Dandong, China) with Cu-Ka radiation (k = 1.5418 Å) at room tem -
perature and 2 θ ranging from 10
◦
to 80
◦
. Raman spectra were measured 
with DXR Raman spectroscopy (Thermo-Fisher Scientific Inc. Waltham, 
MA, USA) to assess the degree of graphitization and surface defect with 
455 nm laser excitation at the range from 2200 to 800 cm
� 1
. Fourier 
transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) spectra were characterized on a 
Spectrum Two infrared spectrometer (PerkinElmer Inc. Waltham, MA, 
USA) to identify surface functional groups. X-ray photoelectron spec -
troscopy (XPS) spectra were recorded with Axis Ultra DLD Kratos AXIS 
SUPRA Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Kratos Analytical Ltd, 
Wharfside, Manchester, UK) to ascertain the surface elemental compo -
sition and molecular structure of the samples. The pore structure of the 
materials was analyzed through the N
2 
adsorption – desorption test at 77 
K, using a specific area surface and pore size analyzer (ASAP 2460, 
Micromeritics, USA). The Brunner-Emmet-Teller (BET) and the density 
functional theory (DFT) model were employed to calculate the specific 
surface areas and the pore size distribution, respectively. Scanning 
Electron Microscopy (SEM) (JSM-7610F using 15 kV accelerating 
voltage) was used to study the morphology of the materials. Thermog -
ravimetric analysis (TGA) was conducted on a simultaneous thermal 
analyzer (NETZSCH STA 449 F3 Jupiter ® , NETZSCH Group, Deutsch -
land, Germany) to analyze the thermal stability of the as-prepared car -
bon aerosol samples.
2.4. Electrochemical measurements
These were firstly conducted in a three-electrode system, employing 
a modified Ni foam as the working electrode, Ag/AgCl, and Pt as the 
reference electrode and the counter electrode, respectively. The elec -
trode preparation process involved the incorporation of 80 % carbon 
aerogel, 10 % acetylene black as the conductive support, and 10 % 
polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) into an N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP) 
solution under ultrasonic dispersion, thus producing a homogeneous 
ink. The resulting ink was then applied in a dropwise deposition manner 
onto the nickel foam in an area of 1 cm
2
. The modified Ni foam was then 
subjected to a drying process overnight in a vacuum oven at 60 
◦
C. The 
mass loading of the active materials in each electrode was set at 1.2 – 1.6 
mg. Cyclic voltammograms (CV) were obtained from different scanning 
rates (10 � 200 mV/s), while galvanostatic charge – discharge (GCD) 
tests were carried out at a current density between 1 and 20 A/g. 
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted within a 
frequency range of 0.01 to 100 kHz, with a potential window of 5 mV. 
All the aforementioned measurements were conducted in 6 M KOH 
electrolyte solution using the CHI660E instrument (Shanghai, China).

This study investigates the influence of oxygen functional groups in biomass-based activated carbon (AC) as an efficient, 
high-performance supercapacitor electrode. To create activated carbons with variable oxygen concentration, the surface of 
produced AC was altered using oxygen as an oxidizing agent at various temperatures. Nitrogen adsorption–desorption iso-
therms, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray analyzer (EDX) analysis, thermogravimetric analysis 
(TGA), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) spectroscopy, Boehm titration and X-ray Photoelectron Spectrometer 
(XPS), are used to characterize the physico-chemical characteristics of the obtained carbons. Afterward, cyclic voltammetry, 
constant current charge–discharge and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were used to evaluate the electro-
chemical properties and behavior of ACs based electrodes. Indeed, the oxidative treatment increases the oxygen functional 
content while reducing the specific surface area. According to the results of the characterization, the electrode test reveals 
that the modified materials improve the electrochemical properties and enhance the material’s double-layer capacitance. The 
AC treated with oxygen at 623 K displayed outstanding capacitance of 550 F  g−1  at specific current of 0.1 A  g−1  in NaOH 
(2 M) electrolyte and exhibits an excellent stability after 1000 cycles with a capacitance retention of 85.5%. In addition to 
being inexpensive, the prepared materials have excellent electrochemical performance and good stability, which make them 
appropriate for supercapacitor applications.

a great deal of interest among many technologies for energy 
storage, due to their high power density, rapid energy stor -
age rate, and long life cycle [3 , 4]. Consequently, electro-
chemical capacitors are gradually finding their way into 
applications such as electric vehicles, portable electronics, 
heavy-duty machinery, storing the energy produced by solar 
cells and other fields [ 5–8]. The supercapacitor’s ultimate 
performance is significantly influenced by the electrode 
material and electrolyte [9, 10]. The development of highly 
efficient electrode materials with a high energy density is 
one important challenge [9 , 11]. Supercapacitors can be 
divided according to their charge storage mechanism into 
three types; (i) Double-layer capacitors, which are associated 
with electrostatic charge accumulation. They are character -
ized by rectangular CV curves and triangular GCD curves; 
(ii) Pseudo-capacitors, where charge storage comes from 
surface faradic reactions and the intercalation mechanism. 
They behave like EDLC materials, with almost rectangular 
CV curves and quasi-triangular GCD curves; Finally, (iii) 
Battery-type SCs, where reactions are controlled by ionic 
diffusion from the electrolyte, with a phase transformation 
reflected in the CV curves by obvious redox peaks, leading 
to the appearance of the potential plateau in the GCD curves 
[12, 13].
Carbon electrode materials such as graphene, carbon 
nanofibers, carbon nanotubes, and activated carbon have 
generally demonstrated promise as active materials for 
supercapacitors [11, 14]. Within these materials, activated 
carbon is most frequently utilized as an electrode due to its 
high surface area, chemical stability, environmental friend-
liness, relatively low cost and well-established scalability 
[15, 16].
One of the major challenges for high performance elec-

incompletely reduced graphene oxides (RGOs) was studied 
by Young Joon Oh et al. [17], revealing a specific capaci-
tance of 220 F  g−1  at the scan of 5 mV   s−1 . Xi-ran Li and his 
team modify activated carbon by  (NH4)2S2O8 oxidation [18],

Abstract
The graphitization and porous structure of carbon materials have been the focus of research on the electrochemical properties 
of supercapacitors. In this work, highly graphitized porous carbon (HPCS) is fabricated from biowaste sunflower shells using 
potassium hydroxide (KOH) as an activator. The effects of the mass ratio of KOH to raw material and activation temperature 
on the electrochemical properties are studied in detail. The results show that highly graphitized porous carbon after activation 
at 800°C for 2 h (HPCS-800–2) exhibits obvious graphitized stripes with a spacing of ca. 0.34 nm and a lower I D/IG value 
(0.797) than that of pristine carbon with non-activation (0.917). The HPCS-800–2 reaches a high specific capacitance of 
403 F   g−1  at a current density of 0.5 A   g−1 . In addition, the HPCS-800–2//HPCS-800–2 symmetric supercapacitor device 
displays outstanding higher energy density of 20.84 Wh   kg−1  than that of the YP50//YP50 device (8.18 Wh   kg−1 ).

Introduction
Supercapacitors, as a new type of energy storage device, 
mainly store energy through charge accumulation or 
reversible surface redox reaction. 1–4 Supercapacitors have 
received increasing attention owing to their fast charging 
and discharging ability, high power density, and long cycle 
life,5–7 and have been widely applied in many fields, such 
as transportation, portable electronics, medical electronics, 
and military equipment. 8,9 According to the energy storage 
mechanism, supercapacitors can be divided into two cat-
egories, namely electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) 
and pseudocapacitors. 10–12 Pseudocapacitors arise from 
fast and reversible oxidation–reduction (redox) or faradaic 
charge reaction of electrode materials, including conductive 
polymers such as polyaniline and  polypyrrole13 and metal 
oxides such as  MnO2  and14  Co3O4.15 EDLCs arise from elec-
trostatic charges accumulated at the electrode–electrolyte 
interface, such as carbon materials including carbon nano -
tubes (CNT), 16 ordered mesoporous carbon, 17 porous car -
bon,18,19 graphene, 20,21 and biomass carbon. 22–24 Among 
these, biomass carbon electrode materials have garnered 
increasing attention because of their abundant sources, low 
cost, and environmentally friendly nature.25–28
Many biomass waste materials are used to produce carbon 
electrodes applied in supercapacitors, such as straw, peel, 
fruit, and animal hair. 29 Kempasiddaiah et al. 30 reported 
mesoporous biomass carbon which was prepared from rad-
ish leaf waste, showing specific capacitance of 129 F   g−1  
at current density of 0.25 A   g−1  with specific surface area 
of about 704   m2   g−1 . Sankar et al. 26 prepared ultrathin 
mesoporous graphite carbon using biomass green tea waste 
as a raw material through a KOH activation process com -
bined with water or hydrochloric acid treatment, exhibit-
ing specific capacitance of 162 F   g−1  at current density of 
0.5 A   g−1 . Sun et al. 31 selected kelp as a carbon source and 
used its natural salt content (Ca, Na, etc.) as a template to 
obtain mesoporous carbon. Consequently, multichannel 
pores were obtained through chemical activation to enrich 
the microporous structure, thereby increasing the specific 
surface area and providing a wealth of effective adsorp-
tion sites. Mesoporous materials not only enhance the ionic 
conductivity of materials, but also improve the wettability 
of materials, which is critical to electrochemical-related

enhancement of specific capacitance is still needed to meet 
high energy requirements. Sunflower is a common plant in 
our lives, with annual global output of tens of millions of 
tons. The seeds can be used not only to produce seed oil, 
but also to make biscuits, among other uses.32 However, the 
shell as a waste by-product has become a serious problem. 
The shells are often dumped or burned on the spot, polluting 
the environment with ash and harmful gases. But in terms of 
the components of the sunflower shell, it contains consider-
able cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin and is considered a 
good precursor for preparing carbon materials. 34,35
For carbon materials, the concerned problems involve 
specific surface area, pore size and distribution, surface 
group, and conductivity.36,37 In this work, highly graphitized 
porous carbon (HPCS) is prepared by a chemical activation 
method using sunflower shell as the raw material and KOH 
as an activator. The temperature and mass ratio of KOH to 
sunflower shells are investigated to adjust the specific sur -
face area and pore size. The influence of the above factors 
on the electrochemical performance is studied. The HPCS 
shows a three-dimensional (3D) porous structure with a 
large specific surface area (1098.07   m2  g−1 ) and lower ID/IG 
value (0.797), exhibiting excellent specific capacitance of 
403 F   g−1  at a current density of 0.5 A   g−1 . The symmetric 
supercapacitor device delivers outstanding energy density 
of 20.84 Wh   kg−1 .
Experimental
Reagents and Materials
Sunflower shells were obtained from local supermarkets 
(Yinchuan City, Ningxia Province, China), KOH and HCl 
were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., 
Ltd., and YP50 was purchased from Kuraray Co., Ltd. The 
reagents were used as received.
Construction of Highly Graphitized Porous Biomass 
Carbon from Sunflower Shells (HPCS)
Pretreatment of Sunflower Shells
The sunflower shells were cleaned using water under stirring 
and ultrasound-assisting to remove the dirt and impurities, 
and then dried at 80°C over 12 h.
Fabrication of HPCS
First, a certain mass of sunflower shells was carbonized at 
300°C for 2 h to prepare the black precursor, denoted as 
SS-300–2. Next, 1 g precursor was soaked in different mass 
amounts of KOH (1, 2, 3, 4 g) in 30 mL water for 12 h 
to absorb all the ions in the solution, and the solvent was 
evaporated completely overnight. Subsequently, the obtained 
powders were carbonized and activated at different tempera-
tures (700°C, 800°C, and 900°C) at a rate of 2°C/min for 2 h, 
respectively. The powders were then immersed in 1 M HCl 
over 12 h and washed with water more than three times until 
the pH reached 7, followed by drying at 75°C for 12 h. The 
obtained samples were abbreviated as HPCS-X–Y (X = 700, 
800 and 900, where Y  = 1, 2, 3, and 4 represent the mass 
ratios of KOH to SS-300–2). In addition, pristine sunflower 
shells were carbonized at 800°C in a tubular furnace for 2 h 
at a similar rate to obtain carbon without pre-carbonation 
and KOH activation, which was labeled CS-800–0.
Material Characterization
The crystal structure of the samples was determined using 
x-ray diffraction (SmartLab, Cu  Kα). The morphology 
information was obtained by scanning electron microscopy 
(SEM, Hitachi SU-5000) and transmission electron micros-
copy (TEM, Talos 200 S). The specific surface area and pore 
size distribution were studied based on  N2 adsorption and 
desorption isotherms (JW-BK200C). Raman spectra were 
measured on a DXR Raman spectrometer. The elemental 
composition and chemical states of the samples were charac-
terized by x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo 
Scientific K-Alpha).
Preparation of Working Electrode
The prepared active material, acetylene black, conducting 
graphite, and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) were mixed 
in a mass ratio of 80:7.5:7.5:5 to form a uniform slurry. 
Subsequently, it was coated on nickel foam of geometric 
surface area of ca. 1  cm2 as current collector (active material 
mass loading of 4 mg   cm−2 ). Then, the working electrode 
was obtained after drying at 80°C for 12 h and pressing at 
10 M Pa for ca. 15 s.
Electrochemical Performance Evaluation
The electrochemical properties were measured by a three-
electrode system comprising a reference electrode (saturated

Abstract
Developing appropriate electrode materials is crucial for achieving supercapacitors with high power output and extended 
cycle life. Among these, biomass-derived carbon electrodes hold a prominent position in supercapacitor applications. How-
ever, these electrodes need to be modified by appropriate methods to increase their performance. In this study, sulphur and 
iodine heteroatom functionalization was performed using a hydrothermal method on activated carbon (SPAC) derived from a 
microalgae precursor through potassium hydroxide activation, resulting in iodine- and sulphur-doped SPAC (iodine@S-doped 
SPAC). Characterization was carried out with Scanning electron microscope (SEM), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy 
(FTIR), X-ray diffraction analysis (XRD), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and nitrogen adsorption/desorption 
analyses. The electrochemical properties of the resulting composite material as a supercapacitor were examined. A specific 
capacitance of 208.95 F/g was achieved with the iodine@S-doped SPAC supercapacitor. The maximum energy density and 
power density of the supercapacitor, derived from the iodine@S-doped SPAC sample, were calculated as 5.11 Wh/kg and 
2000 W/kg, respectively. Additionally, the coulombic efficiency of this supercapacitor was calculated to be 87.57% at a cur-
rent density of 0.06 A/g. It also exhibited a capacity retention of up to 89.72% over 1000 cycles.
Keywords Microalgae · Pyrolysis · Iodine and sulphur doping · Hydrothermal heating · Supercapacitor
1 Introduction
Energy, which is vital for world life, seriously affects the 
economies and the environment of countries around the 
world due to the current dependence on non-renewable fos-
sil fuels [1]. Interest in renewable, environmentally friendly, 
high-performance energy storage devices such as batteries, 
supercapacitors and fuel cells for electrochemical energy, 
which is an important part of clean energy, tends to increase 
[2, 3]. Among these, supercapacitors, in particular, have gar-
nered significant interest from researchers [4–6].
The excellent microstructure and reasonable pore size dis-
tribution of biomass-derived carbon materials enable their 
use in various applications. In particular, the outstanding 
charge storage/release capacity and high cycling stability of 
carbon-based supercapacitors promote their applications in 
energy storage and conversion [7]. The development of low-
cost and renewable biomass-based carbon materials for use 
in energy storage devices is an important issue. As typical 
electrode material for supercapacitors, biomass-based car -
bon precursors are attracting intense interest as a reliable and 
readily available source [8–12]. However, further enhancing 
the performance of such carbon-based materials when used 
as electrodes is an important research topic. Increasing the 
specific surface area and incorporating heteroatom doping 
are widely preferred strategic approaches to improving the 
performance of carbon-based electrode materials. The elec-
trochemical activity of supercapacitors can be significantly 
improved by appropriately doping biomass-derived carbon 
materials with heteroatoms. The incorporation of heter -
oatoms with different electronegativities and atomic radii 
than carbon alters the electron distribution of the material. 
As a result, heteroatom functional groups enhance properties 
such as wettability, redox activity, and electrical conduc-
tivity, thereby promoting pseudocapacitance formation and

Thus, charge transfer kinetics can be positively affected by 
the easy transport of ions at the electrode/electrolyte inter -
face with heteroatom doping [17].
Heteroatoms such as sulphur (S), nitrogen (N), phos-
phorus (P), and oxygen (O) are widely preferred in vari-
ous applications [18]. In supercapacitor applications, car -
bon edges are modified through heteroatom doping, which 
enhances electron conductivity and improves pseudocapaci-
tance via Faradaic reactions [19– 21]. The use of N atoms 
with high electronegativity has been frequently reported in 
heteroatom-doping applications to carbon materials [22, 
23]. Sulphur, which has a larger radius and higher electro-
chemical activity compared to nitrogen, is added to carbo-
naceous materials as a heteroatom, disrupting the electron 
balance density of the material and resulting in different 
bond lengths and bond angles [1 , 24]. Sulphur-doped car -
bon materials also have significant interest in supercapacitor 
applications.
Another important element among heteroatoms is iodine. 
The iodine doping has begun to be considered especially 
in some applications [ 25–27]. There is still little research 
on iodine doping into porous carbon structure. With iodine 
atoms having a relatively high electronegativity (2.66) and 
a larger radius (140 pm) compared to carbon, both the elec-
tronic structure of carbon materials can be optimized and 
the d-spacing can be increased [28]. Thus, we believe that 
investigating how iodine can be integrated into carbon mate-
rials to enhance energy storage performance in supercapaci-
tor applications is of great importance. Doping iodine as a 
heteroatom can significantly increase the electrochemically 
active sites of carbon-based materials [29, 30].
Biomass-based carbon materials are widely used in vari-
ous application areas [31– 33]. Among biomass-based car -
bon materials, algae have attracted great attention in differ-
ent application areas with their important features such as 
fast growth rates and high photosynthetic efficiency [ 34]. 
Spirulina platensis, which has an important place among 
algae and is characterized by rapid growth and wide distribu-
tion, consists mainly of polysaccharides, proteins, and lipids. 
One of the significant properties of Spirulina platensis  is 
its natural nitrogen content. Therefore, it can be utilized in 
various applications without requiring an additional nitrogen 
source for doping. With its low cost and these advantageous 
characteristics, Spirulina platensis emerges as a promising 
candidate for biomass-derived carbon materials as electrodes 
in supercapacitor applications. This study focuses on the 
synthesis of iodine@S-doped SPAC through a series of 
pyrolysis and hydrothermal processes, utilizing Spirulina 
platensis microalgae as the carbon precursor, with S and I 
atoms as heteroatoms for electrode material in supercapaci-
tor applications. The synthesized material was character -
ized using XRD, EDS, SEM, FTIR, and nitrogen adsorption/
desorption analyses. Its electrochemical properties were 
evaluated through CV, GCD, and EIS measurements.
2  Experimental section
2.1  Sample preparation
This experimental study consists of three stages. The first 
stage is the production of activated carbon. The procedure 
for producing activated carbon from Spirulina platensis  
microalgae as a carbon source was reported in another study 
[35]. In summary, microalgae as a carbon precursor (20 g) 
and KOH activator (20 g) as a chemical activator were added 
to an Erlen flask at a ratio of 1:1. The pure water (100 mL) 
was added to this mixture and mixed on a magnetic stirrer at 
room temperature for approximately 1 h. Then, this mixture 
was placed in an oven and impregnated at 80 °C overnight. 
After this process, the samples taken into porcelain cruci-
bles were pyrolysed in a muffle furnace at 600 °C under a 
carbon dioxide atmosphere for 30 min. After the pyrolysis 
process, this sample was left to cool to room temperature, 
washed with hot and cold deionized water, and dried in an 
oven at 105 °C. The sample obtained by this process was 
called SPAC.
In the second stage, sulphur doping was performed with 
sulfuric acid. A certain amount of SPAC (3 g) and 30 mL of 
sulfuric acid diluted with pure water at a 1:3 ratio was added 
to a conical flask [ 35]. This mixture was hydrothermally 
processed in an oven at 105 °C for 24 h. After this process, 
the obtained sample was repeatedly washed with hot and 
cold pure water and was named S-doped SPAC.
The third stage involves adding iodine to the S-doped 
SPAC sample by hydrothermal heating method. To achieve 
iodine doping, S-doped SPAC was mixed with iodine at a 
1:2 ratio in a 30 mL aqueous solution. Heating and mixing 
were carried out via hydrothermal processing on a magnetic 
stirrer at 50 °C for 6 h. Subsequently, the obtained sample 
was washed multiple times with pure water and dried in an 
oven at 80 °C for 2 h. This sample was named iodine@S-
doped SPAC.

sample is presented in Fig.  1.

Abstract: Biomass materials with representative morphologies and compositions were employed to
study the activation effect of KHCO3. As the activation time increased from 1 to 3 h, the products
derived from puffed rice and pleurotus eryngii achieved a hierarchical porous structure, while the
products derived from cotton still presented a microporous structure. In the electrochemical test of a
three-electrode system, the speciﬁc capacitance of these products was 352, 319, and216 F g−1, respec-
tively. In the two-electrode system, the PR-2-based symmetric supercapacitor presented with a speciﬁc

1. Introduction
To face the energy challenges of modern society, it is urgent to vigorously develop
renewable energy sources and storage devices. As a promising candidate technology,
supercapacitors have received wide attention because of their great application value in
the ﬁelds of electric vehicles, power systems, and consumer electronics [1,2].
Based on different energy storage mechanisms, supercapacitors are generally divided
into two categories: electrochemical double-layer capacitors and pseudocapacitors. The
former mainly uses carbon materials as electrodes, while the latter mainly uses transition
metal oxides and conductive polymers as electrodes. In general, metal oxides are often
hampered by the serious aggregation of nanoparticles and low electron transport, resulting
in their poor speciﬁc capacitance in practical applications [3]. The conductivity of these
polymers is excellent; however, signiﬁcant expansion and contraction during charging
and discharging can reduce the mechanical properties and cycling stability of the con-
ductive polymer [4]. By comparison, carbon materials have always been the most widely
studied and applied electrode materials, with the advantages of abundant raw materials,
stable chemical properties, high speciﬁc surface area, and environmental friendliness. Car-
bon materials that are commonly used for the electrode mainly include activated carbon,
graphene, and carbon nanotubes. Compared to graphene and carbon nanotubes, biomass
