Coatings 2023, 13, 1236 2 of 14
material is one of the most popular carbon precursors due to its high porosity, low cost,
and renewability.
As shown by vast amounts of research, the three-dimensional (3D) hierarchical porous
structure of biomass-derived carbon electrode materials can be beneﬁcial in improving the
electrochemical properties of supercapacitors [5–7]. Generally, macropores (>50 nm) are
usually distributed on the surface of the carbon material, which acts as ion reservoirs for
storing huge amounts of electrolyte ions. The mesopores (2~50 nm) provide expressways
for the transport of electrolyte ions. In addition, the existence of micropores (<2 nm) can
signiﬁcantly improve the adsorption capacity of carbon materials and form more electrical
double layers [8].
Chemical activation is one of the common methods to prepare 3D hierarchical porous
carbon materials [9–11]. Compared to obtaining microporous structures through KOH
activation, the decomposition of KHCO3 during the activation process leaves abundant
macropores in carbon materials, which facilitate the formation of hierarchically porous
structures that are rich in macropores, mesopores, and micropores, resulting in an im-
provement in the electrochemical properties of supercapacitors. In addition, from a safety
perspective, KHCO3 is not as corrosive as KOH and is more environmentally friendly. Some
scholars have employed KHCO3 [12–14] as a substitute for KOH and obtained an excellent
activation effect. The activation process of KHCO 3 can be divided into two aspects. On
the one hand, the CO2 and water vapor released by the thermal decomposition of KHCO3
forms a honeycomb structure in the carbon material. On the other hand, decomposition
products further produce abundant mesopores and micropores during high-temperature
activation, resulting in 3D hierarchical porous carbon materials [15,16].
Among the thousands of biomass materials, how to quickly select the optimum carbon
precursor and achieve the desired performance is a cumbersome task. In this work, to study
the impact of KHCO 3 activation on different biomass materials, various representative
biomass materials with typical morphology and composition (Table 1) were adopted to
prepare porous carbon materials through a one-step activation method by using KHCO3
as the activation agent (Figure 1). The sample derived from puffed rice (PR-2) exhibited a
maximum speciﬁc capacitance of 352 F g−1 in the three-electrode system due to its high
speciﬁc surface area and hierarchical porous structure. In the two-electrode system, the
PR-2-based symmetric supercapacitor presented a speciﬁc capacitance of 280.7 F g−1 at
0.5 A g−1 and an energy density of 14.03 Wh kg−1 at 150.04 W kg−1, with an energy density
retention of 73.7% even at the higher power density of 8380.4 W kg−1. After 10,000 cycles of
charging and discharging at 5 A g−1, the speciﬁc capacitance retention of the supercapacitor
reached 108.8%. Based on the experimental analysis, a likely mechanism for the formation
of pores was established for these biomass materials. The results indicate that biomass
materials with a soft layered or network structure are the best candidates to obtain a 3D
hierarchical porous structure.

2. Materials and Methods 
2.1. Material Synthesis 
The porous carbon materials were prepared by a one-step activation method. Typi-
cally, the washed biomass materials were mixed with KHCO3 in a mass ratio of 1:3 before 
they were stirred fully with moderate deionized water. Typically, 5 g of biomass, 15 g of 
KHCO3, and 100 mL of deionized water were mixe d. After the mixture dried at 80 °C, it 
was ground to ﬁne powder by a high-speed ball crusher. Subsequently, the powder was 
put into a tubular furnace at 900 °C in a nitrogen atmosphere for x (x = 1, 2, 3) hours and 
was then naturally cooled to room temperat ure. Afterward, the product was neutralized 
with a suﬃcient 1 M HCl solution and ﬁltered until neutral with excessive deionized wa-
ter. Finally, the product was placed into a vacuum oven to dry at 80 °C for 48 h. In this 
work, cotton, puﬀed rice and pleurotus eryngii were used as the carbon precursor, and 
corresponding samples were named CT-x, PR-x, and PE-x, respectively, where x (x = 1, 2, 
3) is the activation hours. 
2.2. Material Characterizations 
The morphologies of the samples were acquired on a Hitachi SU8010 scanning elec-
tron microscopy (SEM) system. A Bruker D8 ADVANCE diﬀractometer was employed to 
analyze X-ray di ﬀraction (XRD) pa tterns. The speci ﬁc surface areas (SSA) and pore size 
distribution (PSD) were analyzed on a Micromeritics ASAP 2460 instrument. 
2.3. Electrochemical Testing 
To fabricate the working electrode, the as-prepared carbon materials were mixed 
with carbon black and polyvinylidene ﬂuoride according to a mass ratio of 8:1:1. Then, 
the appropriate N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone solvent was injected into the mixture and stirred 
suﬃciently with a magnetic stirrer for 6~8 h until uniform was obtained. Afterward, the 
mixed slurry was evenly coated on foam nickel with a brush and thoroughly dried at 80 
°C under vacuum conditions. Then, the electrode was compressed with a tablet press ma-
chine to ensure close contact between the electrode material and the foam nickel. A plati-
num sheet was employed as a counter electrode, whereas an Hg/HgO electrode served as 
a reference electrode. Furthermore, in the tw o-electrode system, two pieces of PR-2 elec-
trodes were used to assemble the symmetric supercapacitor. All the electrochemical meas-
urements of the as-prepared materials were conducted on a Metrohm Autolab 
PGSTAT302N electrochemical workstation with 6 M KOH aqueous as the electrolyte.

Biomass-based activated carbon materials provide a new approach for the

pacitor cell circuit had an energy density of 7.11 Wkg -1 with a power density of
125.46 Wkg-1 in an H2SO4 electrolyte. These results offer an efﬁcient strategy for
the preparation of high-performance carbon electrodes based on date seeds

1 Introduction
Advances in industry and modern technology have
led to a high energy demand for daily operation and
further development [ 1, 2]. This energy demand is
mostly met by conventional and natural exploitation

of electroactive species, electric double layer capacitor

other [ 9]. EDLC have a higher power density and
longer cycle life than hybrid and PC supercapacitors.
The component consists of two symmetrical elec-

arator[10]. Electrodes are the core of EDLC and play

Activated carbon is a form of carbon that has been

and chemical reactions. Activated carbon is environ-

However, due to environmental pollution and lim-

Moreover, they are potentially applied as activated

Lignin-Derived Activated Carbon as Electrode Material for
High-Performance Supercapacitor
Chenghao Pan 1,2 , Yongfeng Ji 2, Suxia Ren 2, Tingzhou Lei 2,* and Lili Dong 2,*
1 School of Environmental Science and Engineering, Changzhou University, Changzhou 213164, China;

13222666378@163.com (Y.J.); rensuxia@cczu.edu.cn (S.R.)
* Correspondence: leitingzhou@163.com (T.L.); dongli2050@cczu.edu.cn (L.D.)
Abstract: Utilizing lignin-derived activated carbon in supercapacitors has emerged as a
promising approach to alleviating environmental pollution and promoting the high-value
utilization of byproducts in the papermaking industry. In this study, activated carbons
(LACs) were prepared using a simple one-step KOH activation approach and by employing
enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL). The impact of the KOH activation parameters on the
microstructure and capacitive performance of the LACs was investigated by varying the
KOH/EHL ratio and activation temperature. The optimized sample LAC 800-4 showed
an interconnected porous structure with a high surface area of 2285 m 2/g, abundant
micropores, and a small number of mesopores, which makes it a suitable electrode material
for supercapacitors. The sample LAC 800-4 demonstrated a high specific capacitance of
291.3 F/g in a three-electrode system. Under a symmetrical supercapacitor electrode
system, the specific capacitance of the LAC800-4 electrode reached 186.8 F/g at 0.5 A/g. After
10,000 cycles at 20 A/g, the capacitance retention rate remained at 96.1%. The symmetrical
supercapacitor also demonstrated a superior energy density of 6.5 Wh/kg. This work
provides valuable insights into the transformation of low-value natural biomass derivatives
into environmentally friendly, high-performing supercapacitor electrode materials.
Keywords: lignin; activated carbon; KOH activation; supercapacitors
1. Introduction
In recent years, the use of carbon-based supercapacitors in energy storage and con-
version devices has garnered significant attention due to their high energy density, rapid
charge and discharge rates, and superior safety performance [1,2]. Based on the formation
mechanism of double-layer capacitance, the carbon material electrode should contain abun-
dant micropores to provide a high surface area, enough active sites for electron storage,
and an appropriate amount of mesopores and macropores to supply fast transmission and
diffusion channels for the electrolyte [3,4]. Therefore, preparing activated carbon materials
that meet the above requirements has gained considerable attention.
In recent years, biomass has been recognized as an ideal precursor for activated carbon
due to its renewability, chemical stability, low cost, and unique structure. Wu et al. [ 5]
prepared honeycomb-like carbon foam from wheat flour via one-step carbonization. The
unique structure provided the carbon foam with a significant capacitive performance, with a
high specific capacitance of 473 F/g at 0.5 A/g and a high energy density of 29.3 63.5 Wh/kg.
Chen et al. [6] used rice husk as a raw material to prepare hierarchical porous carbon. The
contribution of different rice husk components, including cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin,
Molecules 2025, 30, 89 https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules30010089
Molecules 2025, 30, 89 2 of 11
and SiO2, to the formation of pores was investigated. Lignin mainly contributes to the
formation of mesopores and micropores, which is crucial in obtaining a high specific
capacitance. The optimized sample showed a specific capacitance of 51.4 F/g at 0.5 A/g
in the symmetric supercapacitor, while its capacitance retention was as high as 96.2 % at
20 A/g. Studies have shown that biomass-derived carbon materials could be effectively
employed in supercapacitors. Among the numerous biomass precursors developed, lignin
has attracted significant attention due to its high carbon content, numerous self-doping
heteroatoms, rigid chemical structure, and large and cheap output.
Lignin is the most abundant aromatic polymer in the world. Approximately 70 million
tons of lignin are produced from pulping byproducts annually, but almost 98% of that
lignin is burned as low-quality fuel or discarded directly as waste [7,8]. The conversion of
lignin into carbon-based electrode materials not only alleviates environmental pollution
but also realizes the high-value utilization of lignin. In recent years, some methods for
the preparation of lignin-based carbon materials for use in supercapacitors have been
developed. Zhang et al. [9] prepared carbon materials from lignin with and without KOH.
The carbon material (LC) obtained without KOH showed a large texture with a small
surface area, while the hierarchical porous carbon (LHPC) prepared with KOH showed a
high surface area of 907 m2/g. Benefiting from the hierarchical porous structure, the LHPC
sample presented a superior captive performance, with a specific capacitance of 165.0 F/g
in 1M H2SO4 at 0.05 A/g. Shi et al. [10] fabricated porous carbon from enzymatically hy-
drolyzed lignin and urea through a KOH activation procedure. The influences of activation
temperatures and elemental doping on the microstructure and capacitive performance of
the synthesized ONS-HPC materials were investigated and the ONS-HPC-600 electrode
material presented the best electrochemical performance. It can be concluded that the
activation parameters strongly influence the microstructure and capacitive performance of
carbon materials. However, systematic discussions regarding the influence of the activa-
tion parameters on the pore structure and electrochemical performance of lignin-derived
activated carbon have rarely been reported.
In this study, activated carbons (LACs) were prepared from enzymatic hydrolysis
lignin and KOH using a facile one-step method. The lignin-derived activated carbon was
characterized to analyze the mechanism implicated in the formation of the porous structure
of LACs. The intrinsic regular relationship between the structure and electrochemical
performance of LACs was further discussed. This work will provide a valuable reference
for the fabrication of lignin-derived carbon electrodes for supercapacitors.
2. Results and Discussion
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used to characterize the morphology and
microstructure of the as-prepared samples. As shown in Figure 1a, LAC800-2 exhibited a
bulk structure, in which only the surface was etched. This may be attributed to the low
quantity of the KOH added, which contributed to the low etching degree and relatively
complete carbon skeleton. As the KOH/EHL mass ratio increased, the LAC 800-3 and
LAC800-4 formed a well-developed porous structure. Generally speaking, an appropriate
porous structure should contain a large number of micropores to provide enough active
sites for ion storage, a certain amount of mesopores to provide short and convenient
ion transfer channels, and large pores to provide buffer layers for electrolyte ions [ 11].
Thus, LAC800-3 and LAC800-4, which have interconnected porous structures, may exhibit a
significant capacity for electrochemical energy storage due to the improved electron and
ion transport efficiency. However, the carbon skeleton was over-etched due to the excessive
use of KOH, as indicated in Figure 1d [12]. The activation temperature also has a strong
impact on the porous structure of carbon materials. The LAC600-4 sample showed few pores

ABSTRACT: Supercapacitors are high-power energy storage
devices due to their charge storage capability and long cyclic
stability. These devices rely on highly porous materials for
electrodes providing a substantial surface area per mass, such as
highly porous carbon. Developing high-performance porous
carbon from biomass wastes such as waste-activated sludge and
spent coffee is a sustainable way to reduce adverse environmental
effects, contributing toward a carbon circular economy. In this
study, hierarchically porous carbon with a high surface area of 1198
± 60 m
2
g
−1
was synthesized through a green route. Sodium
acetate was utilized as an environmentally friendly electrolyte. The
long-term stability test at a high current density was conducted,
providing valuable insights into the viability of sodium acetate as a robust electrolyte in supercapacitor application. The
supercapacitor demonstrated an excellent cycle stability of 98.4% after 20,000 cycles at a current density of 10 A g
−1
in sodium
acetate. Further assessment revealed dominant fast surface kinetics. Moreover, a maximum energy density of 15.9 Wh kg
−1
at 0.2 A
g
−1
was achieved. By utilizing highly porous carbon in conjunction with a water-based binder, a substantial improvement of 76% in
capacity with respect to a nonaqueous-based binder was demonstrated.
1. INTRODUCTION
Supercapacitors are characterized by high power density, fast
charging/discharging rates, and remarkable long-term stability
(>10,000 cycles).
1
Energy storage and delivery technologies
such as supercapacitors possess the capability to store and
deliver energy at an extremely fast rate, providing a high
current over a short period. Hence, they are applicable in
electric vehicles (EVs), uninterruptible power supplies (UPS),
and hybrid buses.
2
The most common type of supercapacitor is
an electrochemical double-layer capacitor (EDLC). EDLC
supercapacitors store charges through the adsorption and
desorption of electrolyte ions at electrodes, in contrast to
batteries that depend on electrochemical redox reactions.
3
This
distinction has enabled supercapacitors to achieve impressive
high power densities, surpassing lithium-ion batteries by an
order of magnitude. The electrochemical performance of the
supercapacitors is limited by the electrode materials. It is
crucial to develop highly porous carbon-based electrode
materials featuring a high specific surface area that can be
readily accessed to electrolyte ions. Accessibility of the specific
surface area depends on the pore size distributions. Pore sizes
smaller than 0.5 nm are not accessible to hydroxide ions when
aqueous electrolytes are used (e.g., potassium hydroxide) and
pore sizes below 1 nm are not accessible to organic
electrolytes.
4
Porous carbons are the key component in many applications
including adsorption and energy storage systems such as
supercapacitors and lithium batteries.
5
The demand for porous
carbon is expected to substantially increase over the next few
years. The high-cost petroleum-based active carbon ($4000 per
ton) is the commercial material that is currently being used.
6
The operating voltage window and specific capacitance of the
commercial supercapacitors are 2.7 V and 100−120 F g
−1
in
organic electrolytes and 1.23 V and 200 F g
−1
in aqueous
electrolytes.
2
Biomass-derived porous carbons are considered
the most reliable carbon source due to their low cost,
availability, and sustainability. In recent years, the use of
activated carbons derived from biomass, especially biowaste,
has sparked substantial interest in the energy storage device
community.
7−12
This popularity is primarily due to the
inexpensiveness, sustainability, and abundance of the raw
materials. To date, several biowastes have been utilized to
synthesize activated carbon; however, the applications are still
restricted due to undesirable pore structures. The synthesis
methods play a vital role in controlling the carbonization
process and pore size distributions to meet the required criteria

for supercapacitor applications. The ideal porous carbon for
supercapacitors should possess several key characteristics
including a large specific surface area to accommodate charge
storage, hierarchical pores (micro (<2 nm), meso (2−50 nm),
and macro (>50 nm)) to facilitate fast ion transport diffusion,
and excellent wettability to enhance access of electrolyte ions
to the pores.
13
Waste-activated sludge (WAS) and spent coffee
(SC) are ideal candidates to convert into porous carbon for
energy storage applications due to their high organic content
and their functional groups.
14,15
Tremendous amounts of WAS
(45 million tons) and SC (15.33 million tons) are generated
annually around the world, which will end up mostly in
landfills.
16,17
Landfilling these biowastes releases greenhouse
gases including 28.644 million tons of carbon dioxide and 21
million tons of methane annually.
18,19
Hence, converting waste
to activated carbon for energy storage applications could solve
environmental issues related to waste landfilling. The hydro-
philic nature of WAS and SC due to their surface functional
groups makes the material wettable with aqueous electrolytes
and rapid ion diffusion to the pores, which results in obtaining
a higher capacity.
Traditional transformation routes of biomass to porous
carbon materials involve corrosive chemicals such as hydrogen
fluoride (HF), potassium hydroxide (KOH), and zinc chloride
(ZnCl
2
), which also hinder the economic feasibility, environ-
mental friendliness, and scaling of the processes.
20−24
For
instance, Li et al. synthesized porous carbon from oily sludge
using HF pretreatment, KOH as the activation agent, and
hydrochloric acid (HCl) for the washing step, which resulted
in producing different hazardous waste streams.
25
Also,
utilizing the microwave-assisted process for porous carbon
synthesis is not applicable to large scale due to challenges such
as the lack of uniform heating, safety concerns (thermal
runaway), and energy distribution (limited penetration depth
of microwaves).
26
The production process of activated carbon
needs to be eco-friendly and easy to scale up. Therefore, it is
imperative to use environmentally friendly alternatives for
activating chemicals such as sodium thiosulfate, carbonate salts,
and molten salts (e.g., potassium chloride and sodium
chloride).
27
Utilization of flammable organic electrolytes (e.g., tetrae-
thylammonium tetrafluoroborate (TEA-BF4) in propylene
carbonate or acetonitrile) in EDLCs causes numerous safety
issues. In addition, traditional aqueous electrolytes such as
sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide have limited operating
potential to 1 V.
25,28
Hence, the supercapacitors made with
conventional electrolytes have a low energy density (<10 Wh
kg
−1
).
25
To develop high-energy-density and eco-friendly
supercapacitors, it is essential to use a green electrolyte with
a wider operating potential window (>1 V), which can
maintain capacity for a long operating time (>10,000 cycles) in
a coin cell.
In this study, a green, facile, and scalable route of production
of activated carbon from WAS and SC waste was developed by
using sodium thiosulfate, potassium carbonate, and trisodium
citrate as the green activation agents. Notably, no prior studies
have explored the synthesis of porous carbon from mixtures of
WAS and SC waste using these specified chemicals. The effects
of the activation agents with a molten salt aid (e.g., potassium
chloride), mixing method, and operating temperature on the
physiochemical properties of the activated carbons were
evaluated. The electrochemical performance of supercapacitors
made with synthesized activated carbon was investigated by
incorporating different binding materials into a traditional
aqueous electrolyte. It is worth noting that in this study, a
green electrolyte (sodium acetate) with a wide operating
potential window (∼1.5 V) was used to obtain a high-energy-
density supercapacitor. The kinetic and mass transfer processes
were examined using cyclic voltammetry with an ultrafast scan
rate ranging from 20 to 1000 mV s
−1
and electrochemical
impedance spectroscopy, respectively. To the best of our
knowledge, no prior studies have investigated the long-term
stability test as well as the kinetic and mass transfer process of
a biomass-based supercapacitor using a sodium acetate
electrolyte.
2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
2.1. Materials. Sludge samples were taken from the
Lubbock, Texas, wastewater treatment plant after centrifugal
drying, the last step in the process before landfill disposal.
Spent coffee samples were obtained from premium roast
McCafe ́ after filter brewing. Both spent coffee and sludge
samples were dried in an oven (Across International) at 100
°C overnight (24 h). Sodium thiosulfate pentahydrate
(Na
2

·5H
2
O, 99.7%, Fisher Scientific), potassium carbo-

ABSTRACT
Carbon materials have the advantages of large surface area, high conductivity and stable chemical properties, 
and are widely used in the field of electrochemical energy storage. However, carbon materials currently have 
some problems such as high cost, complicated process and poor electrochemical performance. The development 
of low cost, environmental friendly and high specific capacitance porous carbon materials is of great significance 
for large-scale production and application. In addition, renewable, low-cost biomass materials are ideal pre -
cursors for the preparation of porous carbon materials. In this work, porous carbon materials were synthesized 
using ginkgo leaves as carbon source and KHCO
3 
as activator. The effect of activator mass on the structure and 
composition of porous carbon was studied in detail. The results show that when 3 g activator is added, the 
prepared carbon material (GCK-3) has a specific surface area of up to 2640 m
2 
g
� 1 
and a rich hierarchical pore 
structure (including micro, medium and large pores). In addition, the carbon material retains a certain amount of 
the heteroatoms of the biomass itself, which can generate additional pseudocapacitance. Due to the advantages 
of composition and structure, GCK-3 shows good electrochemical performance and rate performance. A sym -
metric supercapacitor assembled from two identical GCK-3 electrodes has an energy density of 13.7 Wh kg
� 1 
and 
exhibits good cycle stability with a capacitor retention rate of 100 % after 10,000 cycles. The green and low-cost 
carbon source precursor, simple synthesis method and excellent electrochemical properties all indicate that 
ginkgo leaf derived carbon materials have great application prospects.
1. Introduction
With the increasingly prominent resource and environmental prob -
lems, the development and demand of electronic equipment and new 
energy vehicles are increasing rapidly, and the development of low-cost 
and high-performance energy storage equipment has become particu -
larly important [ 1 , 2 ]. Supercapacitors have the characteristics of high 
power density, high coulomb efficiency and long cycle life, which are 
the energy storage devices concerned by many researchers [ 3 – 5 ]. 
Electrode materials play an important role in the electrochemical per -
formance of supercapacitors, and also involve the manufacturing cost of 
supercapacitors [ 6 ]. Therefore, the development of low-cost and 
high-performance electrode materials has become one of the main 
research goals of supercapacitors as energy storage devices.
Porous carbon materials have high surface area, high porosity, 
excellent electrical conductivity and chemical stability, and can be used 
as high-performance electrode materials for supercapacitors. At present, 
porous carbon materials mainly composed of micropores and small 
mesoporous are widely used as electrode materials [ 7 , 8 ]. However, 
porous carbon materials often have poor pore structure and closed 
pores, which is not conducive to the improvement of electrochemical 
properties [ 9 , 10 ]. To solve this problem, the pore size distribution of

preparing porous carbon, which can convert the precursor into porous

ever, it is highly corrosive and easy to form K
2

3 
with carbon mate -
rials, resulting in lower yield [ 14 ]. Relatively speaking, KHCO
3 
is less 
corrosive, low cost, and the melting point is also low, and it can also 
regulate the pore distribution of carbon materials through redox reac -
tion. At present, the preparation of carbon materials using KHCO
3 
as an 
activator has been reported. For example, Li et al. prepared 
iron-modified porous carbon with carbon spheres/nanoplate structure, 
but the preparation process is complicated and is not conducive to 
large-scale production [ 15 ]. Manyala et al. prepared porous carbon 
composed of micropores and mesoporous, but the electrochemical per -
formance was poor [ 16 ]. Feng et al. prepared hierarchical porous car -
bon, but the preparation process is complicated and the reaction 
conditions are harsh [ 17 ].
As a carbon precursor, biomass has the advantages of low cost, no 
pollution, rich resources, etc., and has been widely used in various fields 
(such as adsorption of contaminated water, electrochemical sensors, 
energy storage, supercapacitors, etc.) [ 18 – 20 ]. Among them, ginkgo 
leaves are mainly composed of cellulose, protein, carbohydrates and a 
small amount of inorganic minerals. These substances can provide het -
eroatomic (such as N, S, O) self-doping for carbon materials, which can 
affect the charge distribution of the carbon material, thus forming active 
regions on the surface of the carbon material [ 21 ]. In addition, ginkgo 
leaves have a special structure, and the porous skeleton of its derived 
carbon material can be considered to be composed of carbon nanosheets 
[ 22 ]. Therefore, carbon materials derived from ginkgo leaves should 
have broad application prospects in the field of supercapacitors.
As mentioned above, the mass production and application of porous 
carbon materials are limited due to its complex process, harsh reaction 
conditions and poor electrochemical properties. In order to solve these 
problems, we have chosen a low-cost, renewable ginkgo leaves as a 
precursor and a simple preparation method to synthesize porous carbon 
materials for supercapacitors. The structure-activity relationship be -
tween the structure composition and electrochemical properties of 
porous carbon materials was revealed by exploring the effects of pore 
structure, specific surface area and heteroatoms on electrochemical 
properties. This work has important theoretical significance and prac -
tical application value for the preparation of low cost and high perfor -
mance porous carbon.
2. Experimental
2.1. Synthesis of electrode materials
The purity of the chemical reagents in this experiment was analytical 
grade. Ginkgo leaves come from the same tree in Shanxi Normal Uni -
versity, and the leaves are in the same batch to ensure the consistency of 
the material, so the experimental data obtained have good compara -
bility. The preparation process of porous carbon materials is shown in 
Fig. 1 . First, the ginkgo leaves are washed with deionized water and 
dried. The ginkgo leaves are ground into powder through a grinder and 
passed through a 200-mesh sieve. The sifted 2 g powder was put into a 
nitrogen-protected tube furnace and carbonized at 750 
◦
C for 3 h. The 
heating rate is 5 
◦
C min
� 1
. The obtained product was stirred in 100 mL 2 
M HCl solution for 12 h, and then washed with deionized water several 
times until the pH of the supernatant was neutral. The final product is 
dried at 60 
◦
C, and the resulting carbon material is labeled GC. For 
comparison, 2, 3 and 4 g KHCO
3 
were added to 2 g ginkgo leaf powder, 
respectively. After mixing evenly, it is carbonized in a tube furnace. 
Other experimental conditions remained unchanged, and the obtained 
products were labeled as GCK-2, GCK-3 and GCK-4, respectively.
Structure characterization and electrochemical testing were written 
down in Supporting Information.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Structure and morphology
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of ginkgo leaf derived carbon ma -
terials are shown in Fig. 2 a. All samples show a wide peak at 2 θ = 26
◦
and a weak peak at 2 θ = 44
◦
, corresponding to the (002) and (101) 
crystal faces of the graphite structure (JCPDS No. 41 – 1487), respec -
tively. The diffraction peak at 2 θ = 26
◦
is wider, indicating that the 
prepared carbon material mainly contains a large amount of amorphous 
carbon. The diffraction peak of the carbon material at 2 θ = 7
◦
represents 
the ordered structure of the graphene layer [ 23 ]. Among them, GC and 
GCK-3 have weak diffraction peaks at 2 θ = 7
◦
, and GCK-2 and GCK-4 
have strong diffraction peaks at 2 θ = 7
◦
, indicating that the ordering 
of the graphene layer in GC and GCK-3 is lower than that in GGK-2 and 
GCK-4.
Fig. 2 b shows the Raman spectrum of carbon materials. The D band is 
the characteristic peak of amorphous carbon, and the G band can indi -
cate the distribution degree of sp2 hybrid carbon atoms in carbon ma -
terials, and the intensity ratio (ID/IG) is usually used to measure the 
disorder degree of carbon materials [ 24 ]. In general, a larger ID/IG 
value indicates that the sample has more defects; a smaller ID/IG value 
indicates that the electrons in the sample are easily transported [ 25 ]. 
The figure shows that the ID/IG values of KHCO
3
-activated samples are 
all lower than GC, indicating that electrons are more easily transported 
in KHCO
3
-activated samples. Table S1 shows the Raman shifts in the 
D-band and G-band in different samples (Supporting Information). 
Among them, GCK-3 has the largest blue shift, indicating that it has the 
largest defect density, which is conducive to increasing the electro -
chemical active site [ 26 ]. In addition, the Raman peaks of GC and GCK-3 
are very sharp, indicating the presence of multilayer graphene in the 
sample, which is consistent with the XRD test results [ 27 – 31 ].
Fig. 2 c shows fourier transform infrared spectrophotometer (FTIR) 
analysis of ginkgo leaves and carbon materials. The figure shows that 
ginkgo leaves have a large number of functional groups, for example, the 
peaks at 1318, 1620, 1737 and 2925 cm
� 1 
correspond to C-H, C = C, C = O 
and methyl or methylidene, respectively. The wide peaks at 1070 and 
3426 cm
� 1 
represent the presence of a large number of OH [ 32 ].

Abstract: This study successfully demonstrates the synthesis of foxtail millet carbon-
activated (FMCA) materials using a two-step carbonization process from foxtail millet husk
(FMH). The pre-carbonized biomass-derived millet husk was chemically activated with
KOH at 500 ◦C and subsequently carbonized in an inert argon atmosphere at 800 ◦C in a
tubular furnace. XRD analysis revealed a diffraction peak at 2 θ = 23.67◦, corresponding
to the (002) plane, indicating the presence of graphitic structures. The Raman analy-
sis of FMCA materials showed an intensity ratio (I G/ID) of 1.13, signifying enhanced
graphitic ordering and structural stability. The as-prepared FMC and FMCA electrode
materials demonstrate efficient charge storage electrochemical symmetric devices. Elec-
trochemical analysis revealed the charge–discharge curves and a specific capacitance of
Csp (FMC//FMC) 55.47 F/g and (FMCA//FMCA) 82.94 F/g at 0.5 A/g. Additionally, the
FMCA//FMCA symmetric device exhibits superior performance with a higher capacity
retention of 94.89% over 5000 cycles. The results confirm the suitability of FMCA for en-
ergy storage applications, particularly in electrochemical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs),
making it a promising material for next-generation supercapacitors.
Keywords: foxtail millet husk; biomass; activated carbon; energy storage; supercapacitor
1. Introduction
Energy storage technologies are rapidly evolving, particularly with advancements
in supercapacitors, also known as ultracapacitors, also known as electric double-layer
capacitors, which rely on the rapid and reversible adsorption and desorption of ions at
the electrode–electrolyte interface to store and release energy [1–3]. Recent developments
in symmetrical carbon-based materials have demonstrated significant improvements in
cycle life and performance for both electric double-layer capacitors (EDLC) and pseudo-
capacitance, leading to enhanced efficiency in energy storage systems [ 4,5]. In recent
years, the utilization of metal oxide nanomaterials has unveiled favorable redox behavior,
contributing to long-lasting performance with minimal capacity loss even after thousands
of charge–discharge cycles [6,7]. Meanwhile, biomass hard carbon derived from biomass
and activated carbon materials have emerged as promising alternatives due to their scalable
production, high porosity, and exceptional surface area [8]. These bio-derived carbon-based
hard nanomaterials are essential in optimizing charge storage mechanisms, significantly
Nanomaterials 2025, 15, 575 https://doi.org/10.3390/nano15080575
Nanomaterials 2025, 15, 575 2 of 18
improving both the efficiency and lifespan of supercapacitor devices [ 9]. By leveraging
their unique structural properties and high conductivity, they facilitate faster charge and
discharge cycles while maintaining stable performance over time. This results in more
durable, energy-efficient supercapacitors, contributing to the development of advanced
energy storage technologies with a lower environmental impact [10].
In recent years, agro-waste bio-derived activated carbon is a versatile material that
has garnered significant attention in the field of energy storage due to its high surface
area and porous structure [ 11]. These porous and higher surface properties have the
capacity to store energy through the formation of electric double layers at the carbon–
electrolyte interface [12]. The production of activated carbon from waste materials offers
the use of acid- and alkaline-based surface modifications for a sustainable and cost-effective
approach [13,14]. It is a compelling choice for various energy conversion and storage
applications, particularly supercapacitors, resulting in improved energy density and power
density in supercapacitor devices [ 15]. Various types of activated carbons, including
those commercially available, typically have lower porosity and surface activation than
biomass-derived carbons [16,17]. Biomass-derived carbons exhibit superior surface reaction
capabilities and increased porosity, which promote enhanced ionic storage when activated
with alkaline-based agents such as NaOH, H 3PO4, FeCl 3, and ZnCl 2 [18,19]. Biomass
waste products, often discarded, can be repurposed through large-scale chemical activation
methods to produce high-performance activated carbons. Among various techniques,
alkaline activation, particularly using KOH, combined with pretreatment and thermal
pyrolysis (typically between 600 and 1200 ◦C), significantly enhances surface area and
porosity [20–23].
In addition, alkaline activation converts agricultural and other waste materials into
bio-derived activated carbon materials, offering a sustainable approach for electrode fabri-
cation [24]. Such bio-derived carbons are highly promising electrode active materials for
application in symmetric supercapacitors, batteries, and energy conversion systems due to
their low cost, environmental benefits, and exceptional electrochemical properties [25–28].
Utilizing agro-waste for carbon production thus provides a dual advantage: waste man-
agement and the development of efficient energy storage materials [29]. There are several
biomass agro-waste products utilized with a wide range of applications [30–36].
Among them, foxtail millet husk (FMH) is a rich source of various bioactive com-
pounds that are rich in fiber content. It contains significant amounts of phenolic compounds,
flavonoids, and other phytochemicals that can impact its thermal stability and reactiveness
during activation [37,38]. Its major constituents include cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin
of the plant-available content of silica/silicon [39]. After KOH activation, chemical acti-
vation with KOH allows for the transformation of foxtail millet husk into highly porous
activated carbon. In this process, KOH not only serves as a chemical agent that enhances
pore formation but also increases the total surface area of the resultant carbon material,
often exceeding 1200 m 2/g [40]. The thermal carbonization process typically occurs at
high temperatures, around 600 to 800 ◦C, where biomass undergoes pyrolysis to produce
biochar, thus concentrating carbon content [41].
Foxtail millet husk (FMH) is one such agro-waste product that is reported as having
antioxidant, acetylcholinesterase, and α-glucosidase inhibitory activities [42]. FMH waste
is converted into energy in eco-friendly supercapacitor applications. Foxtail millet husk
(FMH), as ground millet seeds, was once discarded as agro-biomass, but nowadays it is
utilized by researchers as next-generation supercapacitors. The thermally activated carbon
that transforms FMH into a high-performance electrode material redefines sustainability in
energy storage. From FMH, activated bio-derived carbon finds new life in clean energy
applications. The activated carbon has good physicochemical properties essential for

ABSTRACT
Biomass-derived porous carbon (PC) has emerged as a promising candidate for electrode materials in energy 
storage applications, effective pretreatment of the precursor is a key strategy for enhancing the electrochemical 
performance of PC. However, challenges remain in achieving this goal through environmentally friendly, simple, 
and efficient methods. In this paper, a dual-frequency ultrasonic-assisted enzymolysis strategy combined with 
carbonization-activation method was proposed to prepare high-performance garlic peel-derived PC (DUGPC) for 
supercapacitors. Gentle and effective sonobiocatalysis facilitates microstructural regulation and composition 
management of the precursor, granting DUGPC an impressive specific surface area (SSA, 3006 m
2
/g), improved 
pore distribution, low metal impurity content (less than 100 ppm) and high wettability. As anticipated, DUGPC 
demonstrates excellent specific capacitance (408.77 F/g at 1 A/g) and rate performance (retention is 81.8 % at 
50 A/g) surpassing most recently reported biomass-based PCs. In addition, the assembled aqueous symmetric 
supercapacitor achieves an excellent energy density of 15.78 Wh kg
� 1 
at a power density of 50.04 W kg
� 1 
with a 
remarkable cycle stability of 95.5 % after 10,000 cycles at 5 A/g, and the assembled 2.8 V high-voltage organic 
supercapacitor even exhibits an ultra-high energy density of 58.96 Wh kg
� 1 
at a power density of 139.86 W kg
� 1
. 
Significantly, this dual-frequency ultrasonic-assisted enzymolysis strategy is expected to be applicable to various 
biomass wastes and promotes the high-value utilization of biomass in the field of energy storage.
1. Introduction
With the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, the demand 
for energy storage devices continues to emerge in this process due to the 
intermittency of certain clean energy sources, such as wind and solar 
power [1 – 5] . Different from the generally short service life and safety 
risks of batteries, supercapacitors have gradually become one of the 
most promising energy storage technology solutions due to their merits 
of outstanding power density, long cycle life and high reliability [6,7] . 
Electrode materials are a critical component of supercapacitors which 
determine their performance, and porous carbon (PC) has become the 
mainstream choice due to its large specific surface area (SSA), abundant 
source, low price and stable chemical properties [8 – 10] . Biomass, 
including plants, animals and their biodegradable components, is 
considered one of the sustainable and environmentally friendly 
candidates for commercially viable PC precursors [8,11] .
Due to their natural micro-layered structure, PCs with well- 
developed pore structure can typically be obtained from biomass 
(such as scallion peel [12] , sorghum [13] , feather finger grass flower 
[14] , corn straw [15] and walnut shell [16] , etc.) through chemical 
activation, eliminating the need for expensive template methods. 
However, most natural plant cell walls are primarily composed of lignin, 
cellulose and hemicellulose. Lignin serves as a binder, forming a stable 
cross-linked structure between cellulose and hemicellulose. This rigid 
structure, along with its barrier effect, impedes the infiltration of acti -
vators during the carbonization-activation process, resulting in limited 
activation efficiency and porosity [17,18] . Consequently, the micro -
structure of customized precursors before carbonization-activation 
through pretreatment, especially chemical pretreatment, has been 
extensively studied. For example, Yakaboylu et al. used KOH aqueous

solution to chemically pretreat Miscanthus grass to control the micro -
structure, chemistry and active functional groups [19] . Hu et al. con -
structed PC with high porosity by degrading portions of lignin and 
hemicellulose with a mixture of Na
2
SO
3 
and NaOH solutions [20] . While 
chemical pretreatment is effective, biological pretreatment (degrada -
tion) is a notably greener, more sustainable, and simpler approach.
At present, many researchers have reported biodegradation based on 
fungi to prepare PCs, including yeast [21] , Pleurotus ostreatus [22] , 
Neurospora crassa [23] and Trichoderma [24] . However, the harsh cul -
ture conditions and environmental factors affecting microorganisms 
have led to increased interest in enzymes with similar effects, such as 
cellulase and amylase. For instance, Peng et al. treated wood with 
cellulase to form a large number of prefabricated micropores to prepare 
layered porous carbon plates, which exhibited excellent catalytic ac -
tivity in oxygen reduction and oxygen evolution reactions [25] . Wang 
et al. developed carbon materials from cottonseed meal using a 
straightforward enzymolysis strategy with cellulase, the optimized PC 
has a multistage porous structure with high O doping and delivers a high 
specific capacitance of 364 F/g [26] . These findings suggest that cellu -
lase pretreatment enhances the porosity of PCs while offering the ad -
vantages of being green and scalable. Additionally, ultrasound, a 
common enhancement technology in the biological field, is widely 
employed to assist in processes such as organic solvent extraction and 
enzymolysis, improving extraction efficiency and yielding greater 
product quantities [27 – 29] . Nevertheless, there have been few studies 
on the preparation of high-performance PC from biomass using 
ultrasonic-cellulase synergistic pretreatment to date.
Shandong is the leading garlic-producing province in China, with an 
annual output of approximately 4 million tons. It has been reported that 
solid waste, such as garlic peels generated during garlic production, 
accounts for about 22 – 27 % of the total output [30] . Therefore, efficient 
disposal and utilization methods for this waste are urgently needed. In 
this study, we utilized garlic peels as a carbon source to prepare PCs with 
ultra-high SSA as a supercapacitor electrode, employing a dual- 
frequency ultrasonic-assisted enzymolysis strategy. The effects of enzy -
molysis temperature and ultrasonic frequency on the performance of 
PCs were analyzed, and the potential synergistic mechanism of ultra -
sound and cellulase pore-forming was elucidated in this paper. Hence, 
the resulting PC exhibits ultrahigh SSA, competitive capacitive perfor -
mance and energy density that exceed those of previously reported 
biomass-based PCs. Overall, the ultrasound-assisted enzymolysis strat -
egy proposed in this work is expected to be extended to common plant 
precursors, and holds significant promise for developing high- 
performance energy storage materials with controlled pore structures.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials
The raw material (garlic peel) was a thin layer that wraps around the 
garlic clove and sourced from the plantations in Shanghe County, Jinan

China. Cellulase (50 U/mg, obtained from Shanghai yuanye Bio- 
Technology Co., Ltd) was produced through the fermentation of Tri -
choderma viride and other excellent strains. The inert protective gas 
utilized in the experiment is high-purity nitrogen ( > 99.999 %) provided 
by Jinan Deyang Special Gas Co., Ltd. (Shandong, China), and the 
single/dual-frequency ultrasonic generator is a laboratory ultrasonic 
cleaner manufactured by Yunyi Ultrasonic (Shenzhen) Co., LTD (China).

The washed garlic peel was placed in a drying oven at 105

2.2.3. Dual-frequency ultrasonic-assisted cellulase pretreatment

T
) and micropore vol -

micro

Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) method and t-plot method respectively. 
Moreover, the measurement of micropores was based on the Horvath-

ABSTRACT  
The effective strategies to increase the energy density of carbon-based supercapacitors are increasing the specific 
surface area (SSA) and heteroatom doping, however the methods to achieve such outcomes are often time- 
consuming and complicated. Herein, a time-saving and facile method was adopted to fabricate hierarchical 
carbonized wood electrodes with both delignification and partly dissolution/regeneration through NaOH/thio -
urea solution followed by carbonization. The partial dissolution/regeneration treatment not only generates the 
interconnected network structures on the surface of the regenerated wood and improves the porosity, but also 
achieves the efficient co-doping of nitrogen/sulfur heteroatoms. A relatively excellent activation was achieved by 
dissolving for only 3 h, with a SSA of 1416.25 m
2
/g, which was 2.86 times higher than the SSA of the samples 
carbonized directly with delignified wood. Remarkably, the as prepared electrode exhibits superior areal (spe -
cific) capacitance of 6.11 F/cm
2 
(413.6 F/g, 1.0 mA/cm
2
) and durability (98.9%, 12,000 cycles, 50 mA/cm
2
). In 
addition, a symmetrical supercapacitor (SSC) assembled from carbonized regenerated wood has an excellent 
energy density of 1.15 mWh/cm
2 
(51.24 Wh/kg) at a power density of 699 mW/cm (31.11 W/kg). This facile 
doping and activation method may be able to provide a new concept for the carbon electrode preparation of bio- 
based materials.   
1. Introduction 
As one of the most widely used electrochemical energy storage de -
vices, supercapacitors (SCs) performing a crucial function in electro -
chemical storage and release of energy due to their potentially high 
electrochemical efficiency, long operating life, and certifiable safety ( Fu 
et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022 ). The output performance of SCs is heavily 
relevant to the electrode substances. Carbon-based electrodes were 
regarded as promising electrode for SCs due to the presence of large 
specific surface area (SSA), adjustable pore size distribution and high 
electrical conductivity ( Wang et al., 2019b; Yang et al., 2022 ). Unfor -
tunately, the low energy density of carbon-based electrode is the major 
obstacle towards the flexible application due to the lack of structure 
optimization and control of surface properties. Therefore, finding a 
simple way to optimize the structure and control surface properties of 
carbon-based material electrodes can achieve energy density 
improvements. 
Lignocellulosic biomass-derived materials are encountering the most 
flourishing moment due to their versatile properties and wide potential 
applications( Shen and Sun, 2021 ). Controllable preparation of ligno -
cellulosic biomass-derived materials, development of new methods to 
prepare novel biomaterials from lignocellulose, and provision of envi -
ronmentally friendly, low-cost and easily scalable lignocellulosic func -
tional materials are essential to achieve carbon neutrality( Kang et al., 
2021 ). Woody biomass possesses a rich source, a wide variety, low cost, 
degradable, renewable, and a significant anisotropic and hierarchical 
structure, allowing it to be applied directly to SCs without the use of 
other conductive agents or adhesives ( Daotong et al., 2023 ). However, 
wood has a diversity of chemical components and structural complexity 
( Zhao et al., 2020 ). Due to the different distribution of the three major 
components including cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin ( Schubert 
et al., 2022 ), the uneven decomposition of the three components during

the direct carbonization of the natural wood leads to uneven conduc -
tivity and pore distribution in the thick cell walls, which results in still 
unsatisfactory electrochemical properties ( Wang et al., 2021c; Wang 
et al., 2021d; Zhang et al., 2019a ). Therefore, reducing the 
non-uniformity of conductivity and pore distribution due to the 
complexity of the wood itself is the valid methods to enhance the elec -
trode performance. In contrast to the classic bottom-up method of 
delignification in the paper and pulping industry, the top-down 
approach allows the embedded lignin to be removed from the wood 
cell wall structure while maintaining the natural anisotropic structure. 
The carbonization of wood after delignification will minimize the 
inhomogeneous pore structure produced by the complexity of the wood 
and facilitate the regulate the charge/ion transport pathway. 
The large SSA provides active sites that can retain electric charges. 
For instance, in our previous work, the delignified wood carbon elec -
trode obtained by controlling the carbonization temperature and the 
multi-stage carbonization process had a high SSA of 945.09 m
2
/g, this is 
significantly higher than the 357.25 m
2
/g of natural wood and 481.05 
m
2
/g for delignified obtained by one-stage carbonization, its capaci -
tance was 211.3 F/g (0.5 A/g), far exceeding the natural carbonized 
wood (20.6 F/g)( Luo et al., 2022a ). That is, the electrochemical per -
formance is improved by the electric double layer capacitances (EDLC) 
mechanism( He et al., 2022b ). Therefore, the activation of carbon pre -
cursors before or during the carbonization process is one of the effective 
means to increase the SSA. Wang et al. prepared carbonized wood 
through delignification followed by enzyme treatment, the pore gener -
ation was controlled by controlling the ratio and treatment time be -
tween cellulase and delignified wood. The obtained electrode had a high 
SSA (1418 m
2
/g), capacitance (328 F/g, 1 mA/cm
2
) and the assembled 
SSC can achieve areal/volumetric energy density of 0.21 mWh 
cm
� 2
/0.99 mWh cm
� 3 
and durability (86.58%, 15,000 cycles)( Wang 
et al., 2021c ). N, S could cause electron density imbalance and improve 
carbon surface activity due to the electronegativity difference between 
atoms( He et al., 2022a ; Wang et al., 2023 ). The surface functional 
groups could provide additional pseudo-capacitance via redox reaction, 
thus improving the weight capacitance( Lyu et al., 2023 ). Importantly, 
the introduction of heteroatoms into the carbon structure could enhance 
surface polarity and wettability could further overcome the limitations 
of carbon in structure, surface performance and electrochemical per -
formance ( Ma et al., 2020 ). However, the methods that can simulta -
neously achieve an increase in SSA and heteroatom doping were often 
complex, time-consuming and could not be obtained in one step. For 
example, Tang et al. first achieved the doping of N and S double atoms 
by soaking a mixture of delignified wood and trithiocyanuric acid so -
lution, then two high-temperature carbonizations in N
2 
and NH
3
, 
respectively, were performed to obtain larger SSA. The obtained wood 
carbon electrode had a high SSA (1438 m
2
/g), the specific capacitance 
(704 F/g, 0.2 A/g) and superior oxygen reduction reaction performance 
( Tang et al., 2018 ). Therefore, in order to boost the output performance 
of biomass-based carbon, we are very interested in a simple and versatile 
strategy that enables a combination of activated pore generation and 
regulation surface properties. 
Herein, an effective method was adopted to fabricate hierarchical 
carbonized wood electrodes with both delignification and partly disso -
lution/regeneration through NaOH/thiourea solution followed by 
carbonization. The delignification is to obtain a more uniform hierar -
chical structure, and the process of dissolution regeneration of the 
NaOH/thiourea reagent system is also a process of activation and het -
eroatom doping. A relatively high activation effect was achieved in three 
hours, and the SSA obtained after carbonization was 1416.25 m
2
/g, 
much higher than that of 494.89 m
2
/g for direct carbonization after 
delignification. In addition, the doping of N,S double heteroatoms in -
creases the surface wettability and improves the defects and graphiti -
zation degree of the carbon structure. Therefore, the structure of this 
regenerated wood makes it an outstanding substrate for multi- 
functionalities, which makes up for the defects of traditional 
activation and doping methods and opens new opportunities for the 
development of supercapacitors. 
2. Experiment sections 
Detailed preparation and electrochemical test methods were 
included in the Supporting Information . 
3. Result and discussion 
A schematic diagram is shown in Fig. 1 , where we describe the entire 
procedure of converting waste Larch (Natural wood, NW) to a carbon 
material through delignification, regeneration and thereafter carbon -
ization, followed by assembly into a symmetrical supercapacitor (SSC) 
device. First, delignification and bleaching methods were mentioned in 
our previous study (process I) to obtain delignified wood (TW)( Luo 
et al., 2022b ). After delignification, NaOH/thiourea solution was 
introduced to dissolve a portion of the wood cell wall. Regenerated TW-x 
(RTW-x) was obtained after regeneration and drying of the dissolved cell 
walls in ethanol, where the x represents the time of dissolution (process 
II). Specifically, NaOH can not only penetrate the microcrystals but also 
enter the microcrystals to destroy the cellulose molecules, thiourea as 
blockers can prevent the recombination of cellulose molecular chains, 
the synergistic effect enables cellulose to achieve activation and the 
introduction of N and S atoms. NaOH/thiourea solvent is an effective 
inorganic solvent for dissolving cellulose, and NaOH is considered to be 
a useful activator, so the activation and two-element doping can be 
achieved very skillfully by this method. It is worth noting that this 
method has the advantage of being rapid and safe compared to con -
ventional activation and doping methods. RTW-x was carbonized under 
inert gas (N
2
), also to gain conductive carbon wood with extensive 
surface area (Process III), and carbonized RTW-x (CRTW-x) was ob -
tained. This is expected to achieve excellent capacitive performance by 
regulating N/S content and improving porosity through partial dis -
solution/regeneration while preserving the wood microtubule structure. 
3.1. Characterization of RTW-x 
From the physical object displayed in Fig S1a and b, it can be seen 
that compared to NW, the color of TW becomes white due to the removal 
of a large amount of lignin. Particularly, given its outstanding lignin 
solubility, cellulose protection, and low energy consumption, formic

lignocellulosic feedstock ( Wang et al., 2019a ). In addition, the dual 
solvent system is formed by formic acid and water with the character -
istic of a high azeotropic point, which is 107. 6 º C at 101.3 kPa pressure, 
and easy recovery with distillation ( Luo et al., 2022b ). Additionally, 
deep eutectic solvent (DES) is an emerging candidate as compared to 
others due to its high efficiency, recoverability, biodegradability, and 
has a low cost of preparation ( Kesari et al., 2022 ; Sirvio et al., 2015 ). 
DES is expected to be an efficient solvent for obtaining delignified wood 
directly from wood by the "Top-down" method. After dis -

dried RTW did not change significantly. When the dissolution time was 
longer than 3 h, however, RTW crumples after drying, which is detri -
mental to the establishment of wood-based hierarchical porous mate -
rials. Fig. 2 a. ( Fig S2a ) shows the scanning electron microscope (SEM) 
images of TW that presented a more closed block structure. Differently, 
after one hour of dissolution, RTW-1 exhibits a slight volume of pore

interwoven network appeared on the cell wall of RTW-2. RTW-3 shows 
the anisotropic multi-channel structure of the wood is preserved, and in 
the lumen with a nanofiber network is the result of regeneration 
( Fig. 2 d). The original channel structure of RTW-3 facilitates the for -

ABSTRACT
By virtue of its abundant availability, diverse structures, renewability, and cheapness, the rational utilization of 
biomass waste to synthesis porous carbon with a great specific surface area (SSA), high porosity, and superior 
electrochemical capabilities holds substantial significance for energy storage. In this research, waste bamboo 
fibers with a vascular bundle structure were selected as precursors. The porosity and conductive characteristics of 
the materials (ACK-x, x represents the activation temperature) were controllably adjusted by altering the KOH 
activation temperature. The findings suggest that the material ’ s notable expansion in SSA is linked to the rise in 
activation temperature. Notably, ACK-700 has a SSA of up to 2768 m

the structure, which demonstrated outstanding capacitive properties of 492 F g
� 1 
at 0.5 A g
� 1

resistance values (the resistance value for charge transfer as low as 0.81 Ω ) in the three-electrode system. ACK- 
700 demonstrated a capacitive performance of up to 283 F g
� 1 
when assembled into a symmetrical device, 
achieving a high density of energy of 9.82 Wh ⋅ kg
� 1 
while possessing an excellent power density of 123.15 W 
kg
� 1
. The capacitance preservation was 89.44 %, and the Coulomb efficiency reached 100 % after 2000 charge- 
discharge cycles. Most importantly, we successfully demonstrated the practical viability of these materials by 
powering a 2.2 V LED bulb for 20 min using three such symmetrical supercapacitors connected in series. This

Waste bamboo fiber-based porous carbon was prepared from waste 
bamboo fiber as a carbon source after low-temperature carbonization 
with KOH as an activator. Then, the bamboo fiber-based porous carbon 
was characterized and assembled into a symmetric supercapacitor, 
which electrochemical performance was tested and the energy storage 
mechanism was analyzed.
1. Introduction
In view of the irreversible and progressive reduction of fossil fuels, 
developing renewable energy sources have emerged as effective strate -
gies to address the crisis of environmental damage and global warming. 
However, the key issue for the development of renewable energy is the 
availability of high efficiency, affordable and sustainable energy storage 
facilities [ 1 – 3 ]. Supercapacitors (SCs) stand out among other novel en -
ergy storage technologies owing to their affordability, fast responsive -
ness, superior power density, and simple operating environment [ 4 – 6 ]. 
SCs are prevalent utilized in sensors, industrial automation equipment ’ s 
auxiliary power supply, power grid energy storage devices, and new 
energy vehicle power systems [ 7 , 8 ]. On the basis of their energy storage 
techniques, SCs are grouped into pseudocapacitors using redox reactions 
and electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) utilizing physical 
adsorption. Conductive polymers or metal oxides, which typically have 
inadequate cycling stability, are exemplary pseudocapacitors electrodes. 
Despite the fact that these materials increase the device ’ s energy den -
sity, chemical reactions cause the electrode material ’ s structure to 
deteriorate over time, leading to diminished cycling stability [ 9 ]. In 
contrast to pseudocapacitors, EDLCs employ excellently conductive 
carbon materials as electrodes. Among them, the most popular electrode 
material for EDLCs is porous carbon because of its rich pore structure, 
high conductivity, and extensive active specific surface area (SSA). 
These characteristics typically confer excellent capacitive performance 
and robust cycling stability [ 10 ].
Raw materials are a decisive factor in determining the characteristics

of carbon materials [ 11 ]. Currently, majority of porous carbon is based 
on fossil fuels as precursors, which not only costly but also detrimental 
to the environment. Converting biomass into high-quality carbon-based 
electrode materials is of great relevance, particularly in the context of 
achieving “ dual carbon ” goals. Furthermore, biomass has evolved a 
natural spatial structure over hundreds of millions of years, which is 
crucial for energy storage. Biomass waste has become increasingly 
notable due to its renewable, environmentally friendly, and widely 
available sources, such as sargassum [ 12 ], bagasse [ 13 ], walnut shell 
[ 14 ], lotus flowers [ 15 ], and eggshells [ 16 ]. These materials offer 
promising potential for developing advanced energy storage technolo -
gies. It is estimated that biomass waste contributes approximately 10 % 
to the total global energy supply [ 17 ], and the total amount of exploit -
able biomass resources in China is currently equivalent to about 700 
million tons of standard coal. The utilization of waste biomass is not 
optimized in many developing countries due to differing levels of 
awareness about the circular economy and limitations in technological 
capabilities. Consequently, waste biomass is primarily disposed of 
through direct burning for heating, returning to fields, composting, or 
use as fodder. This singular approach to disposal not only results in low 
utilization rates but may also increase greenhouse gas emissions and 
contribute to environmental pollution. Converting it into superior per -
formance, potential porous carbon materials through suitable processes 
holds far-reaching significance for eco-environmental protection and 
sustainable energy development. This approach not only mitigates waste 
but also contributes to the development and implementation of green 
energy strategies.
Among the plethora of biomass waste resources, bamboo stands out 
as one of the fastest-growing plants globally. China, often referred to as 
the “ Kingdom of Bamboo ” , boasts the richest bamboo resources, the 
largest bamboo industry, and the most advanced processing and utili -
zation technologies in the world. During the processing of the bamboo 
industry, a significant amount of bamboo fiber waste is generated. These 
wastes are typically incinerated, leading not only to a squandering of 
resources but also to the emission of large quantities of pollutants such 
as carbon monoxide and dust. This results in severe environmental and 
atmospheric pollution. In fact, bamboo produces incredibly rich 
vascular bundle structures during its fast growth [ 18 ]. Furthermore, 
because of its abundant lignin component, bamboo is a superb precursor 
for carbon materials. Khuong et al. [ 19 ] successfully prepared porous 
carbon materials from bamboo and its solid residue after hydrothermal 
treatment as precursors, which were activated by carbon dioxide and 
showed good adsorption capacity when used as carbon dioxide adsor -
bents. Huang et al. [ 20 ] prepared bamboo-derived carbon-based com -
posites by one-step pyrolysis reaction, which showed excellent 
performance in the field of electromagnetic wave absorption. Yue et al. 
[ 21 ] prepared bamboo-based carbon materials by pre-oxidation and 
secondary carbonization, which exhibited an electrochemical capacity 
of 321 F/g in 6 M KOH electrolyte. Qiu et al. [ 22 ] investigated the role of 
cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin in bamboo chips on supercapacitor 
electrode materials using bamboo chips from a bamboo chopsticks 
processing plant as a carbon source. However, bamboo ’ s structural 
stability results in the retention of several cell wall remnants upon 
carbonization, which limited the material ’ s application in electrode 
materials by producing undeveloped pores, a low SSA, and suboptimal 
capacitance characteristics.
Researchers have developed a variety of synthesis methods to 
enhanced the capacitive properties of biomass carbon, such as activa -
tion, template method, hydrothermal method, molten salt method [ 23 ]. 
Among these methods, activation stands out as a traditional and efficient 
technique for generating porous carbon. Specifically, the original carbon 
skeleton of the biomass can be preserved while producing high-quality 
materials with rich porosity and appropriate distribution by carbon -
ization followed by chemical activation [ 24 ]. Among various chemical 
activation agents, KOH activation is particularly effective in producing 
materials with large SSA and well-distributed aperture, making it a 
widely used activator in the industry. Biomass porous carbon with a 
controllable pore structure can be obtained by carefully adjusting the 
parameters of KOH activation. Bag et al. [ 25 ] investigated the effects of 
KOH concentration and temperature on the properties of porous carbon 
derived from oak wood and prepared carbon materials with a surface 
area comparable to that of commercial activated carbon. Balasu -
bramanian et al. [ 26 ] produced porous carbon from banana leaves by 
adjusting the KOH activation temperature and used it as an electrode 
material for supercapacitors. At a current density of 0.3 A/g, the specific 
capacitance value could reach 391.3 F/g. Zheng et al. [ 27 ] regulated the 
pore structure of kapok flower-based porous carbon by changing the 
ratio of KOH to the precursor. The specific surface area of the porous 
carbon with the optimal ratio could reach 1904 m
2
/g, demonstrating 
excellent electrochemical performance.
In this study, porous carbon materials were generated using waste 
bamboo fibers from paper mills as precursors. Following temperature 
carbonization, the impact of KOH activation process on the micro- 
morphology, porosity, carbon microcrystal content, and electro -
chemical performances of the bamboo fiber-based porous carbon were 
examined. Finally, the material with optimal performance was assem -
bled into symmetric supercapacitors to assess its practical application 
potential. This study is significant in alleviating the problem of resource 
wastage of biomass waste and facilitating the advancement of superior 
supercapacitors.
2. Experiment
2.1. Materials
Waste bamboo fibers from the Anhui paper industry were selected 
for this study. The elemental composition of waste bamboo fibers is 
presented in Table S1 of the Supplementary Information. Sinopharm 
Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd provided the KOH and HCl (36 % – 38 %), 
which were used without additional purification. We bought acetylene 
black and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) from Tianjin Avision Chemi -
cal Technology Co., Ltd.
2.2. Porous carbon preparation from bamboo fiber waste
Waste bamboo fiber-based porous carbon was prepared through a 
sequence of processes including pretreatment, temperature carboniza -
tion, and KOH activation. At first, deionized water was used to wash the 
waste bamboo fibers to get rid of any surface contaminants, then dried, 
and subsequently ground to a 100 mesh size using a crusher to obtain 
waste bamboo fiber powder. 5 g of waste bamboo fiber powder was 
placed in a porcelain boat and compacted. Then it was put into the 
center of a tube furnace. Under a nitrogen atmosphere with a flow rate of 
0.2 L/min, the temperature was progressively elevated from ambient 
temperature to 550 
◦
C at a heating rate of 5 
◦
C/min. This heating rate is 
designed to promote uniform and orderly pyrolysis of the sample, con -
trol the release rate of volatile matter, and lay the foundation for sub -
sequent activation [ 28 – 30 ]. After then, the temperature was kept at 
550 
◦
C for 2 h. This temperature can effectively reduce the loss of carbon 
content and improve the activation efficiency [ 31 , 32 ]. The carbonized 
waste bamboo fibers were collected once they had cooled to ambient 
temperature, and termed as PC, with a yield of approximately 22 %. To 
proceed with activation, 1 g of PC was ground and mixed with 4 g of

Novel onion flower-derived biochar for high-performance sustainable 
supercapacitor applications
Felix A. Kwarteng

KOH-activation
Supercapacitor
ABSTRACT
Onions, scientifically known as Allium cepa L., are commonly used as a vegetable and offer a variety of health 
benefits. However, this study explored a novel part of the onion plant, such as the flower seed cover often 
regarded as waste, by converting it into biochar (BC) via pyrolysis. Through careful optimization and activation 
with potassium hydroxide, the resulting novel biochar exhibited a unique graphitic nanosheet-like structure with 
an impressive surface area of 2538.31 m
2
/g. To serve as a control, rice straw, one of the most commonly used 
biomasses, was also activated using the same protocol. Various techniques, including XPS, HRTEM, SAED, FTIR, 
BET, XRD, and Raman, were used to comprehensively understand the surface and structural properties of the 
biochar. When the novel biochar was tested as an energy storage material, it exhibited a specific capacitance of 
200.37 F/g at 1 A/g and 143.82 F/g at 5 A/g in a 1 M H
2
SO
4 
electrolyte with a three-electrode system. In a two- 
electrode system, it showed 158 F/g at 1 A/g and 102 F/g at 5 A/g, indicating its effectiveness at high rates. The 
long-term cyclic stability analysis demonstrated 100 % capacity retention over 1000 cycles in the three-electrode 
system, and 90.77 % and 74.40 % retention after 5000 cycles and 10,000 cycles, respectively, in the two- 
electrode system. The fabricated symmetric supercapacitor yielded a power density of 500 W/kg and an en -
ergy density of 21.94 Wh/kg at a current density of 1 A/g. These findings provide valuable insights into the 
valorization of biomass in addressing concerns regarding the current energy storage dilemma.
1. Introduction
It is reported that the natural world produces about 50 billion tons of 
land-based biomass each year. Out of this, about 16.7 billion tons are 
used for human purposes, such as feed for livestock, food, grazing, and 
specialized crops for other purposes. What is left off after the con -
sumption of these 16.7 billion tons is about 8.1 billion tons, which can be 
sustainably harvested and recycled into value-added products [ 1 ]. 
However, due to logistical and operational challenges, many of these 
biomasses are left untouched, eventually becoming a menace to the 
environment [ 2 ]. Owing to the high cost of commercially activated 
carbon and the vast tonnages of agricultural biomasses that pile up in the 
environment, scientists have resorted to the valorization of this agri -
cultural biomass waste into biochar to be more economical and sus -
tainable due to the abundance of biomass in the environment [ 3 ].
Biochar is a beneficial substance notably rich in carbon and lignin, 
produced under oxygen-deprived conditions via the thermochemical 
conversion of biomass [ 4 ]. Many plant-based agricultural residues are 
regarded as waste, and human approaches to dealing with this waste 
tend to pollute the environment. A practical and environmentally sus -
tainable way of managing these tons of agricultural waste is by pyro -
lyzing the waste in an anoxic environment to produce biochar [ 5 ]. The 
properties of biochar, such as its large surface area, surface functional 
groups, high porosity, and stability, make it a viable alternative for
