energy applications [ 6 ]. These essential properties are predominantly 
established by the type of feedstock used, the treatment processes 
employed, and the conditions under which pyrolysis occurs.
Furthermore, the drastic depletion of non-renewable fossil fuels for 
energy has become a growing concern, and there is a massive advocacy 
to unearth the potential of renewable resources as a replacement for this 
fossil fuel [ 7 , 8 ]. However, this would need time to come to full light. In 
the meantime, supercapacitors have been introduced as the future of 
energy storage devices [ 9 ]. Many researchers have employed varieties of 
agricultural biomasses such as, corn straw [ 10 ], pinecone [ 11 ], rice 
straw [ 12 – 15 ] rice husk [ 16 ], and peanut shell [ 17 ] into forming biochar 
for supercapacitor applications [ 18 ]. Amongst these, rice straw is one of 
the most commonly used biomasses; hence, it was employed as a control 
sample in this study while detailed attention was given to the novel 
biomass. To strike a balance between cost and performance, agricultural 
biomass has been converted to activated carbon to fabricate electrodes, 
commonly referred to as electric double-layer capacitor (EDLC), for 
supercapacitor applications [ 19 ]. However, these biomass-derived 
electrodes suffer from low energy densities and low-rate capabilities 
but are powerful at possessing high power densities and good cycling 
stability [ 20 ] Additionally, the literature reveals significant variations in 
converting these biomasses into carbonaceous materials for super -
capacitor applications, resulting in prolonged processing times, 
increased energy consumption, relatively low capacitances, and the 
utilization of diverse chemicals for each technique.
For instance, a study conducted by Musyoka et al. [ 21 ] explored the 
transformation of onion peel first into hydrochar, followed by pre ‑ car -
bonization and finally activation using KOH in an argon environment. 
This process yielded porous carbon material that showed promise for 
applications in supercapacitors. Similarly, Dai et al. [ 22 ] investigated 
the synthesis of activated carbon from argy wormwood using two 
different chemicals, H
3
PO
4 
and KOH for supercapacitor applications. In 
a different approach also, García-Mateos et al. [ 23 ] developed activated 
carbon electrodes from lignin fibers through H
3
PO
4 
activation using an 
electrospinning technique. Subsequently, the electrodes underwent 
thermal stabilization at 200 
◦
C, carbonization at 900 
◦
C, and O
2 
treat -
ment under a moderately oxygen-containing N
2 
atmosphere. However, 
it should be noted that these sequential steps in the production process 
of activated carbon led to an increase in its energy consumption and 
lengthened the overall process.
To bridge the deficiencies in EDLC's several researchers have 
developed supercapacitors as a composite of biomass and metal oxides 
known as pseudocapacitors [ 24 – 26 ]. These developed pseudocapacitors 
also tend to increase production costs, and the incorporation of metal 
oxides is also non-renewable sources, thus having a mix of forward and 
backward steps towards attaining sustainable energy. Additionally, 
doping of biochar with heteroatoms such as nitrogen, boron, sulfur, and 
phosphorus also tend to improve the EDLC's energy density while 
maintaining its power densities. However, to some extent, these doping 
strategies distort the characteristic morphology of the developed bio -
char and do not largely improve capacitances in all cases. Hence, con -
stant research about the optimization of EDLC is imperative. To achieve 
optimal energy storage, it is important to have electrode materials that 
possess a high surface area, a good combination of micro and mesopores, 
and a characteristic morphology. This enables the electrode to have a 
large number of active sites, allows for fast transfer of ions from the 
electrolyte to the porous electrode, and provides good cycling proper -
ties, ultimately resulting in a high specific capacitance.
Recently, there has been a rise in the demand for fresh onions, both 
for consumption and medicinal purposes. As a result, onions have 
become the second most important horticultural crop, with around 47 
million tons cultivated annually [ 27 ]. However, onion cultivation also 
produces approximately 500,000 tons of waste each year in Europe [ 21 ]. 
Because onion peels have a strong smell and are unsuitable for landfill 
disposal, finding ways to use them is essential. Many researchers have 
focused on the peel of onions as agricultural waste, but the woody 
biomass that houses the flower seeds has been neglected. This results in 
waste from the flower seed covers, which could be transformed into a 
high-value-added product using optimal processing techniques. More -
over, despite the abundance of onion peels, they also have quite a good 
yield when pyrolyzed, and this could be an added reason for their wide 
usage. For example, Musyoka et al. [ 21 ] made porous carbon from onion 
peel by converting it to hydrochar, pre ‑ carbonizing it, and further 
activating it with KOH in an argon atmosphere for supercapacitor 
application. Krishnappa et al. [ 28 ] and Prajapati et al. [ 29 ] also 
employed onion peel biomass by converting it to biochar to treat a va -
riety of textile dyes, including MB, MO CR, and Cr (VI), of which it was a 
success. It is, therefore, essential to mention that there is currently no 
accurate data on the quantity of biomass generated by onion flower seed 
covers. However, it is known that waste is produced with every onion 
plant harvested. In future studies, research will be conducted to explore 
the potential of this unique biomass in greater detail, and accurate sta -
tistical data will be made available. Until then, this work lays the 
groundwork for fully exploring this unique agricultural biomass.
This study, therefore, explored the chemical activation of novel 
onion flower seed cover and rice straw biomasses via optimal temper -
ature, ramping rate, and mix ratio. The study investigated the suitability 
of the developed biochars as energy storage devices in a three-electrode 
and two-electrode setups. Various analytical techniques, including cy -
clic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge/discharge (GCD), electro -
chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), capacitance retention, and 
response time, were thoroughly investigated. The study placed greater 
emphasis on the novel biochar's surface and structural properties, with 
rice straw serving as the control due to its common use as biomass. 
Consequently, this study makes noteworthy contributions to the field of 
converting innovative agricultural biomasses into high-performance 
supercapacitors for sustainable electrochemical energy storage.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
Potassium hydroxide (KOH, 85 – 100 %), hydrochloric acid (30 – 33 % 
assay), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), sulphuric acid (H
2
SO
4
, 97 %), and N- 
Methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP, 98 %) were purchased from Loba Chemie. 
Graphite foil (99.8 %) was purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific, 
Germany. Carbon black (super p Timcal) and polyvinylidene difluoride 
(PVDF) were also purchased from Sigma Aldrich, Germany. Electrolyte 
solutions, samples, and chemical reagents were cleaned using de-ionized 
water. Onion flower seed cover and rice straw were obtained from local 
supplies in Egypt.
2.2. Processing and development of biochar
After collecting the cover of onion flower seeds (OFSC) and rice straw 
(RS) biomasses, the two were cleaned using de-ionized water to elimi -
nate any dirt or other impurities. The cleaned samples were then dried 
for 24 h at 100 
◦
C in a Binder dry oven. Once dried, the samples were 
ground into fine particles using an RRH-500AK grinder and sieved 
through an aperture of 106 μ m. Next, 7 g of the samples were pre ‑ car -
bonized in a muffle furnace under continuous nitrogen gas at 10 
◦
C/min 
for 2 h at 600 
◦
C and designated as onion flower seed cover biochar 
(OFSCBC) and rice straw biochar (RSBC). After that, the samples were 
impregnated with KOH in a 5:1 ratio, sonicated, and refluxed at 65 
◦
C 
before being activated at 900 
◦
C for 2 h under a continuous nitrogen gas 
flow with the rate of heating set at 10 
◦
C/min. After activation, the 
samples were purified effectively using a rigorous 2-hour wash with 100 
ml of 2 M HCl, followed by rinsing with de-ionized water until the pH 
level reached neutrality. The biochars were then dried for 24 h at 100 
◦
C, 
resulting in the successful development of activated onion flower seed 
cover biochar (Act_OFSCBC) and activated rice straw biochar 
(Act_RSBC) ( Scheme 1 ).

RESEARCH ARTICLE
A comparative study on porous activated carbon derived
from waste biomass with varying oxygen functionalities as
supercapacitor electrodes
Atika | R. K. Dutta
Department of Chemistry, Indian Institute
of Technology Roorkee, Roorkee, India
Correspondence
R. K. Dutta, Department of Chemistry,
Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee,
Roorkee 247667, India.
Email:
r.dutta@cy.iitr.ac.in
Funding information
UGC-DAE-CSR-KC/CRS/19/
TE09/1077/1093
Abstract
Activated carbon derived from biomasses with different oxygen-bearing chemi-
cal constituents has been explored as supercapacitor electrode. The rice straw
(RS) and eucalyptus wood biomasses were selected owing to their contrasting
composition of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin contents. The activated car-
bons of these biomasses are obtained by pyrolysis at 550
/C14 C followed by thermal
activation (700 /C14 C) after treatment with optimized KOH. The specific capaci-
tance of RS-based activated carbon (ACRS-700), measured from galvanostatic
charging-discharging studies at 0.5 A g /C0 1, is much higher (eg, 365 F g /C0 1) than
that of ACEW-700 (168 F g /C0 1). The higher specific capacitance of ACRS-700 is
attributable to: (i) significantly higher surface area (3345 m 2 g/C0 1) comprising
of interconnected micro- and mesoporous structure; (ii) porosity of about
2.0 cm
3/g; and (iii) oxygen-rich hemicellulose contents. The possible charge
storage mechanism in ACRS-700 has been discussed. The real-time application
of ACRS-700 has been demonstrated by lighting up red LEDs using ACRS-
700//ACRS-700 symmetric supercapacitor device, operated with aqueous and
freshly synthesized [Bu 4N+][NO3
/C0 ] ionic liquid as electrolytes. The maximum
energy density (42.7 Wh kg /C0 1) and the power density (1.9 kW kg /C0 1) for ionic
liquid electrolyte are favourable for supercapacitor applications.
KEYWORDS
biomass, charge storage mechanism, porousactivated carbon, supercapacitor electrode,
symmetric supercapacitor device
1 | INTRODUCTION
About 50 billion tonnes of biomasses are generated annu-
ally and these are mostly derived from agriculture and
forestry sources. Management of such huge quantities of
waste biomasses has been a challenging task from envi-
ronment and climate change perspective. There has been
a continuous effort for finding sustainable technology to
utilize this organic carbon-rich waste for generating
wealth, including valuable technological products.
1 In
this regard, conversion of plant-derived waste biomasses
intoactivated carbon has been a lucrative option. This has
been well-studied as adsorbent for environmental
applications.2,3 Lately, porousactivated carbon from
waste biomasses has revealed very promising result as
carbon-based supercapacitors (SCs) to meet the drastic
demand in the energy sector.
4-6 The carbon-based SCs
offer promising futuristic prospect as efficient energy-
storage device(s) due to their fast charging-discharging,
durable cycle life, high-power delivery capabilities, and
Received: 5 October 2023 Revised: 22 November 2023 Accepted: 10 December 2023
DOI: 10.1002/est2.554
Energy Storage. 2024;6:e554. wileyonlinelibrary.com/journal/est2 © 2023 John Wiley & Sons Ltd. 1o f1 6
https://doi.org/10.1002/est2.554

environmental friendliness. 7-9 These types of carbon
materials as SCs correspond to electrical double-layer
capacitors (EDLCs) and store charge via adsorption/
desorption of electrolytic ions at the electrode-electrolyte
interface and offer high power density.
10 The favorable
features of activated carbon (AC) as SCs are associated
with relatively higher electrical conductivity, large spe-
cific surface area with tunable pores, favorable electro-
chemical and thermal stability, and mechanical
properties.
11 The carbon materials, operated at higher
potential as compared to the transition metal-based mate-
rials such as metal oxides(CoO), metal
sulfides(Cu
2MoS4), metal carbides (Fe 3Mo3C/Mo2C), and
metal borides (CoB, NiB, NiCoB). 12-15 Moreover, the scal-
able manufacturing of porousactivated carbon from bio-
mass waste is a feasible option that is lucrative for
production of largescale SCs to meet the requirement of
energy production. In this scheme, one can avoid the
commonly employed strategy of managing large quanti-
ties of agro and forestry wastes via open field burning,
which leads to environmental pollution.
Some of the common biomasses used for developing
supercapacitor electrodes include eucalyptus wood, bam-
boo, rice husk, rice straw, tea leaves, coconut husk,
bagasse from sugarcane, and eucalyptus bark.
16-20 Among
them, rice straw contains some traces of silica along with
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. The silica is expected
to combine with lignocellulose to produce matrix of high
chemical and thermal stability.
21 While on the other
hand, eucalyptus wood-derived AC with hierarchical
porous structure has also been explored for preparation
for supercapacitor application. It is one of the most com-
mon and widely planted species found in 90 countries of
our world due to its rapid growth rate and renewable
availability.
22 Though several methods including
microwave-based heating are available for the prepara-
tion of AC, but direct heating of biomasses for carboniza-
tion at higher temperature has been a preferred one
owing to its ability to process large quantities of bio-
mass.
23 The electrochemical studies of these ACs are pri-
marily focussed on the effect of pore dimensions and
consequential increase in specific surface area as salient
factors for EDLC-type SCs. However, the chemical com-
position of the AC tends to vary due to differences in the
constituents of their source biomasses. This may impact
on the structural and morphological features of the AC,
which consequently alter their electrochemical proper-
ties. For example, lignin-rich biomasses are rich in oxy-
gen functionalities and may act as natural oxygen
dopants in the corresponding AC and might improve
electronic conductivity, surface wettability, and electro-
chemical reactivity at the carbon electrode/electrolyte
interface for accessing electrolyte ion and favor the
charge accumulation capacity.
24 This is consistent with
higher specific capacitances exhibited by carbonaceous
materials doped with heteroatoms, owing to higher
charge densities in dopants of higher electronegativity
than carbon.
25 These studies are mostly based on
nitrogen-doped carbon materials. While supercapacitor
electrodes made with oxygen-functionalized carbona-
ceous materials are less studied. Moreover, the oxygen
functionalities might offer additional redox property-
based pseudocapacitive characteristics for further
enhancing the charge storage process and could also
improve charge migration due to more polar electrode
surface and enhanced wettability of the electrolytes.
26
Looking at these advantages, biomasses with different
chemical composition were chosen for synthesizing
oxygen-rich AC as supercapacitor electrode materials.
The porous and oxygen-enriched AC of these biomasses
were obtained by carbonization method via direct heating
in inert condition. It is followed by alkali-treated thermal
activation. KOH activation is chosen for laboratory scale
due to its low activation temperature and it produces AC
with well-defined micropore distribution, large micro-
pore volume, and a very high surface area. Moreover,
metallic potassium in the carbon matrix expands the
space between carbon atomic layers, and leads to the pro-
duction of more porosity.
27 Several studies on porous AC
obtained from rice straw show high specific capacitance
and the results are attributed to favourable EDLC-based
charge storage owing to formation of very high surface
area. It is however not very clear why rice straw-based
AC exhibits such high surface area while AC derived
from other biomass sources does not. It could be due to
variation in the chemical composition of the biomasses,
particularly in terms of their cellulose, hemicellulose, lig-
nin, ash, and extractives. It is worth studying the correla-
tion of AC derived from strikingly different compositions
of biomasses with their charge storage properties. In view
of this, we have selected two biomasses, that is, rice straw
and eucalyptus wood of strikingly different composition
with respect to lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose to pre-
pare AC for understanding the correlation between com-
position of biomasses and their effect on charge storage
property.
The electrochemical properties of AC obtained from
rice straw and eucalyptus wood biomasses are studied in
a three-electrode set-up. The neutral aqueous electrolyte
(2 M NaCl) has been used, as the acidic and alkaline elec-
trolytes are associated with evolution of H
2 or O 2 gases
when operated at larger potential window and may affect
the stability of the electrode materials in device opera-
tion.28 Besides, ionic liquid-based non-aqueous electro-
lyte has been explored here to achieve higher energy
density requirement by virtue of their ability to operate

Synthesis of mesoporous carbon from banana peels
with silica gel 60 as the hard templates †
Dinda P. N. Nahda, a Aﬁten R. Sanjaya, a Fitria Rahmawati, b Anne Zul ﬁa,c
Afriyanti Sumbodja, d Respati K. Pramadewandaru, e Yuni K. Krisnandi, a
Zico A. Akbar *a and Tribidasari A. Ivandini *a
The synthesis of mesoporous carbon was successfully performed through solid –solid phase reaction
employing banana peel powder as the carbon source and silica gel 60 (SG-60) as the hard template. The
synthesis was initiated by hydrothermal heating to introduce the banana powder to SG-60 surface,
followed by the carbonization process to form the mesoporous carbon. FTIR, Raman, XRF, and XRD
characterization con ﬁrmed the success of the carbonization step, while N
2 physisorption and TEM
characterization con ﬁrmed the mesoporous structure formation of the synthesized carbon with the
template. At an optimum carbon-to-silica precursor ratio of 3 : 1, the synthesized carbon with SG-60
templates proceeds to a speci ﬁc surface area of 476.97 m 2 g−1, which is around 55-fold higher than the
one synthesized without any template. Furthermore, evaluation of the capacitance performances was done
by creating composite electrodes with nickel foam as the support and polyvinylidene di ﬂuoride as the
binder. The evaluation was carried out using cyclic voltammetry in 3.0 M KOH, galvanic charge –discharge,
and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy con ﬁrming a high correlation between the speci ﬁcs u r f a c e
area and the speci ﬁc capacitance. The banana peels-derived mesoporous carbon demonstrates a speci ﬁc
capacitance value of 23.1 F g
−1, measured using the cyclic voltammetry method. Good stability of the
prepared electrode over 2500 voltammetric cycles was also demonstrated, indicating that the use of SG-
60 as the hard template is suitable for synthesizing carbon with mesoporous structure from biomass.
Introduction
Porous carbon materials have been established as a common
material for many applications, including pollutant adsor-
bents,
1,2 supporting catalysts,3 and electrode materials 4,5 due to
their high surface area, good electrical conductivity, high
chemical and physical stability as well as their versatility. 6 To
date, various types of porous carbon materials such as powders,
bers, and tubes have been reported,
7 and extensive methods
have been developed to produce these types of materials. 8
Meantime, mesoporous carbon attracts great attention due to its
advantage in high specic surface and porous volume, providing
low-resistant pathways for the ions through the porous particles.
8
This property is very useful to increase the performance of
carbon as adsorbents, catalysts, or electrodes. Moreover, the pore
structure of mesoporous carbon is uniform and can be
controlled depending on the applications. The optimum pore
structures are supposed to possess smaller pores interconnected
with larger sets of pores, which could achieve high surface area
and eﬃ cient ion di ﬀusion pathways simultaneously.
9
Furthermore, the use of a hard template is one of the
promising strategies to produce a mesoporous structure. The
high stability and good space-con ned e ﬀect of the hard
template can produce the structure of the nal target materials
to perfectly replicate the morphology of the template.
10 A
common example of a hard template for mesoporous carbon
synthesis is silica-based materials, such as SBA-15, 11 MCM-41,12
and MCM-48. 13 These silica templates are popular because of
their well-de ned and tuneable pore structures, which can be
replicated in the carbon structure. Meanwhile, some e ﬀorts to
use more economical hard templates to synthesize mesoporous
carbon have been reported, such as zeolites, clays, and calcium
carbonate.
14–16 Notably, the use of silica gel 60 (SG-60) as a hard
template to synthesize the mesoporous carbon with sucrose as

volume.17 SG-60 refers to a speci c grade of silica gel commonly

On the other hand, biomass materials ( i.e. paper, food waste,
leaves, wood, and leather products) generally abundant, renew-
able, inexpensive, and environmentally benign are potentially
used as precursors to construct high quality carbon materials.
Bananas are the most widely consumed fruits in the world. Based
on data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in
2021, India, China, and Indonesia are the countries where the
highest bananas are produced and consumed. During banana
production and consumption, approximately 40% of the total
banana fruit, in the form of banana peels, is discarded.
18 Banana
peels are rich in nutrients, such as carbohydrates, protein, ber,
and fat. Apart from that, banana peels also contain various
minerals, such as phosphorus, sodium, calcium, iron, magne-
sium, and potassium.
19 The high carbon content in banana peels
has the potential to produce porous carbon materials.
The use of banana peels as the carbon source for producing
activated carbon has been reported to yield a speci c surface
area of 1928 m 2 g−1 aer activation process using ZnCl 2 and
FeCl2.4 Meanwhile, the synthesis of porous carbon from banana
peels, producing a hierarchical material consists of micropores
and mesopores, is reported to yield a speci c area of 1362 m
2
g−1 aer activation process using KOH and ZnCl 2.20 However,
there are limited reports speci cally combining biomass with
hard templates for mesoporous carbon synthesis as this
synthesis involving solid–solid phase reaction. No record shows
the synthesis using hard templates with banana peels as the
carbon source, while studies using similar biomass sources,
such as coconut shells or rice husks, are available.
21,22
Carbon materials have been studied for various applications,
including applications in supercapacitors. Numerous publica-
tions have reported the development of carbon-based materials
for this purpose. The synthesis of porous carbon material is
reported to achieve a speci c capacitance of 74 F g
−1.23
However, the modi cation of carbon materials, such as mixing
with cerium-doped NiO nanocomposite and with MnO 2 nano-
particles can provide signi cant enhancement of the speci c
capacitance to be comparable with conductive polymer, such as
polyaniline (PANI) or metal-based materials, such as NiMoO
4
nanorods.24–27 This remains a strong demand for the develop-
ment of carbon-based supercapacitors, particularly those
derived from environmentally friendly precursors, such as
biomass waste like banana peels.
In this research, mesoporous carbon was synthesized from
banana peel powder using SG-60 as the hard template. The
synthesis was performed by hydrothermal reaction of banana
peel powder suspension in the presence of SG-60 to introduce
the banana peel powder to the SG-60 surface. A erward, the
banana peel powder-coated SG-60 was carbonized to obtain the
graphitic phase of carbon. Characterization a er removing the
hard template carried out using FTIR, Raman, XRD, and XRF
conrmed the formation of graphitic carbon, while TEM and
N
2-physisorption analyses indicated that the mesoporous
carbon structure was successfully formed. Without any addi-
tional activation, a speci c surface area of 476.97 m
2 g−1 and
a total pore volume of 0.67 cm 3 g−1 was achieved, representing
an approximately 55-fold increase compared to the synthesized
carbon performed without any template. Furthermore, the
electrochemical capacitive performance of the synthesized
mesoporous was investigated by using cyclic voltammetry (CV),
galvanostatic charge –discharge (GCD), and electrochemical
impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The result showed that consis-
tent with its higher surface area, the template-used synthesized
mesoporous carbon provides a signi cantly higher speci c
capacitance than the carbon synthesized without a template.
Moreover, good stability of the speci c capacitance value was
observed. The results suggest that the synthesis of porous
carbon materials from biomass with economical hard
templates is promising to be developed.
Experimental
Materials
The banana peels ( Musa paradisiacal sp.) used in this research
were collected from fried banana sellers in Depok, West Java,
Indonesia. To synthesize the mesoporous carbon, silica gel 60
(SG-60), sulfuric acid (H
2SO4), and ethanol were used, while to
perform the electrochemical analysis, polyvinylidene di uoride
(PVDF), dimethylacetamide (DMAc), and potassium hydroxide
(KOH) were used. Commercial mesoporous carbon was applied
to compare the characteristics and performances of synthesized
mesoporous carbon as a supercapacitor. All these chemicals
were purchased from Merck and used without any puri cation.
Milli-Q water with 18.2 MU cm was used to prepare the solution.
The synthesized mesoporous carbon was characterized using
N
2 adsorption and desorption isotherm at 77 K on a Quantach-
rome Quadrasorb-Evo Surface Area and Pore Size Analyzer. The
surface areas were calculated using the Brunauer –Emmett–
Teller (BET) method, and the pore size distributions were
determined using the Barrett –Joyner–Halenda (BJH) method
from the desorption data. X-ray di ﬀraction (XRD) spectra of the
samples were obtained using a benchtop X-ray di ﬀractometer
(Aeris 600 W with GI-XRD or Heating Stage). Fourier transform
infrared (FTIR) spectra were recorded on a Bruker Alpha II FTIR
Spectrometer, with samples ground with KBr and pressed into
thin wafers. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images
were acquired on an FEI Tecnai G2 20 S-Twin electron micro-
scope, equipped with a eld emission gun at an acceleration
voltage of 200 keV using a LaB6 lament and an Eagle ™ CCD
camera. The Raman spectra were performed using a HORIBA
LabRAM HR Evolution Raman Microscope with a 532 nm laser
beam and 1800 g mm

dried under the sun. Then, the banana peels were cut into small
pieces and pulverized into powder. The powder was ltered

An

−4Among

,6Supercapacitors

electrode surface through electrostatic interaction between the

carbon content, low cost, and environmental friendliness.9
,10Plenty

increasing environmental pollution and carbon emissions. To

Because of their rich availability and sustainability, these
biomass-derived materials have become a research hotspot
widely used in different applications, like catalysts, electrodes,
and absorbents.16

The

southern India, producing nutritious edible seeds, healthy and

Abstract—This research focuses on synthesizing biomass-derived porous carbon materials from soybean straw
and corn cob through a one-step molten salt carbonization -activation method, using three molten salt mix-
tures, namely NaCl–KCl, ZnCl 2–KCl, and ZnCl 2–NaCl, as both templates and activators. The synthesized
carbon materials were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD),
Raman spectroscopy, and Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) analyses. A series of electrochemical measure-
ment techniques were employed to investigate their three-electrode electrochemical performances and the
assembled symmetric supercapacitors. The results indicate that the soybean straw-derived carbon prepared
with the ZnCl
2–KCl mixture (denoted as ZK–S) exhibits a high specific capacitance of 197 F g –1  at a current
density of 0.1 A g –1  in a 6 M aqueous KOH electrolyte. The assembled symmetric supercapacitor device
exhibits a specific capacitance of 155 F g –1 , a power density of 50 W kg –1 , and an energy density of
12.84 W h kg–1  at 0.1 A g–1 . Moreover, the ZK–S carbon demonstrates remarkable cycling stability, retaining
over 105% of its capacity after 10 000 cycles, indicating a promising long cycle life. Therefore, this study
emphasizes the potential of soybean straw-derived carbon materials prepared by the molten-salt carboniza-
tion-activation method in promoting the development of high-performance supercapacitors.
Keywords: soybean straw, biomass-derived carbon, molten salt, supercapacitor, electrode materials

1. INTRODUCTION
With the excessive consumption of fossil fuels and
the increasing depletion of energy resources, carbon
dioxide emissions have been continuously rising,
making global warming increasingly severe. The
energy crisis and environmental crisis pose significant
threats to the survival and development of human
society. To address these issues, it is imperative to vig-
orously develop new technologies for energy conver-
sion and storage [1–5]. Energy storage devices such as
conventional capacitors [6], batteries [7], lithium-ion
batteries [8], fuel cells [9], and supercapacitors [10]
have garnered considerable attention from research-
ers. Among them, supercapacitors are regarded as one
of the most promising energy storage devices due to
their higher power density and superior cycle stability
compared to batteries, as well as higher energy density
than conventional capacitors [11]. Electrode materials
are key components of supercapacitors, and their per-
formance directly affects the overall performance and
efficiency of the energy storage devices [12]. Cur-
rently, carbon materials used in supercapacitors
include graphene [13], carbon nanotubes [14], carbon
nanofibers [15], activated carbon [16], and derived
porous carbon materials [17]. Notably, biomass-
derived porous carbon has gained prominence due to
its wide availability, low cost, and environmental
friendliness [18]. These characteristics enable it to
achieve excellent performance and meet the require-
ments of specific applications.
The energy storage performance of biomass-
derived porous carbon materials is primarily deter-
mined by their structural design. Key structural char-
acteristics include porosity, pore size, pore size distri-
bution, pore diameter, and pore length, all of which
affect the specific surface area, ion transport rate, of
the materials [19–21]. Biomass-derived activated car-
bon is typically prepared through chemical methods,
involving two steps: high-temperature carbonization
and activation. The carbonization process removes
volatile substances and hydrocarbons through high-
temperature pyrolysis, converting organic matter into
carbonaceous residues. The activation stage employs
activators (such as KOH) to construct a porous struc-
ture with a large specific surface area [22, 23]. There-
fore, the design of derived porous carbon structures
requires comprehensive consideration of multiple fac-
tors, such as the selection of precursor materials, car-
bonization conditions, preparation methods, template
types, and subsequent activation treatments. Adopting

green, safe, and sustainable methods for the prepara-
tion of derived porous carbon materials, improving
their energy storage performance, and expanding their
application fields are the key objectives of porous car-
bon materials research in the future.
Molten salt has gained widespread use in the
preparation of porous carbon due to its dual role as a
template and activator, which simplifies the synthesis
process and improves efficiency [24–30]. Wang et al.
[31] employed chitosan as the carbon precursor (raw
material) and LiCl–ZnCl
2 molten salt as the template,
successfully fabricating hierarchically porous nitro-
gen-doped activated carbons via a simple one-step
carbonization method. Under a relatively low molten
salt/chitosan mass ratio (3 : 1) and a moderate calci-
nation temperature (1000 °C), the obtained porous
carbon material achieved a maximum specific surface
area of 1317 m
2 g–1  and a nitrogen content of 5.1 wt %.
Liu et al. [32] employed tobacco waste as the biomass
carbon precursor. The carbon material prepared by
carbonization in molten CaCl
2 at 850°C for 3 h exhib-
its a hierarchical porous structure and ideal capacitive
performance. In a three-electrode system with a 1 M
H
2SO4 aqueous electrolyte, the tobacco waste—
derived carbon delivers a specific capacitance of
196.5 F g –1  at 0.2 A g –1 . Moreover, the capacitance
retention rate remains 94% after 5000 charge-dis-
charge cycles at 0.1 A g –1 . Zhang et al. [33] using
ginkgo leaves as the raw material and CaCl 2–KCl
molten salt as the activator and template, N/S co-
doped porous carbon nanosheets were successfully
prepared. The material exhibits a specific surface area
of 1120 m2 g–1  and a specific capacitance of 318 F g –1
(1 A g–1 ) in a three-electrode system, along with excel-
lent rate capability (82% capacitance retention at
10 A g–1 ). Despite these advancements, most studies
have mainly focused on the structural regulation of a
single molten salt system. However, there is relatively
little research on the effects of molten salt carboniza-
tion and activation in different mixed molten salt sys-
tems and the underlying mechanisms. Therefore, it is
crucial to clarify the role of molten salt carbonization
in pore evolution and structural optimization of bio-
mass-derived carbon across different systems. Fur-
thermore, systematic comparative studies on one-step
molten salt carbonation—activation methods for spe-
cial cylindrical materials like soybean straw and corn
cob in various molten salt systems are still lacking, and
their potential structure-property correlations require
further investigation.
In this study, soybean straw and corn cob were
selected as biomass precursors, and porous carbon
materials for supercapacitor electrodes were prepared
via a one-step molten salt carbonization-activation
method. First, the biomass precursors underwent
impurity removal and washing. Subsequently, three
different molten salt systems, namely NaCl–KCl,
ZnCl
2–KCl, and ZnCl 2–NaCl, were mixed with the
pretreated biomass precursors by ball milling. Then,
the ball-milled mixtures underwent high-temperature
carbonization under an inert atmosphere. As a result,
corn cob-derived porous carbons and soybean straw-
derived porous carbons were obtained in NaCl–KCl,
ZnCl
2–KCl, and ZnCl 2–NaCl mixtures, respectively.
X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, scan-
ning electron microscopy (SEM), Brunauer–
Emmett–Teller (BET) specific surface area analysis,
and electrochemical measurement techniques were
employed to characterize the phase composition,
microstructure, pore size variation, and electrochem-
ical performance of the carbon materials. The pre-
pared corn cob-deriver porous carbons in ZnCl
2–KCl
melt exhibits excellent electrochemical performance
in 6 M KOH aqueous electrolyte, delivering a specific
capacitance of 197 F g –1  at 0.1 A g –1 . The assembled
symmetric supercapacitor achieves a specific capaci-
tance of 155 F g–1 , a power density of 55 W kg –1 , and
an energy density of 12.84 W h kg–1  at 0.1 A g–1 . Addi-
tionally, the influence mechanism of the biomass-
derived porous carbon materials on their electrochem-
ical performance and supercapacitor properties was
discussed.
2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTIONS
2.1. Preparation of Biomass-Derived Porous Carbon
Corn cob powder and soybean straw powder (par-
ticle size: 500 mesh) were used as biomass precursors,
while NaCl, KCl, and ZnCl
2 (analytical grade) were
employed as molten salt. The biomass precursors were
pretreated through sequential cleaning, impurity
removal, and drying steps. Three types of molten salt
mixtures (NaCl–KCl, ZnCl
2–KCl, ZnCl 2–NaCl)
were mixed and calcined at 300 °C for 2 h under N 2
atmosphere to remove moisture and volatile impuri-
ties. In a typical procedure, 30 g of pretreated corn cob
or soybean straw was separately mixed with three mol-
ten salt systems: 150 g of NaCl–KCl (75 g NaCl and
75 g KCl), 60 g of ZnCl
2–KCl (44 g ZnCl 2 and
16 g KCl), and 60 g of ZnCl 2–NaCl (42 g ZnCl 2 and
18 g NaCl). Each mixture was mechanically blended
in a ball mill for 1 h. Subsequently, the mixture was
transferred into a tube furnace and heated to 800°C at
a rate of 5 °C min –1  under a nitrogen flow of
120 mL min–1 . After reaching the target temperature,
it was held for 2 h to ensure complete reaction. The
furnace was then turned off and allowed to cool natu-
rally to room temperature. The resulting black powder
was collected and added to deionized water to remove
impurities. The mixture was stirred at 1200 rpm for 6 h
at room temperature, followed by centrifugation. The
precipitate was repeatedly washed with deionized
water and anhydrous ethanol until the pH reached 6.
The obtained black powder was then dried under vac-
uum at 70°C for 12 h. Finally, the corn cob and soy-
bean straw derived carbons prepared in NaCl–KCl,

1. Introduction
The escalating global energy crisis, resulting from excessive fossil 
fuel consumption and accompanying CO
2 
emissions, has intensified the 
demand for sustainable energy solutions and advanced energy storage 
technologies [1] . Among emerging energy storage systems, super -
capacitors (SCs, also known as electrochemical capacitors) have 
garnered significant scientific attention as hybrid devices bridging the 
performance gap between conventional dielectric capacitors and 
rechargeable batteries [2,3] . These devices feature three distinct ad -
vantages over conventional energy storage systems: exceptional char -
ge/discharge kinetics that enable rapid energy delivery within seconds, 
unparalleled cycle stability exceeding 100,000 cycles with minimal 
capacitance decay, and superior power density (typically 10 – 100 times 
higher than lithium-ion batteries) [4,5] . Particularly, electrical 
double-layer capacitors (EDLCs), which rely on physical charge 
adsorption/desorption at electrode-electrolyte interfaces, demonstrate 
remarkable rate capability and cycling performance compared to pseu -
docapacitive systems [2,6] .
Carbon-based materials, including activated carbon, carbon nano -
tubes, graphene, and carbon fibers, are predominantly employed in the 
design of supercapacitor electrodes due to their tunable physicochem -
ical properties and robust electrochemical stability [7,8] . The perfor -
mance of these materials is principally governed by three critical 
parameters: (i) heteroatom doping configurations, (ii) accessible specific 
surface area (S
BET
), and (iii) hierarchical pore architecture [9,10 ] . 
Strategic incorporation of nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, or sulfur het -
eroatoms into carbon matrices induces electron density redistribution, 
which simultaneously enhances electrical conductivity through 
defect-induced charge carrier mobility and introduces

emerged as sustainable alternatives to conventional carbon precursors,

abundant renewable sources, (ii) intrinsic heteroatom self-doping (N, O,

2.2. Synthesis of PC from Osmanthus fragrans
The Osmanthus fragrans -derived carbon materials were synthesized 
via a controlled thermal activation protocol as depicted in Fig. 1 . Fresh

the dual-activator system (ZnCl

The subsequent thermal treatment was conducted in a horizontal

ABSTRACT: Activated carbon (AC) materials were developed via a single-step method from three different biowaste sources and tailored 
for application in carbon dioxide (CO
2
) capture and electrochemical energy storage, combining the concept of biowaste valorisation with 
sustainable environmental and energy applications. This work investigated the use of three underexplored agro-food waste streams as 
precursors, namely flour mill waste (BW1), old corn waste (BW2), and feed waste (BW3), and performed a systematic comparison of their 
conversion under the same activation conditions, as well as characteristics and performance. The developed AC materials demonstrated 
properties such as high graphitization, favorable pore-structure configuration and surface area, and favorable surface characteristics. CO
2 
adsorption experiments at 298 K showed a capacity of 2.55 mmol/g at 1 bar with stability over multiple cycles for AC2, as well as high CO
2
/ 
N
2 
selectivity, reaching 48 at 1 bar (ideal adsorbed solution theory (IAST)) for a 15:85 v/v CO
2
/N
2 
mixture for AC1, suggesting a high 
selective affinity for CO
2 
capture at ambient conditions. Furthermore, electrochemical experiments revealed stable performance as electric 
double-layer capacitors as a result of low solution and charge-transfer resistance, demonstrating capacitive performance in the order of 250 F/g 
at a scan rate of 5 mV/s for AC3, which was tested at different increasing scan rates and determined to retain a capacitance value higher than 
90 F/g at a high scan rate of 100 mV/s. Galvanostatic charge−discharge (GCD) investigations revealed virtually symmetric charge−discharge 
curves with an acceptable rate capability for a symmetric AC3 full cell, retaining ∼70% of initial capacitance despite a 4-fold increase in current 
density, and preserving ∼78% of initial capacitance after 1000 cycles. These results reveal the potential of agro-industrial waste streams- 
derived AC materials for selective carbon capture and electrochemical energy storage, enabling them a simple, potentially scalable, and 
sustainable material platform for such applications. The key contribution is the processing of three previously underutilized agro-food 
industrial biomass wastes into functional AC materials for energy storage and CO
2 
capture via a single-step KOH activation approach, 
allowing for direct comparison and correlation of precursor chemistry. Furthermore, this provides a solid basis for future precursor-specific 
tuning of KOH loading, activation temperature and time, pore structure, and surface functioning to optimize properties and performance.

1. INTRODUCTION 
Activated carbon (AC) from biowaste is a sustainable and cost- 
effective approach to develop porous materials with tunable 
pore structure, high surface area and surface chemistry.
1 
It bears 
potential for environmental protection and energy storage re-
lated applications, including advanced carbon capture and 
electrochemical supercapacitor systems, because of the avail-
ability of various source materials and the highly favorable 
physicochemical properties of the resulting products.
2,3 
Glob-
ally, agricultural waste generation exceeds 1 billion tonnes

annually, much of which is disposed of through landfilling or

4 
Con-
verting these residues into AC provides a value-added waste 
utilization pathway while lowering disposal costs. Furthermore, 
biomass-derived AC can be produced at costs as low as 
1.34 USD/kg, highlighting its potential as a sustainable and 
economically viable alternative to conventional carbon mate-
rials.
5 
The potential of biowaste-derived AC to function as an 
effective adsorbent for carbon dioxide (CO
2
) capture while also 
demonstrating high electrochemical performance for super-
capacitor applications provides new opportunities to address 
two pressing global challenges: CO
2 
accumulation and energy 
crisis.
6 
This concept also establishes structure−property cor-
relations that can be used to rationally design next-generation 
CO
2 
capture based on electrochemically motivated systems. 
CO
2 
capture has emerged as a vital strategy for minimizing 
the impact of climate change.
5,6 
The buildup and rising con-
centration of CO
2 
in the atmosphere leads to global warming, 
making it vital to develop effective technologies for capturing 
and storing greenhouse gases.
7−10 
Among the various tech-
nologies, selective capture by solid adsorbent systems is a po-
tential technique for CO
2 
capture due to its affordability, ease of 
operation in ambient conditions, and low energy 
requirements.
11,12 
AC, with a high surface area, and adjustable 
pore structure and surface chemistry, has been demonstrated to 
be a suitable adsorbent for CO
2 
capture.
13 
In this context, 
attempts have also been made to develop AC adsorbents from 
various biomass sources. For instance, an AC produced from 
lotus seeds had an adsorption capacity of 3.1 mmol/g at 25 °C 
and 1 bar due to high specific surface area of up to 2230 m
2
/g as 
well as tunable ultra-microporosity.
14 
Pine cone-derived carbon 
showed a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 1.91 mmol/g under 
ambient conditions, owing to well-defined microporous struc-
ture and the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups.
15 
Furthermore, tea seed shells were used to produce AC, which 
was then modified with melamine to add more nitrogen, re-
sulting in a CO
2 
adsorption capacity of 3.15 mmol/g at 25 °C 
and 1 bar due to the presence of a microporous structure with 
nitrogen functional groups.
16 
At 1 bar, the CO
2 
uptake of olive 
stone-derived AC, which was produced using an eco-friendly 
bioorganic method and had a high surface area and ultra-
microporous structure, was 4.33 mmol/g (at 30 °C).
1 
Likewise, 
biochar-derived AC produced via KOH activation demonstrated 
steady CO
2 
breakthrough performance, revealing the impor-
tance of activation and micropore framework tailoring for gas 
separation at practical conditions.
17 
Amazonian fruit waste- 
derived AC with well developed narrow microporosity 
showed 4.81 mmol/g of CO
2 
adsorption at 1 bar and 25 °C.
18 
Building on this concept, multisubstrate agricultural waste- 
based AC prepared from a blend of peanut shells, coffee 
husks, corn cobs, and banana peels demonstrated an adsorption 
capacity of 2.01 mmol/g (8.86 wt %) and a CO
2 
removal ef-
ficiency of up to 96.2%.
19 
Recent investigations have shown that heteroatom-doped 
biomass-derived carbons, such as N,S co-doped and boron- 
doped systems, can further enhance CO
2 
uptake and selectivity 
by introducing additional adsorption sites and modulating the 
electronic characteristics of the carbon framework.
20,21 
Col-
lectively, these studies demonstrate that high surface area, 
abundant ultra-microporosity, and heteroatom functionalities 
are key elements influencing CO
2 
adsorption performance, yet 
the adsorption behavior strongly depends on precursor type and 
synthesis method. Desert biomass wastes have recently been 
identified as interesting precursors for high-performance CO
2 
adsorbents.
22 
Asmaly et al.
23 
synthesized AC from Balanites 
aegyptiaca seed shells and reported a large surface area exceeding 
3000 m
2
/g, resulting in a CO
2 
uptake of 5.2 mmol/g at 25 °C. 
Similarly, AC produced from desert date seed husk via KOH 
activation achieved a surface area of ∼2000 m
2
/g and a CO
2

2
/ 
N
2

agricultural waste valorization for carbon capture applications.
24 
Recent reviews have highlighted that biomass- and waste- 
derived AC with abundant ultra-microporosity and tailored 
surface functionalities can achieve CO
2 
capacities exceeding 
6−9 mmol/g under near-ambient conditions.
25 
This superior 
adsorption performance is primarily governed by the pore size 
distribution and surface chemistry of the AC. In particular, 
narrow micropores and ultra-micropores are highly effective for 
CO
2 
capture because their dimensions closely match the kinetic 
diameter of CO
2 
(0.33 nm), resulting in enhanced adsorba-
te−adsorbent interactions through overlapping adsorption 
potentials.
26 
Thus, at 25 °C and 1 bar, AC enriched with ultra- 
micropores have shown CO
2 
adsorption capacities exceeding 
4−6 mmol/g.
27,28 
On the other hand, supercapacitors, also known as electro-
chemical capacitors, are energy storage devices with high power 
density, cyclic performance, and fast charge−discharge rates, 
making them suitable options for applications requiring rapid

and renewable energy systems.
29,30 
Yet, developing cost- 
effective, high-performance supercapacitors that can meet ris-
ing energy demands remains a challenge. AC is one of the most 
popular materials for supercapacitor electrodes due to its large 
surface area, electrical conductivity, and favorable electro-
chemical characteristics.
31 
Based on this, using biomass as a 
precursor, efforts have been made to generate AC exhibiting

vironmental impact of conventional AC sources.

seeds with the synergistic effects of electric double-layer ca-

3

 Penelitian ini bertujuan mengembangkan elektroda karbon monolitik bebas perekat 
berbasis limbah daun lobak yang berasal dari residu sayuran pasar sebagai prekursor 
biomassa untuk aplikasi superkapasitor dengan fokus pada peningkatan kinerja 
kapasitansi volumetrik. Elektroda karbon disintesis melalui tahapan pra -karbonisasi 
biomassa, pencetakan bertekanan tinggi untuk membentuk struktur monolitik, dan 
pirolisis pada suhu 800 °C dalam atmosfer inert tanpa penggunaan bahan pengikat. Dua 
jenis sampel dikembangkan, yaitu karbon tanpa perlakuan (DLK) dan karbon dengan 
impregnasi awal menggunakan larutan H₃PO₄ sebelum proses karbonisasi (DLK -P). 
Karakterisasi dilakukan terhadap perubahan densitas m aterial, morfologi permukaan, 
serta komposisi unsur untuk memahami pengaruh perlakuan kimia terhadap struktur 
karbon yang terbentuk. Hasil analisis menunjukkan bahwa impregnasi awal H₃PO₄ 
mampu menghasilkan struktur karbon yang lebih homogen dan meningkatk an 
konduktivitas material tanpa mengurangi stabilitas mekanik elektroda monolitik. 
Evaluasi elektrokimia menggunakan metode voltametri siklik menunjukkan bahwa 
elektroda DLK -P memiliki respons kapasitif yang lebih baik dibandingkan elektroda 
tanpa perlakua n. Elektroda DLK -P menghasilkan kapasitansi volumetrik sebesar 109 
F/cm3, meningkat signifikan dibandingkan elektroda DLK yang hanya mencapai 53,4 
F/cm³. Nilai ini menunjukkan potensi kompetitif dibandingkan beberapa elektroda 
karbon berbasis biomassa yang telah dilaporkan sebelumnya. Hasil penelitian ini 
menunjukkan bahwa lim bah daun lobak berpotensi dimanfaatkan sebagai sumber 
karbon berkelanjutan untuk superkapasitor. 
Kata kunci:   limbah organik, karbon padat, elektroda, penyimpan energi,

  ABSTRACT 
 This study aims to develop binder -free monolithic carbon electrodes derived from radish 
leaf waste, originating from vegetable market residues, as a biomass precursor for 
supercapacitor applications with a focus on enhancing volumetric capacitance 
performance. The carbon electrodes were synthesized through a sequence of biomass pre-
carbonization, high-pressure compaction to form a monolithic structure, and pyrolysis at 
800 °C under an inert atmosphere without the use of binders. Two types of samples were 
prepared: untreated carbon (DLK) and carbon with prior impregnation using an H₃PO₄ 
solution before the carbonization process (DLK -P). Characterization was conducted to 
examine changes in material density, surface morphology, and elemental composition in 
order to understand the influence of chemical treatment on the resulting carbon 
structure. The results indicate that H₃PO₄ pre -impregnation produces a more 
homogeneous carbon structure and enhances the electrical conductivity of the material 
without compromisi ng the mechanical stability of the monolithic electrode. 
Electrochemical evaluation using cyclic voltammetry shows that the DLK -P electrode 
exhibits a superior capacitive response compared to the untreated electrode. The DLK -P 
electrode delivers a volumetric capacitance of 109 F/cm3, significantly higher than the DLK 
electrode, which only reaches 53.4 F/cm3. These results demonstrate that radish leaf waste 
has strong potential as a sustainable carbon source for supercapacitor electrodes. 
Keywords:   organic waste, solid carbon, electrode, energy storage, supercapacitor

1. PENDAHULUAN 
Pengembangan perangkat penyimpan energi elektrokimia berkelanjutan menjadi kebutuhan strategis seiring meningkatnya 
tuntutan energi bersih dan konsumsi sumber daya yang bertanggung jawab. Superkapasitor berbasis karbon menempati posisi 
penting dalam penciptaan teknologi ini karena stabilitas siklus yang tinggi dan kemampuan pengisian cepat [1]. Dalam beberapa 
tahun terakhir, karbon turunan biomassa telah dieksplorasi secara luas sebagai material elektroda alternatif yang ramah 
lingkungan dan ekonomis, menggantikan karbon sintetis konvensional berbasis sumber fosil [2]. 
Berbagai sumber biomassa telah dilaporkan sebagai prekursor karbon untuk superkapasitor seperti limbah akasia [3], rotan 
[4], kulit manggis [5], kulit singkong [6] dan limbah buah [7].  Namun demikian, sebagian besar studi tersebut masih berfokus 
pada optimasi kapasitansi gravimetrik menggunakan elektroda berbentuk serbuk yang dicampur dengan bahan perekat polimer 
dan kolektor arus tambahan. Pendekatan ini seringkali tidak merepresenta sikan performa perangkat secara realistis karena 
keberadaan komponen non -aktif seperti bahan perekat polimer dapat meningkatkan resistansi internal elektroda dan 
mengurangi luas permukaan aktif yang berperan dalam proses penyimpanan muatan [8], [9]. Berdasarkan studi terbaru kinerja 
volumetrik merupakan parameter utama dalam menyiapkan divais super kapasitor masa depan. Kepadatan partikel bahan 
menjadi bahan pertimbangan dalam menciptakan superkapasitor berkualitas. Baru -baru, karakteristik volumetrik telah dikaji 
intens dengan berbagai pendekatan dan teknik terbaru. Sebagai contoh, Zhu dkk (2025), telah meneliti kinerja volumetrik 
superkapasitor berbasis karbon kayu basal dengan performa 31,4 F/cm3 [10]. Sementara itu, Zhang dkk (2025) mensistesis CNTs + 
rGO sebagai material dasar superkapasitor menghasilkan performa volumetrik 8,43 F/cm 3 [11]. Hasil yang sama juga dilaporkan 
oleh Shi dkk (2025) [12]. Namun, material yang digunakan masih berfokus pada logam oksida dan grafena yang mahal, korosif, 
dan tidak ramah lingkungan. Selain itu, konfigurasi elektroda berbasis serbuk juga cenderung memiliki densitas material yang 
rendah sehingga membatasi kinerj a kapasitansi volumetrik perangkat. Oleh karena itu, pengembangan elektroda karbon padat 
bebas perekat menjadi isu terkini yang relevan untuk meningkatkan efisiensi volumetrik dan kesederhanaan konfigurasi 
perangkat superkapasitor. 
Dalam konteks pengembangan material berkelanjutan, pemanfaatan limbah biomassa lokal tidak hanya memberikan 
alternatif sumber karbon yang ekonomis tetapi juga berkontribusi terhadap pengurangan beban limbah organik yang dihasilkan 
dari aktivitas domestik d an pasar tradisional. Di Kota Pekanbaru, timbulan sampah harian tercatat melebihi 700 ton, dengan 
dominasi sampah organik mencapai sekitar 65%, yang sebagian besar terdiri dari sisa sayuran dan limbah dapur [13]. Limbah ini 
umumnya berakhir di Tempat Pembuangan Akhir (TPA) Muara Fajar yang telah mengalami kelebihan kapasitas, sehingga memicu 
permasalahan lingkungan yang berkelanjutan [14], [15] . Kondisi tersebut menunjukkan adanya peluang strategis untuk 
mengonversi limbah sayur lokal menjadi material karbon fungsional bernilai tambah tinggi. Secara spesifik, limbah sayuran, 
khususnya daun lobak memiliki kandungan lignoselulosa yang relatif ting gi (76%) serta struktur jaringan alami yang berpotensi 
menghasilkan kerangka karbon berpori setelah proses karbonisasi [16]. Karakteristik ini menjadikan limbah sayuran sebagai 
kandidat prekursor karbon yang menarik untuk aplikasi elektroda energi [17]. 
Oleh karena itu, studi ini berfokus pada eksplorasi limbah sayur lokal Indonesia yang dikhususkan pada limbah daun lobak 
sebagai sumber karbon untuk elektroda padat bebas perekat pada aplikasi superkapasitor. Daun lobak dipilih dalam penelitian ini 
karena biomassa ini memiliki kandungan selulosa dan hemiselulosa yang relatif tinggi serta struktur jaringan tanaman yang 
berlapis, yang berpotensi menghasilkan kerangka karbon berpori setelah proses karbonisasi. Elektroda karbon monolitik bebas 
perekat dikembangkan dari biomassa daun lobak melalui pendekatan karbonisasi yang dirancang untuk menghasilkan struktur 
karbon padat dengan kinerja elektrokimia yang optimal. Kinerja perangkat superkapasitor dianalisis dengan penekanan khusus

superkapasitor modern karena lebih merepresentasi kan kapasitas penyimpanan energi dalam volume perangkat yang 
sebenarnya, khususnya untuk aplikasi portabel dan sistem penyimpanan energi dengan keterbatasan ruang. 
 
2. METODE PENELITIAN 
Penelitian ini menggunakan limbah daun lobak sebagai sumber biomassa lokal untuk sintesis elektroda karbon padat bebas

Potassium Bicarbonate-Assisted Pore Regulation of 
Corn-Straw-Derived Interconnected Porous Carbon for 
Supercapacitors 
Xiaodong He1 Zhidong Sun1 Zilong Zhou1 Fanen Zeng2 Chenglong Jing1 Bing Xu2 
1 School of Transportation Engineering, Dalian Jiaotong University, Dalian, China 2 School of Materials Science and Engineering, Dalian Jiaotong University, 
Dalian, China 
Correspondence: Bing Xu ( xb@djtu.edu.cn) 
Received: 30 June 2026 Revised: 19 August 2026 Accepted: 21 August 2026 
Keywords: corn straw | KHCO3 activation | porous carbon | supercapacitor 
ABSTRACT 
Biomass-derived porous carbons are promising electrodes for sustainable supercapacitors, but their performance depends on 
balancing charge-storage sites and ion-transport pathways. Herein, corn straw was converted into interconnected porous carbon 
through mild KHCO3 -assisted activation. The effects of activation temperature and holding time on pore architecture and 
capacitive behavior were comparatively evaluated, and the surface chemistry of the best-performing sample was further examined. 
CSK-750-2, prepared at 750◦C for 2 h, exhibited a hierarchical porous structure containing micropores and mesopores with a 
specific surface area of 1701 m2 g− 1 . Micropores provided abundant surface area for electric double-layer charge storage, whereas 
mesopores facilitated electrolyte-ion transport, and surface oxygen-containing groups may provide a limited Faradaic contribution. 
CSK-750-2 delivered 157 F g− 1 at 0.5 A g− 1 with 86% capacitance retention at 5 A g− 1 . The symmetric supercapacitor achieved 10.5 
Wh kg− 1 at 500 W kg− 1 and approximately 106% capacitance retention after 10,000 cycles. These results highlight the importance 
of balancing micropore-based charge storage and mesopore-assisted ion transport in biomass-derived carbon electrodes. 
1 Introduction 
The increasing demand for efficient energy conversion and 
storage, together with growing environmental concerns, has 
stimulated extensive research into sustainable electrochemical 
energy-storage technologies. Among various energy-storage sys- 
tems, rechargeable batteries generally provide relatively high 
energy density, whereas electrochemical capacitors, particularly 
supercapacitors, have attracted considerable attention because 
of their high power density, rapid charge–discharge capability, 
long cycling life, and operational safety [ 1–8 ]. Recent advances 
in graphene-based and flexible electrochemical energy-storage 
systems have further demonstrated the importance of elec- 
trode architecture, surface chemistry, and electrode–electrolyte 
interactions in determining energy-storage performance [ 9–11 ]. 
Carbon materials have been widely investigated as supercapac- 
itor electrodes because of their physicochemical stability, large 
specific surface area, favorable charge-transport characteristics, 
and tunable pore architecture [ 12–18 ]. In particular, biomass- 
derived porous carbons are promising electrode candidates 
because of their renewable origin, abundant availability, low cost, 
environmental compatibility, and adjustable surface chemistry. 
Engineered biochar and biomass-derived carbon materials have 
also received increasing attention for sustainable energy and 
environmental applications [ 19 ]. 
The capacitive behavior of porous carbon is strongly depen- 
dent on its pore architecture. Micropores mainly provide ion- 
accessible surface area and charge-storage sites, whereas meso- 
pores facilitate electrolyte-ion transport between the external

surface and internal micropores; larger pores can additionally 
serve as ion-buffering reservoirs and shorten transport pathways 
[ 20 ]. Consequently, neither a high specific surface area nor a 
large pore volume alone necessarily guarantees high capacitance. 
Instead, an appropriate balance between accessible micropores 
for charge storage and larger pores for ion transport is required to 
achieve favorable electrochemical performance. Therefore, ratio- 
nal regulation of hierarchical porosity is essential for the effective 
conversion of agricultural and forestry wastes into high-value 
porous carbon electrodes for supercapacitor applications. 
Chemical activation is one of the most widely employed 
approaches for developing porous structures in biomass-derived 
carbons. Strong alkaline activators such as KOH and NaOH are 
commonly used because of their high etching capability and 
pore-forming efficiency. Nazhipkyzy et al. prepared chemically 
activated carbons from karagash and pine sawdust, obtaining 
specific capacitances of 147 and 114 F g− 1 , respectively [ 21 ]. Le Van 
and Luong Thi demonstrated that NaOH activation effectively 
promoted pore development in rice-husk-derived carbon [ 22 ], 
Singh et al. reported biomass-derived activated carbon with a 
specific capacitance of 115 F g− 1 for electric double-layer capacitor 
applications [ 23 ], while Perez-Chavez et al. further compared 
KOH and H3 PO4 activation of corn-husk- and agave-bagasse- 
derived carbons, demonstrating the important influence of the 
activating agent on electrochemical performance [ 24 ]. These 
studies demonstrate the effectiveness of strong alkaline activation 
in developing porous carbon structures. However, the strong 
alkalinity and corrosiveness of KOH and NaOH can increase 
equipment-corrosion risks and post-treatment requirements. 
Moreover, excessive activation may induce severe carbon etching, 
structural deterioration, or an unbalanced pore-size distribution, 
such that the resulting high surface area cannot be fully utilized 
electrochemically. 
Alternative pore-regulation strategies have also been investi- 
gated. Bandara et al. incorporated TiO2 into activated carbon 
derived from Jack wood biochar, obtaining a specific capacitance 
of 147 F g− 1 [ 25 ], whereas Diantoro et al. reported sponge- 
like activated carbon derived from Manihot esculenta tubers 
with a gravimetric capacitance of 146.6 F g− 1 [ 26 ]. Hoffmann 
et al. demonstrated the feasibility of converting potato waste 
into carbon electrodes for supercapacitor applications [ 27 ]. Hor 
and Hashmi prepared hierarchical porous carbon from biomass 
pollen cones through ZnCl2 -assisted activation, achieving capac- 
itances of approximately 126–146 F g− 1 [ 28 ]. ZnCl2 activation 
has also been applied to biomass-derived biochar, including 
corn-cob-derived carbon [ 29 ]. Other activation routes, such as 
molten-salt-assisted carbonization, have also been explored to 
construct porous carbon structures for supercapacitor electrodes 
[ 30 ]. Lee et al. further modified activated carbon through nitric- 
acid treatment and obtained a capacitance of 106 F g− 1 in an 
all-solid-state supercapacitor [ 31 ]. Recent studies have further 
demonstrated the electrochemical potential of biomass-derived 
carbons prepared from different biomass sources and through 
different modification strategies [ 32–34 ]. Collectively, these stud- 
ies indicate that pore development, morphology regulation, and 
surface chemistry can all influence capacitive performance. How- 
ever, approaches involving additional inorganic components, 
metal salts, or strong acids can increase the complexity of material 
preparation and subsequent purification. These considerations 
motivate the development of simpler and milder activation 
strategies capable of simultaneously regulating pore formation 
and preserving the carbon framework. 
Compared with strongly alkaline or metal-salt-based activation 
routes, KHCO3 has emerged as a relatively mild activating 
agent for porous-carbon preparation. During thermal treat- 
ment, KHCO3 decomposes into potassium-containing species 
and gaseous products, which promote carbon etching, pore 
generation, and pore expansion. Such activation can facilitate 
the development of interconnected hierarchical porous structures 
while reducing the likelihood of severe framework destruction. 
Compared with KOH and NaOH, KHCO3 exhibits lower alka- 
linity and corrosiveness, whereas its use also avoids the direct 
introduction of Zn-containing activation residues associated with 
ZnCl2 -based processes [ 28, 35 ]. Therefore, KHCO3 -assisted activa- 
tion provides a promising strategy for balancing pore generation, 
structural preservation, chemical consumption, and environmen- 
tal compatibility. Nevertheless, the relationships among KHCO3 
activation conditions, hierarchical pore evolution, surface chem- 
istry, and the electrochemical behavior of agricultural-waste- 
derived porous carbons remain insufficiently clarified. 
Corn straw (CS), an abundant agricultural residue, contains 
carbon-rich components and intrinsic longitudinal channel- 
like structures, making it a promising precursor for porous 
carbon electrodes. However, the direct conversion of corn 
straw into interconnected porous carbon through a simple 
KHCO3 -assisted activation route, without the use of additional 
templates, transition-metal-based activators, or intentional het- 
eroatom dopants, remains relatively underexplored. In particular, 
the effects of activation temperature and holding time on pore 
architecture, and electrochemical behavior require further clar- 
ification. In this work, CS-derived porous carbons (CSKs) were 
prepared through a KHCO3 -assisted activation strategy, and 
the effects of activation temperature and holding time were 
separately evaluated using a one-factor-at-a-time approach by 
correlating morphology, structural disorder, pore characteristics, 
and electrochemical performance, while the surface chemistry 
of the best-performing sample was further examined. Among 
the investigated conditions, CSK-750-2, prepared at 750◦C for 2 
h, exhibited the most favorable combination of pore structure 
and electrochemical response, delivering a specific capacitance 
of 157 F g− 1 at 0.5 A g− 1 . The present work focuses on the direct 
construction of interconnected porous carbon from corn straw 
through mild KHCO3 activation without additional templates 
or transition-metal-based activators. Particular attention is given 
to the balance between micropore-based charge storage and 
mesopore-assisted ion transport, as well as the possible contri- 
bution of surface oxygen-containing functionalities to capacitive 
behavior. These findings provide a relatively mild and simple 
route for the valorization of corn straw into porous carbon 
electrodes for supercapacitor applications.

2.1 Experimental Materials 
Corn straw was collected from Dalian, Liaoning Province, China.

Unveiling the energy storage potential of valorized 
unripe plantain peel-derived activated carbon
Ayesha Samrin · Mohammed Rehaan Chandan · Igor Levchenko · Katia Alexander  · 
Mandhakini Mohandas
Received: 27 February 2026 / Accepted: 25 August 2026

Abstract
The damage from excess waste generation on the environment has made it necessary to re-think how we 
approach product development and the waste management lifecycle. Within this framework, conversion of 
biowaste into energy storage materials has emerged as an effective means of reducing the environmental 
impact of food production. In this work, activated car-bon with superior supercapacitive properties is produced 
directly from unripe plantain peel by optimizing the use of two different activating agents KOH and ZnCl 2 dur-
ing pyrolysis. Activated carbon Z7 which was pyrolyzed at 700 °C using ZnCl 2 as the activating agent had a 
higher sur-face area of 1636 m 2/g and higher electrochemical performance when compared to activated carbon 
produced under all other experimental conditions. The specific capacitance obtained for Z7 in a two-electrode 
Swagelok set-up was 167 F g −1 at 0.5 A/g and an excellent energy density of 23 Wh/kg at a power density of 
174 W/kg at 0.5 A/g current was obtained. Further-more, a capacitance retention of 79% was achieved after 
4500 cycles at a current density of 5 A/g with a coulombic efficiency of 99%.
Keywords Unripe plantain peels · KOH and ZnCl 2 activation · Porosity · Specific capacitance
Introduction
Driven by the growing population and its increasing use of energy-intensive technologies, the global consump -
tion of energy continues to increase, at a significant cost to the environment. To slow down the depletion of fos-
sil fuels, and reduce associated emissions, there have been significant global efforts to transition to clean forms 
of energy, with a particularly strong focus on renewable energy sources, such as solar or wind. However, their 
intermittent nature as well as potential asynchronicity between peak generation and peak demand necessitates the 
development of efficient systems for energy storage, such as batteries, flywheels, supercapacitors. Supercapaci -
tor is an efficient energy storage system due to its high-power density and high stability. The energy is stored 
in a supercapacitor by two mechanisms, namely (i) Electric double layer (EDLC) and (ii) Faradaic redox reac -
tions. For a clean energy storage system, the electric double layer capacitor (EDLC) materials are highly suitable 
as they are potentially sustainable, have a longer life cycle, chemically stable and are also economical [ 6, 36].

Among promising EDLC materials, activated carbon is one of the most readily available materials with good 
supercapacitive properties [14, 18]. Although activated carbon can be produced from a variety of sources, the use 
of biowaste as the carbon feedstock offers a better choice for the environment [ 22, 38] with an activating agent 
such as KOH, NaOH, NaHCO 3, ZnCl2, HPO3, etc. typically used to chemically activate the carbon in order to 
enhance its properties [4, 28, 33]. Amongst possible biowaste feedstocks, peel from bananas has received notable 
attention due to the substantial volume of waste (almost 32% of the fruit) that is produced during consumption. 
The research has been particularly active in India, as it is the largest producer of bananas globally, according to 
the data from the National Horticulture Board, Ministry of Agriculture, Govt. of India ( https://nhb.gov.in) [34]. 
As banana peel waste contains a high amount of nitrogen and phosphorous, its disposal presents a notable envi -
ronmental hazard, whereas its prolonged decomposition of almost two years contributes to higher greenhouse 
gas emissions [1, 35].
Most of the studies conducted to date on banana peel-derived EDLC materials have focused on the reforming 
of waste from ripe bananas. For example, Tripathy et al., synthesized activated carbons with the highest specific 
capacitance value of 227 F g−1 at 1 A/g in a three-electrode setup with a capacitance retention of 97% after 5000 
cycles. The energy density for the activated carbon was 7 Wh/kg at a power density of 250 W/kg [40]. In another 
example, Lv et al., synthesized a hierarchical porous carbon foam with a specific capacitance of 206 F g−1 at 1 A/g 
and a capacitance retention of 88% [26], whereas Liu et al., prepared an n-doped activated carbon with a specific 
capacitance of 185.8 F g−1 at 5 mV/s and 210.6 F g −1 at 0.5 A/g [25]. Kandasamy et al., investigated the use of 
sulfuric acid to activate the carbon produced from the peel from a triploid cultivar of banana Musa paradisiaca, 
yielding samples with a high specific capacitance of 306.2 F g−1 at 30 mV/s (Kandasamy et al., 2016).
However, in southern parts of India, namely Kerala and Tamil Nadu, unripe plantains are widely used to 
prepare many culinary products, thus yielding a large amount of green plantain peel. While the use of the lat -
ter to prepare activated carbon have been studied for application in oil adsorption [ 41], lead(II) and 3,7-Bis 
(dimethylamino)-phenothiazin-5-ium chloride adsorption [15], reduction of carbon monoxide from biogas [ 11], 
anthracene bioadsorption [2], as a feedstock for ethanol production [46], removal of hexachlorocyclohexane iso-
mers from wastewater [9], and heavy metal adsorption [42], unripe peel-derived EDLC materials have received 
limited attention. Tadesse et al., synthesized activated carbon from raw banana peels using a two-step process 
of carbonization and chemical activation using KOH. They obtained a surface area of 565 m 2/g and a specific 
capacitance of 0.821 F g−1 [37]. Though the surface area is high the specific capacitance values were low which 
could be due to poor pore development or pore accessibility achieved in a two-step synthesis process. The self-
doping of heteroatoms and retention of biomass has been reported to be higher in a single-step process than a 
two-step process as there is biomass loss and also heteroatoms tend to etch out during the activation process [24].
Unripe plantain peels were selected as the biowaste precursor in this work as it has many advantages such as 
high availability, large yield and good scalability when compared to previously reported biomass materials. The 
unripe plantain peels have more rigid and stable lignocellulosic structures containing cellulose, hemicellulose 
and lignin which yields higher carbon content during thermal treatment. Furthermore, it has lower sugar content 
and less volatile content than ripe plantain peels reducing tar formation and structural collapse during thermal 
treatment. These rigid structures have low microbial degradation and are highly suitable for pore development 
and increased char formation required for easy handling and scalable production. Additionally, the plantain peels 
have nitrogen content naturally present paving way to self-doping of nitrogen [3].
This work aimed to optimize the synthesis process to obtain activated carbon with a high surface area and 
higher specific capacitance value from unripe plantain peel in a single step. To do that, a single step carboniza -
tion with activation by either KOH or ZnCl2 was chosen, and the surface and electrochemical properties of thus-
produced materials were analyzed for energy applications. The impregnation ratio was selected as 2:1, where 2 is 
the mass of activating agent and 1 is the mass of the carbon source based on its performance in our previous work 
[33]. Such pyrolysis strategy based on chemical activation enables the direct transformation of unripe plantain 
peel, a structurally complex agricultural biowaste, into high-performance nanostructured carbon, where the use
