Carbon aerogel is an excellent conductive porous carbon material, but suffers from poor mechanical properties 
and fatigue resistance, which greatly limits its application as a flexible electronic device. Herein, the cellulose 
nanofibers/reduced graphene oxide carbon aerogel (BCRCA) with a unique layered structure was prepared by 
bidirectional freezing technique and thermal annealing. BCRCA's layered structure gives it ultra-low density

Notably, the BCRCA assembled into a wearable strain sensor exhibits a stable current signal for real-time

1. Introduction 
Due to the rapid growth of unsustainable consumption and the 
increasing consumption of fossil fuels, environmental problems have 
become increasingly prominent, so new technologies closely related to 
new energy conversion and storage have attracted more and more 
attention [ 1 ]. Among them, the new technologies represented by flexible 
supercapacitors and strain sensors have caused extensive research in 
intelligent robots, intelligent textiles, wearable electronic devices, and 
other advanced fields [ 2 – 4 ]. Lightweight, high power and energy den -
sity, long cycle life, high mechanical flexibility, low cost, high sensitivity 
and fast response speed are the basic requirements of these electronic 
devices [ 5 – 8 ]. For example, smart textiles have high sensitivity and fast 
response ability as multifunctional sensors and heaters for personal 
health management, which was expected to enable disease diagnosis, 
early warning and personal hyperthermia [ 9 ]. 
Carbon aerogels (CAs) are an emerging carbon-based material, 
which is favored by many researchers because of its ultra-high specific 
surface area, rich pore structure and good electrical conductivity 
[ 10 – 12 ]. CAs are usually obtained by carbonizing aerogels in an inert 
atmosphere, and their unique porous structure makes them widely used 
in electromagnetic shielding [ 13 ], sensors [ 14 ], and supercapacitors 
[ 15 ]. However, these carbon aerogels usually have a disordered porous 
structure, which is easy to collapse, and it is difficult to obtain excellent 
compression properties and fatigue resistance [ 16 ]. This is not condu -
cive to the stability and durability of carbon aerogel in practical 
applications. 
Cellulose nanofiber (CNF) is a kind of environment-friendly natural 
polymer material with many advantages, such as stable chemical 
properties, high elastic modulus, and biodegradation [ 17 – 19 ]. The 
unique nanostructure of CNF enables it to be freeze-dried into CNF 
aerogel with a three-dimensional network structure [ 20 ]. After 
carbonization of CNF aerogel under inert gas, carbon aerogel materials 
with conductive properties can be obtained directly. However, pure CNF 
carbon aerogels not only undergo severe volume shrinkage and defor -
mation during the carbonization process, but also it is difficult to pro -
vide satisfactory capacitance by directly using it as an electrode material 
for supercapacitors [ 21 , 22 ]. To solve these problems, CNF is usually

China.

Diamond & Related Materials 140 (2023) 110555
2
combined with other materials (such as carbon materials [ 23 ], 
conductive polymers [ 24 ], metal compounds [ 25 ], etc.) to prepare 
composite carbon aerogels with excellent conductive and mechanical 
properties. Graphene is a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice structure 
carbon material, which stands out among many carbon materials 
because of its high conductivity and large specific surface area [ 26 ]. 
Unfortunately, the interaction of van der Waals forces and π - π bonds 
between graphene sheets tends to cause the sheets to stack and 
agglomerate [ 27 ]. This seriously hinders electrolyte ion diffusion and 
charge transfer, greatly limiting the further application of graphene in 
supercapacitors and sensor functional devices. Therefore, how to 
reasonably design and use the inherent characteristics and advantages of 
CNF and graphene to build high-performance electronic devices with 
special structures is still a huge challenge. 
Directional freezing is a method for synthesizing bionic porous ma -
terials and bionic layered composites [ 28 ]. Temperature gradient is an 
important factor in directional freezing because it can regulate the di -
rection of ice crystal growth [ 29 ]. Specifically, after the uniform 
colloidal suspension is cooled, the ice crystals gradually nucleate in the 
direction of the temperature gradient. At the same time, solute particles 
are pushed between ice crystals to obtain a oriented structure. In recent 
years, anisotropic aerogels prepared by directional freezing technology 
have been applied in various fields. Compared with traditional random 
freezing, directional freezing aerogels have a suitable microstructure 
and excellent properties [ 30 ]. In this paper, we have carefully designed a 
method to control the nucleation and growth of ice crystals under a 
double temperature gradient to achieve a highly ordered layered 
structure of carbon aerogel. Bidirectional carbon aerogel has more 
outstanding mechanical and electrochemical properties than random 
and single direction carbon aerogel. At the same time, this layered 
structure can generate more conductive paths under pressure, thus 
achieving high sensitivity. Therefore, the dual directional carbon aero -
gel can be effectively used for multifunctional applications in super -
capacitor electrodes and strain sensors. 
Herein, we have prepared a multifunctional nanocellulose/reduced 
graphene oxide carbon aerogel (BCRCA) through a simple bidirectional 
freezing, freeze-drying, and high temperature carbonization strategy. 
BCRCA has ultra-low density and good mechanical compression prop -
erties. Excellent performance is attributed to: (i) CNF acts as a physical 
spacer to effectively prevent the agglomeration of graphene sheets; (ii) 
The two-dimensional carbon skeleton of graphene oxide (GO) can 
reduce the excessive shrinkage of CNF during carbonization and give 
carbon aerogel excellent mechanical strength; (iii) The bidirectional 
freezing method is beneficial for obtaining parallel and ordered lamella, 
effectively achieving stress transfer and electrolyte ion transfer. BCRCA 
as electrode material for supercapacitors has excellent electrochemical 
properties. It also has good sensing performance, can easily monitor 
human activity and shows excellent signal stability. Therefore, the 
BCRCA has excellent application prospects in electrochemical energy 
storage materials and wearable electronic devices. 
2. Experimental section 
2.1. Materials 
CNF dispersion was purchased Zhongshan NanoFC bio-materials Co.,

and a carboxyl content of 1.02 mmol/g. GO was purchased from Suzhou

0.2 – 10 μ m and a thickness of ~1 nm. Deionized water was prepared by

2.2. Preparation of bidirectional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel (BCRCA)

1:1, stirring, and ultrasonic 30 min to obtain the mixed suspension. 
Transfer the mixture suspension to the cube plastic mold and place it on

vice consists of a curved copper plate immersed in liquid nitrogen at one 
end and hot water at the other (95 
◦
C) to create a temperature gradient. 
After complete freezing, the samples was frozen in a lyophilizer ( � 60

C,

◦
C under argon for 120 min to obtain 
the layered bidirectional CNF/RGO carbon aerogel, named BCRCA. For

ABSTRACT  
Lignin-activated carbon (AC) composites were employed as electrode active materials to develop more envi -
ronmentally friendly Supercapacitor (SC) materials with enhanced properties. This way, the hydroquinone/ 
quinone moieties present in lignin molecules added Faradaic processes to the system, and the capacitance of the 
active material increased, making it appropriate for future applications requiring more efficient and sustainable 
active materials. Lignin, a sustainable biobased aromatic polymer high in carbon content, was deposited on AC 
surface employing ultrasound (US) system, and for a better deposition, AC was treated with HNO
3
. Since the 
composition and properties of lignin can vary depending on their isolation process, two different types of lignin 
were used: Kraft lignin (KL) and Organosolv lignin (OL), and the effects on the chemical and electrochemical 
composition were deduced. Physicochemical, morphological, and electrochemical analyses were carried out on 
the lignin-AC composite to determine the optimum material combination and treatment process. It was observed 
that the acid treatment was effective in enhancing the functionality and porosity of the surface. Additionally, it 
improved the deposition of lignin and facilitated the formation of hierarchically porous structures on the surface 
of treated activated carbon (TAC), with different tendencies depending on the lignin employed. The creation of 
highly porous structures also resulted in enhanced electrochemical performance in materials. This validated the 
process, where eco-innovative technologies like US forces and employment of lignocellulosic biomass compounds 
like lignin were used as sustainable and efficient alternatives for obtaining electrochemically active materials.   
1. Introduction 
Lignin-based electrode materials are gaining interest due to their 
sustainability and high availability. Most of the works of lignin incor -
poration into batteries are based on its conversion into carbon materials, 
and substitution of the currently used non-renewable fossil-based car -
bons [ 1 ]. Lignin is a promising candidate due to its high carbon content 
and unique aromatic nature. Moreover, by modulating its structure, 
different carbon materials can be obtained to meet the diverse re -
quirements of different battery types. Porous carbons derived from 
lignin have been fabricated as active materials of electrodes [ 2 ]. Lignin- 
derived carbons have also been used as active materials in SCs [ 3 ], with 
studies exploring different activation processes, including carbonization 
and combinations with polymers like polyacrylonitrile (PAN) or 
different metal oxides [ 4 ]. However, these processes are energy 
demanding. Therefore, alternative approaches to incorporate lignin into 
Energy Storage (ES) materials without the need for prior carbonization 
are gaining interest [ 1 , 5 – 7 ]. 
Numerous research works have focused on producing and studying 
composite or hybrid materials by combining lignin with other carbo -
naceous materials or conducting polymers. These efforts aim to enhance 
the properties of the resulting materials. Depending on their targeted 
application, different properties are needed. Nevertheless, one common 
characteristic of enhanced properties of carbon materials is their specific 
surface area (SSA). The porosity is a key factor for the battery perfor -
mance, as it eases the diffusion kinetics and strengthens the conductivity 
network of the conductive ions [ 8 ]. Activated carbon is a commonly 
used material for this reason, but different methodologies have been

2
carried out to increase the SSA and pore size distribution (PSD), for a 
further enhanced specific capacitance [ 9 – 11 ]. AC is used for many 
different applications, ranging from adsorbents to ES devices, all 
needing high SSA for better performance. It is also relatively inexpen -
sive, stable, and easily processable. Several methods have been carried 
out to increase the SSA of AC. The most widely used method is the 
treatment with concentrated HNO
3 
[ 12 – 14 ]. Other works have studied 
the effect of different concentrations of HNO
3 
solutions for the AC 
treatment, which have verified that the concentrated HNO
3 
brings the 
best results [ 15 ]. This treatment not only increases the porosity of the 
surface of the material but also increases the oxygen-containing func -
tional groups, subsequently enhancing its performance [ 16 – 18 ]. 
Although the SSA plays an important role in the improvement of the 
capacity, it does not necessarily mean that all the pores will be elec -
trochemically accessible in contact with the electrolyte. Indeed, the type 
of pore plays an important role, since mesopores (2 – 50 nm wide pores) 
can adsorb more and larger ions than micropores ( < 2 nm wide pores) 
[ 19 ]. Nevertheless, micropore-sized carbon SCs have been proven to 
contribute to charge storage by absorbing electrolyte ions bigger than 
the pores of the carbon [ 20 ]. 
Another approach for enhanced carbon SCs is the fabrication of 
hybrid materials or composites. Double-layer (DL) carbon materials 
have been combined with pseudocapacitance materials to expand their 
capacitance. This enhancement occurs due to the addition of Faradaic 
processes happening on the redox groups of the pseudocapacitance 
materials [ 21 ]. A sustainable approach to the synthesis of hybrid ma -
terials is the incorporation of lignin into AC materials. Lignin is the 
second most abundant polymer on earth and is considered a plausible 
substitute for many materials, such as ES device materials [ 22 ]. It is 
regarded to be a pseudocapacitance material due to the hydroquinone/ 
quinone moieties present in its molecules. Combining these lignin 
properties with the non-Faradaic processes happening in AC, more 
sustainable materials with enhanced capacitance can be obtained. 
Therefore, another current target in the development of novel ES device 
materials is achieved by using inexpensive, abundant, and efficient 
materials, promoting a shift toward more sustainable practices and en -
ergy [ 23 ]. 
From the different ES devices in the market and under development, 
SCs have gained significance in the last decades [ 24 ]. SCs, along with 
Lithium Ion Batteries (LIBs), are among the most promising devices for 
the energy transition [ 25 ]. They are usually used in cases where high 
currents are needed, but they have low capacitance, and therefore, can 
only be used for short times. SCs have a greater capacity and can also be 
recharged without damage, filling the gap between capacitors and 
conventional batteries [ 26 ]. 
SCs electrodes are mainly based on carbonaceous materials that 
possess high surface area and appropriate pore-size distribution for the 
necessary capacitance. Many works are focusing on the development of 
novel materials with enhanced properties for this application, due to the 
estimated high demand [ 27 ]. Similar to the case of batteries, lignocel -
lulosic materials, especially lignin, are making their way to be consid -
ered as a feasible alternative. 
The lignins employed in all the works for the development of ES 
materials are lignosulfonates (LS), or alternatively Kraft lignins. LS have 
been widely employed due to their appealing properties like water sol -
ubility. Nevertheless, its obsolete extraction procedure has resulted in 
Kraft being the most employed pulping process worldwide. This process 
generates substantial amounts of KL as waste, which has high potential 
for valorization. Nonetheless, keeping in mind the utilization and 
implementation of green processes to obtain more ecological materials, 
the organosolv method stands out as the most sustainable lignin isola -
tion process. It promotes an integral biorefinery product valorization 
[ 28 ]. 
However, to the best of our knowledge, no work implementing OL 
can be found in the literature. Therefore, a novel approach involving the 
incorporation of OL into AC and the subsequent comparison of these 
analogous materials with KL has been carried out. Despite the less sus -
tainable extraction process of KL in comparison to OL, massive quanti -
ties of this type of lignin are extracted every year as a side product from 
paper and pulp industry. Consequently, integrating KL into higher-value 
products represents a sustainable method for creating innovative 
advanced materials from waste such as lignin. 
Various physicochemical and morphological techniques were used to 
assess differences in the composition, chemical properties, and 
morphology of the materials. Fourier Transformed Infrared spectros -
copy (FTIR), Elemental Analysis (EA), X-Ray Photoelectron Spectros -
copy (XPS), Brunauer – Emmett – Teller (BET) method and Scanning 
Electron Microscopy (SEM) were utilized for this purpose. Moreover, 
electrochemical measurements were conducted to determine the mate -
rials ’ electrochemical performance. Cyclic Voltammetry (CV), Electro -
chemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) and Galvanostatic Charge 
Discharge (GCD) measurements were performed to study polarization 
processes, determine specific capacitance values, and gather informa -
tion about porosity. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Materials 
KL was precipitated from Kraft liquor and OL was extracted from 
Eucalyptus globulus chips, both provided by Papelera Ziku ˜naga (Hernani, 
Gipuzkoa) and characterized in a previous work [ 29 ]. Granulated acti -
vated carbon (7440-44-0, Panreac) was purchased. AC was treated with 
concentrated nitric acid (HNO

) (65 %, 7697-37-2, Panreac). N-Methyl-

275,000, 24937-79-9, 
Aldrich) were used for the slurry preparation, and a glassy carbon

2.2. Treatment of activated carbon 
To prepare the TAC, AC was milled and then mixed with concen -

The surface deposition of KL and OL onto AC and TAC was carried

Empty Fruit Bunches for Asymmetric Supercapacitors

ABSTRACT: The rapid demand for sustainable, high-performance energy
storage has accelerated the development of biomass-derived electrode materials
for next-generation supercapacitors. However, the intrinsically low electrical
conductivity and limited electrochemical activity of many metal oxide electrodes
remain major challenges that restrict their practical application. In this work, a
novel Fe-doped ZnO/activated carbon composite derived from oil palm empty
fruit bunches (Fe-ZnO/AC) was successfully synthesized via a hydrothermal
method and employed as an electrode material for asymmetric supercapacitors.
ZnO was selected for its low-cost, abundance, nontoxicity, and facile synthesis,
while Fe doping was introduced to enhance electrical conductivity, charge-
transfer kinetics, and redox activity. Simultaneously, activated carbon derived
from empty fruit bunch (EFB) waste provides a conductive, porous carbon
matrix that facilitates ion diffusion and electron transport. This study highlights
the synergistic integration of Fe-doped ZnO with activated carbon, enabling simultaneous enhancement of conductivity,
electrochemical performance, structural stability, and sustainability within a single-electrode system, a strategy that remains rarely
explored for asymmetric supercapacitor applications. The Fe-ZnO/AC electrode exhibited a high specific capacitance of 458.2 F g
−1
at 0.1 A g
−1
in a three-electrode configuration. In an asymmetric two-electrode configuration, the device delivered specific
capacitances of 179.7 and 102.3 F g
−1
for the coin cell and flexible cell, respectively. The corresponding energy densities reached 35.9
and 20.5 W h kg
−1
with power densities of 239.7 and 240.4 W kg
−1
, respectively. These findings demonstrate the excellent
electrochemical performance, stability, and energy storage capability of the Fe-ZnO/AC composite, highlighting its strong potential
as a low-cost, sustainable, and high-performance electrode material for next-generation asymmetric supercapacitors.
1. INTRODUCTION
The global demand for high-performance, environmentally
friendly, and efficient energy storage systems continues to rise
in line with the rapid advancement of modern technologies.
Among various options, supercapacitors have attracted
significant attention due to their density, rapid charge−
discharge capability, and excellent cycling stability compared
to conventional batteries.
1−5
However, their relatively low
energy density remains a limitation.
6
Consequently, the
development of advanced electrode materials capable of
simultaneously delivering high capacitance and long-term
stability has become a research focus. In this context, transition
metal oxides and porous carbon materials are emerging as
promising candidates, as they offer complementary charge-
storage pseudocapacitance and electric double-layer capaci-
tance (EDLC) mechanisms, respectively.
7−9
Supercapacitors generally store energy through two primary
mechanisms, EDLC and pseudocapacitance. In EDLC systems,
charge storage occurs through the electrostatic accumulation of
electrolyte ions at the electrode/electrolyte interface without
involving faradaic reactions, enabling excellent power capability
and long-term cycling stability.
10,11
Porous carbon materials,
including activated carbon, graphene, and biomass-derived
carbon, are widely utilized as EDLC electrodes due to their
high electrical conductivity, large accessible surface area, and
hierarchical pore structures. In contrast, pseudocapacitive
materials store charge through rapid and reversible faradaic
reactions involving surface redox processes, providing higher
specific capacitance than conventional carbon-based electro-
des. Transition metal oxides have attracted considerable
attention as pseudocapacitive materials because of their
multiple oxidation states and rich redox activity. However,
their practical applications are often limited by poor electrical
conductivity and structural instability during repeated charge−
discharge cycles.
12
Therefore, integrating transition metal
oxides with porous carbon materials represents an effective
strategy to combine the high capacitance contribution of

pseudocapacitive reactions with the superior conductivity and
stability of EDLC-based carbon frameworks.
10−13
Zinc oxide (ZnO) is considered one of the most promising
metal oxides due to its natural abundance, low cost, non-
toxicity, and notable redox activity. However, its poor electrical
conductivity and limited electrochemical stability due to
structural degradation and residual impurities significantly
restrict its electrochemical performance.
14−24
To overcome
these limitations, two widely adopted approaches include metal
doping and composite formation with a conductive carbon
matrix. Among various dopants, iron (Fe) has been shown to
effectively enhance the electrical conductivity and charge
carrier concentration of ZnO. Kumar et al. (2023) reported
that Fe-doped ZnO exhibited a specific capacitance of 286 F
g
−1
in a three-electrode configuration, demonstrating the
positive effect of Fe incorporation on charge transfer kinetics.
25
In another study, integration of ZnO with activated carbon
(AC) was widely investigated to enhance surface area and
facilitate ion transport.
26
Selvakumar et al. (2010)
27
reported a
ZnO/AC nanocomposite with a specific capacitance of 160 F
g
−1
, while Yadav et al. (2022) obtained 77.7 F g
−1
from a ZnO-
AC composite derived from walnut shell waste.
28
These
highlight the synergistic contribution of the EDLC behavior of
carbon and the pseudocapacitive properties of ZnO, although
the overall performance remains moderate.
In recent work, Saka and Levent (2024) demonstrated that
nitrogen- and ZnO-doped carbon particles derived from waste
biomass can improve electrochemical performance, yielding
high-capacitance electrodes suitable for energy storage
applications.
29
Recent studies have demonstrated that oil
palm empty fruit bunch (EFB)-derived activated carbon is a
highly promising electrode material for supercapacitors owing
to its naturally abundant carbon content and well-developed
porous structure. Yulianti et al. reported hierarchically porous
EFB-derived activated carbon with a specific surface area of
1215 m
2
g
−1
and an outstanding specific capacitance of 459.28
F g
−1
, where the presence of naturally occurring SiO
2
enhanced
electrode wettability.
30
More recently, biomass-derived acti-
vated carbon prepared from EFB achieved a specific surface
area of up to 1375 m
2
g
−1
, delivering a specific capacitance of
346 F g
−1
together with 82.9% capacitance retention after 5000
charge−discharge cycles, further confirming the excellent
potential of EFB-derived carbon for sustainable electro-
chemical energy storage.
31
Despite these encouraging advances, most reported studies
have focused on optimizing the porous carbon framework itself
or introducing heteroatom functionalities to improve the
capacitive performance. The combination of EFB-derived
activated carbon with Fe-doped ZnO to simultaneously exploit
the high electrical conductivity and large surface area of
biomass-derived carbon together with the enhanced pseudo-
capacitive activity of Fe-modified ZnO has rarely been
investigated. This represents an important opportunity for
the development of low-cost, sustainable, and high-perform-
ance electrode materials.
In this study, Fe-ZnO/AC composites were synthesized via a
hydrothermal method and comprehensively evaluated in both
three-electrode and asymmetric two-electrode configurations.
The results demonstrate that the synergistic effects of Fe
doping and ZnO-carbon hybridization with a locally abundant,
waste-derived carbon matrix significantly enhance the redox
activity, electrical conductivity, and cycling durability. Distinct
from previous studies, this work integrates Fe doping and
ZnO-carbon hybridization within an EFB-based activated
carbon matrix, achieving improved electrochemical perform-
ance through a fully biomass-supported material architecture.
This integrated approach offers an effective and sustainable
material design approach for the development of high-

ABSTRACT
Corn straw is the second most produced agricultural residue globally, and the efficient utilization of this resource 
is of great environmental and economic importance. The study utilized Fenton-like reagents for the pretreatment 
of corn straw, followed by carbonization and activation. It was found that the activated carbon samples pre -
treated with Fenton-like reagents exhibited remarkable microporous structures with good electrochemical 
properties. Specifically, activated carbon samples treated with a 0.1 M concentration of FeCl
3 
solution and 3 wt%

. The findings of the life cycle assessment demonstrate that the utilization of Fenton-like reagent 
pretreatment resulted in a substantial reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and ecotoxicity in comparison with 
conventional methodologies. The study observed a near 30 % decrease in CO
2 
emissions and a 59 % reduction in 
terrestrial ecotoxicity. This pretreatment method has been demonstrated to enhance activation efficiency while 
concomitantly reducing the amount of activator required. This study demonstrates the potential of Fenton-like 
reagent pretreatment technology in improving the electrochemical performance of activated carbon and 
reducing environmental impact, providing a green and efficient process path.
1. Introduction
Corn straw is the second most produced agricultural residue on a 
global scale. The annual yield of corn straw is 1,661,250 tonnes, rep -
resenting 27.2 % of the total agricultural waste [ 1 – 3 ]. Conventional 
methods of handling maize straw, such as incineration or haphazard 
piling, have been shown to result in a range of environmental issues. 
These include air pollution (e.g., PM2.5, CO
2
) and methane emissions, 
which can trigger eutrophication of water bodies and affect soil micro -
bial communities [ 4 , 5 ]. The carbonization of corn straw to produce 
capacitive carbon materials offers numerous advantages in terms of 
environmental sustainability. Its entire life cycle eco-efficiency is sub -
stantial, making it well-suited to the development of a carbon-neutral 
and circular economy [ 6 , 7 ]. Capacitive carbon materials have a long 
service life in supercapacitors, enabling carbon sequestration for a 
longer period compared to the natural decomposition of straw (1 – 2 
years to release carbon) [ 8 – 12 ].
Corn straw has a widely distributed vascular bundle. The secondary 
cell wall of straw consists of cellulose (which provides the backbone), 
hemicellulose (which connects the cellulose), and lignin (which fills the 
cross-links) to form a dense composite system. When the straw is used 
for high-capacitance activated carbon, the denseness of the secondary 
wall hinders the diffusion of the activator, resulting in an uneven dis -
tribution of pores that affects subsequent activation processes [ 13 , 14 ]. 
Consequently, activators that are more than 2 – 3 times the mass of the 
feedstock are employed to activate high-performance activated carbon 
materials using conventional process methods [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, 
Fenton-like reagent pretreatment was employed to minimize the quan -
tity of activator during the fabrication of high-performance activated 
carbon materials.
Fenton reagents and their analogues (Fenton-like) represent a class 
of advanced oxidation technologies grounded in the utilization of hy -

The concept of Fenton ’ s reagent is utilized to deliberately disrupt the 
structural integrity of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin in plants. 
Reference is made to the lignin dimer model in Fig. 1 to simulate the 
behavior of treatment with the Fenton-like reagent. It is predicted that 
this process will weaken the plant structure and result in the formation 
of fine plant tissues [ 24 , 25 ]. This is anticipated to ease the subsequent 
carbonization and activation steps, which may allow for a reduced 
quantity of KOH to be utilized as an activator in order to achieve the 
desired outcomes. Additionally, this approach could be developed into a 
more environmentally friendly pretreatment technology. The reduced 
quantity of activator employed in this method leads to an increased 
reliance on ferric chloride and hydrogen peroxide. As a result, there is a 
need for a more comprehensive evaluation method — specifically, a life 
cycle assessment — to scientifically ascertain its environmental impact.
Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is a methodology that is employed to 
determine the most sustainable approach by considering various envi -
ronmental impact parameters. Consequently, the incorporation of such 
evaluations into biochar production studies is strongly suggested to 
accurately assess its energy-saving and emission-reduction benefits, as 
previously proposed by 
¨
Ogmundarson et al. and Yu et al. [ 26 , 27 ]. In 
recent years, there has been a gradual increase in the number of studies 
related to analyzing biomass energy storage applications using whole 
life cycle assessment. Kulkarni et al. [ 28 ]. found that the environmental 
impacts of the production of battery-grade graphite from biomass as a 
precursor using an electrochemical graphitization process were lower 
than those of conventional methods. Antic Gorrazzi et al. [ 29 ]. investi -
gated the potential of Cyperus papyrus biochar as an electrode material. 
Their findings demonstrated that, despite electrical conductivity and 
mechanical strength limitations, low-temperature biochar has a signif -
icantly lower carbon footprint than graphite. These studies highlight the 
crucial role of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) in identifying sustainable 
pathways for biochar production. They also illustrate the potential of 
biochar to minimize environmental impact and serve as a feasible 
alternative to conventional graphite in energy storage applications.
In this study, activated carbon was prepared using Fenton-like re -
agent pretreatment to evaluate its performance as a capacitive material. 
A life cycle assessment was conducted to determine whether this method 
qualifies as a green treatment technology.

Short-Process Preparation of Ultrathin Spherical Hierarchical Porous
Activated Carbon by Spray Pyrolysis of Papermaking Black Liquor for
Electrochemical Energy Storage
Yuelin Guo, Yang Yan, Ming Xu, Xiaojia Zhang, Yuan Zhang, Xiaofeng Wang, Xuezhi Song, *
and Zhenquan Tan *
Cite This: Read Online
ACCESS
 Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations

ABSTRACT: Black liquor is a typical wastewater and troublesome pollutant in the
papermaking industry, which is rich in lignin, hemicellulose, and residual alkali. Here,
we developed a short and e ﬃ cient process to prepare spherical hierarchical porous acti-
vated carbon from papermaking black liquor. The precursor was prepared by spray pyrol-
ysis of black liquor, where carbonization of black liquor, preliminary activation, and pore
formation are achieved under the synergistic e ﬀects of high temperature, water vapor, and
sodium/potassium hydroxides. The further activation was carried out using the residual
sodium and potassium compounds in the precursor material as etching agents.
Hierarchical porous amorphous carbon was achieved with the merits of ultrathin-walled
(10–20 nm) porous hollow spheres and a large amount of thin, bending, and reticular car-
bon nanosheets. Owing to its unique morphology, microstructure, and hierarchical pores,
the optimized sample AC700 presents a large speci ﬁc surface area of 2104.3 m
2 g–1 and a
pore volume of 1.139 cm 3 g–1. When evaluated as the cathode material of lithium-ion
capacitors, AC700 presents a high speci ﬁc capacity of 67.3 mAh g –1 within 2.0–4.0 V, along with excellent rate capability and cycling
stability. This work o ﬀers an e ﬃ cient and scalable pathway for high-value utilization of papermaking black liquor.
KEYWORDS: porous carbon, activated carbon, spray pyrolysis, black liquor, hierarchical pores, lithium-ion capacitors
1. INTRODUCTION
With the popularization of arti ﬁcial intelligence and battery-
driven electri ﬁcation, the demand for high-performance energy
storage devices is becoming increasingly urgent. 1–3 Lithium-
ion capacitors (LICs), characterized by high-power density,
excellent cycling stability, and relatively high energy density,
are considered promising candidates for applications requiring
rapid charge/discharge and long cycle life.
4,5 The performance
of LICs greatly depends on the properties of electrode mate-
rials.
6–8 Among various candidates, biomass-derived activated
carbon materials (orange peel, 2 coconut shells, 9 rice husks, 10,11
soybean straw, 12 wood,13 persimmon cores, 14 biowastes,6 etc.),
featuring high speci ﬁc surface area, hierarchical porosity, and
facile synthesis, are the most widely employed electrode mate-
rials for LICs
8,15 and supercapacitors,16 as well as catalyst carrier
materials.17,18
Lignin is a naturally occurring macromolecular polymer and
the second most abundant biopolymer in plants after cellulose,
making it one of the most abundant aromatic biomass resources
on Earth. Owing to its relatively high carbon content and favor-
able carbonization behavior, lignin has been widely regarded as
a promising precursor for the preparation of activated carbon
and other porous carbon materials.
19 For example, Nune
et al. 20 prepared porous carbon via lignin carbonization, which
exhibited a speci ﬁc surface area of 1092 m 2 g–1 and a capaci-
tance of 114 F g –1. Qiu et al. 21 synthesized a lignin-derived
mesoporous carbon cage by multi-stage explosion through ther-
mal decomposition of calcium oxalate (CaC
2O4), achieving a
speciﬁc surface area of 1175.6 m 2 g–1. Wang et al. 22 prepared
porous carbons derived from sodium lignosulphonate using
chemical activation and template methods, where KOH-
chemically activated porous carbons exhibited the largest spe-
ciﬁc surface area of 1998.4 m
2 g–1. Despite these advances,
the large-scale utilization of lignin remains challenging due to
its heterogeneous structure and the need for complicated
extraction processes.
Black liquor is the wastewater in the papermaking industry,
which contains substantial amounts of lignin, together with

some hemicellulose-derived fragments and residual alkali. 23,24
Black liquor contains approximately 90% of the pollutants gen-
erated during the papermaking process. 25,26 At present, black
liquor is typically treated and discharged after pollutant
removal,
27 or concentrated and burned as a low-value fuel. 28,29
Alternatively, lignin can be recovered through acid precipita-
tion,30,31 membrane separation,32 or ﬂocculation precipitation25
processes. However, these treatment and recovery routes gener-
ally involve complex procedures, high energy consumption, and
additional environmental burdens, which limit the e ﬃ cient and
high-value utilization of lignin in black liquor. It is of great sig-
niﬁcance to ﬁnd novel ways for the e ﬃ cient treatment of black
liquor from papermaking.
Spray pyrolysis is a new technique developed in recent years
for fast preparation of powder materials.
33,34 The solution is
atomized and sent into a high-temperature furnace, where the
sample undergoes instantaneously series of processes, such as
solvent evaporation, solid particle formation, particle drying,
thermal decomposition, sintering, etc., and then obtains super-
ﬁne powder materials.
35 The operation process is simple, and
the ﬁnal product can be obtained in one step. Huang et al. 34
prepared a highly e ﬃ cient catalyst of Fe 0.18Co0.82 alloy anchor-
ing on the nitrogen-doped porous carbon hollow sphere by
spray pyrolysis. Kubo et al. 36 synthesized N-doped nanoporous
carbon from ZIF-8 metal –organic framework via a one-step
ultrasonic spray pyrolysis process, achieving a speci ﬁc surface
area of 1059 m 2 g–1. Taking the characteristics of papermaking
black liquor and spray pyrolysis into account, fast spray pyroly-
sis is thus an ideal method for preparing black liquor-derived
activated carbon, as it o ﬀers environmental and energy storage
beneﬁts.
In this work, a short-process strategy based on spray pyrolysis
is developed to directly convert papermaking black liquor into
spherical hierarchical porous activated carbon. By coupling spray
pyrolysis with in situ alkali-metal activation, carbonization and
activation are achieved sequentially within a single system, elimi-
nating the multistep lignin extraction and the addition of an
external activating agent required in the conventional process.
During spray pyrolysis, the residual sodium and potassium spe-
cies in black liquor are transformed into active etching agents
and subsequently promote deep pore formation during post-
heat treatment, resulting in a hierarchical architecture composed
of thin-walled porous hollow spheres interconnected with carbon
nanosheets. The resulting material is an oxygen- and sulfur-co-
doped amorphous carbon with a high speci ﬁc surface area
(2104.3 m
2 g–1) and a large pore volume (1.139 cm 3 g–1), out-
performing the commercial activated carbon YP50 (Kuraray
Co., Ltd, Japan). When evaluated as a cathode for lithium-ion
capacitors, the optimized sample (AC700) delivers a speci ﬁc
capacity of 67.3 mAh g
–1 (121.1 F g –1)w i t h i n2 . 0–4.0 V, along
with excellent cycling stability and rate capability. In summary,
this work demonstrates an e ﬃ cient and scalable approach for
the high-value conversion of papermaking black liquor into
advanced electrode materials.
2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
2.1. Materials
The black liquor was obtained from Yueyang Forest and Paper Co.,
Ltd. As listed in Table S1 , the total dissolved solids are 124 g L –1,
and the total organic carbon (TOC) is 21.3 g L –1. The concentrations
of OH -,N a +,K +, and S are 5.54, 20.83, 2.724, and 1.773 g L –1,
respectively. The concentrations of other impurities are below 0.1 g
L–1. The commercial activated carbon YP50 was purchased from
Kuraray International Trade (Shanghai) Co., Ltd.
2.2. Material Preparation
Spherical hierarchical porous activated carbon (SHPAC) was prepared
by a short process of spray pyrolysis, followed by activation, as illus-
trated in Figure 1 . Apart from water and nitrogen, papermaking black
liquor served as the sole raw material for the synthesis of SHPAC.
The black liquor was ultrasonically atomized using nitrogen as the car-
rier gas. The atomized droplets, along with nitrogen (5 L min
–1),
entered a furnace tube of a vertical furnace from the bottom and exited
from the top. The resulting product was collected by a nickel mesh
ﬁxed at the outlet of the furnace tube. The as-obtained material, com-
posed primarily of carbon and Na/K-containing compounds, was used
as the precursor for subsequent activation. High-temperature etching
activation for pore formation was carried out by utilizing the Na/K
compounds present in the precursor as an in situ activating agent.
The precursor was placed in a tubular furnace under an inert atmo-
sphere, heated to 800 °C at a rate of 3 °C min
–1, maintained for 2 h,
and then naturally cooled to room temperature. The resulting material
was washed with deionized water to remove Na 2O and K 2O, yielding
SHPAC. The precursors obtained at pyrolysis temperatures of 600,
650, and 700 °C were denoted as P600, P650, and P700, respectively.
Higher temperatures (e.g., 750 °C) were not employed because they
would signi ﬁcantly promote the water –gas reaction (reaction of H
2O
with C) during spray pyrolysis, which gasi ﬁes the carbon material
and makes the collection of any solid product nearly impossible. The
corresponding activated samples derived from P600, P650, and P700
were named AC600, AC650, and AC700, respectively.
2.3. Material Characterization
The contents of impurities in the raw material (black liquor) and ﬁnal
product were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma (ICP, Thermo
Scientiﬁc, iCAP PRO X) and a carbon –sulfur analyzer (LECO,
CS600). The morphology and elemental distribution of the samples
were characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL,
JSM-IT1700HR), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping,
and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI, Titan G2 60-300).
The microstructure was analyzed by X-ray di ﬀraction (XRD, Rigaku,
RINT-2000) and Raman spectroscopy (Renishaw, U.K.). Functional
groups and bonding information were collected by Fourier transform
infrared (FTIR, Thermo Scienti ﬁc, Nicolet iS20) spectroscopy and
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, Thermo Scienti ﬁc, K-
Alpha). Brunauer –Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area and pore size

ABSTRACT
The synthesis of porous hard carbon from coconut biomass waste using physical activation through pyrolysis and 
chemical activation with orange juice as an organic activator at varying temperatures, including 500 
◦
C, 600 
◦

and 700 
◦
C, has been carried out. The purpose of this research is to develop materials for faradaic-type super -

ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET), cyclic voltammetry 
(CV), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). BET analysis showed that the PHC-700 sample 
exhibited a relatively high specific surface area with porous characteristics and a narrow pore size distribution 
around 17 – 18 nm. The PHC-700 sample also exhibited the best electrochemical performance with a specific 
capacitance of 485.23 F/g and a total resistance of 24.29 Ω . GCD measurements revealed stable triangular 
curves, indicating good charge-discharge reversibility and confirming the superior capacitive behavior of PHC- 
700. The study confirmed that the higher the temperature used, the better the supercapacitor electrode obtained. 
This is evidenced by the pores on the surface that help improve the quality of the electrode and the XRD test 
results which are directly proportional to the increase in temperature. It is hoped that this research can enhance 
understanding of supercapacitor electrode applications.
1. Introduction
The rapid development of the global economy and shifts in energy 
consumption patterns are posing a significant challenge to environ -
mental sustainability [ 1 ]. In an international context, the increasing 
energy demand is driven by rapid urbanization, industrialization, and 
the growing use of electronic devices in almost all aspects of human life. 
On the other hand, the supply of fossil fuels, the primary source of 
traditional energy, is dwindling and becoming increasingly limited. This 
not only impacts energy security but also contributes to accelerated 
global climate change, which is primarily caused by greenhouse gas 
emissions resulting from the burning of fossil fuels. In light of these 
concerns, the search for more environmentally friendly and sustainable 
solutions to meet the world ’ s energy needs has become increasingly 
urgent. One of the alternatives that has garnered significant attention is 
renewable energy, particularly solar and wind energy. These two energy 
sources are considered a promising solution because they are environ -
mentally friendly and do not produce carbon emissions, which is crucial 
in mitigating the impact of global climate change.
Solar energy, obtained through solar panels, and wind energy, ob -
tained through wind turbines, are abundant and renewable natural re -
sources. The main advantages of these energies are their unlimited 
availability and their ability to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. In 
addition, these two sources of energy play a crucial role in creating a 
more decentralized energy model, where each individual or community 
can produce and manage their energy. However, despite their great 
potential, the use of renewable energy such as solar and wind also comes 
with significant challenges. One of them is the dependence on external 
factors that are difficult to control, namely the weather. Solar energy can 
only be generated when the weather is clear, while wind energy can only

be utilized when there is sufficient wind. This leads to instability in the 
energy supply, which, in turn, risks disrupting a stable electricity supply.
To address this issue, it is crucial to develop efficient energy storage 
systems. Energy storage technologies such as batteries and hydrogen- 
based energy storage systems can be an essential solution in address -
ing fluctuations in renewable energy availability. With the ability to 
store energy generated during peak periods (for example, during sunny 
days or in strong winds), it can be used during times of high demand or 
when the weather is unfavorable. This innovation in energy storage 
technology is key to creating a more reliable and sustainable renewable 
energy system. Energy storage has become one of the primary focuses in 
21st-century technological innovation, given the global challenges 
posed by growing energy needs and the worsening environmental crisis. 
The decreasing supply of fossil fuels, the need to reduce carbon emis -
sions, and the increasing reliance on volatile renewable energies, such as 
solar and wind power, further emphasize the urgency to develop effi -
cient and environmentally friendly energy storage technologies. One 
technology that is emerging as an efficient alternative for energy storage 
is the supercapacitor (SC). SCs offer significant advantages over con -
ventional batteries as they can handle much higher power levels and can 
charge and discharge energy quickly without requiring prior charging 
[ 2 ].
Unlike batteries that rely on electrochemical processes to store and 
release energy, SCs store energy through electrostatic mechanisms, 
which allows for much faster and longer-lasting charge and discharge 
cycles. Although SC have a lower energy density compared to batteries, 
their advantage lies in their ability to operate more efficiently in situa -
tions that require sudden power surges, such as in electric vehicles, 
portable electronic devices, and renewable energy systems. Much of the 
rechargeable energy storage industry is currently focused on developing 
electrochemical energy storage systems that combine power, energy 
density, and lower cost per unit of storage capacity. Innovations 
continue to enhance the performance of SC, particularly in terms of 
energy density and manufacturing cost, which is expected to make this 
technology more competitive and relevant in meeting future energy 
demands, as well as providing more sustainable long-term solutions to 
global energy challenges [ 3 ]. The three most common types of SCs are 
known as electric double layer capacitors (EDLC; non-Faradaic), pseu -
do-capacitors (Faradaic), and composite SCs. EDLCs are notable for 
having a low specific energy density and requiring charge deposition at 
the electrode electrolyte interface. Pseudo-capacitors can achieve high 
specific capacitance through fast and reversible redox reactions; how -
ever, this comes at the expense of decreased cycle stability. Thus, due to 
its superiority in research using the pseudo-capacitor (Faradaic) type, 
SC ’ s low specific energy value prevents it from being used in various 
contexts despite its outstanding characteristics. Therefore, developing 
new cathode materials for SCs that maintain low cost, high specific 
power, and long life is a significant focus in this research field [ 4 ].
One very promising electrode material for use in supercapacitors is 
porous hard carbon. This material has a highly porous structure, which 
allows for an increase in electrode surface area, thereby increasing en -
ergy storage capacity. Porous hard carbon is formed through the process 
of carbonizing organic matter at high temperatures, resulting in a ma -
terial with a dense and stable pore network. This porous structure en -
ables electrolyte ions to move more freely and efficiently during energy 
charge and discharge cycles, directly improving the performance of 
supercapacitors, particularly in terms of power and cycle stability. In 
addition, porous hard carbon exhibits good electrical conductivity, 
which is crucial for accelerating the energy charge and discharge pro -
cesses, making it highly efficient in applications that require rapid 
response. Another advantage is its stability at high temperatures, as well 
as its resistance to corrosion and degradation during extended periods. 
Therefore, the use of porous hard carbon as an electrode material is 
expected to enhance the performance of supercapacitors in industrial 
and consumer applications, such as renewable energy storage, electric 
vehicles, and portable electronic devices, making it a highly relevant 
material choice for future innovations in energy storage technologies 
[ 5 ].
To develop porous hard carbon with optimal performance, utilizing 
biomass-based activators is a promising alternative. One potential 
source of biomass is orange juice waste, which contains various organic 
acids, such as citric acid, ascorbic acid, and malic acid [ 6 ]. The primary 
advantage of this content is its ability to induce pore formation during 
the carbonization process through the mechanism of thermal decom -
position and the formation of pore-building gases, including CO
2 
and 
water vapor. Additionally, these compounds play a role in dissolving the 
amorphous part of the carbon, resulting in a porous structure with a 
larger surface area. Not only that, but the presence of metal ions and 
minerals in orange juice, such as potassium (K), calcium (Ca), and 
magnesium (Mg), can also act as catalysts that promote the development 
of micro- and mesopores. With these advantages, the utilization of or -
ange juice as an activator not only improves the ion storage capacity and 
conductivity of the electrode but also supports the concept of circular 
economy by processing waste into valuable materials in sustainable 
energy technology.
Based on the background above, the researcher took the initiative to 
create a faradaic supercapacitor electrode material made of porous hard 
carbon synthesized from coconut biomass waste. In the method of 
making porous hard carbon, physical activation is carried out through 
pyrolysis and chemical activation using organic activator orange juice. 
Then characterization is carried out using X-ray diffraction (XRD), 
scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET), 
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and Electrochemical impedance Spectroscopy 
(EIS) to determine the properties of this material. It is hoped that this 
research can fulfill SDGs (Sustainable Development Goals) number 7 
related to Clean and Affordable Energy.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
The coconut biomass waste and orange juice were obtained from 
Langkat, Indonesia. Ethanol and distilled water were bought from CV. 
Rudang Jaya, Indonesia [ 45 ]. Vacuum oven, pyrolysis equipment and 
other supporting equipment using basic Physics laboratory facilities 
from the Universitas Sumatera Utara [ 7 ].
2.2. Preparation of porous hard carbon (PHC)
The preparation of porous hard carbon from coconut biomass waste 
is achieved through chemical and physical activation methods. First, the 
coconut biomass waste was broken into small pieces and then washed 
with distilled water and ethanol to remove impurities present in the raw 
material, then the water content in the coconut biomass waste was dried 
in a vacuum oven at 100 
◦
C for 12 h. Then the carbon powder obtained is 
chemically activated, which is a process carried out by mixing the 
sample powder with an activator substance, namely 200 mL of orange 
juice, which is then stirred with a magnetic stirrer at a speed of 15.000 
rpm, and then processed using the maceration or soaking method for 1 
day. After that, the carbon was washed until the pH was neutral and 
filtered. Then, physical activation using the pyrolysis method was car -
ried out at 500 
◦
C, 600 
◦
C, and 700 
◦
C, each for 2 h. The resulting hard 
carbon was labeled PHC-500, PHC-600, and PHC-700. further grinding 
and ball mill processes were carried out to obtain a smaller size. And 
finally the PHC is ready to be tested [ 8 ].
2.3. Fabrication of electrodes
The working electrode was made by mixing the sample with PVDF as 
a binder, acetylene black for a conducting agent, and a weight ratio of 
80:15:5. The mixed material was added to the NMP solution to create a 
slurry. As a current collector, aluminum foil was used to cover the slurry,

Keywords: Heated tobacco waste; Carbonized tobacco leaf; Metallic heating element; MnO 2 
electrodeposition; Asymmetric supercapacitor; Recycling. 
 
In this study, an integrated recycling strategy is developed to  utilize the organic and metallic 
components collected from used heated tobacco as active materials and current collectors for 
an asymmetric supercapacitor (ASC) . Residual t obacco leaves are carbonized to obtain 
carbonized tobacco leaves (CTL), while metallic heating elements (MHEs) are directly reused 
without melting, reshaping, or additional processing. The MHEs maintain their morphology , 
surface characteristics,  and electrical continuity after tobacco use . A CTL-based slurry  is 
coated onto the MHE to fabricate the CTL/MHE negative electrode, and MnO2 is subsequently 
electrodeposited for 10–30 min to prepare MnO2-CTL/MHE positive electrodes. The electrode 
prepared using 15 min deposition time (M15 -CTL/MHE) exhibits favorable Mn 4+/Mn3+ 
surface states and high electrochemical performance for use as positive electrode. The 
asymmetric supercapacitor device assembled by M15 -CTL/MHE and CTL/MHE operates 
stably over 0–2.0 V and exhibits a gravimetric specific capacitance of 39.2 F g−1 at 1 A g −1. 
The device further achieves a maximum energy density of 23.6 Wh kg−1 and a power density 
of 10.0 kW kg−1, retains 81.8% of its initial capacitance after 3000 cycles, and successfully 
illuminates a 1.8 V red light-emitting diode. These results demonstrate the direct integration of 
multiple components from a single waste product into functional energy storage device.

Abstract: How to address the destruction of the porous structure caused by elemental doping
in biochar derived from biomass is still challenging. In this work, the in-situ nitrogen-doped
porous carbons (ABPCs) were synthesized for supercapacitor electrode applications through pre-
carbonization and activation processes using nitrogen-rich pigskin and broccoli. Detailed characteri-
zation of ABPCs revealed that the best simple ABPC-4 exhibited a super high specific surface area
(3030.2–3147.0 m2 g−1) and plentiful nitrogen(1.35–2.38 wt%) and oxygen content (10.08–15.35 wt%),
which provided more active sites and improved the conductivity and electrochemical activity of
the material. Remarkably, ABPC-4 showed an outstanding specific capacitance of 473.03 F g −1 at
1 A g−1. After 10,000 cycles, its capacitance retention decreased by only 4.92% at a current density
of 10 A g−1 in 6 M KOH. The assembled symmetric supercapacitor ABPC-4//ABPC-4 achieved a
power density of 161.85 W kg−1 at the maximum energy density of 17.51 Wh kg−1 and maintained
an energy density of 6.71 Wh kg−1 when the power density increased to 3221.13 W kg−1. This study
provides a mixed doping approach to achieve multi-element doping, offering a promising way to
apply supercapacitors using mixed biomass.
Keywords: hybrid biomass; porous carbon; heteroatom doping; supercapacitor
1. Introduction
Energy, a concept that is often mentioned, has an irreplaceable place in our daily lives.
Natural energy sources such as solar and wind energy could not be directly exploited.
These sorts of energy forms were mostly turned into electric energy or other types of
energy through the transformation of natural energy forms to suit the development needs
of humans [1–3]. Until recent centuries, humans had mostly obtained energy from fossil
fuels. However, the consumption of a huge number of these fuels could not accomplish
long-term sustainable development, and environmental degradation was also severe [3–6].
To effectively solve the problems of energy structure and environmental pollution, one of
the main research directions to efficiently reduce environmental pressure is the creation of
energy storage materials utilizing biomass resources [7,8]. Among these, supercapacitors
were widely utilized in railways, electronic communication, vehicles, and other industries
as a type of energy storage material with high power density, high charging rate, extended
cycle life, and environmental friendliness [9–11].
Electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs), dummy capacitors, and hybrid supercapaci-
tors are the three types of supercapacitors [12]. As an example, the charging and discharging
process of the most popular electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) among these three
Nanomaterials 2024, 14, 1368. https://doi.org/10.3390/nano14161368 https://www.mdpi.com/journal/nanomaterials
Nanomaterials 2024, 14, 1368 2 of 16
types was realized by the storage and release of charges between inert carbon-based ca-
pacitors and electrolytes in the environment [12,13]. Scientists have worked for decades
to develop conductive polymers, carbon-based compounds, transition metals, and other
electrode materials [14,15]. Carbon-based capacitors, for example, could be made from a
variety of biomass found in nature, including waste biomass from industrial and agricul-
tural output [16,17]. This was not only because biomass includes a high concentration of
carbon elements, but it could also significantly reduce consumption caused by additional
environmental development and enable the recycling of certain biomass [11,18–20]. Fur-
thermore, because of their high specific surface area (SSA), good pore size distribution, and
low acquisition cost, many carbon-based materials prepared from biomass are frequently
the first choice for making high-performance supercapacitors [21,22].
Numerous study findings exist on the synthesis of electrode materials from biomass
carbon at the moment. With the continued investigation of these findings, it became clear
that the essence that influenced the power of supercapacitors was ion transmission time [23].
Myriad approaches exist to improve this, such as creating carbon nanomaterials with
improved pore structure using one-dimensional or two-dimensional plant materials [24] or
realizing additional pseudo-capacitance effects by doping heteroatoms [25–27]. However,
even if biomass materials with a better structure were chosen, the method of doping
heteroatoms at the moment was primarily realized by the reaction of inorganic reagents [28],
such as nitrogen atom doping by soaking in ammonia water solution or phosphorus and
sulfur co-doping by soaking in phosphoric acid and sulfuric acid solution [29]. Depending
on the kind, concentration, and reaction time of inorganic chemicals, these approaches
more or less degraded the initial excellent carbon pore structure [ 30]. As a result, more
research was required to achieve the preparation process of heteroatom doping while not
degrading the carbon nanostructure of biomass.
Pigskin, a frequent material waste from the kitchen, was high in collagen and nitrogen.
During pyrolysis, these proteins decompose to form nitrogen-doped carbon materials,
which are known to improve electrical conductivity and enhance the electrochemical
properties of the composite. Broccoli was a member of the Cruciferae family, which
included plants with a high sulfur content [31]. The carbonization of broccoli contributes
to the formation of a porous carbon structure. The presence of nitrogen from pigskin can
prevent the collapse of these porous structures during pyrolysis, resulting in a more stable
and interconnected pore network. This enhanced electrochemical properties, conductivity,
and stability. These improvements make the composite material a promising candidate for
various applications in energy storage and catalysis [32].
Herein, in situ, nitrogen-doped porous carbons (ABPCs) were prepared using nitrogen-
rich pigskin and broccoli as precursors through pre-carbonization and activation processes
for electrochemical application. The effect of different mixing ratios of pigskin and broccoli

Abstract
This research investigates the use of machine learning (ML) to improve the performance of conducting polymer-based 
electrodes in supercapacitors, which leverage both electric double-layer capacitance (EDLC) and pseudocapacitive charac-
teristics. Six ML models—Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Decision 
Tree (DT), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN)—are evaluated for their ability 
to predict the specific capacitance of electrodes using an experimental dataset comprising Polyaniline (PANI), Polypyrrole 
(Ppy), and Polythiophene (PTh). Performance metrics included Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), 
and R-squared  (R2). Among the models, MLP demonstrates superior predictive accuracy, achieving the lowest MAE of 0.1452

 R2 values of 0.9399 and 0.9354, their errors are comparatively higher than MLP. These results highlight the effectiveness of 
advanced ML techniques in enhancing supercapacitor technology and indicate the potential of these models to predict and 
optimize conducting polymer-based electrode materials for improved performance.

Abstract
This complete investigation presents a combined experimental and computational 
Approach to emergent high-performance nickel cobalt sulfide (NiCo 2S4) 
nanostructures for Supercapacitor applications. NiCo 2S4 samples were synthesised 
via a two-step solvothermal Method at temperatures of 120–180 °C (designated 
NCS1-NCS4) and scientifically characterised using XRD, BET, SEM, XPS and FTIR.

Fg− 1 from cyclic voltammetry and 375 Fg − 1 from galvanostatic Charge-discharge

thickness of 200 nm for device development. This integrated methodology provides 
a comprehensive framework for the rational design of transition metal sulfide 
electrodes, with applications in electric automobiles, portable semiconductor 
technology, renewable energy storage, and industrial power systems.

The valorization of biomass residues into advanced carbon materials offers a promising route 
toward more sustainable supercapacitor technologies. Birchwood was evaluated as a 
sustainable precursor for activated carbon electrodes in aqueous supercapacitors. Carbon was 
produced via carbonization, grinding, and activated at 700 or 800 °C using varying quantities 
of NaOH. Structural characterization (N₂ sorption at 77 K, XRD, Raman, SEM, elemental 
analysis, XPS) indicated specific surface areas up to 2401 m 2 g-1 and a temperature‑dependent 
pore architecture: predominantly microporous at 700 °C and mixed micro/mesoporous at 
800 °C. Electrochemical performance was assessed in symmetric CR2032 coin cells with a 
phosphate buffer electrolyte, using CV and GCD. The highest specific capacitance reached 
247 F g-1, exceeding that of commercial carbon Kuraray YP-80F by up to 115% under given 
test conditions. Although more pronounced graphitic structures develop after treatment at 
800 °C and may enhance conductivity, they also coincide with reduced surface area and 
consequently do not improve capacitance. Samples activated at 700 °C generally delivered 
superior capacitance and competitive rate capability, likely due to enhanced microporosity 
which increases the accessible surface area for electric double‑layer formation. These results 
suggest birchwood is a viable high‑value feedstock for carbon-based supercapacitor electrodes.

In recent years, the incorporation of transition metals such as iron 
(Fe) into biomass-derived carbon systems has demonstrated significant

synthesizing and evaluating a novel Fe-incorporated chitosan@SiO ₂ @ -

trode material with significant potential for next-generation energy 
storage applications, aligning with the broader trend of utilizing

ABSTRACT
Water scarcity and salinity pose critical challenges that necessitate the development of efficient 
desalination processes for brackish water treatment. This study investigates the use of activated carbon 
derived from date palm pollen as a potential electrode material for batch capacitive deionization (CDI). 
Activated carbon exhibits an exceptionally large surface area of 2586.9 m²·g −1, as determined by 
Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area analysis, which provides numerous sites for electrostatic ion 
accumulation during CDI operation. When activated carbon is used as an electrode in batch CDI 
experiments with a 500 ppm NaCl feedstock at an applied cell voltage of 1.2 V, the electrode exhibits a 
salt adsorption capacity (SAC) of 38.0 mg·g−1 after 120 min of adsorption. These results indicate effective 
electrosorptive salt removal from brackish water under practical operating conditions. Additionally, 
electrochemical measurements reveal that the activated carbon electrodes exhibit a high specific 
capacitance of 92 F·g −1, indicating efficient storage of electric charge in electric double layers. The high 
SAC and specific capacitance and the large BET surface area confirm that the date-palm-pollen-derived 
activated carbon is a promising electrode material for batch CDI desalination systems.

explosion, rapid industrialization, and climate change. Additionally, water quality is declining owing to 
pollution generated by agricultural activities and industrial emissions [1],[2]. Thus, new methods have

significantly lower energy consumption, has a reduced environmental impact due to the chemicals used,

ABSTRACT
Over the years, porous carbons have garnered immense research interest due to their abundance, 
cost-effectiveness, and promising performance across a range of applications, including energy 
storage, gas separation, and catalysis. With growing demand for eco-friendly materials, biomass-
derived hard carbons have gained increasing attention. This study investigates the potential of 
porous carbons synthesized from locally sourced bay leaves by carbonizing at varying 
temperatures for batteries and supercapacitor applications. The porous carbon produced at 800 ℃ 
demonstrated an impressive specific capacitance of 689 F g−1 at a current density of 1 A g−1 in a 2 
M NaOH electrolyte. The device attained an energy density of about 33.3 Wh kg −1 at a power 
density of 1098.8 W kg −1. Moreover, porous carbon synthesized at a mild carbonization 
temperature exhibits excellent battery performance, delivering a reversible capacity of 310 mAh 
g−1 at 30 mA g−1, with high capacity retention and rate capability. This work presents a viable path 
towards low-cost, scalable, and sustainable waste (bay leaves) for producing porous hard carbon 
and demonstrates its use for energy storage applications.

NaOH-Activated Bamboo Carbon with Hierarchical Porosity for High-
Performance Electrochemical Capacitors 
 
E. C. Udochukwu1,2*, O. E. Onyelucheya1, A. C. Orga1,3 and I. S. Ike1, 3 
Department of Chemical Engineering, Federal University of Technology, Owerri, Nigeria1

1. Introduction 
The global shift toward sustainable energy systems necessitates the development of advanced 
energy storage technologies capable of mitigating the intermittent nature of renewable energy 
sources such as solar and wind [1], [2] . Electrochemical capacitors (ECs), commonly known as 
supercapacitors, have gained significant attention as promising candidates in this transition due to 
their high-power density, fast charge–discharge rates, and excellent cycle stability [3]. Compared to 
conventional batteries, ECs offer superior operational safety and reliability; however, their relatively 
low energy density continues to constrain their widespread adoption in large -scale ap plications, 
including electric vehicles and grid-level energy storage systems. 
Article information  Abstract 
 
Article History 
Received 08 October 2025 
Revised   27 October 2025 
Accepted 18 November 2025 
Available online 02 December 2025 
 This work reports the development of an electrode material derived from 
bamboo stem via NaOH activation, integrating hierarchical porosity, and 
surface functionalization for electrochemical capacitor applications. The 
synthesized carbon exhibits a flaky, fibrous morphology with micro –
mesoporous networks as confirmed by SEM, and a predominantly 
amorphous structure with short -range graphitic ordering from XRD. 
Elemental analysis via EDS reveals a high ca rbon content (94.65%) and 
nitrogen content (3.4%), which enhances charge storage and electrical 
conductivity. BET and BJH analyses indicate a high surface area (865 –
1147 m²/g), a pore volume of 0.552 cm³/g, and an average pore diameter 
of 2.43 nm, favourab le for ion diffusion and electrolyte access. 
Electrochemical testing demonstrates a high specific capacitance of 833 
F/g at 0.5 A/g, attributed to combined electric double -layer capacitance 
and pseudocapacitive contributions from oxygen- and nitrogen-containing 
functional groups, as evidenced by FTIR and CV (b = 0.787; 21% 
diffusion-controlled contribution). Electrochemical impedance 
spectroscopy shows a low equivalent series resistance of 0.2 Ω, while 
charge–discharge cycling confirms excellent stability w ith 94% 
capacitance retention after 5000 cycles. The CV and GCD further confirm 
its potency for efficient charge transport and high energy storage 
performance. These findings highlight the potential of bamboo -derived 
activated carbon as a sustainable and c ost-effective electrode material. 
However, the overall energy and power densities remain constrained by 
the narrow voltage window of the aqueous electrolyte and the limited 
cycling evaluation, indicating the need for further study with other 
electrolytes with higher voltage window and long-term testing. 
 
 
Keywords: 
Electrochemical energy storage, Extra 
capacitance from surface reactions, 
NaOH treatment, Nitrogen-doped 
carbon, Porous structures

ECc store energy through two primary mechanisms: electrical double -layer capacitance (EDLC) 
[4], wh ich involves non -faradaic ion adsorption at the electrode/electrolyte interface, and 
pseudocapacitance, which results from faradaic redox reactions associated with surface functional 
groups or transition metal compounds [5], [6]. The overall performance of ECs is largely dependent 
on the intrinsic properties of the electrode material, particularly its specific surface area, pore 
structure, electrical conductivity, and surface chemistry [7]. Among various c andidates, carbon-
based materials have emerged as the dominant class for supercapacitor electrodes, owing to their 
high surface area, tunable porosity, low density, and excellent chemical stability [8]. However, 
conventional activated carbons are often derived from fossil -based or synthetic precursors, raising 
environmental and economic concerns that conflict with the broader goals of sustainability and 
carbon neutrality [9]. 
 
In response, there has been a growing inter est in biomass -derived carbons as eco -friendly 
alternatives that align with circular economy principles [10]. Biomass precursors, including coconut 
shells, rice husks, sawdust, and corn stalks, have demonstrated promising performance when 
properly activated and functionalized [11]. Among these, bamboo has emerged as a particularly 
attractive candidate due to its fast growth rate (up to 1 m/day in some species), abundant availability 
in tropical and subtropical regions, and favourable lignocellulosic composition [12]. Rich in 
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, bamboo biomass provides a carbon-rich framework suitable for 
conversion into porous carbon structures. Its naturally hierarchical vascular architecture further aids 
the deve lopment of interconnected micro -, meso -, and macropores essential for efficient ion 
transport and charge accumulation [13]. 
 
Despite its potential, the use of bamboo-derived carbon in supercapacitors remains underexplored, 
particularly in the context of tailored chemical activation and heteroatom doping. Previous studies 
have reported specific capacitance values ranging from 150 to 400 F/g using physical activation or 
simple pyrolysis [14], which are lower than those achieved with advanced processing techniques. 
One key challenge lies in engineering a pore structure that optimally balan ces micropores (for 
increased surface area and energy density) with mesopores (to facilitate ion diffusion and power 
delivery) [15]. Additionally, improving the surface chemistry through nitrogen and oxygen doping 
can introduce faradaic red ox-active sites, thereby enhancing pseudocapacitive behaviour and total 
capacitance [16]. 
 
Chemical activation using alkali hydroxides, especially NaOH and KOH, has been shown to 
significantly enhance porosity and surface area of carbon materials. NaOH, in particular, reacts 
effectively with carbonaceous precursors to form pore -generating gases and salts, yielding well -
developed hierarchical pore systems [17]. When combined with thermal treatment under inert 
atmosphere, NaOH activation can produce highly porous carbon with tailore d textural and 
electrochemical properties. The incorporation of nitrogen -containing functional groups during 
carbonization or activation, particularly species such as pyridinic-N and pyrrolic-N has been widely 
associated with enhanced electrochemical performance, including increased capacitance, improved 
wettability, and higher electrical conductivity [18]. 
 
This study reports the synthesis of NaOH-activated carbon derived from bamboo waste, specifically 
sourced from discarded scaffold material. The objective was to address the performance limitations 
typically observed in conventional biomass-derived carbons for electrochemical energy storage. The 
precursor underwent controlled pyrolysis  followed by chemical activatio n to induce hierarchical 
porosity. The resulting material was thoroughly characterized using scanning electron microscopy

Abstract 
Porous carbon material s were synthesized from bamboo shoot shells through carbonization and static air 
activation.  The physicochemical properties of bamboo shoot shell -based porous carbon (BBC) were observed 
by scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, X -ray photoelectron spectroscopy, 
and N 2 adsorption desorption analysis. BBC has an optim al hierarchical porous structure that displays a

ABSTRACT
With the development of computer technology, a variety of machine learning models have been used to predict
the electrochemical performance of energy storage devices. In this study, the elemental analysis, industrial
analysis and structural composition, activation conditions, and current density of biomass are innovatively
selected as input conditions from the biomass raw material characteristics perspective and predict specific
capacitance based on the light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM) and deep neural network (DNN) algo-
rithm. Meanwhile, the prediction effects of the contrast capacitance under seven different input combinations are
compared. The results show that the combination prediction effect of retaining all features is the best, and the
industrial analysis and structural composition of biomass have a greater impact on the model than elemental
analysis, this conclusion is also verified by SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) value analysis, indicating that
they are essential for the model. It is also found that the Light GBM model has more advantages, with R
2
of 0.951,
mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.090, and Root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 14.756. This study builds a key
bridge between the basic composition information of biomass raw materials and the electrochemical perfor-
mance. Also, it helps to understand the related formation mechanism of biomass-derived carbon materials.
1. Introduction
With the increasing emphasis on renewable energy and the
increasing demand for addressing climate change, the demand for effi-
cient energy storage technologies is becoming more and more urgent.
Therefore, creating innovative and effective energy storage solutions has
emerged as a significant global challenge [ 1 ]. Among the spectrum of
energy storage devices, supercapacitors, as a new form of energy stor-
age, have become highly promising candidates. Their advantages lie in
their high power density, wide temperature range, and economical and
environmentally friendly characteristics [ 2 , 3 ]. The selection and per-
formance of electrode materials have a crucial impact on the overall
performance and cost of supercapacitors. As a key component of the
supercapacitor structure, it directly determines its key parameters such
as electrochemical performance, energy density, power density, and
cycle life [ 4 ]. Among many electrode materials, biomass-derived carbon
has been widely used in supercapacitors due to its high specific surface
area (SSA), low cost, high porosity, large-scale production, and
environmental friendliness [ 5 , 6 ].
Although supercapacitors have been particularly widely used, man-
ufacturers are still seeking higher energy-density supercapacitors to
meet the needs of transportation, energy, and aerospace. [ 7 ] The com-
plex composition and structure of biomass make the synthesized carbon
materials often exhibit inhomogeneity [ 8 , 9 ]. Moreover, biomass-
derived carbon materials have irregular pore structures and single-
pore channels, resulting in an increase in the diffusion distance and
resistance of ions in the electrolyte, which significantly reduces the rate
performance of assembling supercapacitors [ 10 ]. Therefore, various
methods have been tried to prepare high-performance porous carbon
materials, such as the molten salt method, activation method, hydro-
thermal carbonization method, and template method [ 11 – 12 ]. In many
experiments preparing porous carbon materials for supercapacitors, a
common method is to chemically or physically activate biochar [ 11 , 12 ].
Physical activation involves subjecting carbon materials to high-
temperature atmospheres (CO2, O2, etc.) to form pores [ 13 ]. Chemi-
cal activation, on the other hand, involves using acids or strong bases
