Machine learning enabled property prediction 
of carbon‑based electrodes for supercapacitors
Rajat Kushwaha1, Mayank K. Singh1, Sarathkumar Krishnan1, and Dhirendra K. Rai1,* 
1 Sustainable Energy and Environmental Materials (SEEM) Lab, Department of Metallurgical Engineering and Materials Science, 
Indian Institute of Technology, Indore, Simrol, Indore 453552, India
ABSTRACT
For supercapacitor electrodes, carbon is one of the most sought materials. Many 
synthetic strategies have been reported for carbon materials with a wide range 
of features in terms of surface area, porosity, the extent of the disorder, and 
the presence of various doping elements. Though there are many reports on the 
independent impact of these properties on supercapacitive outcomes of carbon 
materials, the collective effect of these features on the supercapacitive behavior 
is still not well understood. Therefore, it is imperative to explore new methods 
to predict the supercapacitive performance of carbon material without attempt-
ing experimentation. In this regard, this work reports on the comparative effi-
cacy of five machine-learning (ML) techniques for estimating the capacitance of 
carbon-based supercapacitors, including Linear Regression, Lasso Regression, 
XGBoost, Random Forest Regressor, and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN). We 
gathered data from various research papers and articles to prepare the dataset, 
followed by Data Cleaning and Feature Selection to select the best parameters 
for training our Machine Learning model. Additionally, five factors were cho-
sen to determine their effects on capacitance: voltage window, specific surface 
area  (m2/g), pore size (nm),  ID/IG ratio, and extent of N-doping. Out of five ML 
approaches, XGBoost, Random Forest Regressor, and Artificial Neural Networks 
(ANN) produced respectable prediction results when tested against actual data. 
More significantly, this project demonstrates the promise of Machine-Learning 
in selecting suitable materials for energy storage applications.
Introduction
Compared to batteries, supercapacitors possess the 
unique advantages of fast charging and discharg-
ing, high power density, and longer cyclic life [1 , 2]. 
However, the energy they can store is much less than 
the batteries. Such difference in behavior is mainly 
because of different charge storage mechanisms oper-
ating in batteries and supercapacitors. While charge 
storage in a battery is achieved by electron transfer

across the electrode–electrolyte interface [3 ], there is 
simple ion accumulation at or near the electrode in 
the case of supercapacitors [4]. Because of high power 
density and rapid charging, supercapacitors are 
increasingly appealing to various sectors, including 
transportation, aircraft, and communications [5 –7]. 
Electrodes are the most crucial part of supercapaci-
tors. Carbon-based materials have been extensively 
employed as electrode materials for supercapacitors 
due to their outstanding chemical and physical quali-
ties, low cost, easy availability, significant capacitance, 
and high electrical conductivity associated with their 
large specific surface area [8–10].
Researchers are keen to boost the specific capaci-
tance of carbon-based electrodes to improve super-
capacitors’ performance. For instance, numerous 
attempts have been made to alter the pore structure, 
add surface functional groups, and increase specific 
surface area to enhance the capacitance [11– 15]. Nev-
ertheless, presently there is no accepted guiding prin-
ciple that can adequately explain ways to enhance 
capacity; hence, the work of modification on capaci-
tor electrodes only depends on a few empirical ideas 
or hazy theoretical models [16]. The workable solu-
tion to this issue is to derive conclusions from a lot 
of data. In this connection, Machine Learning (ML), 
one of several data science technologies, is useful for 
establishing a predicted link between input and out-
put variables [17].
Since ML techniques can effectively and accurately 
anticipate property connections by utilizing datasets 
that are already accessible, this can be a perfect tech-
nique to predict the materials properties without actu-
ally attempting the experiment [18– 26]. Hence, with 
appropriate data set feed, ML can be implemented to 
obtain an advanced evaluation method for predicting 
the capacitance of carbon-based electrodes for super-
capacitors. Most of the time, data sets to feed ML for 
materials property predictions (primarily electrical, 
optical, and mechanical) are derived from theoretical 
calculations [27] or large-scale projects such as Materi-
als Genomic Initiative [28]. However, such approaches 
are not viable for carbonaceous materials as their com-
position is constant, which is carbon. Therefore, the 
possible dataset input for carbon materials should be 
based on their microstructures, degree of the disor-
der, and extent of different dopings. Moreover, for 
supercapacitive property prediction, experimental 
conditions, such as potential window and type of 
electrolyte, can also be used as the data set. Therefore, 
simply extracting data from the available publications 
and establishing a relationship between multivari-
ate information and performance is the most logical 
course of action.
More than 1000 publications concerning carbon-
based supercapacitors have been compiled by Zhu 
et al. [29]. It has been the source for the extraction of 
more than 10,000 data points, which include physi-
cal and chemical characteristics of the carbon mate-
rial (specific surface area, pore size, the ratio of  ID/IG, 
and doping elements) and the experimental conditions 
(such as electrolyte, test voltage window, and corre-
sponding specific capacity). Using these data points 
and theoretically derived input values, there have been 
reports on ML-assisted supercapacitive prediction of 
carbon-based materials [ 29]. For example, Zhao and 
co-workers have reported on the use of Linear regres-
sion [30], Lasso regression [31], and Artificial Neural 
Networks (ANN) [32] models of ML to predict super-
capacitive features of carbonaceous electrodes. During 
the application of ML, the ANN model has been used 
in most cases [ 33, 34], which has been able to fetch 
respectable predictions upon comparison with the test 
data. However, ANN is costly in terms of time and 
computer power, requiring hectic training [35]. Moreo-
ver, ANN is known to overfit the simple dataset [36]. 
To the best of our knowledge, the efficacy of superca-
pacitive behavior prediction of carbon materials using 
XGBoost, Random Forest Regressor models of ML has 
not been attempted and compared with other reported 
models, such as Linear regression, Lasso regression, 
and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN).
Here, we introduce ML to forecast how well carbon 
materials will perform in terms of capacitance. Although 
ML encompasses a vast array of various techniques, 
this report focuses on the efficacy comparison of Linear 
regression, Lasso regression, XGBoost, Random Forest 
Regressor, and ANN in predicting the carbonaceous 
material supercapacitive behavior. A least-squares 
function known as a linear regression equation is used

[30]. Lasso, in contrast, is a regression analysis technique

Abbas A. Abdullahi1, Ahmad Abbas Dalhatu2, Abdul‑Rahman Faisal Al‑Betar1, Syed Shaheen Shah3, 
Syed Masiur Rahman4,6, Tawfik A. Saleh1, and Md. Abdul Aziz4,5,*

ABSTRACT
This study presents a machine learning (ML)-driven framework for optimizing 
the design of polyaniline (PANI)-based supercapacitors, a promising material 
for energy storage. The framework integrates experimental data and advanced 
optimization techniques to systematically investigate the effects of key fabrication 
parameters such as mesh size, deposition cycles, voltage window, and operating 
potential on performance metrics, including specific capacitance, energy density, 
and internal resistance (IR) drop. Two ML models, gradient boosting regressor 
(GBR) and random forest regressor (RFR), were trained on 145 experimental data-
sets, achieving high predictive accuracy  (R2 > 0.95). Bayesian optimization (BO) 
was used to identify the global optimum fabrication conditions, resulting in sig-
nificant reductions in mean absolute percentage errors 15% for energy density, 
20% for capacitance, and 7% for IR drop. Feature importance analysis, includ-
ing SHAP and partial dependence plots, revealed that mesh size and operating 
potential were the most influential parameters, aligning with electrochemical 
theories on ion transport and polymer growth. This integrated approach not 
only accelerates the design and optimization of PANI-based supercapacitors but 
also minimizes material waste and provides a scalable, interpretable pathway for 
ML-driven optimization in the development of high-performance, cost-effective 
energy storage devices.

GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT
Introduction
Supercapacitors play a pivotal role in the advancement 
of smart energy storage technologies. The intermittent 
availability of energy required for routine activities 
necessitates the development of efficient and reliable 
storage systems across various applications, including 
those in optics. As a result, there is a growing impe-
tus to investigate alternative energy storage solutions, 
such as rechargeable batteries [ 1], fuel cells [ 2], and 
supercapacitors [3]. Supercapacitors have gained sig-
nificant attention due to their favorable characteristics, 
notably high power density and substantial specific 
capacity [4–6]. The overall performance and efficiency 
of supercapacitors are critically influenced by the 
properties and design of the electrode materials used. 
Polyaniline (PANI) is a prominent conductive poly-
mer for electrode materials due to its high theoretical 
capacitance, adjustable conductivity, environmental 
stability, and cost-effectiveness. It has been extensively 
studied for supercapacitor applications, especially in 
asymmetric and hybrid configurations [7, 8].
One promising strategy involves electrodepositing 
PANI onto conductive substrates such as stainless-
steel mesh, which provides a robust, flexible, and 
conductive platform [ 9]. Nevertheless, optimizing 
the electrodeposition conditions to maximize capaci-
tance and energy density while minimizing the IR 
drop remains a challenging task. The IR drop, a sud-
den voltage loss occurring at the onset of discharge, 
is one of the major performance-limiting factors in 
PANI-based supercapacitors. It reflects the internal 
resistance of the device, influenced by several inter-
dependent variables, including the morphology and 
conductivity of the electrode, interface contact, elec-
trolyte composition, and electrode design [10]. Exper-
imentally, researchers have sought to mitigate this 
issue through extensive parametric tuning, adjusting 
electrodeposition techniques (e.g., cyclic voltammetry 
(CV) vs. galvanostatic methods), scan rates, electrolyte 
concentrations, operating potential window (OPW), 
and cycle numbers [11]. However, the sheer number 
of combinatorial possibilities introduces complex-
ity, cost, and time delays to the experimental design 
process.
In this context, machine learning (ML) presents 
a transformative approach to materials optimiza-
tion, particularly for electrochemical systems where 
parameter interactions are non-linear and data rich. 
By training ML algorithms on experimentally acquired 
datasets, predictive models can be built to identify 
patterns and recommend optimized conditions faster 
and more accurately than traditional trial-and-error 
methods. In recent years, ML has shown promise in 
predicting battery cycle life [12], optimizing catalysts 
[13], and guiding material synthesis pathways [14]. 
However, its application in supercapacitor fabrica-
tion, particularly for optimizing electrodeposition 
parameters to address IR drop and enhance energy 
performance, remains underexplored. Although ML 
models have shown significant promise in predicting 
the specific capacitance and energy density of super-
capacitors, they encounter several limitations that can 
affect their accuracy and generalizability [15– 17]. A 
primary concern is their reliance on the quality and

face, making nanoporous carbon materials particu-

Sachit Mishra 1,2,6, Rajat Srivastava 1,3,6, Atta Muhammad 1,4, Amit Amit 1, Eliodoro Chiavazzo 1, 
Matteo Fasano 1* & Pietro Asinari 1,5
Hybrid electric vehicles and portable electronic systems use supercapacitors for energy storage owing 
to their fast charging/discharging rates, long life cycle, and low maintenance. Specific capacitance 
is regarded as one of the most important performance-related characteristics of a supercapacitor’s 
electrode. In the current study, Machine Learning (ML) algorithms were used to determine the impact 
of various physicochemical properties of carbon-based materials on the capacitive performance of 
electric double-layer capacitors. Published experimental datasets from 147 references (4899 data 
entries) were extracted and then used to train and test the ML models, to determine the relative 
importance of electrode material features on specific capacitance. These features include current 
density, pore volume, pore size, presence of defects, potential window, specific surface area, oxygen, 
and nitrogen content of the carbon-based electrode material. Additionally, categorical variables 
as the testing method, electrolyte, and carbon structure of the electrodes are considered as well. 
Among five applied regression models, an extreme gradient boosting model was found to best 
correlate those features with the capacitive performance, highlighting that the specific surface area, 
the presence of nitrogen doping, and the potential window are the most significant descriptors for 
the specific capacitance. These findings are summarized in a modular and open-source application 
for estimating the capacitance of supercapacitors given, as only inputs, the features of their carbon-
based electrodes, the electrolyte and testing method. In perspective, this work introduces a new wide 
dataset of carbon electrodes for supercapacitors extracted from the experimental literature, also 
giving an instance of how electrochemical technology can benefit from ML models.
Electrochemical capacitors (supercapacitors) are electrochemical devices that are extensively used for energy stor-
age due to promising characteristics such as high-power density, electrochemical stability, fast charge/discharge 
rates, safe operation mode, high power density, and long cycle  life1–3. These characteristics enable their use in a 
broad range of energy storage applications, e.g., for hybrid electric vehicles, portable electronics, and memory 
backup  systems4–6. Other than energy storage, there are some further interesting applications of supercapaci-
tors such as heat-to-current conversion of low-grade thermal  energy7 and renewable energy extraction using 
a supercapacitor from water  solutions8. Supercapacitors have been primarily classified into two types based on 
their charge storage mechanism: (i) electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs), which store electrical charge via 
ion adsorption at the electrode surface, and (ii) pseudo-capacitors, which store charges via reversible Faradaic 
redox reactions (see Fig.  1). Generally, EDLCs have superior cycle stability but lower specific capacitance in

stability  instead9,10. The current study focuses on EDLC supercapacitors and their optimization.
For the optimization of the electrochemical performance of EDLC supercapacitors, it is critical that the elec-
trode materials have commendable physicochemical properties, including appropriate pore size distribution, 
high specific surface area, high electrical conductivity, as well as electrochemical and mechanical stability for 
good cycling  performance9. Numerous materials have been synthesised and used as supercapacitor electrodes in 
recent years, including porous  carbon11–13, hierarchical porous  carbon14–16, activated  carbon10,17,18,  graphene9,19,20, 
rGO-PANI  nanocomposite21, carbon  nanotubes22–24,  In2O3-loaded porous  carbon25, and carbon  aerogels26,27. 
Among these electrode materials, carbon is the most frequently used due to its versatility and  uniqueness28. 
It exists in various forms (e.g., graphite, diamond), dimensionalities (fibres, fabrics, foams, and composites), 
ordered and disordered structures (depending on the degree of graphitization), with commendable electrical 
 conductivity29,30. The catalytic, optical, mechanical, and electrochemical properties of carbon make it an excel -
lent material for energy conversion and storage  applications31. Additionally, its well-established synthesis and 
activation methods enable its use as an electrode in supercapacitors with an appropriate pore size  distribution32.
Porous and activated porous carbon (AC) and hierarchical porous carbon (HPC) have been proposed in the 
literature for carbon electrodes (see Supplementary Note 1 for a detailed review). Because of its high specific 
surface area (SSA), improved electrical conductivity, adjustable pore sizes, electrochemical stability and low cost, 
porous carbon offers significant promise for use as the  electrode33–36. These properties make AC an excellent 
material for a variety of applications, including water purification, gas separation and storage, and electrode mate-
rials for capacitors, fuel cells and  batteries37. Differently from AC, hierarchical porous carbon material contains 
pores in a wide range of length scales, namely macro- (> 50 nm), meso- (2–50 nm), and micro- (< 2 nm) scales. 
The presence of macropores in HPC allows high-rate ion transport and acts as an ion reservoir. Furthermore, 
the interconnected mesopores provide low resistance pathways for the diffusion of ions; whereas the high SSA of 
micropores enhances the adsorption of ions at the pore  surface38. These unique properties of HPC gained recent 
interest in the selection of electrode materials for supercapacitors.
Besides the SSA and pore volume, there are also several other factors that influence performance of electrodes 
in supercapacitors, such as surface functional groups and conductivity. These can be modified by introducing 
heteroatoms—HA (nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur, etc.) in the carbon electrodes, which do not only enhance the 
wettability, but also improve electronic conductivity of activated  carbon39. Nitrogen doping on carbonaceous 
material as electron donor is useful for enhancing the specific capacitance via faradaic reaction and enhancing 
 wettability16. Similarly, oxygen doping improves the surface wettability, which in turn improves the supercapaci-
tor  performance39. Sulphur doping on carbonaceous material increases its bandgap, thus enhancing the electron 
donor properties and changing the electronic density of state. Sulphur doping also increases wettability, which 
in turn decreases the diffusion resistance that occurs between the electrode and electrolyte  ions40.
In perspective, graphene is a promising electrode material for supercapacitors too, due to a high electrical 
conductivity, high SSA, and excellent mechanical  strength41,42. Its porous structure also facilitates charge transport 
in the supercapacitor. The SSA of graphene is highly tuneable according to the requirement of supercapacitor 
electrode for energy storage applications. Also, the presence of highly movable free π electrons on its orbital are 
responsible for the exceptionally high electrical  conductivity41. Furthermore, the electrical behaviour of graphene 
can be improved through  functionalization43 and heteroatom  doping44.
Numerous attempts have been made to increase the specific capacitance of supercapacitors by utilizing differ-
ent types of carbon electrodes with varied pore size distributions, high specific surface area, diverse morphologies, 
and modified surface  chemistry45. However, the influence of these physicochemical parameters on the specific 
capacitance of supercapacitors has not been completely understood. Additionally, conventional theories and 
models are incapable of capturing with sufficient accuracy the microscopic details of the underlying physical 
mechanisms affecting ion transport, which are essential for accurately predicting the capacitive performance of

Electricity has emerged as the principal currency of energy exchange in the modern 
world. The recent increase in the acceptance of electrically operated automobiles such 
as e-bicycles, e-mopeds, electric cars, hybrid buses, and e-rickshaws has amplified the 
demand and dependency on electrical power [ 1– 5]. The global rise in living standards 
can be largely accredited to increasing reliance on electrical power. The development of

Discover Electronics
Abstract
The design architecture of electrode materials plays a pivotal role in shaping the 
electrochemical performance of supercapacitor. The dimensionality of electrode 
material proposes trade-off between specific surface area, pore architecture, 
mechanical strength and flexibility. This review undertakes a comprehensive 
classification of electrode materials into zero-dimensional, one-dimensional, two-
dimensional, and three-dimensional architectures, further correlating their structural 
characteristics with surface area, electrical conductivity, and ion transport dynamics. 
Various classes of materials, including carbon-based nanostructures, transition metal 
oxides, transition metal dichalcogenides, MXenes, and metal–organic frameworks, 
are analysed with respect to morphology-dependent performance characteristics. 
The design of heterostructures and multi-dimensional electrodes, as well as various 
synthesis methods, and the crucial elements of sustainability and scalability, are also 
taken into account. Furthermore, viewpoints for future avenues that pave the way 
for the development of supercapacitors are presented. Overall, this review aims to 
bridge the understanding between dimensional architecture, synthesis approach 
and performance, offering acuity in rational material design strategies for sustainable, 
high-performance supercapacitor systems.

the development of SC electrode is receiving extensive attention due to its paramount 
role in energy storage. Focused research efforts are directed toward the development 
and optimization of advanced electrode materials for commercial supercapacitor [ 27–

Abstract
Biomass-derived porous carbons are promising electrode materials for sustainable
electrochemical energy storage, yet their capacitance depends on coupled precursor and
process variables that are difficult to optimize experimentally. Here, we present a
source-aware materials-informatics framework for predicting the specific capacitance of
biomass-derived carbon electrodes directly from raw precursor descriptors and processing
conditions. A literature-curated dataset comprising elemental composition, proximate
analysis, lignocellulosic structure, and activation variables was evaluated with support
vector regression (SVR), Random Forest (RF), a deep neural network (DNN), LightGBM,
and XGBoost, together with an ensemble strategy, across seven feature combinations.
XGBoost delivered the strongest test performance, reaching R2 = 0.948 for the most
informative feature block. Beyond model ranking, the study emphasizes validation realism
by contrasting conventional random splits with source-aware evaluation, showing that
random partitions can substantially overestimate apparent generalization. Across models,
current density, activation temperature, holding time, ash content, and volatile matter
emerged as the most influential predictors. The resulting workflow provides practical
guidance for precursor screening, process-window definition, and data-driven design of
biomass-derived supercapacitor electrodes. The guidance applies within the precursor and
process regime represented by the training corpus; experimental verification is
recommended for excursions beyond it.
1 Introduction
The escalating global demand for efficient energy storage technologies, driven by the increasing
emphasis on renewable energy and the urgent need to address climate change, has positioned super-
capacitors as increasingly important devices in energy storage technologies. They are used in many
areas such as electric vehicles, renewable energy storage systems and portable electronics due to
their high power density, long cycle life and fast charge/discharge capabilities [1, 2]. One of the main
parameters determining the performance of supercapacitors is capacitance, which is directly related
to the surface area, porosity and chemical structure of the electrode materials. Traditionally, carbon-
based materials such as activated carbon have been preferred as electrodes. However, in terms of
sustainability and cost-effectiveness, the use of agricultural biomass waste as carbon electrode precur-
sors is becoming increasingly popular [3–5]. Activated carbon produced from biomass is important
both in terms of environmental benefits and contribution to the circular economy. These materials
are obtained by converting agricultural wastes such as rice husk, coconut shell, apricot kernel shell
and bamboo into high surface area carbons through carbonization and activation processes [6]. This
approach both reduces costs and offers an innovative solution in waste management. However, the

fractionation and delignification with industrial potential
Karo Almassi Tighi
*
, Rama Layek, Ikenna Anugwom
Department of Separation Science, LUT University, Mukkulankatu 19, Lahti, 15210, Finland

Sustainability
Economic viability
ABSTRACT
Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) represent a new generation of environmentally friendly solvents that show great 
promise for sustainable lignocellulosic biomass separation. The article presents an original assessment of DES 
formulations through advanced computational modeling and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, which 
reveal essential mechanistic details that previous reviews have not fully explored. This work reviews MD sim -
ulations, DFT, and ML methods to study detailed hydrogen-bonding systems and proton-catalytic and ionic in -
teractions between DESs and biomass components, which leads to their high selectivity for lignin and 
hemicellulose extraction. The review establishes a fundamental understanding of DESs by studying their 
chemical makeup and physical characteristics, and experimental results when processing different biomass 
materials. The review combines molecular-level findings with process optimization methods, economic assess -
ments, and sustainability impact evaluations. The review establishes a complete understanding by connecting 
atomic-scale interactions to industrial-scale applications through computational modeling, which enables the 
creation of optimized DES-based biorefinery systems.
1. Introduction
Growing global demand for energy and materials, coupled with 
climate concerns and fossil fuel depletion, drives the search for renew -
able alternatives. Lignocellulosic biomass and microalgae offer prom -
ising, sustainable raw materials used in producing energy sources, 
chemical products, and industrial compounds, lessening the usage of oil, 
along with limiting environmental outcomes.
The environmental viability and process effectiveness of the different 
methods of breaking down biomass face multiple essential barriers in 
their conventional approaches. The NaOH/urea pretreatment from 
agricultural residues of rice straw enhances plant-based polysaccharides 
like cellulose and hemicellulose, achieving high yields but producing 
excessive salts, which need costly removal procedures ( Dong et al., 
2018 ). Application of organic liquids for hemicellulose and lignin 
removal from poplar through organic acid/solvent blends proves effec -
tive yet remains impractical because it requires substantial solvent 
volumes and produces harmful compounds ( Yang et al., 2020 ). The 
conventional methods experience three major drawbacks, which include 
equipment corrosion, high operational costs, and complex chemical 
recovery procedures, thus limiting their suitability for large-scale 
sustainable biomass processing ( Rastogi and Shrivastava, 2017 ). 
Organic solvents used in conventional processes face multiple draw -
backs, including their volatile nature and corrosive effects on equipment 
and toxic properties, which prevent their use in biomass processing 
( Hong et al., 2020 ). Specific advantages associated with ionic liquids 
(ILs) make them attractive for lignocellulosic biorefinery applications 
because they are non-flammable, have low vapor pressure, and lack 
volatility ( Wang et al., 2017 ). The extensive deployment of ILs is limited 
by their expensive production costs and challenging preparation 
methods.
Deep eutectic solvents (DES) present an environmentally friendly 
solution to traditional biomass pretreatment procedures through their 
ability to overcome major challenges, including high energy re -
quirements and corrosive or expensive chemical usage. The pretreat -
ment process with DES produces better glucose yields and maintains 
stable cellulase enzymes while decreasing both energy requirements and 
environmental effects ( Liu et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2018; Sai and Lee, 
2019 ). The DES method operates without requiring severe processing 
conditions or expensive solvents that traditional methods need. The 
fractionation of complex biomass microalgae through biomass process -
ing using DES composed of lactic acid (LA) and choline chloride (ChCl)

of untreated biomass by more than double (7.7%) ( Yu et al., 2024a ). 
Introduction of 0.5 aqueous molar equivalent to the solvent system 
modified its polarity and increased its hydrogen bond acidity (from 1.37 
to 1.42) and alkalinity (from 0.52 to 0.54), which led to 89.4% lipid 
extraction and 84.2% protein dissolution. The research demonstrates 
DES as a promising method for complete biomass processing that com -
bines efficiency with environmental sustainability. Fig. 1 illustrates the 
application of DESs in the fractionation of lignocellulosic biomass and 
the subsequent utilization of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin as 
renewable feedstocks for the production of value-added materials and 
chemicals.
DESs have the highest potential among other solvents to be consid -
ered as green solvents, which stems from their distinctive characteris -
tics. The solvents possess several key characteristics, which include 
structural integrity, high dissolution efficiency, excellent biological 
tolerance, affordable manufacturing expenses, and reduced evaporative 
loss with straightforward preparation procedures. These solvents exhibit 
distinctive features, which include low toxicity and tunability, thus 
showing promise for pollution prevention and sustainability initiatives 
( Ee et al., 2023 ).
While the potential of DESs is widely acknowledged, this review aims 
to provide an original assessment by leveraging advanced computa -
tional modeling and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to reveal 
essential mechanistic details that previous reviews have not fully 
explored. Our objective is to establish a fundamental, molecular-level 
understanding of DES-biomass interactions and connect these atomic- 
scale phenomena to industrial-scale applications and economic viability.
The review follows this structure to achieve its purpose. It starts by 
explaining how lignocellulosic biomass exists and why it needs efficient 
fractionation methods. Thereafter, it explains what DESs consist of and 
their industrial value and chemical properties. Our main contribution 
appears in the following sections, which explain biomass fractionation 
through DESs and provide detailed molecular dynamics and thermo -
dynamic studies of DES systems. The study also examines simulation and 
modeling approaches, including machine learning and kinetic models, 
which serve as essential tools for DES performance prediction and 
optimization beyond experimental data. Furthermore, it moves into 
practical aspects, which include industrial process optimization, DES- 
based process sustainability evaluation, economic feasibility assess -
ment, and scalability issues. Finally, there is a summary of acquired 
knowledge and proposed research paths for the field. This review unites 
fundamental molecular studies with process optimization and economic 
evaluations to create a complete system for building efficient, environ -
mentally friendly, and cost-effective DES-based biorefineries.
2. Lignocellulosic biomass: challenges and fractionation 
requirements
Biorefineries use lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) as their primary 
feedstock because this renewable resource exists abundantly in quanti -
ties reaching 200 gigatons per year. The development of sustainable bio- 
based industries depends heavily on lignocellulosic biomass which 
comes from agricultural and forest residues and energy crops including 
both herbal and woody types and specialty crops ( Kumar et al., 2020; 
Rai et al., 2022 ). The production of LCB through halophytes which are 
salt-resistant plants growing on salt-damaged lands provides a 
cost-effective sustainable solution that frees up arable land and fresh -
water resources ( Fugol et al., 2023; Jankowski et al., 2020; Li et al., 
2023a; Rajput and Sheikh, 2019 ).
Lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) contains three primary biopolymers 
which include cellulose as a linear crystalline glucose polymer and 
hemicellulose as a branched amorphous heteropolysaccharide and 
lignin as a complex aromatic polymer that together form more than 70% 
of the biomass. Recent studies have identified proteins along with in -
organics and resins and other compounds as minor constituents in 
addition to the main three biopolymers ( Hallac and Ragauskas, 2011; 
French, 2017 ). The chemical diversity of these components is demon -
strated through their molecular structures which are shown in Fig. 2 .
Cellulose contains a highly structured and resistant framework that 
consists primarily of glucose units that bond through glycosidic linkages. 
The biomass section contains high crystallinity because of its intra- and 
intermolecular hydrogen bond connections. Different biomasses show 
varying levels of polymerization. The degree of polymerization in agri -
cultural residues reaches 900 units, but woody biomass contains be -
tween 4000 and 5500 units ( Hallac and Ragauskas, 2011 ).
Lignin, the second most abundant natural polymer, is a hydrophilic 
phenolic substance present in the plant cell wall that provides greater 
resistance to microbial attacks ( Sakakibara, 1980 ). Chemically, it is a 
highly complex polymer with plant-specific compositions and linkage 
motifs, lacking a defined primary structure; instead, it consists of 
random phenylpropanoid (C9) polyphenols primarily linked by aryl -
glycerol ether bonds between the phenolic units of para-coumaryl 
alcohol (H-type), coniferyl alcohol (G-type), and sinapyl alcohol 
(S-type). The majority of a plant's lignin (75 – 85%) is located within the 
considerably larger volume of the secondary cell wall ( Holtman et al., 
2003 ).
LCB maintains its structural integrity because of the complex 
bonding between its components, which creates a major processing 
obstacle. The biopolymers maintain strong covalent bonds between 
lignin-carbohydrate complexes (LCCs) and hydrogen bonds that create a 
three-dimensional cross-linked matrix structure ( Sun et al., 2023 ). Fig. 3
shows detailed lignin linkage types which demonstrate the complex 
nature of the structure. The strong bonding network protects poly -
saccharides from enzymatic and microbial breakdown while making it 
difficult to separate individual components, and affects both biomass 
physical characteristics and processing complexity. The strategic

The disposal of cigarette butts (CB s) is a global
issue. CB s are physically small and do not easily de -
grade, which poses significant toxicity risks to a 
wide range of organisms, including aquatic species,
insects, and both domestic and wild animals when it

from the presence and environmental release of nu -

sometimes reaching millions of dollars [11 ]. B ecause 
of the sheer volume of cigarette use, the resulting 
waste dispersion, removal costs, and the hazardous 
substances found in persistent butts, it is crucial to 
prioritize solutions for this problem [12 , 13 ].
Despite the toxic effects of CB  waste on the envi-
ronment, CB s can be recycled into valuable prod -
ucts. Various researchers have examined treatment
methods for CB s to minimize their ecological foot-
print and repurpose the waste into secondary raw 
materials or commercially available goods.
Several review articles report on CB  pollution and 
their toxicity to the environment. Early reviews re -
ported on their toxicity and environmental distribu -
tion, highlighting the release of heavy metals and mi-
croplastics to the aquatic and terrestrial environment.
Marinello et al. [14 ] emphasized recycling methods 
of CB s and cellulose acetate recovery, while Kurmus 
and Mohajerani [15 ] reported on the toxicity of CB s 
and their valorization strategies. Again, B attista [16 ]

ery technologies and Morales-Vera et al. [17 ] ex -
plored the biodegradation of cellulose acetate by mi-
crobial approaches.
Although reported reviews on the impact of CB s on 
the environment and valorization techniques have

emerging valorization strategies. This includes as -
sessing the types and concentrations of toxic ele -

cigarette butts, their compositional characteristics,
their filter structure, and the nature of contaminants 
released into water systems. In addition, we explore 
recent case studies, and the potential reuse and socio-
economic implications of CB  pollution. Collectively,
this study provides an integrated understanding of
CB -related pollution and its broader environmental
implications.

ABSTRACT  
Green energy-based power generation is a most rising topic in scientific society. Carbon water interaction-based 
hydrovoltaic (HV) power generation is a futuristic current research theme to generate power; however, the actual 
process remains an open question. Here in this work, a novel three-dimensional (3D) tubular HV device is 
fabricated, and its voltage distribution is analyzed. Under ambient conditions, a single tubular activated carbon 
hydrovoltaic (TAC) device can generate a voltage of up to 0.9 V and a current of up to 0.7 mA. Moreover, the 
outstanding power deliver from TAC is nearly 600 μ W for 1.2 g of active materials, and it is stable for more than 
ten days without any external light, wind, or heat. Further voltage improvement is tested with various factors 
such as light, heat, and humidity. Based on water flow-induced potential, 4 TACs can light an LED for successive 
ten days under ambient conditions (without any external energy supply). Moreover, the fabricated TAC device 
shows excellent self-life after one year of the experiment. Overcoming the two-dimensional (2D) HV devices, this 
self-charging 3D tubular high-power configuration is a low-cost HV device based on activated carbon and has 
advantages for practical applications.   
1. Introduction 
The increase in energy consumption due to the rapid development of 
population and modern technologies has been a significant concern in 
energy crisis over the recent years [ 1 , 2 ]. Green energy-based technol -
ogies are well developed and improved to reduce carbon footprints for a 
better tomorrow. Popularized technologies like piezoelectric [ 3 ], 
photovoltaic [ 4 – 6 ], thermoelectric [ 7 ], and photodetector [ 8 ]

technologies have inspired to develop new technical approaches for 
generating electric power in a sustainable manner using nanotech -
nology. However, most of the technologies are expensive and hard to 
manage in large-scale applications. Generally, carbon is a highly abun -
dant, low-cost material on earth that is popularized in various fields such 
as EM shielding [ 9 ], supercapacitor [ 10 ], freshwater production [ 11 , 
12 ], etc. Activation were carried out to attach the functional groups on 
carbon and modify the porosity, which gives excellent properties suit -
able for several applications. Recently, the generation of electric power 
via solid-liquid ( carbon-water ) interaction (CWI) was found promising to 
demonstrate potential induction without any high external energy 
consumption [ 13 ]. Briefly, power generation through water evaporation 
is an emerging green technology called hydro-voltaic (HV) to produce 
power through carbon-water molecular interaction. In this approach, 
water molecules are pumped to the top by capillary action, the resulting 
voltage is generated by the gradient of charges of the water molecules 
interacting with functional groups-rich carbon nanostructures. Any 
water-like liquid, droplet, moisture, or vapour leads to interaction with 
carbon nanostructures to generate the HV effect. When water passes 
through the functional groups rich carbon substrate, it forms an electric 
double layer (EDL). This type of interaction along the length of device is 
varies, as the amount of water molecules differ along the length. The 
amount of H
+
ions in the vertical porous media varies, forming a 
gradient of EDL which can create an electric potential along the device. 
This mechanism is schematically shown in Fig. 1 . 
Voltage generation from CNT was reported in the year 2003 [ 14 ]. So 
far, colossal carbon-based materials exhibit the HV effect without 
non-uniformity of pressure along its length. Yet, the impact of HV is an 
ultimate future technology to fabricate a power generator with low 
energy consumption. Several theories were used to explain the mecha -
nism behind the hydro voltaic, such as the electric double layer and 
pseudocapacitance mechanism [ 15 , 16 ], ion diffusion-induced mecha -
nism [ 17 ], and so on. However, the explanation for the HV working 
mechanism remains controversial. Diverse devices were being devel -
oped for hydrovoltaic power generation, like moisture-induced elec -
tricity generation [ 18 ], droplet movement-induced power generation 
[ 19 ], flow-induced electricity generation [ 20 ], and evaporation-induced 
electricity generation [ 21 ]. Of these methods, evaporation-induced 
power generation is natural and efficient in producing a high potential 
and current; generally, in this method, the abundance of functional 
groups in the carbon results in voltage generation when the water 
molecules interact via capillary flow. Plasma treatment to add func -
tional groups, [ 18 , 22 ] and hydroxide-based materials [ 23 ], were used to 
enhance the interaction between carbon and water. Also, the structural 
change in the device could be a factor in enhancing the evaporation for 
better CWI. However, all the existing HV-based reports show consider -
able voltage [ 23 , 24 ], of the order of 1 V [ 13 ], but the induced electric 
current from the device is in the range of few nA to μ A [ 13 , 25 , 26 ]. 
Notably, external sources like light, heat, or wind (apart from ambient 
conditions) also essential to generate power from the devices. All re -
ported HV devices are thin film-based structures that are limited by the 
low possibility of CWI. Also, arranging this 2D device at a particular 
angle for better capillary is complicated for a large-scale practical 
application and requires external energy. 
Here a novel 3D tubular hydrovoltaic device was fabricated that uses 
activated carbon (TAC) and water to generate high voltage and 
considerable current with less dependency on external energy such as 
light, heat, or wind. Converting 2D to 3D HV devices can show a higher 
possibility of CWI. This could be very useful for potential applications. 
Moreover, the device shows shelf-life of more than one year. This 
method can overcome other reported HV devices under ambient con -
ditions to generate electric current for practical electronic applications. 
The capillary flow of water is varied with different radii tubes to prove 
that the potential induction due to the substance ’ s interplay with water 
molecules. 
2. Experimental 
2.1. Device fabrication 
A typical device fabrication process is illustrated in Fig. S1 , and the 
actual device image is attached in Fig. S2 . Briefly, both side openable 
acrylic 3 mm thickness and 50 mm long tube was taken and washed with 
double distilled (DI) water. Two aluminum foil electrodes were con -
nected along two ends of the tube and tiny pores were made using direct 
punching (less than 1 mm diameter) uniformly in the bottom part of the 
electrode ( Fig. S1a ). The commercial cotton fiber was attached to the 
bottom electrode for the continuous water supply and wettability 
( Fig. S1b ). Powdered activated carbon (made from coconut husk) was 
fully packed inside the tube, as shown in Fig. S1c (average weight of 
carbon is 1.2 g). The final device was taken to analyze the hydro-voltaic 
effect. To understand the CWI, different diameters and various lengths of 
tubes were used to vary the water pumping rate. Three different di -
ameters (1 cm, 1.5 cm, and 2 cm) ( Fig. S3 ) with the same length (5 cm) 
TAC were fabricated with the same amount of carbon to analyze the 
diameter dependence of CWI and named TAC1, TAC1.5, and TAC2. 
From the hydrovoltaic measurement, TAC1.5 performed best. Therefore, 
we selected this device for further measurements. Three different length 
tubes (4 cm, 5 cm, and 6 cm) with the same diameter TAC1.5 were also 
constructed to confirm the capillary rise and mentioned as TAC4, TAC5, 
and TAC6, respectively. Moreover, to differentiate this new 3D from 
other existing 2D designs, the same amount of carbon (1.2 g) was taken 
to construct a 2D HV device.

Abstract
The use of conventional heat transfer fluids has many limitations, and industrial applications require efficient 
heat transfer systems. Existing cooling systems suffer from low thermal conductivity and poor heat transfer, 
which result in reduced efficiency and high power consumption. This study proposes an optimised artificial 
neural network (ANN) and genetic algorithm (GA)-based artificial intelligence model to predict the thermal 
conductivity and viscosity of graphene nanoplatelets (GNP)–Cellulose nanocrystals (CNC)/Ethylene Glycol 
(EG)-water hybrid nanofluids, thereby improving heat transfer performance. Single GNP and hybrid GNP/CNC 
nanofluids are studied, with field-emission scanning electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy 
used to characterise nanoparticles. A two-step preparation method was used for thermal conductivity and vis -
cosity measurements across temperatures (30–80 °C) and volume concentrations (0.02–0.2 vol%). The research 
employs a combined experimental analysis and modern machine learning methods, including ANN and GA, to 
develop an optimised predictive model. The results indicate a considerable improvement in thermal conductiv -
ity, with GNP/CNC hybrid nanofluids at 0.2 vol% and 80 °C showing a 52.77% increase over the base fluid. 
The rheological behaviour analysis reveals that viscosity increases with volume concentration and decreases

1 Introduction
The limitations of classical heat transfer fluids have underscored the need for effective cooling approaches, par -
ticularly as modern thermal management systems become increasingly sophisticated. Nanofluids are one pos -
sible solution, consisting of microstructures dispersed in a base fluid (such as water, ethylene glycol, oil, or 
glycerol), which offer improved thermophysical properties. The tunability of these fluids, achieved by modifying 
nanoparticle characteristics, enables unprecedented versatility across various applications [ 1]. Recent contribu-
tions include hybrid nanofluids, whose composition comprises multiple nanomaterials that interact synergisti -
cally, resulting in enhanced performance. These hybrid systems improve thermal performance by optimising the 
thermal networks and aspect ratios of different nanomaterials [ 2]. Their use encounters real-world difficulties, 
namely increased viscosity, which requires higher pressure drops and pumping power [ 3]. Thus, a critical area 
that needs further investigation and optimisation is the trade-off between improved thermal performance and 
system power efficiency. The growing need for thermal management systems has spurred in-depth investigations 
into advanced heat-transfer materials. This followed Choi’s [ 4] groundbreaking work introducing nanofluids, 
which demonstrated improved thermal properties arising from suspending nanoparticles in base fluids. This work 
has since attracted tremendous research activity in various fields, including chemistry, energy, and industry [ 5]. 
Carbon nanostructure-based fluids have been widely studied, with a focus on carbon nanotubes [ 6], graphene 
derivatives, and their hybrids [ 7]. Graphene nanoplatelets (GNP) are among the most promising materials, bal -
ancing the challenging thermal performance of monolayer graphene with the proven stability and cost-effective 
properties of graphitic carbon. These innovations help overcome the fundamental limitation of classical cooling 
systems: the low thermal conductivity of the heat-transfer fluids.
On the other hand, there are considerable research gaps in hybrid nanofluids. Although considerable work has 
been done on single-carbon nanostructures, hybrid arrangements that offer synergistic advantages have not been 
extensively studied. The interaction mechanism between nanofluid composition and thermophysical properties 
in multi-nanofluid systems is not entirely understood. While graphene nanoplatelets possess various promising 
properties, challenges in dispersion stability and long-term performance warrant further exploration. A detailed 
study of the optimisation of combinations of carbon nanostructures and their synergy to date for thermal conduc-
tivity enhancement is still lacking. Such a gap is critical to the cost-effectiveness and practicality of realistic ther-
mal management systems. In addition, although machine learning methods can predict nanofluid characteristics, 
there is an opportunity to combine genetic algorithms with neural networks to optimise hybrid nanofluid charac-
teristics. This combination has been barely explored. Graphene-based nanofluids have recently gained consider-
able interest due to significant advancements in thermal management systems and the availability of GNP in the 
market. Despite this, the specific surface area of GNP continues to increase, leading to a strong tendency toward 
aggregate formation via van der Waals forces, which remains a major hurdle for thermal applications requiring 
stable dispersion [7]. To overcome this limitation, researchers investigated different innovative methods. Kulan-
daivel et al. [8] explored the use of environmentally friendly GNP-palm oil and CNC hybrid alternatives. GNP 
nanofluids based on water were examined by Bansal et al. [ 9], who investigated possible behaviours as a func -
tion of concentration over a volume concentration range of 0.0125% to 0.0375%. Carbon-based materials have 
evolved for several generations in thermal applications, from simple carbon black to distributed nanostructures 
[10], such as functionalised carbon nanotubes [11]. Over the last decade, carbon spheres of various sizes, ranging 
from the nanostructure scale to the mesoscale, have emerged individually. Among these, graphene nanoplatelets 
have shown great promise, providing a practical compromise between the remarkable characteristics of graphene 
and low-cost manufacture [12]. These multi-layered graphene flakes retain many of graphene’s attractive proper-
ties while enhancing cost-effectiveness for industrial applications.

(ANFIS), and support vector machines (SVMs). These AI approaches have accurately predicted the thermophysical

ABSTRACT: Developing oxygen reduction reaction (ORR)
catalysts with high efficiency and stability represents a key
requirement for zinc-air batteries. Employing a mixture of iron
nitrate nonahydrate, citric acid, and ammonium persulfate as
precursors and g-C
3
N
4
as a sacrificial template, this study
synthesized Fe, N, S co-doped porous carbon nanosheets via
ball-milling and one-step pyrolysis, offering a solvent-free and
simple process. In alkaline electrolyte, Fe-NSC 1000 exhibited
outstanding ORR performance, showing onset and half-wave
potentials of 1.00 and 0.896 V, respectively. Fabricated into the
cathode of a zinc-air battery, it offered outstanding durability (up to
1025 h at 5 mA cm
−2
) in addition to a specific capacity of 760.65
mA h g
Zn

and a peak power density of 145.65 mW cm

. This
work provides a simpler and greener strategy for designing iron-based sulfur-doped ORR catalysts, driving forward zinc-air battery
technology.
1. INTRODUCTION
Given the global shift in energy systems alongside the
implementation of the “dual-carbon” strategy, zinc-air batteries
(ZABs) have emerged as a critical energy storage technology to
overcome traditional energy dependency and resource
constraints, owing to their advantages including economic
viability, excellent theoretical energy density, and ecological
compatibility.
1−3
Nevertheless, the practical application of this
technology remains constrained by several core challenges: the
sluggish ORR kinetics at the air cathode, the prohibitive cost of
commercial Pt/C, and the insufficient catalytic activity of non-
noble metal catalysts.
4−6
Consequently, creating low-cost ORR
catalysts based on non-noble metals with both high activity and
excellent durability has emerged as a key route to optimize the
energy mix and safeguard energy security.
Heteroatom doping is a widely adopted strategy for
modulating carbon materials’ electronic configuration and
defect abundance for better catalysis.
7−12
Nitrogen (N) doping
represents the most prevalent form. Owing to its relatively high
electronegativity, the carbon skeleton’ electronic configuration
can be tuned by nitrogen atoms, thereby inducing the
formation of additional defects and creating active sites such
as graphitic nitrogen.
13−15
Owing to their role in facilitating
oxygen adsorption and electron transfer, these active sites bring
about a pronounced increase in the ORR catalytic performance
of the material.
16
However, external doping with nitrogen
alone can easily lead to excessive nitrogen incorporation,
thereby compromising the overall structural stability of the
material.
17,18
Therefore, selecting a nitrogen-rich template as a
nitrogen source is crucial for achieving effective N-doping
while maintaining structural integrity. Moreover, as a self-
sacrificial template, g-C
3
N
4
can be directly converted into
nitrogen-doped porous carbon during high-temperature
carbonization. The g-C
3
N
4
possesses a graphite-like planar
structure and has been extensively studied owing to its
distinctive features, such as excellent thermal stability, robust
stability, tunable structure, and chemical inertness.
19
For
instance, Qin et al. utilized g-C
3
N
4
as a support to synthesize
double-shelled carbon nanospheres (FSCN-NS).
20
In this
system, g-C
3
N
4
also served as a protective agent; its stable
supporting effect effectively mitigated chemical corrosion,
thereby ensuring that the as-prepared FSCN-NS exhibited
exceptional structural stability and durability during the ORR
process at the fuel cell cathode. This not only effectively
compensates for the loss of nitrogen at elevated temperatures
but also circumvents the cumbersome process of removing the
template using complex etching steps, fully demonstrating its
unique advantages as a self-sacrificial template.
21,22
Furthermore, sulfur doping can expand the interlayer
spacing of materials, which facilitates the transport of reactants

23−25
First-principles
studies based on density functional theory further confirm that
sulfur dopants can also introduce significant spin polarization
into the carbon lattice, thereby enhancing the oxygen
reduction reaction performance.
26
Gu et al. compared the
ORR and oxygen evolution reaction activities of graphdiyne
doped with different heteroatoms (B, N, P, S) through density
functional theory (DFT) calculations.
8
The computational
results revealed that S-doped graphdiyne exhibits the optimal
ORR activity, which is primarily attributed to the relatively
high positive charge density on its active centers. Beyond
single-heteroatom doping, multi-heteroatom co-doping is also
recognized as an effective strategy for enhancing ORR catalytic
performance. Among these, nitrogen/sulfur (N/S) co-doping
has been extensively investigated due to its superior perform-
ance arising from the synergistic effects.
27−30
N/S co-doped
three-dimensional nanoporous carbon materials were success-
fully prepared by Chen et al. through a combined approach of
self-assembly and carbonization, utilizing a hybrid of covalent
triazine framework and sodium lignosulfonate (CTF@LS) as a
multifunctional precursor.
31
Theoretical calculations demon-
strate that the combined effect of nitrogen and sulfur
heteroatom doping significantly facilitates the desorption of
*OOH and its conversion to *O, thereby markedly
accelerating ORR process.
Previous studies have demonstrated that iron-based catalysts
possess advantages such as outstanding stability, high catalytic
activity, and economical viability.
32−34
Specifically, Fe−N−C
enhance ORR activity of individual active sites by forming
highly active FeN
X
sites within microporous graphitized
carbon, achieving a level of performance that equals or
overtakes traditional platinum catalysts.
35−37
Chen et al.
developed a 3D bifunctional catalyst,denoted FeN
x
/N,S−C,
containing co-doped nitrogen, sulfur, and iron, using a simple,
eco-friendly molten salt-assisted route.
38
It is the combination
of uniformly dispersed FeN
x
sites, surrounding S heteroatoms,
and the 3D porous architecture that synergistically provides
the catalyst (FeN
x
/N,S−C) with high accessibility, abundant
open pores/channels, and dense active sites that facilitate mass
transfer. In actual catalytic environments, multiple components
typically work in synergy. Iron-based catalysts often contain
adjacent species such as Fe
x
Oγ, Fe, and Fe
3
C. Although these
components are not the most direct active sites themselves,
they significantly influence the reduction/desorption behavior
of peroxide intermediates in ORR, thereby boosting the
intrinsic ORR activity of FeN
x
.
39−44
Recent studies have further reported a variety of non-noble-
metal catalysts and air-electrode designs for oxygen electro-
catalysis and ZABs.
45−48
Collectively, these representative
studies highlight the importance of integrating active-site
regulation with porous-structure engineering and efficient
mass-transfer pathways to improve ORR activity and practical
battery performance.
Despite these advances, considerable attention has been
devoted to heteroatom composition, active-site configuration,
porous-structure engineering, and electrode architecture,
whereas the influence of pyrolysis temperature on the
evolution of the carbon framework, Fe-containing species,
and ORR performance within a fixed precursor system has
been less systematically clarified. Therefore, in this study, a
facile method combining ball milling with one-step pyrolysis
was employed to successfully synthesize a hierarchically porous
carbon nanosheet material (denoted as Fe-NSC), using ferric
nitrate nonahydrate, ammonium persulfate, and citric acid as
precursors, and g-C
3
N
4
as a sacrificial template. The effect of
temperature regulation on its catalytic activity was sub-
sequently investigated. In contrast to literature methods that
typically involve complex solvent systems, multi-step reactions,
or harsh conditions, this method consists of only two steps:
solvent-free ball milling and one-step pyrolysis. This strategy
significantly streamlines the experimental procedure, and
enhances experimental reproducibility.
49
Electrochemical test
results demonstrate that Fe-NSC 1000 exhibits superior ORR
catalytic activity and superior durability over commercial Pt/C
when tested in 0.1 M KOH. The catalyst also demonstrates
exceptional battery performance when assembled into a zinc-
air battery. In summary, the Fe-NSC material developed in this
study integrates advantages such as high catalytic activity, and
facile synthesis, making it highly promising for ZABs.

Urea, citric acid, ammonium persulfate, and iron(III) nitrate

Abstract:
Key challenges in designing high-performance metal–organic framework (MOF)-based 
supercapacitor electrodes include optimizing precursor concentration and properly predicting 
electrochemical performance. In this article, we provide an integrated experimental and 
machine learning (ML) framework to optimize Co-MOF-coated nickel foam electrodes 
manufactured via a simple and scalable dip-coating process. Concentration-dependent 
structural and morphological evolution was validated by X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning 
electron microscopy (SEM), with the 3 mmol Co precursor electrode (NFC3) showing the most 
uniform coating and superior electrochemical performance. The improved NFC3 electrode was 
built into an NFC3//NFC3 symmetric supercapacitor with a specific capacitance of 19.97 F 
g−1 at 1 A g−1 and 72% capacitance retention after 1000 charge–discharge cycles. 
Electrochemical studies, such as cyclic voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge–discharge 
(GCD), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), Ragone analysis, b-value and Dunn's 
analysis, demonstrated that the charge storage process was mostly surface-controlled 
capacitive. Five ML regression models were trained using experimentally generated CV data 
to predict the electrochemical current response. Among these, the Random Forest model had 
the highest prediction accuracy (R² = 0.999825, RMSE = 1.28 × 10⁻⁴ A, MAE = 3.10 × 10⁻⁵ 
A). The proposed experimental-ML framework provides an effective technique for optimizing 
MOF-based electrodes and accelerates the data-driven creation of high-performance symmetric 
supercapacitors.
Keywords: Co-MOF; Nickel foam electrode; Symmetric Supercapacitor; Machine Learning; 
Random Forest Regression; Electrochemical Energy Storage; Current Response Prediction.

The rapid expansion of renewable energy systems, electric vehicles (EVs), portable devices 
and smart power grids has created an urgent demand for energy storage technologies with high

However, the intermittent nature of these sources needs the use of efficient energy storage 
systems to ensure continuous power delivery and increase grid stability [4–7]. Supercapacitors 
are remarkable for their high-power density, quick charge/discharge ability, excellent cycling

considerable attention [8–10]. These advantages make them particularly desirable for

gadgets, wearable devices and hybrid energy storage systems [2,11,12]. However, further

increase the energy and power performance without affecting the long-term cycle stability to 
sustain efficient electrochemical performance at high current densities  [13–15].

pseudocapacitors and hybrid supercapacitors according to charge-storage mechanism [16–20].

densities [18–20].  However, nonlinear electrochemical behaviour arising from the intricate 
interaction between electrode structure, electrolyte and operating circumstances makes

1. Introduction
With the rapid advancement of next-generation electronics and 
portable energy devices, there has been a growing demand for advanced, 
multifunctional materials that can perform two key functions: energy 
storage and chemical or biosensing interfaces. In these situations, 
bifunctional electrode materials have emerged as strong contenders, 
specifically those with high electrochemical performance, coupled with 
molecular recognition and sensitivity in detection. [ 1 – 6 ] The two-way 
capability of such a feature is instrumental in system integration 
design, particularly for wearable electronics, implantable devices, and 
smart sensors, where component miniaturization is necessary without 
compromising versatility. Supercapacitors, also known as 
electrochemical capacitors, are best recognized for their high-power 
density, long cycle life, and fast charge-discharge capabilities. Their 
energy density typically lags behind that of batteries. [ 7 ] To enhance 
performance and multifunctionality, scientists have increasingly tar -
geted nanostructured materials with pseudocapacitive responses, high 
redox activity, and high surface areas for interaction with the electro -
lyte. [ 3 , 8 – 12 ] However, electrochemical sensors require materials with 
improved electrical conductivity, surface reactivity, and chemical 
selectivity. Creating a material that performs both functions efficiently is 
a synergistic combination of high conductivity, electroactive surface 
sites, and structural stability.
Reduced graphene oxide (rGO), which is a derivative of graphene, is 
among the most interesting materials in this group. Its superior

properties, including a high theoretical surface area (~2630 m
2
/g), high 
carrier mobility, chemical stability, and tunable surface chemistry, make 
it an ideal backbone for hybrid architectures. [ 13 ] In addition, its oxy -
gen functionalities and intrinsic defects not only contribute capacitance 
through faradaic mechanisms but also provide active sites and binding 
sites for sensing purposes. [ 14 – 19 ] Among all the synthesis routes, 
microwave-exfoliation has been of particular interest as a rapid, envi -
ronmentally friendly, and scalable method to synthesize rGO sheets with 
reduced layer numbers, high defects, and intact conjugated networks. 
[ 20 , 21 ] The rapid dielectric heating in the microwave process causes 
thermal shock-induced exfoliation, which prevents restacking and fa -
vors the development of defect-rich rGO with high electrical conduc -
tivity. The method also enables homogeneous heating and rapid reaction 
kinetics, making it highly desirable for heat and sensor devices.
However, despite its advantageous properties, rGO-based electrodes 
often exhibit limited specific capacitance, mainly due to the restacking 
of graphene layers and the absence of faradaic reactions, which restricts 
their energy storage capacity. To overcome these limitations, developing 
hybrid materials that combine the high conductivity and surface area of 
rGO with the pseudocapacitive behaviour of transition metal oxides has 
gained considerable interest. Transition metal oxides, such as MnO ₂ , 
NiO, Co ₃ O ₄ , and TiO ₂ [ 22 – 24 ], offer high theoretical capacitance due to 
their ability to undergo fast and reversible redox reactions. Among 
these, titanium dioxide (TiO ₂ ) is particularly attractive due to its low 
cost, abundance, non-toxicity, environmental compatibility, and chem -
ical stability. [ 25 ] Although TiO ₂ alone suffers from low electrical con -
ductivity, when combined with conductive carbon-based materials, such 
as rGO, it can contribute significantly to enhanced electrochemical 
performance through synergistic effects. [ 26 – 28 ]
In this communication, we try to test the same nanocomposite ma -
terial for two distinct applications: supercapacitor and sensors. It dem -
onstrates its multifunctionality and real-world practicality. For the 
reduction of graphene oxide (GO), a microwave-assisted method was 
employed. This technique is a highly efficient approach, achieving rapid 
exfoliation within seconds, whereas conventional reduction methods 
typically require several hours.
A microwave-exfoliated reduced graphene oxide/titanium dioxide 
(ME-rGO/TiO ₂ ) nanocomposite was synthesized and employed as a 
bifunctional electrode material for energy storage and sensing applica -
tions. The morphology, structure, and surface chemistry of the ME-rGO/ 
TiO ₂ composite were investigated using X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Fourier 
Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Field-Emission Scanning 
Electron Microscopy (FESEM), and Raman spectroscopy, demonstrating 
successful exfoliation and composite formation. The capacitive perfor -
mance was evaluated through electrochemical analyses, including cyclic 
voltammetry (CV), galvanostatic charge-discharge (GCD), and electro -
chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The composite exhibited a high 
specific capacitance, good rate performance, and excellent cycle life, 
demonstrating potential as a suitable material for high-performance 
supercapacitors. Furthermore, its sensing capability was also exam -
ined using a model redox analyte, dopamine (DA), in which case the 
composite electrode exhibited high sensitivity, low detection limit, and 
satisfactory selectivity. Apart from enhancing the fundamental under -
standing of interfacial synergy between rGO and TiO ₂ , this research 
suggests a novel approach to the synthesis of bifunctional nanohybrids 
for integrated electrochemical devices. The ME-rGO is used here as a 
conducting but defective matrix, while the addition of TiO ₂ disrupts both 
redox sites and analyte adsorption capability. Combined, these features

ABSTRACT
Recent years have seen remarkable progress in the integration of Density Func-
tional Theory (DFT) calculations and Machine Learning (ML) techniques, par-
ticularly within the realm of materials science. This review delves into this bur-
geoning field, focusing on their application to MXenes, a significant family of 
two-dimensional (2D) materials comprising transition metal carbides, nitrides, 
or carbonitrides. MXenes have garnered attention for their remarkable proper-
ties and versatile applications, including catalysis, gas sensing, and energy stor-
age. We further investigate the integration of ML methodologies, utilizing vari-
ous algorithms to predict MXene properties with high accuracy and efficiency. 
Through a comprehensive literature analysis, we underscore the synergistic rela-
tionship between DFT calculations and ML approaches, showcasing how their 
combined use accelerates MXene discovery and optimization for diverse techno-
logical applications. Additionally, we discuss current challenges and future direc-
tions in leveraging these computational techniques to advance our understanding 
and utilization of MXene materials. This review serves as a valuable resource for 
researchers at the intersection of computational methods and materials science, 
offering insights into state-of-the-art techniques for predicting MXene proper-
ties, performance, and guiding future research endeavors in this dynamic field.

has significantly reshaped the landscape of modern 
materials science, enabling breakthroughs in energy, 
electronics, and environmental technologies. Follow-
ing the pioneering work on graphene, extensive efforts 
have been devoted to the synthesis, processing, and 
functionalization of 2D materials using scalable tech-
niques such as printing and additive manufacturing, 
which have facilitated their integration into flexible 
and wearable devices [1 , 2]. In parallel, the develop-
ment of 2D semiconductor nanosheets has opened 
new opportunities in photocatalysis and solar energy 
conversion, highlighting the critical role of dimen-
sionality in tailoring material properties [3 ]. Among

ABSTRACT
Recently, MXenes have become effective electrode materials for devices including 
batteries, supercapacitors (SCs), sensors, antennas, and optoelectronic devices, as 
well as for sustainable energy storage. They are promising choices for a variety of 
energy conversion and storage materials due to their metallic conductivity, good 
hydrophilicity, and ability to act as ideal templates for developing other materi-
als with tunable features. Recent advances in energy devices and storage using 
MXene as electrode materials are outlined in this article. The fundamental ideas 
of energy storage and renovation systems are examined. The following sections 
highlight the special qualities of Green Synthesis Methods for MXenes. Potential 
fixes for issues that arose during the development of MXene were investigated, as 
was the use of Machine learning techniques as cutting-edge approaches to MXene 
product optimisation. Additionally, MXene’s applications in energy conversion 
devices, such as supercapacitors, catalysis, various batteries, and electrochemi-
cal sensing were highlighted. A discussion of potential future opportunities for 
MXene-based materials in energy industries for sustainable technology wraps 
up the study.

Li	micro	batteries	like	electrodes	or	supercapacitors	(Y e	et	
al.	2024).	 Li2T iO3	has	widely	been	regarded	as	a	promis-

nized	as	one	of	the	best	solid	tritium	breeder	materials	under

Li	 atomic	 density,	low	 activation	 energy,	strong	 chemical	
stability,	and	efficient	tritium	release	at	low	temperatures.	To	
fully	harness	the	potential	of	 Li2T iO3,	a	comprehensive	
characterization	of	its	mechanical	properties	is	required	(Hu	
et	al.	2024;	Xu	et	al.	2022;	Goswami	and	Murphy	2020).
The	technology	and	application	of	artificial	intelligence	
have	reached	a	high	level	of	maturity,	with	many	scholars	
introducing	 experimental	 data	 and	 artificial	 intelligence	
modelling	 theory	 into	 rolling	 process	 optimization	 and	
mechanical	property	prediction	(Kibrete	et	al.	2023;	Amal-
lah	et	al.	2020;	Tanasehte	et	al.	2020;	El	Hana	et	al.	2024).	
This	has	led	to	the	emergence	of	new	data-driven	methods	
based	 on	 big	 data,	 such	 as	 machine	 learning	 (ML),	 in	 the	
field	of	materials	science	(Elkhal	et	al.	2021,	2022;	Hader	et	
al.	2020;	Tanasehte	et	al.	2022).	The	application	of	machine	
learning	 reduces	 overall	 computational	 costs	 and	 shortens	
the	development	cycle	(Huang	et	al.	2023),	and	its	use	has	
been	 prevalent	 across	 diverse	 domains	 such	 as	 computer	
vision,	data	analytics,	and	bioinformatics	(Iqbal	and	Kumar	
2023;	 Nafea	 et	 al.	 2024).	 It	 has	 also	 played	 a	 key	 role	 in	
material	 characterization,	 enabling	 the	 discovery	 of	 novel	
material	 structures	 and	 facilitating	 the	 accurate	 prediction	
of	material	and	molecular	properties	(Akinpelu	et	al.	2024;	
Fedik	 et	 al.	 2022).	 Tawfik	et	 al.	 (2020)	 applied	 ML	 algo-
rithms	to	predict	the	thermal	properties	of	crystals,	demon-
strating	the	potential	of	data-driven	approaches	for	property	
estimation	in	complex	materials	(Tawfik	et	al.	2020).	And	
several	studies	have	successfully	applied	ML	to	predict	the	
mechanical	properties	of	metals,	composites,	and	ceramics,	
as	 shown	 by	 Kibrete	 et	 al.	 (2023).	 Similarly,	Gogineni	 et	
al.	(2024)	demonstrated	that	ML-based	models	can	reliably	
correlate	structural	descriptors	with	macroscopic	mechani-
cal	performance	(Manhas	et	al.	2025).
Furthermore,	 the	 integration	 of	 machine	 learning	 has	
enabled	 the	 development	 of	 models	 that	 predict	 both	 the	
functional	 relationship	 describing	 a	 material’s	response	 to	
an	 electric	 field	 and	 its	 electronic	 properties,	 such	 as	 the	
band	 gap	 (Sudha	 et	 al.	 2022).	 Similar	 approaches	 have	
been	 proposed	 as	 an	 alternative	 route	 for	 predicting	 the	
mechanical	 strength	 of	 concrete.	As	 a	 branch	 of	 artificial	
intelligence,	machine	learning	leverages	large	datasets	and	
statistical	learning	algorithms	to	construct	predictive	mod-
els	with	improved	accuracy	and	reduced	computational	cost	
(Ben	Chaabene	et	al.	2020).
Three	 machine	 learning	 models	 were	 employed	 in	 an	
approach	 to	 supervised	 learning	 (Liu	 Duanyang	 2023).	
The	 predictive	 models	 of	 linear	 regression	 (LR),	 random	
forest	(RF),	and	XGBoost	were	employed	to	forecast	spe-
cific	 mechanical	 properties	 of	 Li2T iO3,	 including	 elas-
tic	 anisotropy	 (A),	 the	 shear	 modulus	 (G_VRH),	 the	 bulk	
modulus	(K_VRH)	using	the	VRH	approximation,	and	the	
Poisson’s	ratio	(ν)	(Ji	et	al.	2018).
While	 machine	 learning	 has	 seen	 increasing	 adoption	
in	 materials	 science,	 its	 application	 to	 specific,	 under-
represented	 systems	 such	 as	 lithium	 titanate	 ( Li2T iO3,)	
remains	 limited.	 This	 study	 addresses	 that	 gap	 by	 devel-
oping	 predictive	 models	 for	 the	 mechanical	 properties	 of	
Li2T iO3,	a	perovskite	compound	with	promising	applica-
tions	in	energy	storage	and	nuclear	fusion	(Sengodan	et	al.	
2022;	Stepišnik	et	al.	2021).
To	this	 end,	 we	 construct	 and	 benchmark	 three	 super-
vised	 learning	 models:	 Linear	 Regression	 (LR),	 Random	
Forest	 (RF),	 and	 XGBoost	 using	 physically	 interpretable	
descriptors	 derived	 from	 density	 functional	 theory	 (DFT)	
calculations,	 including	 volume,	 nsites,	 space	 group,	 and	
kpoint_density,	obtained	 via	 the	 Matminer	 framework.	 In	
this	work,	we	combine	DFT	derived	data	with	explicit	fea-
ture	engineering	on	structural	descriptors	to	construct	a	com-
pact,	 physically	 interpretable	 input	 space	 for	 the	 machine	
learning	models.	The	combination	of	domain	relevant	fea-
tures	 and	 systematic	 model	 comparison	 distinguishes	 this	
work	from	broader,	less	material-specific	studies	and	con-
tributes	to	the	growing	body	of	ML-assisted	materials	prop-
erty	prediction.
This	 work	 contributes	 to	 Sustainable	 Development	
Goals	 related	 to	 clean	 energy	 technologies	 and	 industrial	
innovation	 by	 accelerating	 the	 prediction	 and	 optimiza-
tion	of	energy-relevant	ceramic	materials	using	data-driven	
machine	learning	approaches.

ever, most existing models are constructed based on speciﬁcd o m a i n
knowledge, potentially introducing biases that impact their performance.
Here, we propose a machine learning framework rooted in electron conﬁg-
uration, further enhanced through stack generalization with two additional
models grounded in diverse domain knowledge. Experimental results validate
the efﬁcacy of our model in accurately predicting the stability of compounds,
achieving an Area Under the Curve score of 0.988. Notably, our model
demonstrates exceptional efﬁciency in sample utilization, requiring only one-
seventh of the data used by existing models to achieve the same performance.
To underscore the versatility of our approach, we present three illustrative
examples showcasing its effectiveness in navigating unexplored composition
space. We present two case studies to demonstrate that our method can
facilitate the exploration of new two-dimensional wide bandgap semi-
conductors and double perovskite oxides. Validation results fromﬁrst-
principles calculations indicate that our method demonstrates remarkable
accuracy in correctly identifying stable compounds.
Designing materials with speci ﬁc properties has long posed a sig-
niﬁcant challenge in the ﬁeld of materials science 1– 3. A major hurdle
stems from the extensive compositional space of materials, wherein
the actual number of compounds that can be feasibly synthesized in a
laboratory setting only represents a minute fraction of the total space.
This predicament, often likened to ﬁnding a needle in a haystack,
necessitates effective strategies to constrict the exploration space
4,5.
By meticulously evaluating the thermodynamic stability, it becomes
plausible to winnow out a substantial proportion of materials that are
arduous to synthesize or endure under certain conditions, thereby
notably amplifying the ef ﬁciency of materials development. The
thermodynamic stability of materials is typically represented by the

However, the conventional approaches for determining com-
