hull typically requires experimental investigation or density functional

within a given phase diagram. The computation of energy via these

compound stability, its widespread use has paved the way for the
development of extensive materials databases, such as Materials Pro-

8.T h e s e
databases enable researchers to leverage cutting-edge statistical
methodologies under the purview of artiﬁcial intelligence and machine
learning.
A growing number of researchers have utilized machine learning
to predict compound stability
9– 16. This trend has been primarily driven
by the emergence of extensive databases6,17– 22, which provide a large
pool of samples for training machine learning models 23– 27,e n s u r i n g
their predictive ability. By leveraging these databases as training data,
machine learning approaches enable rapid and cost-effective predic-
tions of compound stability
7,20,28– 37. For example, Dipendra et al.
developed a deep learning model called ElemNet, which uses the ele-
mental composition of compounds to predict their formation
energy
29. Despite these advancements, current machine learning
methods for predicting compound stability suffer from poor accuracy
and limited practical application. One major issue is the signiﬁcant bias
introduced by machine learning models that rely on a single hypoth-
esis. Training a model can be likened to a search for the ground truth
within the model’ s parameter space, gradually approaching it through
optimization algorithms
38. However, the lack of well-understood che-
mical mechanisms in materials39 often leads to models built on idea-
lized scenarios. Consequently, the ground truth may lie outside the
parameter space or even far from its boundaries, diminishing the
accuracy of predictions. For instance, ElemNet ’ sa s s u m p t i o nt h a t
material performance is solely determined by elemental composition
may introduce a large inductive bias
29, reducing the model ’ s effec-
tiveness in predicting stability.
In this study, we propose an ensemble framework based on
stacked generalization (SG)40,41, which amalgamates models rooted in
distinct domains of knowledge. Our approach involves the integration
of three models into this ensemble framework to construct a super
learner
42.T h eﬁrst two models are drawn from existing literature, while
the third, named Electron Con ﬁguration Convolutional Neural Net-
work (ECCNN), is a newly developed model designed to address the
limited understanding of electronic internal structure in current
models. The resulting super learner, designated Electron Con ﬁgura-
tion models with Stacked Generalization (ECSG), effectively mitigates
the limitations of the individual models and harnesses a synergy that
diminishes inductive biases, ultimately enhancing the performance of
the integrated model. In our experiments, the proposed model yields
an AUC of 0.988 in predicting compound stability within the Joint
Automated Repository for Various Integrated Simulations (JARVIS)
database. Furthermore, we observed a considerable enhancement in
sample efﬁciency, as our model attained the equivalent accuracy with
only one-seventh of the data required by the existing model. Addi-
tionally, we applied our model to explore new two-dimensional wide
bandgap semiconductors and double perovskite oxides and unveiled
numerous novel perovskite structures. Subsequent validation using
DFT further underscored the high reliability of our model.
Results
Model development
The machine learning models discussed in this study are primarily
composition-based. Currently, two types of models are available for
predicting the properties of inorganic compounds: structure-based
models and composition-based models
43,44. Structure-based models
contain more extensive information, including the proportions of each
element and the geometric arrangements of atoms. However, deter-
mining the precise structures of compounds can be challenging
7,45.I n
contrast, composition-based models do not encounter this issue, but
they are often perceived as inferior due to their lack of structure
information. Nonetheless, recent research has demonstrated that
composition-based models can accurately predict the properties of
materials, such as energy and bandgap
45. More importantly, in the
discovery of novel materials, composition-based models can sig-
niﬁcantly advance the ef ﬁciency of developing new materials, given
that the composition information can be known as a priori. While
databases like the Materials Project (MP) contain extensive structural
information, this data is often unavailable or difﬁcult to obtain when
exploring new, uncharacterized materials. Structural information
typically requires complex experimental techniques such as X-ray
diffraction or electron microscopy, or computationally expensive
methods like Density Functional Theory (DFT). These approaches are
time-consuming, costly, and require signiﬁcant expertise and specia-
lized equipment. In contrast, compositional information can be readily
obtained by sampling the compositional space, making it more
accessible for high-throughput screening and the exploration of new
materials. Therefore, this study mainly considers models that utilize
chemical formula-based representations as input.
Composition-based models usually require specialized proces-
sing of composition information before it can be used as input for the
model. The data directly extracted from the chemical formula only
consists of the proportion of each element, providing minimal insight.
As a result, it is challenging to develop a high-performance model
based solely on this information. In addition, models that solely
incorporate element proportions, known as element-fraction models,
cannot be extended to account for new elements. If an element is not
included in the training database, the model will not be able to predict
the effects of that element
46. Consequently, before incorporating
composition information as input for the model, it is necessary to
create hand-crafted features based on speciﬁcd o m a i nk n o w l e d g e .
Due to the limited understanding of the relationship between
material properties and composition, introducing theories or
assumptions about the property-composition relationship into
composition-based models can lead to signiﬁcant biases. At the algo-
rithmic level, it is common to make assumptions that favor one solu-
tion over others. For example, convolutional neural networks (CNN)
assume that information exhibits spatial locality, enabling weight
sharing through slidingﬁlters to reduce the parameter space
47. Except
for biases in the model itself, prior knowledge is also introduced when
transforming the element proportions into model inputs. These
assumptions, however, have limited applicability and can result in
poor generalization performance.
For instance, Roost assumed that the unit cell within a crystal can
be viewed as a dense graph, with at oms represented as nodes con-
nected by edges. However, it is essential to acknowledge that not all
nodes in the unit cell have strong interactions with eachother
48.
Therefore, incorporating such assumptions can lead to limitations in
model performance. By recognizing these constraints, we can better
understand the trade-offs involved in model design and strive to
develop more robust and generalizable models.

technique, which amalgamates models grounded in diverse knowl-
edge sources to complement each other and mitigate bias, conse-

Introduction
With the rapid advancement of biomedical technology, the 
demand for simulating and intervening in biological sig -
nals has been growing exponentially [ 1–3]. As a crucial 
component of biological signaling, neural signal trans -
mission presents higher requirements for bionic electro -
chemical devices due to its complexity and rapid response 
characteristics. SCs [ 4], renowned for their fast charging-
discharging capabilities and high power density, share 
similarities with neurons' rapid-response mechanisms 
[5], making them a focal point in bionic electrochemical 
device research. Applying SCs to biological signal simu -
lation—particularly neural signal transmission—not only 
drives progress in neural interface technology [ 6] but also 
provides innovative solutions for biomedical equipment 
[7].
This article systematically explores the application 
potential of SCs in biosignal simulation [ 8], with a par -
ticular focus on their role in neural signal transmission. 
The review first introduces the fundamental principles,

Abstract
This review examines the potential of supercapacitors (SCs) in simulating biological signals, with a particular focus 
on neural signaling applications. Owing to their rapid charge–discharge kinetics and high power density, SCs exhibit 
functional parallels with neuronal response mechanisms, positioning them as promising candidates for bioinspired elec -
trochemical devices. The paper begins by outlining the fundamental principles, material architectures, and performance 
characteristics of SCs. Subsequently, it establishes the theoretical framework for biological signal simulation, encom -
passing neural signal propagation mechanisms and the properties of bioelectrical signals. The core discussion centers 
on supercapacitor-based neural signal simulation, addressing the similarities in dynamic behavior with neuronal activity, 
supported by experimental findings and computational modeling. Current technological limitations, including material 
optimization, structural design, and biocompatibility challenges, are critically analyzed alongside potential solutions. The 
review concludes by highlighting emerging applications in neural interfaces and biomedical devices, while identifying key 
research directions for future investigation. This synthesis highlights the distinct advantages of SCs in bioelectronic signal 
emulation and underscores the need for continued exploration in this interdisciplinary field.

Overview of SCs
Basic Principle of SCs
SCs, also known as electrochemical capacitors, realize 
energy storage through the electric double layer effect and 
the Faraday pseudocapacitance effect (Fig. 1a–c) [13]. The 
basic principles include the following two aspects:
Electric Double Layer
The electric double layer (EDL), a well-established fun -
damental in electrochemistry, arises from physical charge 
adsorption at the electrode–electrolyte interface, enabling 
rapid, non-Faradaic energy storage [ 14]. The formation 
of EDL primarily depends on the electrode materials' 
high specific surface area and good electrical conductiv -
ity. Electrode materials with high specific surface area 
provide more active sites, thereby enhancing the charge 
storage capacity of EDLs [ 15]. Simultaneously, excellent 
electrical conductivity ensures efficient charge transport 
within the electrode, which is essential for achieving rapid 
energy cycling. The physical adsorption characteristics of 
EDL imply that its charge storage mechanism differs from 
chemical reactions in batteries [ 16]. In EDLCs, charges 
are stored through physical adsorption on ions on the elec -
trode surface—a highly reversible process enabling nearly 
infinite charge–discharge cycles. Additionally, the thick -
ness and ion distribution of EDLs influence their interac -
tion with external electric fields, affecting phenomena like 
Joule heating (Fig. 2a–c) [ 17]. The Poisson-Boltzmann 
equation forms the theoretical basis for describing EDLs, 
with advanced models like the fractional-space general -
ization accounting for spatial complexity (Fig. S1e and f) 
[18]. The electric double layer effect not only holds signifi-
cant applications in energy storage but also shows promis -
ing potential in thermal management and nanoscale heat 
transfer [16]. For instance, in studies investigating extreme 
near-field heat transfer, the influence of the electric double 
layer on heat flux at metal surfaces was examined (Fig. 
S2a and d) [ 20], revealing that the contribution of the 
electric double layer to heat flow far exceeds predictions 
from traditional heat transfer theories [ 21]. Therefore, 
the electric double layer effect is a crucial phenomenon 
in electrochemical and energy science, which relies on 
electrode materials' high specific surface area and excel -
lent conductivity. The physical mechanisms of the electric 
double layer are being thoroughly understood so that the 
performance of energy storage and conversion devices can 
be further optimized [ 22].
Faraday Pseudocapacitance Effect
The Faraday pseudocapacitance effect is another key 
charge storage mechanism in supercapacitors (SCs), 
involving fast, reversible surface redox reactions that pro -
vide higher energy density than pure EDL mechanisms 
(Fig. 3a–e) [ 24]. Compared to traditional double-layer 
capacitors, pseudocapacitors exhibit higher energy density 
and power density, making them particularly effective for 
applications that require fast charging/discharging, such 
as electric vehicle start-stop energy recovery and rapid 
response requirements in biosignal simulation [ 25]. The 
energy storage performance of SCs relies on both double-
layer capacitance and/or pseudocapacitance [ 26], with the 
latter stemming from rapid reversible surface redox reac -
tions. MOFs, emerging electrode materials, have garnered 
attention due to their superior capacitance performance 
compared to conventional materials. However, MOF-
based SCs still face practical challenges, including low 
potential windows, limited cycle life, and poor rate per -
formance [27].
Nevertheless, MOFs' unique and tunable chemical 
structures offer multiple pathways to enhance supercapaci -
tor performance [ 28]. This fast surface-redox process is 
crucial for high-power applications. For instance, Nb 2O5 
electrodes demonstrate the ability to retain pseudocapaci -
tive properties of nanoscale materials. They exhibit no 
half-infinite diffusion limitation even during extremely 
short charging times (within one minute), achieving a high 
specific capacitance of 380 F/g and an area capacitance of 
0.46 F/cm2. This indicates that optimizing electrode mate -
rials and structures can significantly enhance the energy 
density and power density of SCs [ 30]. Furthermore,

Spark Plasma Sintered Binder-Free Carbon Electrodes for 
Decoupled Water Electrolysis
Mārtiņš Vanags1, Mairis Iesalnieks1, Toms Valdemārs Eiduks1, Artūrs Plūdons1, Krišjānis 
Šmits2,3, Reinis Drunka1, Ints Šteins1, Andris Šutka1*

Riga Technical University, P. Valdena Str. 3, Riga, LV-1048 Latvia
Abstract
Water electrolysis is the dominant approach for producing green hydrogen from renewable 
energy, providing an alternative to fossil fuels. Conventional water electrolysis faces many 
problems due to the intermittent nature of renewable power and the need for a membrane to 
avoid the formation of an explosive gas mixture. To avoid the use of a membrane, the 
decoupled water electrolysis approach has been introduced, where one catalyst electrode is 
replaced by a solid redox mediator. So far, redox mediators for decoupled electrolysis have 
been prepared using fluoropolymer binders, which pose a serious environmental burden and 
are facing a ban. This is a limiting factor for further implementation of emerging decoupled 
water electrolysis technology. In this work, we report a binder-free charcoal electrode for use 
as a redox mediator electrode in acid and alkaline decoupled water electrolysis. The binder-
free redox mediator electrodes were prepared by a solvent-free spark plasma sintering. The 
sintering temperature was optimised to obtain a volumetric redox mediator with a high specific 
capacitance of 175 F g-1 and a specific charge capacity of 41 mAh g-1 at a current density of 50 
mA g-1. The observed values are higher than reported in the literature for volumetric carbon-
based supercapacitor materials. 
Keywords: Spark plasma sintering, decoupled electrolysis, activated charcoal, double-layer 
capacitor.
Introduction
The energy sector is currently undergoing a transformation from fossil to renewable energy 
sources (solar, wind, hydropower, tidal, etc.) [1]. Renewable energy is inexhaustible, and it 
does not pollute the environment. However, they are characterised by intermittency. Energy 
consumers require stability, availability, and energy security; therefore, there must be a stable, 
efficient, and secure connection between the renewable energy production plant and consumers. 
One of the most promising is “green hydrogen”.

Green hydrogen is hydrogen produced by water electrolysis powered by renewable energy 
sources. Since 2021, green hydrogen production has risen by 50 %, reaching a production 
capacity of 1 million tonnes per year (Mtpa). In parallel, the installed capacity of water 
electrolysers has grown ninefold, and electrolyser production has increased fourfold, 
highlighting the growing role of hydrogen in the global energy transition. The International 
Energy Agency (IEA) has also strongly recommended further increases in green hydrogen 
production [2].
In water electrolysis, water is split into hydrogen and oxygen. A conventional electrolysis cell 
consists of two metal catalyst electrodes (anode and cathode) immersed in an aqueous 
electrolyte. An oxygen evolution reaction (OER) occurs on the anode, and a hydrogen 
evolution reaction (HER) occurs on the cathode. As a result, hydrogen and oxygen are 
produced by consuming electricity and splitting water.
Currently, the highest technology readiness levels (TRLs) available for low-temperature 
electrolysis are alkaline electrolysers (AWE), proton exchange membrane electrolysers 
(PEMWE), and anion exchange membrane electrolysers (AEMWE). The voltage efficiencies 
of these electrolysers range from 60-80 % for AWE, 65-82 % for PEMWE, and 52-67 % for 
AEMWE [3]. 
All of the aforementioned water electrolysers use membranes or diaphragms to separate the 
cathode and anode and prevent the formation of an explosive mixture of oxygen and hydrogen. 
There are several challenges for existing membrane-based water electrolysis. The diaphragm, 
or membrane, typically does not exceed 0.5 mm in thickness, which causes cross-diffusion of 
hydrogen and oxygen. Moreover, oxygen is released at twice the volume of hydrogen; therefore, 
pressure management is required to avoid membrane deformation and rupture. In addition, 
membranes used in water electrolysis increase the overpotential for gas generation due to the 
resistance of ion exchange and transport across the membrane [4]. Membranes are made from 
harsh fluoropolymers, and their manufacturing and exploitation cause severe environmental 
issues [5].
For this reason, decoupled water electrolysis (DWE) has recently been proposed to split water 
without using membranes [6]. In this concept, one of the metal/catalyst electrodes in a water 
electrolysis cell is replaced by a solid redox electrode, and the membrane is removed. The 
process is typically cyclic. In one cycle, the OER reaction occurs at the metal electrode while 
the redox electrode is reduced. In the second cycle, the HER reaction occurs at the metal 
electrode, and the redox electrode is oxidised [7]. In such a process, simultaneous release of 
oxygen and hydrogen is avoided. 
Redox mediator electrode selection and design are critical for the successful construction of a 
DWE device for H 2 production. Turning attention to solid-state redox electrodes, they are 
typically charge-storage electrodes that can be divided into three major groups according to the 
charge-storage mechanism: battery-type [8], pseudocapacitive [9], and electric double-layer 
capacitance electrodes [10]. Electrodes must meet specific criteria for successful decoupled 
electrolysis. Redox potentials of electrode materials should lie between the OER and HER 
onset potentials; the materials should be durable for long-term redox cycling, non-corrosive in

Sustainable amorphous porous carbon for 
efficient removal of industrial dyes
Dayane G. Domingos1* , Beatriz Lima Santos Klienchen Dalari2 , 
Marina C. de Moraes1, Antonio I. Ramos Filho3 , Luís A. M. Ruotolo4 , 
Maria Ángeles Lobo-Recio1 , and Maria Eliza Nagel-Hassemer1
1Department of Environmental Engineering, Center of Technological Sciences (CTC), Federal

2Department of Environmental and Sanitary Engineering, School of Engineering and Applied 
Sciences, University of Vale do Itajaí (UNIVALI), Itajaí, Santa Catarina, Brazil
3Department of Materials Engineering, Center of Technological Sciences (CTC), Federal University 
of Santa Catarina (UFSC), Florianópolis, Santa Catarina, Brazil
4Department of Chemical Engineering, Center for Exact Sciences and Technology (CCET), 
Federal University of São Carlos (UFSCar), São Carlos, São Paulo, Brazil
Abstract
Cork, a porous biopolymer, is composed of hollow prismatic cells with thin walls 
arranged in a compact honeycomb-like structure, making it a promising material 
for adsorption applications. In this study, cork-derived activated carbon (CAC) 
was synthesized through pyrolysis followed by chemical activation using solid 
potassium hydroxide, with the aim of producing an efficient adsorbent for the 
removal of industrial dyes. The structure, morphology, and functional groups of the 
CAC were characterized using Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area analysis, 
scanning electron microscopy, thermogravimetric analysis, Fourier transform 
infrared spectroscopy, and X-ray diffraction. BET surface area analysis revealed a 
high specific surface area of 1,793 m 2/g, favoring strong adsorption capacity. Batch 
and fixed-bed column experiments were conducted to evaluate the adsorption 
performance toward two representative dyes: Methylene blue (MB) and reactive red 
(RR). The pseudo-second-order kinetic model accurately described the adsorption 
behavior, while the Langmuir isotherm model indicated monolayer adsorption for 
MB, and the Freundlich model better fitted the heterogeneous adsorption of RR. The 
maximum adsorption capacities (q m) were 250 mg/g and 105 mg/g for MB and RR, 
respectively. Overall, the results demonstrate that the produced CAC exhibits high 
adsorption efficiency and holds significant potential for application in industrial 
effluent remediation and the treatment of water contaminated with persistent dye 
compounds.
Keywords: Activated carbon; Adsorption; Cork; Industrial effluents

resources.1-3 Within this context, the reuse of industrial waste stands out as a key strategy

technologies. Among the most relevant waste materials, 
cork stoppers—by-products of the wine industry—
represent a promising resource owing to their low carbon 
footprint and renewable characteristics.
Cork, derived from the cork oak tree ( Quercus suber), 
is widely recognized as a renewable natural material 
characterized by low density, flexibility, and high resistance 
to chemical degradation. 4 Despite its economic and 
environmental relevance, a significant amount of used 
cork stoppers is not properly treated, resulting in the loss 
of valuable resources and environmental issues such as 
waste accumulation in landfills. 5-7 Moreover, direct use 
of cork stoppers is limited, as their physical and chemical 
properties deteriorate during use. In this scenario, 
valorizing cork waste through chemical and thermal 
transformations emerges as a promising alternative to 
reduce the environmental impact associated with its 
disposal.5,6
At the same time, the increasing contamination of 
water bodies by industrial effluents has become a global 
concern. Among the most persistent pollutants are 
synthetic dyes, extensively used in the textile, paper, 
plastic, and leather industries. These organic compounds 
exhibit high toxicity, chemical stability, and resistance 
to conventional degradation processes, making their 
treatment and removal particularly challenging. The 
presence of these dyes in wastewater not only degrades 
environmental quality but also poses significant risks 
to human health and aquatic biodiversity. Therefore, the 
development of effective and affordable technologies for 
the treatment of these pollutants has become a priority in 
the environmental field.8,9
In this context, activated carbon produced from 
lignocellulosic waste, such as cork, has gained considerable 
attention as a viable and sustainable adsorbent. Activated 
carbon is characterized by its high surface area, tunable 
porosity, and excellent adsorption capacity, making 
it highly effective for treating industrial effluents. 10 
Producing activated carbon from cork stopper waste not 
only addresses the issue of waste reuse but also offers a 
low-cost and efficient alternative for the removal of organic 
pollutants.11-13 Studies indicate that the porous structure of 
activated carbon, characterized by the ratio of micropores 
to mesopores, plays a crucial role in the adsorption of 
different types of pollutants, including industrial dyes.14
Activated carbon production is widely recognized 
as a well-established and consolidated process, applied 
in various industrial and environmental applications. 16 
However, recent advances in its manufacturing have 
gained attention, with a focus on structural modifications 
and improvements that enable more precise control over 
its physicochemical properties. These developments 
include innovative synthesis methods that regulate pore 
formation, as well as surface functionalization to enhance 
its performance in specific applications, such as the 
removal of organic and inorganic pollutants from aqueous 
systems.14,16-18
Pore-structure control, with particular attention to the 
ratio between micropores, mesopores, and macropores, 
has become one of the most studied parameters due to its 
direct influence on the material’s adsorption capacity. 19,20

Coal possesses a dense, cross-linked structure and strong π - π stacking interactions that hinder activator pene -
tration and cause excessive graphitization, which limits its application in zinc-ion hybrid capacitors (ZIHCs). 
Herein, we propose a synergistic deep eutectic solvent (DES) swelling and in-situ air carbonization strategy to 
fabricate defect-rich, heteroatom-doped porous carbon from raw coal. Utilizing the ZnCl

covalent interactions of coal are disrupted, which significantly increases its fraction of free volume from 16.29% 
to 31.45% to facilitate deep activator penetration. During the subsequent air carbonization, the DES functions as 
a condensed-phase flame retardant to prevent over-burning, alongside serving as an in-situ activator and P 
dopant. The in-situ formation of thermally stable C-O-C bridge bonds introduces spatial steric hindrance that is 
proposed to promote a local hybridization shift from sp
2

carbon. This effectively inhibits the tight 
stacking of aromatic sheets and suppresses excessive graphitization. The optimized carbon is characterized by a

carbon, with potential to extend to diverse precursors for structurally and compositionally rich carbon materials.
1. Introduction
Benefiting from their high safety, low cost, and fast charge transport 
kinetics, zinc-ion hybrid capacitors (ZIHCs) have attracted extensive 
research attention as potential energy storage candidates [ 1 ]. Due to 
their excellent electrical conductivity, tunable pore structures, and su -
perior electrochemical stability, porous carbons are widely utilized as 
cathode materials in ZIHCs [ 2 ]. Because the cathode crucially dictates 
the capacity and rate performance of ZIHCs, rationally designing porous 
carbon cathodes featuring both hierarchical porous channels and a 
highly active interface is important [ 3 ].
Coal serves as a cost-effective and carbon-rich precursor that con -
tains a 3D network. In this network, aliphatic chains and ether linkages 
connect polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and strong π - π 
stacking interactions also exist [ 4 ]. While such a highly aromatic 
structure endows coal-derived carbons with outstanding intrinsic con -
ductivity and structural stability, the tightly cross-linked matrix and 
potent intermolecular forces severely impede the diffusion of activators 
[ 5 ]. Consequently, the derived carbon materials often suffer from 
inhomogeneous pore evolution and constrained specific surface areas. 
Moreover, high-temperature carbonization in an inert atmosphere cau -
ses intense condensation and aromatization in PAH-rich coal [ 6 ]. This 
process preferentially produces highly graphitized carbons that lack 
structural defects and reactive sites. This highly ordered lattice config -
uration fails to offer adequate Faradaic charge compensation, thus 
severely limiting the overall electrochemical performance [ 7 ].

Synergistic Design of Biomass Materials for Moisture‐ 
Induced Electricity Generation
Wangxin Liu | Yanhua Guan | Guanghui Song | Chuanling Si | Lin Dai
State Key Laboratory of Bio‐based Fiber Materials, College of Light Industry and Engineering, Tianjin University of Science and Technology, Tianjin, China
Correspondence: Lin Dai ( dailin@tust.edu.cn )
Received: 1 July 2026 | Revised: 29 August 2026 | Accepted: 9 September 2026
Keywords: biomass | clean energy | hydrovoltaic effect | ion transport | moisture‐induced electricity generation
ABSTRACT
Harvesting the dispersed, low‐grade energy stored in atmospheric moisture has emerged as an attractive route toward 
distributed and sustainable power generation. Moisture‐induced electricity generation (MEG) converts chemical potential 
changes associated with water sorption, ion dissociation, selective ion transport, and interfacial charge transfer into electricity 
without requiring light, wind, or a liquid water supply. Natural biomass is a promising material platform because its polar and 
ionizable groups and hierarchical pore channels support moisture uptake, carrier generation, and directional ion transport. 
However, a single biomass material is unlikely to simultaneously provide high ionic conductivity, a persistent gradient, efficient 
charge collection, and wet‐state stability. This minireview presents a synergistic design framework across molecular, structural, 
and device levels. Biomass chemistry regulates carrier generation and ion selectivity, hierarchical structures maintain water 
activity and ion concentration gradients, and device integration coordinates ionic transport, charge collection, and structural 
stability. We first outline the fundamental mechanism of biomass‐based MEG and then compare cellulose, sodium alginate, 
lignin, proteins, chitosan, and microbial materials in terms of their properties, functions, limitations, and suitable application 
scenarios. Performance optimization strategies are further summarized as ionic regulation, gradient construction, and composite 
integration. Finally, we discuss the main challenges of conversion efficiency, operating lifetime, wet‐state durability, and 
biomass variability, together with future directions for practical and sustainable moisture energy harvesting.
1
|
Introduction
Rising global energy demand and the pursuit of carbon 
neutrality have intensified the search for clean and sustainable 
energy solutions. In this context, technologies capable of har -
vesting dispersed, low‐grade energy from ambient environments 
are emerging as a promising complementary pathway [ 1, 2 ]. The 
atmosphere, nearly ubiquitous yet long underexploited, repre -
sents one such reservoir, containing approximately 12,900 km
3 
of water vapor at any given time, with about 495,000 km
3 
of 
water circulating through the atmosphere each year via the hy -
drological cycle [ 3 ]. The adsorption and desorption of water 
molecules at material surfaces are accompanied by pronounced 
changes in chemical potential; if these can be directed into an 
electrical signal, energy can be harvested continuously in the 
absence of light, wind, or a liquid‐water supply. Building on this 
idea, moisture‐induced electricity generation (MEG) has 
advanced rapidly in recent years [ 4, 5 ]. For example, protein 
nanowires derived from Geobacter sustain self‐maintained po -
wer output under ambient humidity [ 6 ], adsorption–evaporation 
synergistic systems extend the continuous output of a single 
cycle to several hundred hours [ 7 ], and emerging platforms such 
as supramolecular hydrogels push the current to the milliampere 
level [ 8, 9 ], moving the technology from a concept toward 
practical use [ 5, 10 ].

With the rapid development of this field, the research focus has 
correspondingly shifted from the early synthetic polymers and 
carbon nanomaterials toward natural biomass [ 8, 11, 12 ]. Bio -
molecules are intrinsically rich in polar and ionizable groups, 
such as hydroxyl, carboxyl, amino, and sulfonic acid moieties, and 
possess native fibrous networks and hierarchical pore channels, 
combining moisture uptake, ion generation, and ion transport 
within a single material (Figure 1 ). They are also abundant, low‐ 
cost, biodegradable, and renewable, aligning well with green 
electronics and sustainable energy [ 13 ]. This rationale is corrob -
orated by analyses of water‐biopolymer interactions, which 
identify hydrophilic groups, interfaces, and hierarchical struc -
tures as key to water sorption and transport [ 14 ], and by reviews of 
bio‐hydrovoltaic systems (both living and non‐living) [ 11 ] and 
cellulose‐enabled generators driven by moisture, evaporation, 
osmosis, or droplets [ 15 ]. In contrast, this minireview focuses on 
ambient‐moisture electricity generation across diverse biomass 
families. We adopt a comparative lens that directly links each 
material's chemical functionality and hierarchical architecture to 
its performance in moisture sorption, ion transport, and gradient 
retention. Given that a single biomass rarely optimizes all these 
attributes simultaneously, we argue that progress lies in the 
rational combination of complementary components rather than 
in the pursuit of a universal candidate.
Here, we aim to construct a comprehensive framework that 
encompasses the full pathway from biomass feedstocks, through 
the mechanisms of water‐to‐electricity conversion, to material 
synthesis and performance optimization strategies (Figure 1 ). 
Biomass functional groups and native structures dictate mois -
ture uptake, ion generation, and transport; multiscale in -
terventions (molecular ionic regulation, structural gradient 
construction, and device‐level composite integration) offset the 
limitations of any single material and maintain electrical output. 
Synergy is realized by aligning biomass properties with the 
mechanism and integrating cross‐scale complementary func -
tions. This logic connects the mechanism discussed in Section 2
with biomass comparison and selection in Section 3 , perfor -
mance optimization in Section 4 , and the biomass‐specific 
challenges and opportunities in Section 5 .
2
|
Fundamental Mechanism of Moisture‐ 
Induced Electricity Generation
The broader hydrovoltaic effect refers to the generation of 
electricity from the direct interaction between water and 
nanostructured materials [ 16 ]. As one branch of this effect, 
MEG converts a water‐chemical‐potential difference into elec -
tricity through four coupled processes: water sorption, ion 
dissociation, ion transport, and interfacial charge transfer [ 6, 10 ] 
(Figure 2 ). Hydration increases carrier density and mobility, but 
useful output also requires the driving gradient to be main -
tained. The following subsections introduce only the relations 
needed to connect biomass chemistry and structure with voltage 
and current.
2.1
|

chemical potential between two locations in the device. In this 
review, adsorption refers to the binding of water at material 
surfaces, absorption refers to water uptake into the material 
bulk, and sorption is used as the general term encompassing 
both processes. For vapor‐exposed regions, water activity can be

ABSTRACT: As urgent demands increase in energy-grid systems, supercapacitors have been
further documented as highly promising energy-storage technologies across a range of
applications owing to their high-power density, rapid charge−discharge capabilities, and
prolonged endurance life. Porous carbon-based materials, particularly those derived from
metal−organic frameworks (MOFs), are prominent candidates for supercapacitor electrode
materials owing to their customizable inner-pore structures and superior electrochemical
properties. In this work, we systematically manipulate the carbonization temperature (700−900
°C) of Al-NDC-MOF to tailor the hierarchical pore structure, defect density, and surface
chemistry of the resulting porous carbons (AC-Al-NDC-x), aiming to unravel the structure−
performance−device correlations required for stable dual-ion storage. Systematic character-
ization reveals that carbonization temperature plays a crucial role in regulating pore structure
hierarchy, defect density, and surface functional groups. As a result, the optimized sample (AC-
Al-NDC-800) exhibits balanced electrochemical performance, enabling its application as both
positive and negative electrodes in symmetric and asymmetric two-electrode devices. This behavior is attributed to the synergistic
effect of micropores for charge storage, mesopores for ion transport, and appropriate surface functionalities for interfacial stability.
Although the achieved energy density and cycling stability are comparable to previously reported porous carbon systems, this work
highlights a rational design strategy for balancing pore structure and surface chemistry to achieve stable dual-ion storage under
practical two-electrode conditions.

supercapacitors, two-electrode devices
1. INTRODUCTION
As advancements in electrochemical energy storage technology
continue, supercapacitors (SCs) have demonstrated distinct
advantages in various applications owing to their high-power
density, rapid charge−discharge capabilities,
1,2
and exceptional
cycling stability.
3,4
They have become indispensable compo-
nents in sectors such as industry,
5,6
energy,
7−9
and trans-
portation.
10,11
However, their relatively low energy density
presents a significant challenge for widespread adoption. This
limitation is primarily determined by the energy storage
mechanism, structural stability, and efficiency of the interfacial
reactions of the electrode materials within the different
operating potential windows.
Porous carbon-based materials, recognized for their high
specific surface area, customizable inner-porous net structure,
and excellent electrical conductivity, are regarded as prime
candidates for active SC electrode materials.
12,13
Among these,
carbon-based materials derived from metal−organic frame-
works (MOFs) have emerged as a focal point in contemporary
research owing to their significant advantages, such as a
designable and tunable precursor structure and a controllable
thermal conversion process.
14−17
By meticulously adjusting
process parameters, such as carbonization temperature and
activation intensity, it is possible to synergistically optimize the
key properties of MOF-derived carbon materials, such as the
specific surface area, pore structure distribution, defect density,
and surface chemical composition, thereby enhancing their
electrochemical energy-storage performance.
18−20
Numerous
studies have demonstrated that these materials can achieve a
high specific capacitance in three-electrode systems and exhibit
good rate capability in two-electrode devices.
21−24
Aluminum-based MOFs constructed from conjugated
aromatic ligands represent a promising yet relatively underex-
plored category of precursors for porous carbon electrodes,
although several recent studies have begun to explore Al-MOF-
derived carbon materials for supercapacitor applications,

indicating emerging but still limited research efforts in this
area. In particular, Al-NDC-MOF, assembled from 1,4-
naphthalenedicarboxylate ligands, features an extended π-
conjugated framework and a robust coordination structure.
During carbonization and activation, aluminum species can be
effectively removed, enabling the formation of high-purity
carbon materials while retaining framework-derived pore
characteristics. These features provide a favorable structural
basis for generating porous carbons capable of supporting
charge storage in both negative and positive potential regions.
Nevertheless, systematic investigations on Al-NDC-MOF-
derived carbon materials remain limited compared with those
on ZIF-type or transition-metal-based MOFs.
More importantly, the relationship between the structural
characteristics of Al-NDC-MOF-derived porous carbons and
their electrochemical behavior across different potential
windows has not yet been fully clarified. In practical
supercapacitor operation, electrode materials are required to
function under both negative and positive polarization
conditions, where the charge storage behavior and interfacial
responses can differ significantly. How the pore structure
hierarchy, carbon framework characteristics, and surface
chemical composition collectively influence electrochemical
performance remains insufficiently understood. This issue
limits the rational design of Al-MOF-derived carbon electrodes
for practical device applications.
To address these issues, this study synthesized a series of
MOF-derived porous carbon materials (denoted as AC-Al-
NDC-x) using Al-NDC-MOF as the precursor through
controlled carbonization and chemical activation processes.
Rather than pursuing solely a new material design, this work
focuses on elucidating how the incremental structural changes
induced by carbonization temperature influence the balance of
charge-storage behavior in negative and positive potential
windows. We aim to establish a clear structure−performance−
device correlation that links the hierarchical pore architecture,
defect chemistry, and surface functional groups to the dual-
potential electrochemical behavior in practical two-electrode
supercapacitors.
2. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS
2.1. Experimental Materials
1,4-Naphthalenedicarboxylic acid (1,4-NDC), aluminum chloride
hexahydrate, polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), N,N-dimethylformamide
(DMF), deionized water, absolute ethanol, sodium hydroxide
(NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH), nickel hydroxide (Ni(OH)
2
),
and commercial activated carbon (AC) were used.
2.2. Synthesis Methods
2.2.1. Synthesis of Al-NDC-MOF. Al-NDC-MOF was synthe-
sized with minor modifications based on the previously reported
literature.
27
Specifically, 1.081 g of 1,4-naphthalenedicarboxylic acid
(1,4-NDC, 5 mmol) was dissolved in 20 mL of N,N-dimethylforma-
mide (DMF). Meanwhile, 1.207 g of aluminum chloride hexahydrate
(5 mmol) and 0.100 g of PVP were dissolved in 20 mL of deionized
water. The two solutions were mixed and stirred for 15 min, then
transferred into a 100 mL stainless-steel autoclave lined with Teflon.
The autoclave was placed in a blast drying oven and maintained at
120 °C for 12 h for the reaction.
After the reaction completed, the system was cooled down to room
temperature. The resulting white solid product was collected by
centrifugation, washed twice with absolute ethanol and deionized
water, respectively, and then freeze-dried for 12 h. The final white
powder was designated as an Al-NDC-MOF.
2.2.2. Carbonization and Alkali Washing. A certain mass of Al-
NDC-MOF was weighed and placed in a porcelain boat, which was
then transferred into a tube furnace. Carbonization was carried out at
700 °C for 2 h under a nitrogen atmosphere, with a heating rate of 4
°C/min. The obtained black powder was added into 20 mL of 10
mol/L NaOH solution, heated to boiling and kept boiling for 30 min.
After cooling to room temperature, the mixture was stirred
continuously for 12 h. The solid product was separated by
centrifugation, washed with deionized water until the filtrate reached
neutral pH, and freeze-dried for 12 h to obtain C−Al−NDC-700.
2.2.3. Activation. C−Al−NDC-700 and KOH were mixed
uniformly at a mass ratio of 1:3. A small amount of deionized water
and absolute ethanol (approximately 1 mL in total) was added into
the mixture, which was then soaked for 12 h. The resulting mixture
was transferred into a porcelain boat and placed in a blast drying oven
at 75 °C to evaporate the solvents, yielding a black viscous slurry. The
slurry was transferred into a tube furnace and activated at 600 °C for 2
h under a nitrogen atmosphere, with a heating rate of 4 °C/min. The
activated product was washed repeatedly with deionized water until
neutral pH, separated by centrifugation, and freeze-dried for 12 h to
obtain the activated porous carbon, designated as AC-Al-NDC-700.
AC-Al-NDC-800 and AC-Al-NDC-900 were synthesized following
the identical procedure, with only the carbonization temperature
altered. The material synthesized at a carbonization temperature of
800 °C was named AC-Al-NDC-800, while that synthesized at 900 °C
was named AC-Al-NDC-900, with all other experimental conditions
kept unchanged.

Recovery of Cathode and Solid Electrolyte in All-Solid-State Sodium-
Ion Batteries with Superhigh Selectivity

ABSTRACT: Metals in spent all-solid-state sodium-ion batteries
(ASIBs) pose severe environmental pollution, resource depletion,
and health risks. However, selective and sustainable recovery of
these metals from ASIBs remains highly challenging. Herein, we
introduce a coordination-solvation dual-regulation (CSDR) mech-
anism that enables, for the first time, the recovery of both the
cathode and solid electrolyte from ASIBs with exceptional
selectivity and high sustainability. Guided by this CSDR
mechanism, amino acid−based green solvents are employed with
a dual function: abundant functional groups provide coordination
sites for target metal ions while facilitating favorable solvation
interactions, collectively enabling metal leaching. Mechanistically,
the superior Na over Zr selectivity originates from differential
binding energetics, Na
+
forms stable chelate complexes with amino acid ligands with lower binding free energies, whereas Zr
4+
,
owing to its higher charge density and stronger hydrolysis tendency, exhibits weaker coordination affinity and poorer solvation
compatibility, thus remaining preferentially in the solid residue.
1. INTRODUCTION
Renewable energy sources (solar energy,
1−5
biomass energy,
6,7
hydrogen energy
8,9
) paired with electrochemical energy
storage (batteries,
10−12
supercapacitors
13−15
) are pivotal
areas of research for supplying power to next-generation
consumer electronics and electric vehicles. Sodium-ion
batteries (SIBs) are a promising next-generation energy storage
solution because of their abundant resources, widespread
availability, and low cost.
16−23
In particular, all-solid-state
sodium-ion batteries (ASIBs) constitute a critical advancement
toward next-generation energy storage, characterized by high
energy density, long cycle life, and inherent safety.
24−28
However, the rapid expansion of the ASIBs industry will
bring the challenge of exponential growth in battery waste in
the near future, such as cathode Prussian blue analogues (e.g.,
Na
2
Mn[Fe(CN)
6
], NMF) and solid electrolyte sodium-ion
conductive ceramic (Na
3
Zr
2
Si
2
PO
12
, NZSP). The improper
disposal of these materials not only causes a waste of resources
but also poses significant risks to ecosystem health and public
safety.
29
Thus, the establishment of green and efficient
recycling strategies is necessary for the long-term sustainable
development of the ASIB industry.
In recent years, novel green solvent systems, such as ionic
liquids (ILs), deep eutectic solvents (DESs), and low-melting
mixture solvents (LoMMSs), have demonstrated distinct
advantages in the field of battery recycling. ILs are room-
temperature liquid salts composed of anions and cations with
tunable properties, such as low volatility, high thermal stability,
and excellent solubility.
1,30−38
DESs are multicomponent
mixtures formed via noncovalent interactions that are widely
used in separation, metal extraction, and electrochemistry.
39−42
LoMMSs are a simple extension of DESs that lower the
melting point of their components, making them promising
candidates for dissolution, separation, and catalysis.
43,44
Unlocking the underlying mechanism is the critical bottle-
neck for green and selective ASIB recovery. However, the
existing green technology fails to provide the precise regulation
mechanisms needed to enhance recovery efficiency.
45−51
For
example, Chen et al.
51
utilized an amino acid−based DES to
leach Na
4
Fe
3
(PO

2
P

O

(NFP) cathodes; however, the
simultaneous leaching of Na (87.5%) and Fe (83.3%) resulted
in low selectivity, and the underlying mechanism was not

elucidated. Therefore, it is necessary to elucidate the

sustainable recovery.
Herein, we propose a coordination-solvation dual-regulation
(CSDR) mechanism using amino acid−based LoMMSs for the
selective recovery of metals from spent ASIBs. NMF and
NZSP were selected as the typical cathode and solid
electrolyte, respectively. Amino acids (Figure 1a) are chosen
as the hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) for LoMMSs due to
their green and biodegradable nature, as well as the ability of
their amino and carboxyl groups to coordinate effectively with
metals. Notably, the functional amino and carboxyl groups in
HBAs not only offer strong coordination sites for metals but
also influence the solvation effect, enabling fine-tuning of metal
ion solubility and selectivity. By balancing coordination and
solvation regulation, the CSDR mechanism achieves remark-
able metal selectivity, thereby allowing efficient separation of
target metals from both the cathode and solid electrolyte.

Unravelling Biocoke Structural Evolution and Delayed
Coking Effects
Shaikat Chandra Dey 1 | Seong-Min Cho 1 | Jose A. Gonzalez-Aguirre 1 | Md. Nazrul Islam 1 | Ravindra Kumar Bhardwaj 2 |

Directorate, National Laboratory of the Rockies, Golden, Colorado, USA | 3Worfolk Consulting, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA | 4Department of Biological
and Agricultural Engineering, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, North Carolina, USA | 5Bioenergy Science and Technology Directorate, National

Keywords: anode | biocoke | biographite | delayed coking | lithium-ion batteries | pyrolysis oil | sustainable aviation fuel
ABSTRACT
Catalytic graphitization of biomass-derived carbon offers a promising route to produce biographite as a sustainable alternative to
petroleum-based synthetic graphite for lithium-ion battery (LIB) anodes. This study investigates the physicochemical properties of
biocokes produced from pyrolysis oil at carbonization temperatures ranging from 150°C to 500°C. Using an iron (Fe) catalyst,
graphitization was performed at 1500°C, significantly lower than the /C243000°C required for conventional synthetic graphite. The
effects of introducing an intermediate-temperature hold (400°C –600°C) prior to graphitization were evaluated, simulating a
“delayed coking ” process to enable the coproduction of sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs). Chemical structure evolution during
biocoke formation was analyzed, and proposed mechanisms are presented. Biographites produced via the delayed coking pathway
exhibited high crystallinity and excellent electrochemical performance in both half-cell and full-cell LIB configurations. The full
cells exhibited an initial discharge capacity close to the theoretical capacity of the NMC622 cathode (175 mAh/g at 4.2 V), and high
capacity retention (/C2488%) after 150 cycles. Notably, the graphitic and electrochemical properties remained stable across the range
of intermediate hold temperatures. These findings provide a foundation for optimizing temperature parameters in delayed coking
systems to enable scalable, integrated production of biographite and SAFs from pyrolysis oil.
1 | Introduction
Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) were developed and
commercialized as high-performing and cost-effective energy stor-
age systems. Since commercialization in 1991, LIBs have revolu-
tionized the electrochemical energy storage technology owing to
their high energy density, light-weight nature, small size, high
Coulombic efficiency (CE), long cycle life, good rate performance,
high working voltage, minimal self-discharge, negligible memory
effect, etc [ 1–5]. The LIBs are extensively used in portable
electronic devices, grid energy storage, and electric vehicles
(EVs). The EVs, powered by LIBs, can achieve longer driving
ranges and are transforming the automotive sector by offering a
sustainable, environmentally friendly mode of transportation with
lower carbon emissions [ 6]. In 2023, almost 14 million EVs were
sold worldwide, with a 35% year-on-year increase, indicating the
rapid adoption and growing confidence in EVs as a sustainable
transportation solution [ 7]. Due to the increased popularity of
EVs, the demand for LIBs is increasing exponentially.

Among the various essential components in LIBs, the active mate-
rials are most widely studied, as they are responsible for the revers-
ible intercalation and deintercalation of lithium ions (i.e., Li+)[ 8].
Commercial LIBs use graphite as the anode active material,
together with a binder and conductive carbon. Graphite is pre-
ferred because of its high gravimetric capacity (theoretical maxi-
mum /C24372 mAh/g), low delithiation potential (/C250.2 V vs. Li/Li+),
high CE, extended plateau capacity, long cyclability, good rate per-
formance, low voltage hysteresis, cost effectiveness, environmental
friendliness, etc [ 9–15]. Both natural and synthetic graphites are
used in the commercial LIB cells. Natural graphite is extracted
from geographically constrained natural reserves. Mining, refin-
ing, and beneficiation of natural graphite require substantial
energy and lead to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. These pro-
cesses are also associated with the generation of mining dust and
the utilization of toxic hydrofluoric acid [16]. Compared to natural
graphite, synthetic graphite offers greater consistency and tunabil-
ity. Thermal treatments of soft carbon precursors (e.g., petroleum
coke) at very high temperatures (/C243000°C) make synthetic graph-
ite. It is worth noting that graphite is considered a critical material,
and synthetic graphite has the potential to provide a secure and
reliable supply chain for graphite in LIBs. However, the produc-
tion of synthetic graphite involves nonrenewable feedstocks and
emits GHG. Additionally, the process is energy-intensive (i.e.,
costly) and takes longer times [ 17].
Catalytic graphitization of renewable biocarbon is an emerging
alternative approach to sustainably produce anode-grade biogra-
phite for LIBs at low temperature and shorter time, overcoming
the key limitations of synthetic graphite [ 18–21]. Group VIII
transition metals, e.g., iron [ 22], cobalt [ 23], or nickel [ 24],
can catalyze the graphitization process via a dissolution-
precipitation mechanism [22] and/or a formation-decomposition
mechanism [25]. Among these transition metals, iron-based cat-
alysts are mostly used because of relatively higher carbon solu-
bility in iron, d-orbital electron vacancies, availability, low cost,
etc [26, 27]. Although iron can be used in many different forms to
catalyze the graphitization process, reduced metallic iron powder
is preferred over other available forms such as salts, oxides, orga-
nometallics, etc [ 13].
Feedstock selection is another key variable to consider for scal-
able production of biographite [ 18, 28]. To date, various biocar-
bon feedstocks have been catalytically graphitized such as
softwood [20], hardwood [ 29], glucose [ 30], lignin [ 23], lignocel-
lulose [ 31], cellulose [ 32], hemicellulose [ 33], biochar [ 34],
bagasse [ 35], coconut coir [ 36], corn straw [ 37], waste coffee
grounds [ 38], passion fruit shells [ 39], olive pomace [ 40], beech
[41], fiberboard [ 12], paper towel [ 19], etc. An emerging feed-
stock for catalytic graphitization is pyrolysis oil (also known
as bio-oil), which is derived from the fast pyrolysis of biomass.
Given the scalable production of biographite, pyrolysis oil offers
several key advantages, including low inorganic content, high
carbon content, and easier handling and transportation [ 42–44].
Our recent study explored the mechanism of iron-catalyzed
graphitization of pyrolysis oil. Catalyst loading was optimized,
and the effects of temperature and pyrolysis oil aging were also
studied. The optimal biographite demonstrated promising perfor-
mance as anode active material in LIB half-cells [ 22]. However,
the process ’s scalability was challenged by several factors. Our
follow-up work addressed the key challenges in processing
pyrolysis oil into LIB-grade graphite via iron catalysis at scale,
including viscosity, iron-induced foaming, swelling, and aging.
To address these challenges, five pathways were explored, includ-
ing (i) defoamer use, (ii) use of iron oxide (Fe 2O3) as graphitiza-
tion catalyst, (iii) pH adjustment of pyrolysis oil, (iv) pyrolysis oil
coking at 300°C–500°C, and (v) thermal pretreatment of pyrolysis
oil at 150°C –200°C. The low-temperature pretreatment pathway
successfully addressed the aforementioned challenges and pro-
duced highly crystalline biographites showing impressive electro-
chemical performance in LIB half-cells [ 45].
The objective of this study was to thoroughly characterize the
physicochemical properties of products obtained via pretreat-
ment and coking of pyrolysis oil at 150, 200, 300, 400, and
500°C under inert nitrogen flow and without iron catalyst.
For simplification, the products obtained at five temperatures
are called biocokes, hereafter, and named BC-150, BC-200,
BC-300, BC-400, and BC-500, respectively. Biographites were
made from BC-150 at 1500°C using iron catalyst following an
intermediate hold step (i.e., delayed coking) at three different
temperatures (400, 500, and 600°C) for 1 h. The biographites
were purified via acid refluxing and named BG-400, BG-500,
and BG-600, hereafter. The electrochemical performance of
these biographites was tested as anode active materials in
LIB half-cells and full-cells.
2 | Experimental Section
2.1 | Materials
This study utilized pyrolysis oil, collected from Ensyn Technologies
Inc. (Ontario, Canada), as feedstock for the preparation of biocokes
and biographites. The oil was produced through fast pyrolysis of
woody biomass and had a dark brown opaque appearance. The spe-
cific gravity of the supplied pyrolysis oil sample was 1.15 –1.25 at
20°C, and the pH was 3.2. Reduced iron in powder form (particle
size < 10 μm; 99.9% trace metals basis; Sigma–Aldrich) was used as
a catalyst for the graphitization of biocoke. Hydrochloric acid
(HCl, 37% w/w; Fisher Scientific) was applied to chemically separate
residual iron from the product after graphitization. Conductive
carbon black (C45, Timcal), styr ene-butadiene rubber (SBR, MSE
Supplies LLC), carboxymethyl c ellulose (CMC, MSE Supplies
LLC), and Milli-Q water were used to prepare the electrode. The
electrolyte for half-cell testing was purchased from Tomiyama
Pure Chemical Industries, Ltd, and comprised 1.2 M lithium hexa-
fluorophosphate (LiPF6) in a 3:7 weight ratio of ethylene carbonate
(EC)/ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC).
2.2 | Preparation of Biocokes
Biocokes were prepared as described in our previous work [ 45].
Briefly, the raw pyrolysis oil was heated at five different temper-
atures, i.e., 150°C (5 h), 200°C (1 h), 300°C (1 h), 400°C (1 h), and
500°C (1 h). The experiments were conducted under nitrogen flow
(100 mL/min) to ensure an inert atmosphere. Figure 1a–e repre-
sents the experimental conditions (temperature, hold time, heat-
ing rate, and cooling rate) used for biocoke preparation. The raw
pyrolysis oil did not solidify into biocoke when pretreated at 100°C
for an extended period (12 h), and therefore was not considered for
further study.

ABSTRACT
Uncontrolled bleeding under wet and deformable conditions remains a major challenge for conventional he -
mostatic materials, which often suffer from limited tissue adhesion and poor mechanical adaptability. Here, we 
developed an injectable sodium alginate hydrogel ionically cross-linked with Ca
2
⁺ and reinforced with hazelnut 
branch-derived biochar (HB) to improve structural stability and local hemostatic performance. The HB- 
containing hydrogel exhibited pronounced shear-thinning behavior, high injectability, enhanced wet tissue 
adhesion, and self-healing efficiency exceeding 80%, while achieving an adhesive strength of approximately 
420 kPa. Physicochemical characterization indicated homogeneous HB incorporation and Ca
2
⁺ retention by HB, 
which may influence the local ionic environment of the hydrogel network. In vitro studies demonstrated good 
cytocompatibility and hemocompatibility. In hemostatic assays, 6A7C-HB exhibited a blood clotting index (BCI) 
of 4.45%, markedly lower than that of the commercial oxidized cellulose hemostat Surgicel ® (26.98%), and 
shortened the clotting time to 4.4 min compared with 7.5 min for the untreated blood control and 7.2 min for 
Surgicel ® . In vivo evaluation in rat tail transection and liver injury models showed effective hemorrhage control, 
reducing blood loss by approximately 45 – 55% compared with untreated controls, while subcutaneous implan -
tation demonstrated acceptable biocompatibility without evidence of significant systemic toxicity or adverse 
histopathological responses. These findings demonstrate that HB reinforcement provides a simple and effective 
strategy for developing injectable alginate hydrogels with improved mechanical adaptability and localized he -
mostatic performance under wet and deformable conditions.
1. Introduction
Uncontrolled hemorrhage remains a major cause of mortality in 
trauma and surgical settings [ 1 , 2 ]. Therefore, effective hemostatic de -
vices are needed to promote rapid coagulation of blood, wound 
covering, and improved clinical outcomes. Among these, hemostatic 
hydrogels have attracted attention due to their good biocompatibility 
and ability to maintain a moist wound environment [ 3 , 4 ]. They are 
typically constructed from natural polysaccharides (e.g., chitosan and 
alginate) [ 5 , 6 ] and synthetic polymers such as polyvinyl alcohol, poly -
ethylene oxide and its derivative copolymers, and polyacrylate [ 7 ].
In addition to their hemostatic properties, features such as inject -
ability and self-healing are important in the design of multifunctional 
hydrogels, as they provide a significant advantage in medical practice

[ 2 , 8 ]. For example, their ability to conform to irregular geometries of 
wounds makes them suitable for use in minimally invasive treatments. 
However, when applied in a physiological environment, hydrogel 
structures are generally susceptible to deformation or mechanical 
damage caused by body movements or external pressure, which may 
reduce their functional performance [ 9 ]. To address these issues, 
injectable [ 10 ] and self-healing [ 11 ] hydrogels have been suggested. 
Self-healing hydrogels incorporate reversible dynamic interactions that 
enable the hydrogel network to repair itself upon damage, thereby 
enhancing durability and functionality in medical applications [ 12 ]. 
Nevertheless, maintaining structural integrity during injection and 
subsequent deformation remains an important challenge [ 13 ]. To 
address this limitation, reinforcing phases such as carbon-based nano -
materials [ 14 ], metal ions [ 15 ], and small molecules [ 16 ] can be 
incorporated into the hydrogel network. For locally applied hemostatic 
materials, sufficient contact with wet and mechanically dynamic tissue 
surfaces is also important for maintaining the material at the bleeding 
site [ 17 , 18 ].
Herein, we present a multifunctional hydrogel platform composed of 
99% natural components and designed to combine injectability, struc -
tural stability, self-healing, wet-surface retention, and localized hemo -
static performance. To enhance structural stability and recovery while 
preserving injectability, sustainably sourced hazelnut branch biochar 
(HB) was produced through controlled carbonization and activation 
processes and incorporated as a particulate reinforcing phase ( Fig. 1 a). 
Sodium alginate (SA), used as the polymer matrix, was stabilized with an 
ionic cross-linking strategy using Ca
2
⁺ ions. A small amount of poly -
vinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was added to increase the mechanical and 
chemical stability of the network by forming interchain hydrogen 
bonding interactions ( Fig. 1 b). The central question of this study was 
whether HB incorporation could improve resistance to mechanical 
disruption and structural recovery of the ionically cross-linked SA/PVP 
hydrogel while preserving the shear-thinning injectability required for 
application to irregular wound surfaces. Despite a water content of 97%, 
the resulting hydrogel exhibited high structural integrity and could be 
injected and conform to irregular surfaces ( Fig. 1 c). HB incorporation 
improved the self-healing behavior of the hydrogel, allowing it to 
maintain its functional integrity after mechanical damage ( Fig. 1 d). The 
system showed retention on wet tissue surfaces and hemostatic activity 
( Fig. 1 e). In a conceptual use case ( Fig. 1 f), the hydrogel was shown to 
conform to irregular wound surfaces following minimally invasive in -
jection, maintain local contact, and provide a physical barrier at the 
bleeding site. The incorporation of HB into the ionically cross-linked SA/ 
PVP hydrogel resulted in a multifunctional material that combines 
structural integrity, self-healing, tissue contact, and hemostatic perfor -
mance on a single platform. Owing to its simple fabrication process and 
predominantly natural composition, the hydrogel shows potential for 
biomedical applications that require injectable and locally acting he -
mostatic materials.
2. Materials and methods
Detailed descriptions of the materials, instrumentation, experi -
mental protocols, and statistical analyses are provided in the Supple -

2.1. Preparation of hazelnut branch biochar
Hazelnut branch-derived biochar (HB) was obtained from the 
hazelnut branch via carbonization and activation. The hazelnut branch 
was milled ( ≤ 250 μ m), carbonized in a horizontal tube furnace under

◦

◦

and activated under the same furnace conditions at 800
◦
C. Residual 
KOH was removed by washing with 1 M HCl until the pH reached 
neutrality, followed by drying at 60
◦
C for 48 h ( Fig. 1 a).

Supercapacitors make up for the shortcomings of batteries in
the realm of fast charge and discharge devices

density, cycle stability, maintenance cost, and safety.

Numerous two-dimensional materials have been investigated
and harnessed for use in supercapacitors (SCs), such as

transition metal carbide/nitride (MXene),

and

11
Among them,
metallic 1T phase molybdenum disulfide (MoS
2
) is one of the
most promising electrode materials for supercapacitors
12−17
owing to its well-defined layered structure, which provides
large surface area and thereby results in more electric double-
layer storage capacitance per unit voltage.
18,19
Moreover,
metallic 1T phase MoS
2
holds higher electrical conductivity
than semiconducting 2H phase MoS
2
,
20

According to the ionic adsorption mechanism of electric
double-layer capacitors (EDLCs),

between the nanosheets will be conjugated on the surface of

ance of functionalized 1T MoS

Keywords: capacitive deionization | MXene | resource recovery | selective ion separation
ABSTRACT
Selective ion separation is essential for effective water treatment and resource recovery. Conventional techniques, such as 
adsorption, coagulation/flocculation, and membrane technologies, suffer from low selectivity, substantial cost, and high energy 
requirements. Alternatively, ion separation using capacitive deionization (CDI) has shown strong potential for energy efficiency, 
cost‐effectiveness, environmental sustainability, and selective removal. However, traditional carbon electrodes used in CDI have 
limitations for selective separations. MXene‐based electrodes present an attractive alternative for CDI due to their exceptional 
electrochemical properties. Nevertheless, MXenes are typically unstable over extended cycles, and to achieve ion selectivity, 
controlled interlayer spacing adjustment is required. Methods such as hybridization and functionalization can improve the 
selectivity properties of MXenes by tailoring their interlayer spacing. Several studies have reported the use of MXenes as CDI 
electrodes; however, most focus on brackish water desalination, while selective ion separation is rarely addressed. This review 
presents an in‐depth analysis of the role of modified MXene electrodes in advancing ion‐selective CDI technologies, exploring 
various strategies to achieve the desired selectivity. Moreover, it highlights critical challenges that hinder scalability and 
practical implementation. Finally, the review showcases the strategic roadmap for future opportunities toward next‐generation 
water purification and resource recovery solutions.
1
|
Introduction
Water scarcity and wastewater generation have become critical 
challenges of the 21st century due to increasing population and 
industrial growth [ 1, 2 ]. Projections indicate that global water 
demand may rise by over 50% in the coming decades, whereas 
nearly one‐fourth of major urban centers are already under sig -
nificant water stress [ 3 ]. Consequently, the need for water recla -
mation and resource recovery is growing rapidly to bridge the 
increasing gap between water demand and supply. Similarly, 
wastewater generation is progressively rising. Every year, the 
world produces around 380 billion m
3 
of municipal wastewater. 
This number is expected to rise by 24% by 2030 and 51% by 2050 
[ 4 ]. Yet, wastewater is predominantly regarded as a problematic 
waste stream and is typically treated as a pollutant requiring 
removal. However, wastewater presents a valuable resource, 
containing recoverable water, energy, and high‐value nutrients.
To meet the increasing water demand, desalination technologies, 
including reverse osmosis (RO), membrane distillation, and 
electrodialysis, are found to be more efficient technologies in 
comparison with others [ 5–7 ]. However, these technologies often 
suffer from high energy consumption required for pumping or

heating, membrane fouling, as well as high capital and mainte -
nance costs [ 8 ]. Despite a significant reduction in energy con -
sumption from 20 to 2–4 kWh m
− 3 
[ 9 ], RO remains an energy‐ 
intensive process to fulfill the water demand. Therefore, the 
need for an alternative nonpressure‐driven water reclamation 
technology still exists to make the process less energy‐intensive 
and sustainable. In addition, industrial wastewater consisting of 
ions or charged pollutants requires ion removal and selective ion 
recovery. Conventionally, coagulation, softening, adsorption, and 
membrane technology are applied to treat ion‐containing waste -
water. Again, the high cost of chemicals, membranes, adsorbents, 
and adsorbent disposal challenges make the abovementioned 
technologies less sustainable. These ion‐containing waters and 
wastewaters often contain valuable resources, including lithium, 
precious metals, nitrate, and phosphate, which could be recov -
ered for value‐adding and the circular economy.
Over the past decades, electrochemical ion separation technol -
ogies have evolved significantly, diversifying in both device 
types and target applications. However, novel pseudocapacitive 
materials remain to be explored for various purposes, including 
selective ion separation, resource recovery, and water reclama -
tion. A brief capacitive deionization (CDI) timeline is summa -
rized in Figure 1 [ 10 ].
Several improvements in CDI have been made in terms of cell 
architecture, system design, and optimization of operational pa -
rameters [ 10 ]. Researchers shifted their focus toward exploring 
alternative electrode materials and identified pseudocapacitive 
materials as highly suitable for CDI applications (Section 2.2 ). 
Pseudocapacitive materials bridge the gap between capacitive and

for High-Performance Hybrid Supercapacitors

ABSTRACT: Currently, the primary bottlenecks that hinder the
widespread application of supercapacitors are low energy density
and narrow potential windows. Herein, the hybrid supercapacitor
with high energy density and wide potential window is constructed
via an in situ self-assembly method employing RGO-induced
flower-like MOF(Ni). Benefiting from the synergistic effect
between RGO and MOF(Ni), the interfacial interactions are
effectively improved, and the contact area with the electrolyte is
enhanced, which increases the ion transfer kinetics and overall
electrochemical performance. The MOF(Ni)@RGO electrode
exhibits a specific capacitance of 1267.73 F g
−1
at a current
density of 1 A g
−1
. Crucially, the assembled MOF(Ni)@RGO//
BC with a broad potential window and good stability employing a
MOF(Ni)@RGO anode and biomass carbon cathode, combined with a 2 M PVA-KOH gel-electrolyte, achieves a maximum energy
density of 70.16 Wh kg
−1
at a power density of 2200.09 W kg
−1
, outperforming most reported supercapacitors. This hybrid
supercapacitor exhibits excellent stability and high energy density, providing a novel strategy for further large-scale applications.
KEYWORDS: supercapacitors, induced, self-assembly, metal−organic framework, RGO
1. INTRODUCTION
Metal−organic frameworks (MOFs) represent a burgeoning
category of materials distinguished by metal clusters intricately
connected to organic ligands through coordinated bonds.
Remarkably, the meticulous choice of metal and organic
ligands during synthesis engenders the substantial latitude in
tailoring MOFs with diverse morphologies, sizes, and pore
architectures.
1−3
Consequently, MOFs hold significant poten-
tial for applications across various fields, including adsorption,
4
detection,
5
catalysis,
6−8
separation,
9,10
and energy storage.
11−13
The MOFs with high specific surface area, controllable
structure, and inherent pseudocapacitive sites make them
exceptionally promising contenders for deployment as
electrode materials in supercapacitors. Currently, two primary
strategies are employed for MOFs in supercapacitor electrodes:
(1) direct utilization of MOFs to store electrical energy via the
electrochemical double-layer capacitor mechanism, leveraging
their inner surfaces;
14,15
(2) MOFs employed as sacrificial
templates or precursors, facilitating the transformation into
final materials (e.g., metal-based hydroxides, oxide, sulfides,
and porous carbon materials) by a straightforward annealing
method.
16−19
Despite notable advancements in energy storage,
the challenges of insufficient conductivity, electrochemical
instability, and limited capacitance in MOFs persist as current
obstacles demanding resolution.
To address the challenges of MOFs, the research focus has
shifted to composites with carbon-based materials possessing
superior electrical conductivity and structural stability (such as
carbon nanotubes, graphene oxide (GO), reduced graphene
oxide (RGO), and metal carbides).
20−24
Therefore, the GO

et al.

and a capacitance

asymmetric supercapacitor (GM-LEG@Ni-MOF//AC) was
assembled with GM-LEG@Ni-MOF and activated carbon
(AC) as the positive and negative electrodes, respectively. The
GM-LEG@Ni-MOF//AC energy density was 32.7 Wh kg
−1
at
a power density of 750 W kg
−1
. Zhang et al.
26
prepared NiO/
C/rGO by pyrolysis of the Ni-MOF precursor on GO. The
capacitance of the NiO/C/rGO hybrid electrode was 496 C
g
−1
at a current density of 1 A g
−1
. Furthermore, the hybrid
supercapacitor composed of NiO/C/rGO and sodium citrate-

Despite RGO with a distinctive thin-layer structure, remark-
able electrical conductivity, robust mechanical properties, and
substantial specific surface area that can accelerate the

the supercapacitors assembled with the prepared electrode
materials still suffer from narrow voltage window, suboptimal

Based on the existing issues of MOFs/GO composites and
drawing inspiration from cauliflower plants, which employ
their leaves not only for nutrient transport but also to protect
themselves from external damage. Herein, we design RGO-
induced flower-like MOF(Ni) in situ self-assembled compo-
sites (MOF(Ni)@RGO) with high electrical conductivity and
excellent electrochemical performance. This remarkable out-
come can be primarily ascribed to the synergistic effect of
RGO with MOF(Ni), effectively enhancing the interfacial
interaction and overall electrochemical performance. Further-
more, the substantial specific surface area and abundant pore
structure of MOF(Ni)@RGO contribute to an increased
contact area with the electrolyte, ensuring efficient charge
transport and storage and improving ion transport kinetics.
Notably, a hybrid supercapacitor is assembled with MOF(Ni)
@RGO and biomass carbon as the anode and cathode,
respectively. The supercapacitors have high energy/power
densities and good cycling stability under a wide potential
window.

Sustainable Removal of Pesticides from Water Using Biochars
Derived from Conocarpus and Lemon Tree Waste
Sayed M. Saleh, Sherif B. Abdel Ghani, Fahad M. Alminderej,* and Osama I. Abdallah*
