ABSTRACT: Pesticide residues in aquatic systems pose persistent risks to
ecosystems and public health, underscoring the need for low-cost and
sustainable remediation strategies. In this study, biochars prepared from
Conocarpus branch waste (CBB) and lemon tree branch waste (LBB) via
slow pyrolysis at 450 °C were evaluated as adsorbents for two widely
applied agrochemicals: imidacloprid (IMI) and myclobutanil (MYC).
Comprehensive physicochemical characterization (SEM, TEM, BET, and
elemental analysis) revealed mesoporous structures with distinct surface
features. Batch adsorption experiments demonstrated strong dependence
on solution pH, adsorbent dosage, contact time, and initial pesticide
concentration. Under near-neutral conditions (pH 7.0, 5 g L
−1
, 25 °C, 24
h), maximum capacities reached 8.69 mg g
−1
(IMI) and 12.31 mg g
−1
(MYC) for CBB. Adsorption kinetics followed a pseudo-second-order
model (R
2
> 0.98), while equilibrium data fit both Langmuir and the Freundlich isotherms (R
2
≥ 0.99). Thermodynamic analyses
(ΔG° = −1.3 to −4.5 kJ mol
−1
; ΔH° = −16.4 to −29.8 kJ mol
−1
) indicated spontaneous, exothermic processes dominated by
physisorption. The reusability of both biochars across multiple cycles further confirmed their practical applicability. These results
highlight pruning-waste biochars as effective and sustainable alternatives to conventional adsorbents for mitigating pesticide
pollution in water.
1. INTRODUCTION
Pesticides play a vital role in modern agriculture, serving as
essential tools for controlling pests and diseases while
significantly enhancing crop yields and ensuring food security.
1
With the continuous growth of the global population, the
demand for food production is expected to increase,
necessitating a greater reliance on pesticides to sustain
agricultural output.
2
However, despite their advantages, the
widespread use of these products has raised serious environ-
mental and health concerns. As pesticides are extensively
applied, their residues and degradation byproducts can
infiltrate aquatic ecosystems through spray drift, surface runoff,
and leaching, posing substantial threats to water quality,
biodiversity, and human health.
3,4
Furthermore, contamination of groundwater and aquifers
exacerbates these concerns, creating long-term environmental
and public health challenges.
5,6
Among the widely used
pesticides, imidacloprid (1-[(6-chloro-3-pyridyl)methyl]-N-
nitroimidazolidin-2-ylideneamine) (Figure 1a), a neonicoti-
noid insecticide synthesized in 1985, has become one of the
most prevalent insecticides globally.
7,8
Its application spans soil
treatment, seed coating, and foliar spraying.
9−11
However,
imidacloprid exhibits high water solubility, increasing its
potential for leaching into surface and groundwater systems.
12
Its environmental persistence has resulted in frequent
detections in water bodies worldwide.
13
Myclobutanil (2-(4-
chlorophenyl)-2-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-ylmethyl)-hexanenitrile)
(Figure 1b), a broad-spectrum systemic fungicide from the
azole class, is widely used in agriculture to combat fungal
pathogens,
14−18
resulting in its widespread detection in soil

19,20
This growing concern has prompted
research into sustainable methods for pesticide removal, with
biochar emerging as a promising solution due to its adsorptive
properties, cost-effectiveness, and environmental compatibil-
ity.
21−24
Biochar is a stable, carbon-rich material produced through
the pyrolysis of biomass under limited oxygen conditions.
23,24
It has gained attention for pesticide remediation due to its
porous structure, chemical stability, and high density of
functional groups, which enable the adsorption of a variety
of organic and inorganic contaminants.
25−28
Various feedstocks, including agricultural wastes,
29−33
wood-
based derivatives,
34−37
and animal manure,
38
have been
extensively investigated for the synthesis of biochar. The
choice of feedstock has a significant impact on the
physicochemical properties of the resulting biochar and its
performance in environmental applications.
Recent research has further emphasized the potential of
biochar for removing pesticides from water and soil systems,
highlighting the influence of solution pH, temperature, contact
time, and initial contaminant concentration on adsorption
efficiency.
22,39−41
Due to its affordability and environmental
benefits, biochar is increasingly regarded as a viable alternative
to activated carbon.
42,43
Given biochar’s significant potential, exploring novel biochar
sources for enhanced pesticide removal is essential. Despite
existing studies, limited research has investigated the
adsorption behavior, isotherm models, and kinetic properties
of imidacloprid and myclobutanil using Conocarpus branches
biochar (CBB) and lemon branches biochar (LBB) in aqueous
systems. This study aims to fill this gap by examining the
thermodynamics, adsorption kinetics, and equilibrium iso-
therms governing the removal of these pesticides by CBB and
LBB. The key objectives include: (1) characterizing the
physicochemical properties of the biochars, including surface
area, porosity, elemental composition, and morphological
features; (2) assessing the impact of pH, contact time, and
initial pesticide concentration on removal efficiency; (3)
elucidating the adsorption mechanisms involved in pesticide
retention; and (4) evaluating the regeneration potential and
adsorption performance of CBB and LBB in actual
contaminated water samples compared to conventional
adsorbents.
Pesticides play a crucial role in modern agriculture, serving
as indispensable tools for controlling pests and diseases while
significantly improving crop yields and ensuring global food
security.
1
With the continuous growth of the world population,
the demand for agricultural output is expected to rise,
inevitably driving greater reliance on pesticides.
2
However,
despite their agricultural benefits, the intensive and widespread
use of pesticides has raised serious environmental and health
concerns. Residues and degradation byproducts can infiltrate
aquatic ecosystems via spray drift, surface runoff, and leaching,
threatening water quality, biodiversity, and human health.
3,4
Groundwater and aquifer contamination further exacerbates
these risks, creating long-term environmental and public health
challenges.
5,6
Among the widely applied pesticides, imidacloprid (IMI) (1-
[(6-chloro-3-pyridyl)methyl]-N-nitroimidazolidin-2-ylidene-
amine) (Figure 1a) is a neonicotinoid insecticide first
synthesized in 1985 and now among the most extensively
used globally.
7,8
Its applications span soil treatments, seed
coatings, and foliar sprays.
9−11
Imidacloprid’s high water
solubility promotes leaching into surface and groundwater,
contributing to its frequent detection in aquatic environments
worldwide.
12,13
Similarly, myclobutanil (MYC) (2-(4-chlor-
ophenyl)-2-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-ylmethyl)-hexanenitrile) (Fig-
ure 1b), a systemic triazole fungicide, is widely applied to
control fungal pathogens.
14−18
Its persistence and widespread
usage have led to frequent detections in soil and water
systems.
19,20
These concerns underscore the urgent need for
sustainable methods to mitigate pesticide contamination in
aquatic environments.
Biochar has emerged as a promising remediation material
due to its porous structure, high surface functionality, chemical
stability, and cost-effectiveness.
21−24
Produced by pyrolysis of
biomass under oxygen-limited conditions, biochar is a stable,
carbon-rich material capable of adsorbing diverse organic and
inorganic contaminants.
23−28
A wide range of feedstocks�
agricultural wastes,
29−33
wood derivatives,
34−37
and animal
manures
38
have been explored for biochar production, with
feedstock type strongly influencing physicochemical properties
and environmental performance.
Recent studies have highlighted the efficiency of biochar in
removing pesticides from soil and water, with adsorption being
strongly influenced by solution pH, temperature, contact time,
and initial contaminant concentration.
39−41
Compared with
activated carbon, biochar is increasingly recognized as a cost-
effective and sustainable alternative.
42,43
Although biochars
from diverse feedstocks have been investigated for pesticide
remediation,
21−24,32,37,38
relatively few studies have systemati-
cally examined the adsorption behavior, isotherm models, and
kinetic mechanisms of imidacloprid and myclobutanil. To the
best of our knowledge, no prior work has focused on biochars
derived from Conocarpus branch waste (CBB) or lemon
branch waste (LBB), despite their abundance as pruning
residues in arid and semiarid regions.
This work advances pesticide remediation by valorizing
locally abundant pruning wastes�Conocarpus and lemon
branches�into low-temperature biochars tailored for arid/
semiarid municipalities. Beyond addressing a methodological
gap for imidacloprid and myclobutanil, we target formulation-
strength sprayer rinsates, benchmark their performance against
conventional adsorbents, and articulate a techno-economic
rationale�encompassing low embodied energy and cost, local
feedstock supply, and simple regeneration�that enables
decentralized, on-farm predischarge treatment within a circular
economy framework. Accordingly, this study investigates the
adsorption performance of CBB and LBB for removing
imidacloprid and myclobutanil from aqueous systems. The
specific objectives are to: (1) characterize the physicochemical
properties of CBB and LBB (surface area, porosity, elemental
composition, morphology); (2) assess the influence of pH,
contact time, and initial pesticide concentration on removal
efficiency; (3) elucidate adsorption mechanisms via kinetic and
isotherm modeling; and (4) evaluate regeneration potential
and performance in contaminated water relative to conven-
tional adsorbents.

2.1. Preparation and Characterization of Biochar. Air-
dried pruning residues from Conocarpus and lemon trees were
sorted to remove dust, bark fragments, and leaves; the branch
fractions only were retained for pyrolysis. Sorted material was
washed with deionized water, oven-dried at 105 °C to constant
mass, cut to 2−3 cm, and then pyrolyzed at 450 °C for 4 h

Tailored activated carbons from biomass components for aqueous 
PFAS adsorption
Delaney E. Clouse
a
, Jianzhou He
b
, Dengjun Wang
b
, Virginia A. Davis
a , *
a

ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
PFAS
Activated carbon
Biomass waste
Water treatment
ABSTRACT
The US Environmental Protection Agency recently released strict regulations limiting per- and polyfluoroalkyl 
substances (PFAS) in drinking water. In response, this study used activated carbons derived from biomass waste 
components for effective water treatment. By varying the composition of feedstock mixtures, perfluorobutane 
sulfonic acid adsorption efficiencies ranged from 31 to 98 %, indicating that biomass structure influences PFAS 
sorption. Activated carbon from a feedstock mixture of 50 % lignin, 35 % cellulose nanocrystals, and 15 % 
cellulose nanofibers achieved over 98 % removal of three regulated and four unregulated PFAS compounds 
without requiring additives or surface functionalization.
1. Introduction
The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently introduced 
regulations aimed at reducing exposure to six per- and polyfluoroalkyl 
substances (PFAS), commonly known as “ forever chemicals, ” in drinking 
water [1] . These guidelines are expected to benefit 100 million people, 
preventing thousands of deaths and many PFAS-related illnesses. To 
meet these regulations, utilities are exploring granular activated carbon 
(AC) to remove PFAS from water sources.
Agricultural residues, which accumulate and contribute to environ -
mental and health hazards, offer a sustainable and abundant source for 
producing AC [2,3] . This biomass is mainly comprised of lignin and 
cellulose, both of which have been shown to contribute to the formation 
of the AC structure [4] . However, the relationship between biomass 
components on AC structure and their effectiveness as PFAS sorbents has 
yet to be fully understood. This research aims to fill this gap by inves -
tigating how the structure of AC derived from lignin (LIG) and cellulose 
influences their PFAS adsorption efficiency. The investigation includes 
an initial screening experiment to identify the most effective AC derived 
from LIG, cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), and cellulose nanofibers (CNFs) 
for adsorbing short-chain PFAS. Once the best-performing AC was 
identified, experiments were repeated to understand the material ’ s 
adsorption behavior on seven common PFAS.
2. Materials and methods
PFAS compounds were selected to include anionic (PFBA, PFBS, 
PFOA, and PFOS), zwitterionic (6:2 FTAB), and cationic (PFHxSAmS 
and PFOSAmS) species with varying chain lengths to understand PFAS 
structure-dependent adsorption by AC. Further details of each model 
PFAS are presented in Table S1. Feedstock biomass characterization 
results using previously established methods [4] are provided in 
Table S2.
Eight mixtures of biomass components were chosen to create a range 
of surface areas (SSA) and microporosity. AC were prepared as described 
previously [4] and named using the system listed in Table 1 AC-5 was 
duplicated in this work to understand batch-to-batch variations. In 
addition to the nine AC samples described, a common wood biochar was 
activated using the same protocol. This compares the adsorption effi -
ciency of tailored AC to AC produced from currently available biochar. 
The SSA and micropore analysis were measured on a Micromeritics 
TriStar II 3020 using BET analysis, surface charge of the best AC was 
determined using zeta potential, and elemental analysis was conducted 
using x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). More details on BET 
sample preparation and analysis techniques can be found in Supple -
mentary Material.
Batch adsorption experiments of individual PFAS were conducted in 
triplicate to explore the efficiency of tailored AC for removing PFAS in 
water. AC and individual PFAS stocks were diluted to 0.1 g/L and 500

µ g/L , respectively, in 1 mM NaCl. The resulting solutions had a pH of 7.0 
± 0.1. Adsorption experiments ran for 48 h, when previous studies have 
shown that equilibrium is reached [5] . Samples were centrifuged and 
filtered to remove any AC particles. PFAS concentration was analyzed 
using a Thermo Scientific Vanquish ultrahigh-performance liquid 
chromatography system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 120 mass 
spectrometer. Details on programs, parameters, and calibration methods 
can be found in our recent papers [5,6] . Minitab software was used to 
probe any potential relationships.
3. Results and discussion
BET analysis results ( Table 1 ) reveal that all AC exhibit high SSAs 
with varying micropore fractions. The reported range of SSAs and 
microporosity in Table 1 underscores the importance of feedstock ma -
terial selection, as specific properties can be tailored based on relative 
ratios of LIG, CNC, and CNF. AC composed of a blend of biomass com -
ponents exhibit greater SSAs and micropore fractions, highlighting the 
synergistic effects of biomass components [4] . AC-Bio exhibits a similar 
SSA to other AC, containing microporosity 17 % higher than any other 
sample. An unpaired t -test indicates a non-significant difference (p- 
value = 0.054) between AC 5-1 and AC 5-2, suggesting minimal varia -
tion between sample batches.
The effectiveness of various biomass-derived AC for the adsorption of 
two short-chain compounds, PFBA and PFBS, and the adsorption ca -
pacity at equilibrium (Q
e
) are presented in Fig. 1 a and Table S3, 
respectively. PFBS adsorption efficiencies were over 30 % for all AC and 
as high as 98 %, exceeding the results of commercial activated carbons 
[7] . When analyzing the adsorption data, the authors noticed apparent 
trends between SSA, CNF, and PFAS adsorption efficiency, so analysis of 
variance was used to verify if these relationships were significant. There 
is a significant trend (R
2 
= 0.84) between SSA and PFBS adsorption, as 
shown in Fig. 2 a and Table S4. Notably, AC-7 and AC-8, which present 
the highest SSA, exhibited exceptional PFBS adsorption efficiencies of 
95 % and 98 %, respectively. These findings surpass previous biochar 
studies by 6 – 80 % due to the high SSA achieved during the activation 
process [8 – 10] .
The adsorption efficiency of PFBA was below 40 % across all mix -
tures due to its greater hydrophilicity compared to PFBS and the 
generally lower adsorption affinity of carbonaceous materials towards 
carboxylate versus sulfonate PFAS. As shown in Fig. 2 b, PFBA removal 
efficiency generally increased with SSA, but an R
2 
of 0.45 highlights that 
additional factors are also influential. AC-8 achieved a notable PFBA 
adsorption efficiency of 33 %, a significant achievement for an experi -
ment conducted at room temperature. In contrast, previous studies using 
powdered or granular AC often required acidic conditions or surface 
functionalization of the carbons to achieve PFBA removal levels. For 
example, Huang et al. [11] achieved a maximum PFBA removal effi -
ciency of approximately 10 % using silicon modified AC, and Zhang 
et al. [12] reported a PFBA removal capacity of 20 % using commercial 
granular AC, which is 13 % lower than the removal capacity reported 
here under similar conditions. These findings advance short-chain PFAS 
adsorption, demonstrating that AC derived from a mixture of biomass 
components offer desired properties for efficient water treatment.

RESEARCH ARTICLE
Unveiling the Crosslinking Architecture Governed Carbon 
Yield in Phenolic Resin-Derived Porous Carbons for 
Cost-Effective Energy Storage 
Zhaojin Li Chenze Di Di Zhang Huilan Sun Qujiang Sun Qiujun Wang Fei Yuan Ranran Li 
Bo Wang
Hebei Key Laboratory of Flexible Functional Materials, School of Materials Science and Engineering, Hebei University of Science and Technology, Hebei, China 
Correspondence: Huilan Sun ( sunhl@hebust.edu.cn) Bo Wang ( wangbo@hebust.edu.cn) 
Received: 4 June 2026 Revised: 23 July 2026 Accepted: 25 July 2026 
Keywords: activated carbon | carbon yield | crosslinking degree | phenolic resin | porous carbon | supercapacitor 
ABSTRACT 
Porous carbons are indispensable for supercapacitors and as hosts for silicon anodes in next-generation lithium-ion batteries, 
yet their commercialization is crippled by the low carbon yield of phenolic resin precursors. What fundamentally controls the 
yield and how to improve it have long puzzled both academia and industry. Here, we address the root cause by systematically 
tuning the formaldehyde-to-phenol (F/P) molar ratio. We discover that the methylene bridge density in the cured resin is the key 
determinant of carbon yield. At the optimal F/P ratio of 2.0, the resin achieves the most complete crosslinked network, boosting 
the porous carbon yield from below 36% (PC-1.0) to 47.15% (PC-2.0), without compromising pore development. PC-2.0 retains a 
high specific surface area of 2580.6 m2 ⋅g− 1 and delivers an outstanding specific capacitance of 371.8 F ⋅g− 1 at 0.5 A ⋅g− 1 . Moreover, 
it exhibits a high capacitance retention of 95.76% after 10 000 cycles at a current density of 10 A ⋅g− 1 , demonstrating competitive 
advantages over various electrode materials reported in recent years. Quantitative analysis confirms a strong positive correlation 
between methylene content and yield, solving the long-standing puzzle. This work provides a simple, scalable strategy to break 
the yield-performance trade-off, reducing raw material cost by 16.47% compared with commercial resin. 
1 Introduction 
Against the backdrop of the escalating global energy crisis 
and worsening environmental degradation, the development 
of advanced and sustainable electrochemical energy storage 
technologies has become pivotal to achieving the societal goal 
of carbon neutrality [ 1–4 ]. The pursuit of carbon neutrality 
has driven the rapid diversification of electrochemical energy 
storage technologies, ranging from alkali metal-ion batteries 
[ 5, 6 ], supercapacitors [ 7 ], and aqueous zinc-ion batteries to 
emerging systems such as ammonium-ion batteries [ 8–11 ], 
hybrid-ion batteries [ 12 ], and zinc-ion hybrid capacitors [ 13–15 ], 
as well as biofuel-based energy conversion devices [ 16 ]. In many 
of these systems, porous carbons, owing to their high specific 
surface area (SSA), tunable pore structure, excellent electrical 
conductivity, and good chemical/thermal stability, demonstrate 
irreplaceable potential in these fields [ 17, 18 ]. Porous carbon 
not only serves as a catalyst support for biofuel production, 
reducing catalyst deactivation [ 19 ], but also functions as an ideal 
electrode material for electrical double-layer capacitors (EDLCs) 
in supercapacitors, delivering high power density and ultra- 
long cycle life [ 20 ], and additionally acts as an excellent host 
for silicon-based anodes, mitigating the volume expansion dur- 
ing charge/discharge processes, among other applications [ 21 ]. 
However, despite its immense performance potential, the com- 
mercialization of phenolic resin-based porous carbon remains

severely constrained by the high cost of raw materials. Compared 
with inexpensive precursors such as biomass or coal, the phenolic 
resin route allows for more precise control over pore structure 
and yields superior electrochemical performance [ 22, 23 ]. Never- 
theless, it holds a relatively low market share, primarily because 
of the higher precursor cost. More importantly, the generally low 
carbon yield during pyrolysis and activation directly inflates the 
unit production cost of the final material, thereby weakening its 
competitiveness in price-sensitive application scenarios. 
For a long time, the research community has devoted extensive 
efforts to enhancing the electrochemical performance of porous 
carbons, with strategies primarily focused on heteroatom doping 
to introduce pseudocapacitance, fine-tuning of pore structure 
through template methods or activator regulation, and optimiza- 
tion of pyrolysis and activation conditions [ 24–27 ]. Although 
these efforts have improved the specific capacitance or ion 
transport kinetics of the materials to a certain extent, they have 
generally overlooked a more fundamental bottleneck for indus- 
trialization: the low carbon yield of phenolic resin precursors 
during carbonization. The excessively low yield means that a 
large amount of raw material is lost in the form of volatile 
matter during the conversion process, which not only results in 
resource waste but also directly leads to a significant increase in 
the cost of the final product. A deeper core scientific question 
thus emerges: what factors fundamentally determine the carbon 
yield of phenolic resin? How can the carbon yield be improved 
while ensuring that the critical porous structure and electro- 
chemical performance are not significantly compromised? These 
two fundamental questions have become key obstacles limiting 
the large-scale application of high-performance porous carbons 
in the energy storage industry. Existing studies have mostly 
focused on post-carbonization modifications, with relatively little 
attention paid to the resin synthesis stage. Investigating the 
chemical structure of the precursor itself and how it affects its 
thermal stability and resistance to etching during subsequent 
high-temperature treatment may be the key to unraveling the 
mystery of carbon yield. 
In response to this long-standing conundrum, the present study 
proposes the following hypothesis: the final carbon yield of 
phenolic resin-based porous carbon is likely predetermined by the 
crosslinking network integrity of its precursor, and, in particular, 
by the degree of methylene ( ─CH2 ─) bridging. To verify this 
hypothesis, we deliberately forgo complex doping or composite 
strategies and instead adopt an exceedingly simple, fundamental, 
and highly controllable synthesis parameter, the formaldehyde- 
to-phenol molar ratio (F/P), which serves as a core lever to 
systematically regulate the crosslinking degree of the resin. By 
varying the F/P ratio, we aim to alter, at the molecular level, 
the crosslinking extent and methylene bridge content of the 
resin network. We employ a combination of characterization 
techniques, including Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy 
(FT-IR), solid-state 13 C nuclear magnetic resonance (ssNMR), 
and nanoindentation testing, to quantitatively characterize the 
crosslinking structure and mechanical properties of the resins 
prepared at different F/P ratios. The distinct advantage of this 
strategy is that it does not rely on expensive additives or complex 
post-treatment processes, thereby inherently possessing natural 
feasibility and economic viability for industrial scale-up from the 
outset. 
Herein, by systematically designing a series of phenolic resins 
with different formaldehyde-to-phenol molar ratios and employ- 
ing ssNMR and FT-IR spectroscopy, this study reveals the 
key structural parameters governing the porous carbon yield, 
elucidates the underlying mechanisms, and ultimately provides 
a simple, efficient, and universally applicable strategy for the 
rational design and large-scale production of low-cost, high- 
performance porous carbon electrode materials, thereby serving 
practical energy storage applications such as supercapacitors and 
silicon anodes for lithium-ion batteries. 
2 Experimental Section 
2.1 Experimental Materials 
Phenol (C6 H5 OH, 99%), formaldehyde (CH2 O, 37%), ammonia 
solution (28%), and hydrochloric acid (37%) were purchased from 
Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. Activated 
carbon was purchased from Fujian Xinsen Carbon Industry Co., 
Ltd., and commercial phenolic resin was purchased from Hebei 
Zetian Chemical Co., Ltd. 
2.2 Synthesis of Phenolic Resin 
Phenolic resins were synthesized from phenol (P) and formalde- 
hyde (F) by varying the molar ratio of formaldehyde-to-phenol. 
In a typical synthesis, 23.5 g (0.25 mol) of phenol was added 
into a round-bottom flask and heated to 80◦C in a water bath. 
Then, 1.5 mL of ammonia solution (28%) was added, followed by 
the addition of a specific volume of 37% formaldehyde solution 
according to the desired molar ratio, for example, 37.5 mL for a 
formaldehyde-to-phenol ratio of 2:1. The mixture was stirred and 
heated at 80◦C for 2 h, and subsequently subjected to vacuum 
distillation at 60◦C to remove impurities. The resulting resins 
were designated as PF- x , where x represents the molar ratio of 
formaldehyde-to-phenol ( x = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, and 3.0). Finally, 
the resins were transferred into PTFE beakers and cured by 
sequential heating at 80◦C for 1 h, 120◦C for 1 h, and 160◦C for 
3 h. After curing, the resins were ground to obtain resin particles. 
2.3 Synthesis of Porous Carbon 
The porous carbon was synthesized via a two-step process 
consisting of pre-carbonization and KOH activation. Briefly, 
2 g of the as-prepared phenolic resin was placed in a tube 
furnace and heated to 600◦C at a rate of 5◦C ⋅min− 1 under Ar 
atmosphere, and held at this temperature for 3 h. After cooling, 
the resulting char was mixed with KOH at a mass ratio of 1:3 
and ground thoroughly to obtain a homogeneous mixture. The 
mixture was then transferred to a tube furnace and heated to 
800◦C at 5◦C ⋅min− 1 under an Ar atmosphere, held for 3 h, and 
subsequently cooled to 300◦C at a rate of 5◦C ⋅min− 1 , followed by 
natural cooling to room temperature. The product was washed 
repeatedly with hydrochloric acid and deionized water, and 
finally dried in an oven at 70◦C for 8 h. The resulting porous 
carbons were designated as PC- x , where x corresponds to the 
molar ratio of formaldehyde-to-phenol in the precursor resin 
( x = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, and 3.0). For comparison, porous carbon

ABSTRACT
Biomass-derived carbon materials represent stable, cost-effective and environmentally friendly electrocatalyst for 
oxygen evolution reaction (OER) and hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). In this work, a self-supporting coconut 
shell carbon (SCC) catalyst featuring a three-dimensional (3D) hierarchical porous structure was reported by in 
situ ammonia etching. The SCC-1100-NH
3 
exhibited outstanding OER performance, achieving a current density 
of 10 mA cm
� 2 
at an overpotential of 294 mV and a potential of 1.52 V vs RHE. The unique structural config -
uration also offered the catalyst excellent durability with stable operation for at least 98 h. It was believed that 
the hierarchical porous structure enhances electrical conductivity and the formation of vacancy-coupled 
pentagon defects which act as active sites. This work provides a new strategy for designing defect-rich metal- 
free biomass-derived carbon electrodes.
1. Introduction
Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is a critical process in renewable 
energy technologies, yet its practical application is hindered by intrin -
sically slow kinetics involving a four-electron transfer, which leads to 
high overpotentials ( η > 200 mV) [ 1 – 3 ]. This inefficiency remains a key 
obstacle in devices such as electrolysers, regenerative fuel cells and 
metal-air batteries. Although noble metal oxides (e.g., IrO
2 
and RuO
2
) 
represent the state-of-the-art OER catalysts due to their high activity and 
stability [ 4 ], their high cost and limited availability impede widespread 
use [ 2 , 5 ]. Moreover, under harsh oxidizing conditions, these catalysts 
often suffer from dissolution or surface reconstruction, further under -
mining their long-term stability. These challenges have motivated the 
search for cost-effective and durable alternatives. Metal-free carbon- 
based materials such as biomass-derived carbons, graphene and carbon 
nanotubes [ 6 ], have gained increasing attentions because of low cost, 
tunable electronic properties, high stability, and the use of earth- 
abundant precursors.
The OER on metal-free carbon catalysts operates through a mecha -
nism fundamentally different from that of conventional metal-based 
oxides [ 7 ]. Instead of relying on metal d-orbitals, the catalytic activity 
stems from modifications to the electronic structure of the carbon 
framework. Heteroatom doping with elements such as nitrogen, boron, 
phosphorus and sulfur, enables precise redistribution of charge within 
the carbon matrix. For instance, pyridinic nitrogen provides lone elec -
tron pairs, while graphitic nitrogen enhances conjugation, and both ef -
fects promote charge polarization to form highly active sites that may 
act synergistically to improve electrocatalytic performance [ 8 – 12 ]. 
Notably, engineered carbon defects can exhibit higher catalytic efficacy 
than even pyridinic-N sites in certain doped graphitic carbons [ 13 ], 
establishing defects as emerging active centers in carbon-based elec -
trocatalysis. Structural imperfections such as vacancies, edges and to -
pological defects break the continuity of the sp
2
‑ carbon network. This 
exposes carbon atoms with mixed sp
2
/sp
3 
hybridization, altering local 
electron density and creating regions of enhanced charge that favor the 
adsorption of OH
�
and stabilize key intermediates like *OOH, thereby 
lowering the Gibbs free energy barrier [ 14 – 16 ]. Dangling bonds at 
defect sites also strengthen interactions with hydroxy species, promot -
ing O
–
O bond formation [ 14 , 17 ]. Therefore, designing carbon archi -
tectures with a high density of defects is an effective strategy for 
improving metal-free OER catalysts. Biomass-derived carbon materials 
have attracted considerable interest in this regard due to their innate 
heteroatom doping and abundant structural defects. During pyrolysis, 
cross-linking reactions produce polyaromatic compounds with limited 
long-range order. At elevated temperatures, however, highly crystalline 
graphitic microdomains can develop [ 18 ]. During thermal treatment, 
structural defects such as dislocations, grain boundaries, vacancies and 
micropores could be formed through thermal stress and etching by

Powder-based catalysts continue to dominate electrocatalysis owing 
to mature fabrication protocols and broad applicability. However, their 
implementation necessitates polymeric binders and conductive addi -
tives for electrode assembly. These inactive components, while essential 
for structural integrity and electrical connectivity, introduce detri -
mental effects: they physically mask active sites, impeding reactant ac -
cess; promote interfacial degradation during prolonged electrochemical 
cycling; and compromise mechanical robustness, collectively under -
mining long-term electrode durability [ 22 , 23 ]. These limitations have 
accelerated the development of self-supporting electrocatalysts. Such 
systems eliminate auxiliary additives, leveraging intrinsic architectures 
that provide efficient mass transport pathways and maximized active 
site exposure. Concurrently, their monolithic design confers superior 
mechanical stability and enhanced electrochemical resilience, offering a 
promising alternative to conventional powder-based configurations. 
Nevertheless, achieving optimal performance requires navigating the 
critical trade-off between activity and robustness. The central challenge 
lies in engineering self-supporting catalysts with idealized three- 
dimensional (3D) porous architectures that simultaneously deliver 
high catalytic efficiency and operational stability.
Leveraging its inherent fibrous layered structure, which carbonizes 
into a naturally porous framework rich in interconnected channels, co -
conut shell serves as an advantageous precursor material. Subsequent 
etching of this structure can yield highly conductive carbon scaffolds 
featuring 3D interconnected lamellar channels abundant in defects 
[ 24 , 25 ], providing numerous active sites for OER while maintaining 
excellent mechanical strength and structural stability [ 26 , 27 ]. There -
fore, to fabricate porous and defect-rich self-supporting coconut shell 
carbon (SCC) plates from discarded coconut shell, this study employed 
ammonia (NH
3
) etching during the pyrolysis process. At elevated tem -
peratures, NH
3 
decomposes into reactive species (NH
2
, NH, and H) [ 28 ]. 
Atomic hydrogen (H) etches the carbon skeleton, generating micropores 
and structural defects [ 21 ]. Concurrently, NH
2 
radicals provide active 
nitrogen atoms that either substitute carbon atoms within the lattice or 
occupy defect sites, forming nitrogen-doped configurations such as 
pyridinic N and graphitic N [ 29 ]. Furthermore, nitrogen-containing 
groups can displace oxygen-containing functional groups in the pre -
cursor, optimizing the surface chemistry. Crucially, this combined 
etching and nitrogen doping disrupts the carbon layer regularity, 
inducing lattice distortion, thereby effectively introducing structural 
defects and creating a wealth of active sites [ 30 – 33 ]. Among the syn -
thesized materials, the SCC samples prepared under NH

and electrochemical properties. Notably, the etched coconut shell car -
bon retained high mechanical stability. Abundant active sites, structural 
defects, nitrogen doping, and robust mechanical integrity collectively 
contribute to the SCC-1100-NH
3 
material with exceptional OER activity 
and stability in alkaline media.

Abstract
Here we report an effective and facile method for preparing porous carbons (CSCK-T-x) with highly
developed hierarchical porosity for high-performance supercapacitor by one-step KOH activation of
coconut shell carbon. The effects of carbonization temperature (T, oC) and KOH/C ratio (x) on the
structure and electrochemical properties were studied systematically. The as-prepared CSCK-800-2
displayed two concentrated mesopores at 4 nm and 14 nm. The unique hierarchical structure of CSCK-
800-2 enables it to have low ion transport resistance and high ion-accessible surface area, which
contributes to outstanding electrochemical performance. Furthermore, it possessed the highest BET
speci�c surface area of 2143.6 m2·g− 1 with a pore volume of 1.34 cm3·g− 1 among the CSCK-T-x. In a
three-electrode test system, CSCK-800-2 exhibits a high speci�c capacitance of 317 F·g− 1 at a current
density of 0.5 A·g− 1 and considerable rate retention of 68% at 20 A·g− 1. The symmetrical supercapacitor
that was based on CSCK-800-2 showed a maximum energy density of 13.5 Wh·kg− 1 at 0.5 A·g− 1 in 6M
KOH electrolyte. Besides, it also exhibited a superior cycling stability with 99.7% of the capacitance
retention after 10000 cycles at 5 A·g− 1.
1. Introduction
With the increasing demand for energy from transportation electri�cation and smart grids, as well as the
gradual depletion of fossil fuels, it is signi�cant to develop e�cient, low cost, eco-friendly and high-
performance energy storage equipments [1]. Supercapacitors (SCs) have received extensive attention for
their excellent cycling stability and high power density. [2]. However, its low energy density has become a
key factor restricting its wider development. Therefore, it is necessary to improve the energy density of
SCs to satisfy urgent demand for uninterruptible power supplies. The charge storage mechanisms of SCs
can be divided into the electric double-layer capacitors (EDLC) which rely on electrostatic attractions
between ions and charged electrode surface, such as carbon materials [3]; and pseudo capacitance
based on the highly reversible redox reactions on the surface or in the bulk phase of the electrode
materials, such as transition metal oxides [4], transition metal hydroxides [5] and conductive polymers [6].
Many factors contribute to the performance of SCs, such as the electrochemical performance of electrode
materials, electrolyte selection and potential window of the electrode, etc. Among these factors, the
performance of electrode material is the most important factors affecting its electrochemical
performance. In EDLC phenomenon, ion interaction between electrode/electrolyte interfaces is essential
for e�cient charge-discharge process. The electrode material needs to have large speci�c surface area

stability of rice husk-derived activated carbon-
based supercapacitors in KOH electrolyte †
Dechen Liu, ab Wenli Zhang, b Haibo Lin *b and Nan Lin *c
Rice husk-derived activated carbon prepared via KOH activation usually has high speci ﬁc capacitance due
to its high oxygen content and high speci ﬁc surface area, which is regarded as a promising candidate for
supercapacitor electrodes. However, the poor cycling stability of supercapacitors based on rice husk-
derived activated carbon in KOH electrolyte severely limit its commercial application. In this study, the
inﬂuence of di ﬀerent positive-to-negative electrode mass ratios on the cycling stability of
supercapacitors was systematically investigated using rice husk-derived activated carbon as electrode
materials. The results show that increasing the positive-to-negative electrode mass ratios signi ﬁcantly
enhances the cycling stability of supercapacitors. In this process, the continuous increase in positive
electrode potential is e ﬀectively suppressed, which avoid the oxidation of the positive electrode. When
the positive-to-negative electrode mass ratio is increased from 1 to 2, the capacitance retention of the
supercapacitors signi ﬁcantly increases from 27.9% to 96.4% after 10 000 charge –discharge cycles.
Meanwhile, the speci ﬁc capacitance is only reduced by 9.1%. The supercapacitor with positive-to-
negative electrode mass ratio s of 1 and 2 shows energy densities of 10.68 W h kg
−1 and 9.54 W h kg −1
at 0.5 A g −1, retaining 46.8% and 43.4% of energy densities at 20 A g −1. Adjusting the positive-to-
negative electrode mass ratio does not signi ﬁcantly a ﬀect the electrochemical properties of
supercapacitors. Thus, this work unfolds a new strategy for enhancing the cycling stability of activated
carbon-based supercapacitors in alkaline electrolytes and a viable route for practical energy storage
applications of rice husk-derived activated carbon in supercapacitors.
Introduction
Carbon-based supercapacitors (SCs) are regarded as a prom-
ising energy storage device owing to their long cycle life, high
power density, and fast charge/discharge capability.
1–3 Among
various carbon materials, activated carbon (AC) has been widely
investigated as an electrode material for SCs because of its high
specic surface area, abundant raw materials, excellent elec-
trical properties and low cost.
4–6 ACs with high speci c surface
area generally possess high speci c capacitance, which endows
SCs with high energy density. Therefore, signi cant research
eﬀorts have been dedicated to preparing ACs from various
precursors to achieve high speci c surface area. 7–9 Rice husk
(RH), due to its abundance and low cost, has been extensively
employed in the preparation of activated carbons through
chemical activation processes. Prior investigations have shown
that KOH activation enables rice husk-derived activated carbon
(RHC) to achieve exceptional speci c surface areas up to 3000
m
2 g−1.10,11 Furthermore, KOH activation simultaneously
introduces abundant oxygen-containing functional groups on
the surface of the ACs.
12 Although oxygen-containing functional
groups contribute the pseudocapacitance in AC, they simulta-
neously compromise cycling stability, especially in the KOH
electrolyte system.
13,14 During electrochemical processes, the
unstable oxygen-containing functional groups are prone to
undergo irreversible redox reactions. This not only causes
a rapid decline in the capacity initially provided by these func-
tional groups but also leads to progressive pore structure
blockage in the electrode material.
12
In our previous studies, comparable electrochemical degra-
dation behavior was observed in SCs employing RHC electrodes
and KOH electrolyte.
15 Meanwhile, it has been found that
capacity fading in SCs originates from the severe oxidation of
the positive electrode, which results from the continuous
increase in positive electrode potential during cycling. This
oxidative degradation correlates with the accumulation of
oxygen-containing functional groups on the positive carbon

Experimental
Materials
Rice husk was sourced from a rice milling facility in Changchun
City, Jilin Province. Additional chemicals (analytical grade) were
procured from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. High-
purity nitrogen and deionized water were used throughout the
experimental procedures.
Preparation of RHC
Firstly, the RH was thoroughly washed to remove impurities and
then dried at 80 °C in an oven for 10 hours. Subsequently, the
dried RH was pulverized into ne power. RH powder was sub-
jected to carbonization at 500 °C with 10 °C min
−1 under
a nitrogen atmosphere. The carbonization process was main-
tained continuously for 1 hour. The carbonized rice husk was
then mixed uniformly with KOH solution at a 1 : 4 mass ratio,
and the mixtures were dried at 110 °C for 24 hours. Following
this, the dried mixtures were activated at 700 °C for 1 hour. The
activated samples were rinsed to neutral pH with deionized
water. Finally, the activated carbon dried at 110 °C for 24 hours.
The nal activated carbon labelled as RHC.
Material characterization

evaluated by an ASAP 2010 Micromeritics instrument with N

structure were characterized using a Scanning electron

Abstract
In this study, sugarcane bagasse (SCB), an abundant agricultural byproduct, was trans-
formed into activated carbon via a controlled thermochemical pyrolysis route for high-
performance energy storage applications. Herein, we utilized the activated carbon derived
from pure sugarcane bagasse (SCB-AC) and further activated using KOH (SCB-KOH-AC)
as an electrode material in aqueous symmetric supercapacitor configurations. The synthe-
sized activated carbon was subjected to analysis using a range of characteristics including
FT-Raman spectroscopy, which was employed to confirm the functional groups present in
the carbon materials. The XPS analysis provided insights into the elemental composition
and ionic states. The SEM analysis revealed that both activated carbon and KOH/activated
carbon materials exhibited a layered or stacked, albeit slightly random, orientation. Electro-
chemical studies demonstrated that the synthesized carbon electrodes exhibited impressive
specific capacitance values of (SCB) activated carbon (132.20 F/g) and KOH-activated, pure
SCB AC (SCB-A) 253.41 F/g at 0.5 A/g. Furthermore, the SCB KOH-activated carbon (AC)
electrode revealed a higher specific capacitance value and A//SCB-A symmetric devices
delivered energy density reaching 17.91 Wh/kg and power density up to 2990 W/kg.
The KOH-activated carbon electrode demonstrated remarkable cycling stability retaining
93.89%, even after 10,000 cycles. These results suggest that the sugarcane bagasse-derived
activated carbon is a sustainable and low-cost candidate for next-generation supercapacitor
electrodes. The results demonstrate enhanced capacitance, stability, and pore structure
tailored for energy storage applications. The KOH-activated carbon SCB carbon symmetric
device with symmetric electrodes exhibited a suitable bio-mass carbon for future energy
storage applications.
Keywords: energy storage; sugarcane bagasse (SCB); prolysis synthesis; electrochemical
measurements; supercapacitors
1. Introduction
Activated carbon (AC) is a knowingly larger porous material with an extensive internal
surface area, making it an ideal candidate for supercapacitor applications. The formation
of these tiny pores is achieved by activating a carbon precursor through methods such
as KOH (potassium hydroxide) activation. During this process, KOH reacts with the
Nanomaterials 2025, 15, 1028 https://doi.org/10.3390/nano15131028
Nanomaterials 2025, 15, 1028 2 of 19
precursor at elevated temperatures, creating intricate pore networks and significantly
enhancing the surface area [1]. Compared to standard activated carbon, KOH-activated AC
features a higher surface area, adjustable pore size distribution, and potentially improved
electrical conductivity due to the incorporation of potassium [2]. This increased porosity
contributes to superior performance in supercapacitors. Supercapacitors serve as a bridge
between batteries and traditional capacitors, offering faster charging and discharging
capabilities than batteries and higher energy density than standard capacitors. Activated
carbon typically decomposes into gaseous products such as carbon dioxide (CO2), carbon
monoxide (CO), and small amounts of hydrocarbons when exposed to temperatures above
500 ◦C. The specific decomposition products and their proportions can vary depending
on the type of activated carbon and the conditions of decomposition, such as the presence
of oxygen or other reactive gases. The high surface area of AC facilitates efficient charge
storage through electrostatic adsorption, where electrolyte ions accumulate within the
pores, contributing to the overall capacitance of the supercapacitor. KOH activation further
enhances capacitance by introducing oxygen-containing functional groups on the AC
surface, which promote even better ion adsorption.
The activation of carbon using KOH has emerged as a highly effective method for
enhancing the material’s properties, particularly for applications in CO 2 capture and
supercapacitors [3]. The quality of activated carbon can be significantly influenced by
various operational parameters, including particle size, temperature, residence time, and
heating rate [4]. Among these factors, temperature is the most critical and effective. The
literature reports the yield of SCB (sugarcane bagasse)-activated carbon ranging between
14% and 56%. SCB-activated carbon has diverse applications, such as soil amendment,
wastewater treatment, adsorbent in water, and accompanying cementitious material [5].
The study also highlights several gaps in knowledge, including cost wise analysis and the
evaluation of using bagasse as fuel in sugar manufacturing versus producing activated
carbon. Sugarcane bagasse-activated carbon has significant prospective to enhance a highly
attractive carbonaceous material with wide-ranging applications across various industries.
Activated carbon is a highly potential material valued for its large surface area, high
porosity, and tunable surface chemistry, making it suitable for diverse applications such
as energy storage, environmental remediation, and chemical processing [6]. However, its
performance characteristics depend strongly on the source material and activation method.
In recent years, biomass-derived activated carbons have gained significant attention as
sustainable and cost-effective alternatives to conventional carbon materials. Among these,
sugarcane bagasse, a lignocellulosic agro-waste generated in large quantities by the sugar
industry, has emerged as a promising precursor due to its high carbon content and renew-
able nature [7]. In this study, we report the synthesis of activated carbon from sugarcane
bagasse using KOH chemical activation and investigate its electrochemical performance
in symmetric supercapacitor devices. Unlike traditional activated carbon types, which
are often optimized for filtration or adsorption (e.g., granular, powdered, and extruded
forms) [8], our approach is focused on engineering the pore structure and surface proper-
ties of sugarcane-derived carbon specifically for energy storage applications. This work
demonstrates the potential of converting agricultural waste into high-performance elec-
trode materials, contributing to the advancement of environmentally friendly technologies.
It is used in processes such as removing volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from air. Fi-
nally, by selecting the appropriate type of activated carbon, industries can achieve efficient
and targeted removal of contaminants in various applications, including air and water
purification, odor control, and even gold recovery in mining [8].

Abstract: Discarded sports waste faces bottlenecks in application due to inadequate dis-
posal measures, and there is often a neglect of enhancing resource utilization efficiency
and minimizing environmental impact. In this study, nanoporous biochar was prepared
through co-hydrothermal carbonization (co-HTC) and pyrolytic activation by using mixed
goose feathers and heavy-metals-contaminated pine sawdust. Comprehensive character-
ization demonstrated that the prepared M-3-25 (Biochar derived from mixed feedstocks
(25 mg/g Cu in pine sawdust) at 700 ◦C with activator ratios of 3) possesses a high specific
surface area 2501.08 m 2 g−1 and abundant heteroatomic (N, O, and Cu), exhibiting an
outstanding physicochemical structure and ultrahigh electrochemical performance. Com-
pared to nanocarbon from a single feedstock, M-3-25 showed an ultrahigh capacitance of
587.14 F g−1 at 1 A g−1, high energy density of 42.16 Wh kg−1, and only 8.61% capacitance
loss after enduring 10,000 cycles at a current density of 10 A g−1, positioning M-3-25 at the
forefront of previously known biomass-derived nanoporous carbon supercapacitors. This
research not only introduces a promising countermeasure for the disposal of sports waste but
also provides superior biochar electrode materials with robust supercapacitor characteristics.
Keywords: sports waste; supercapacitor; co-hydrothermal carbonization; capacitive performance
1. Introduction
With the swift advancements in global science and technology coupled with the
accelerated pace of industrialization, a substantial quantity of sports and daily necessities
have been manufactured to cater to the demands of individuals for sports training and
for work or day-to-day life [ 1–3]. However, the lack of proper measures for effective
resource utilization has led to waste of recyclable resources, the occupation and pollution
of land resources, and the destruction of ecological balance [4–6]. The recently concluded
Paris Olympic Games garnered extensive attention towards solid waste management
and associated environmental challenges [7]. The Olympic Games leverage a significant
Molecules 2025, 30, 26 https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules30010026
Molecules 2025, 30, 26 2 of 16
amount of infrastructure that utilizes waste plastic, cardboard, wood, and other materials
as environmental protection measures, largely reducing carbon emissions and minimizing
environmental pollution [8]. Globally, 2.01 billion tons of waste is generated annually and
by 2050 this is estimated to hit 3.4 billion tons. Lignocellulosic biomass comprises almost
63% of the total waste mass [9]. Materials with high resource recovery value derived from
used sporting goods waste and infrastructures, such as badminton feathers, wood, pine
sawdust, etc., are still not effectively recycled. Due to the high global demand for wood
and the widespread distribution of the wood processing industry, the amount of discarded
pine sawdust is considerable [10,11]. Failure to devise an effective strategy for managing
this sporting goods waste not only undermines the objective of green and sustainable
development but also constitutes an additional waste of resources and energy.
Since the industrial revolution, the excessive consumption of fossil fuels, including
coal, oil, and natural gas, has triggered global environmental problems, encompassing an
energy crisis and global warming, which has stimulated the exploration of new alternative
energy sources [12–14]. Supercapacitors (SCs) with fast charging speed, long cycle life, high
energy density and power density, and geared towards green environmental protection,
provide a promising method for the rapid storage of renewable energy and show a wide
range of applications in new energy power generation systems, consumer electronics, auto-
motive transportation and other fields [15–17]. Feathers from poultry used in badminton,
such as goose feathers, chicken feathers, duck feathers, etc., have an extremely high nitrogen
content [18]. Doping them into biochar as an exogenous nitrogen element can not only omit
the chemical nitrogen doping steps, but also increase the content of heteroatoms in biochar,
enrich its pore structure and surface active sites, and improve its stability [ 19–22]. How
to utilize discarded sports equipment, specifically badminton shuttlecocks, as a potential
recyclable resource and to compound it as an auxiliary material into the preparation process
for biochar, proposing reasonable resource utilization measures, and producing excellent
nitrogen-rich electrode materials, is a project full of hope and challenge.
Based on the need to improve the performance of supercapacitors, the doping of
nitrogen, oxygen, and other heteroatoms in biochar is regarded as an effective method to
effectively enhance the performance of carbon-based supercapacitors [23,24]. For example,
Geng et al. [25] used Spirulina platensis as the carbon and nitrogen source to prepare porous
carbon, which showed abundant heteroatomic oxygen (13.78%) and nitrogen (2.55%) and
had an exceptional capacitance of 348 F g−1. Yu et al. [26] synthesized P-doped hierarchical
porous carbon by using Typha orientalis leaves with high phosphorus content, possessing a
large specific surface area (SSA) of 1975 m2 g−1 and a high specific capacitance of 324 F g−1
provided by P self-doping. Samage et al. [27] researched N, O, and Fe self-doped electro-
active carbon material for zinc-ion hybrid capacitor derived Solanum melongena, which
delivered an excellent specific capacitance of 313.08 F/g. However, most reports have only
concentrated on how to dope more heteroatoms to enhance the electrochemical performance
of supercapacitors, ignoring the importance of circular stability and sustainability and not
proposing a promising approach for addressing the large amount of solid waste with
potential for recycling. Although the doping of elements such as nitrogen and oxygen
can induce pseudo-capacitance effects, it simultaneously introduces irreversible redox
reactions [28,29]. While these reactions may initially elevate the total specific capacitance by
augmenting pseudo-capacitance, their irreversible nature leads to the gradual diminution
of pseudo-capacitance over numerous constant current charge–discharge cycles, ultimately
resulting in capacitance degradation [ 30,31]. Therefore, apart from pursuing the high
specific capacitance of biochar, how to endow it with circular stability, sustainability, and
as an effective measure to deal with the recycling potential of sports solid waste is also
worth noting.

1. Introduction
Flexible and high-performance energy storage devices are urgently 
needed to meet the growing demands of wearable electronics, smart 
sensors, and portable systems. Among various candidates, super -
capacitors have garnered significant attention due to their fast char -
ge – discharge rates, high power densities, and long cycle life [ 1 – 8 ]. 
However, achieving a simultaneous combination of high energy density, 
mechanical flexibility, and environmental sustainability are key and 
urgent problems for practical application in electrochemical energy 
storage devices [ 9 ]. Conventional electrode materials and organic 
electrolytes commonly used in supercapacitors are often costly, toxic, 
and incompatible with flexible device configurations [ 10 ].
To address these issues, biomass-derived porous carbon materials 
have emerged as promising electrode materials due to their inherent 
sustainability, adjustable pore structure, very good chemical and ther -
mal stability and low cost [ 11 – 19 ]. A variety of biomass precursors, 
including coconut shells [ 20 ], straw [ 21 ], metaplexis shell [ 22 ] and 
agricultural waste, have been successfully converted into activated 
carbon with tailored pore architectures and excellent electrochemical 
performance. Nonetheless, many of these biomass sources either lack 
mechanical resilience or involve complex processing. Therefore, 
achieving excellent bending stability and high capacitance in all-solid 
supercapacitors remains challenging, leaving ample room for further 
development in flexible applications.
In this context, Setaria viridis, a ubiquitous fast-growing weed with 
minimal agricultural value, offers a unique opportunity. Its stalks are 
composed of naturally aligned vascular bundles with a hollow tubular 
morphology, providing a favorable template for constructing inter -
connected porous carbon frameworks. Utilizing such underexploited 
agricultural residues not only reduces production costs and environ -
mental burden but also enables the design of 3D carbon skeletons with 
enhanced ion transport channels and mechanical integrity.
In this study, we report the synthesis of porous carbon from Setaria 
viridis stalks via direct carbonization and KOH activation. The resulting 
materials exhibit tunable pore structures and favorable graphitic fea -
tures depending on the activation temperature. When applied in flexible 
supercapacitors using a PVA/H
2
SO
4 
gel electrolyte, the best-performing

2. Experiment
2.1. Synthesis
The Setaria viridis stalks utilized in this study were harvested from 
the Tianjin University campus. The chemicals utilized in this study were 
of analytical reagent grade and were used without any additional pu -
rification steps.
The process is listed in Fig. 1 . The Setaria viridis stalks were rinsed 
thoroughly with distilled water and dried at 60 
◦
C for 12 h. Subse -
quently, the dried stalks were finely chopped, rinsed again with distilled 
water, and dried at 80 
◦
C for another 12 h. The prepared raw materials 
were then subjected to carbonization in a tubular furnace under argon 
atmosphere for a duration of 1 h at 400 
◦
C, resulting in the sample 
designated as SVS-400. Next, the SVS-400 sample was combined with 
KOH in a mass ratio of 1:4 for the process of activation. Starting from 
room temperature, the temperature was increased at a rate of 5 
◦
C min
� 1

◦
C, 900 
◦
C, and 1000 
◦
C, respectively, 
and held for 1 h. Finally, the activated materials were rinsed with 
deionized water to neutral and named as SVS-800, SVS-900 and SVS- 
1000 respectively. In addition, The Setaria viridis stalk-based porous 
carbon materials SVS-3-900 and SVS-5-900 were prepared under the 
same conditions at an activation temperature of 900 
◦
C using different 
ratios of M
C
:M
KOH 
= 1:3 and 1:5, respectively, in order to compare the 
effect of activation ratios on structural properties.
2.2. Preparation of electrodes and all-solid-state supercapacitor
Activated carbon material, acetylene black and PTFE binder were 
mixed in the ratio of 8:1:1 by mass and then an appropriate amount of 
anhydrous ethanol was added with constant stirring to homogenize the 
mixture in a mortar and pestle. The paste obtained was pressed into a 
uniform thin sheet electrode with a diameter of 0.8 cm and 300 μ m 
thickness using a tablet press, and then dried with oven at 110 
◦
C for a 
duration of 4 h. The mass of each electrode was controlled to be around 
2 mg. The symmetric supercapacitor is assembled from a CR2032 cell 
case by placing two electrodes of the same mass on the surface of hy -
drophilic carbon paper, with a polypropylene film (polypropylene film, 
thickness: 25 μ m, poriness: 41 – 55 %) acting as a diaphragm. Then, a 
conventional symmetrical supercapacitor was assembled and encapsu -
lated under 10 MPa pressure in the order of stainless steel case, spacer, 
electrode set, spacer, and case, and the measurements were repeated at 
least three times for each set.
The all-solid-state flexible supercapacitor was assembled with two 
identical electrodes prepared according to the above-mentioned 
method. The electrolyte is PVA/H
